# INTRODUCTION

The history of Witchcraft is a subject as old and as wide as the world. For the purpose of this work, I define Witchcraft to include Sorcery, Black Magic, Necromancy <note>the practice of communicating with the dead to predict the future</note>, secret Divination, Satanism, and every kind of harmful <note>original: "malign"</note> occult art. This subject immediately presents a writer with a very difficult problem. He is forced to make a choice, and his dilemma is made no easier by the fact that he is acutely aware that, whichever path he chooses, he leaves himself open to damaging and not irrelevant <note>original: "not impertinent"</note> criticism.

Since it is essential that his work be kept within a reasonable length, he may choose to attempt a bird’s-eye view of the entire subject—spanning from China to Peru, and from the rhythmic chants of primitive humans at the dawn of life to the latest spiritualist <note>original: "spiritistic"</note> fads and manifestations seen at yesterday’s séance <note>a meeting where people attempt to contact the spirits of the dead</note> or circle. In that case, his writing will almost certainly be thin and often superficial. On the other hand, he may instead concentrate on one or two features in the history of Witchcraft. He can deal with these at some length, emphasize a few forgotten facts whose importance is currently neglected or unrealized, and use new material resulting from painstaking research. However, this second method comes at the cost of inevitable omissions, gaps <note>original: "hiatus"</note>, and self-denial. He must avoid fascinating side-topics and valuable inquiries, remaining silent when he would gladly enter into further discussion and explanation.

Fully aware of its drawbacks and dangers, I have selected the second method. When dealing with a topic such as Witchcraft, where it is impossible to record more than a tenth <note>original: "tithe"</note> of the facts, I believe it is better to provide a well-documented account of certain aspects rather than to attempt a somewhat cluttered and confused overview <note>original: "conspectus"</note> of the whole. Indeed, even at its best, such an overview is bound to have significant gaps <note>original: "lacunæ"</note>, no matter how carefully one tries to make it complete. I am aware, then, that there is hardly a paragraph in this present work which might not easily be

<summary>In the introduction, the author defines his broad scope of "Witchcraft" and explains his decision to focus deeply on specific, documented aspects of history rather than providing a superficial overview of the entire global phenomenon.</summary>

...could be expanded into a page. There is scarcely a page which might not, to its great advantage, become a chapter, and certainly not a chapter that would not be vastly improved if it were expanded <note>original: "elaborated"</note> into a full volume.

As I have said, many omissions are a necessary consequence of the plan I have adopted. Indeed, I suspect this would be true of any plan that attempts to cover a subject as universal as witchcraft. I can only offer my apologies to those students who come to this history expecting to find details of Finnish magic or the sorceries of Lapland. I also apologize to those who wish to inform themselves about Tohungaism <note>the traditional religious and medicinal practices of Māori healers</note> among the Māori people, Hindu devilry and enchantments, the Berserkers <note>original: "Bersekir"</note> of Iceland, Siberian Shamanism, the blind *Pan-su* and *Mutang* <note>original: "Pan Sus and Mutangs"; traditional Korean shamans and fortune-tellers</note> of Korea, the Chinese *Wu-po* <note>female shamans in Chinese tradition</note>, Serbian lycanthropy <note>the mythical transformation of people into wolves</note>, Voodooism, or the dark lore of ancient Scandinavia and Islam. I trust my readers will believe that I regret the absence of these topics from my work as much as anyone, but in any human endeavor, there are practical limitations of space.

In a complementary companion volume, I intend to treat the outbreaks of witchcraft in specific locations, such as the British Isles, France, Germany, Italy, New England, and other countries. Many famous cases—the Lancashire witch trials, the activities of "Witchfinder General" Matthew Hopkins, Gilles de Rais, Gaufridi, Urbain Grandier, Cotton Mather, and the Salem sorceries—will then be discussed in some detail.

It is a surprising fact that among English writers, the history of witchcraft in Europe has not received adequate attention from serious historians in recent years. They strangely fail to recognize the importance of this tragic belief as both a political and social factor. Magic, the origin of magical cults and ceremonies, the rituals of primitive peoples, traditional superstitions, and their related <note>original: "ancillary"</note> lore have been the subject of vast and scholarly <note>original: "erudite"</note> studies. However, these are mostly written from an anthropological and folklorist point of view. The darker side of the subject—the history of Satanism—seems hardly to have been attempted.

Possibly one reason for this neglect and ignorance lies in the fact that the heavy and crude materialism, which was such a prominent feature of English thought during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, intellectually rejected the supernatural. It attempted, not without some...

...succeeded in substituting a dull system of respectable morality for religion. Since witchcraft was considered entirely debunked <note>original: "exploded"</note>, it would, at best, possess merely an interest for historians of the curious. Even so, the revisiting <note>original: "exhumation"</note> of a disgusting and contemptible superstition was not to be encouraged. It was thought more appropriate to forget the uglier side of the past. This was the attitude that prevailed for more than a hundred and fifty years. 

When witchcraft was discussed by narrowly prejudiced and ineffective writers such as W.E.H. Lecky <note>William Edward Hartpole Lecky (1838–1903), an Irish historian known for his rationalist views</note> or Charles Mackay <note>Author of "Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds" (1841)</note>, they were only interested in debating the possibility of the accounts given by earlier authorities. They began with the premise that these earlier authors were all mistaken, exaggerated, short-sighted <note>original: "purblind"</note>, and misled. However, time has had its revenge, and this "rationalistic superstition" is dying fast. The extraordinary popularity of and immense devotion to Spiritualism <note>original: "Spiritism"</note> alone would prove that. Meanwhile, the widespread interest in mysticism is an even healthier sign that the world will no longer be content to be fed on empty husks and useless straw. These are only two indications out of many, and they are by no means the most significant.

It is quite impossible to appreciate and understand the true lives of men and women in Elizabethan and Stuart England, in the France of Louis XIII and his son <note>Louis XIV, the "Sun King"</note>, or in the Italy of the Renaissance and the Catholic Counter-Reformation <note>original: "Catholic Reaction"</note>—to name but three countries and a few specific periods—unless we realize the part that witchcraft played in those ages within the affairs of these kingdoms. All classes were involved, from the Pope to the peasant, and from the Queen to the cottage girl <note>original: "gill"</note>.

Since actors are "the summaries and brief chronicles of the time," <note>A reference to Shakespeare's *Hamlet*, Act 2, Scene 2</note> I have provided a concluding chapter that deals with witchcraft as it was seen on the stage, mainly concentrating on the English theater. Such a review has not been attempted before. Since witchcraft was such a formidable social evil and so intertwined with all levels of society, it is obvious that we can find few better contemporary illustrations of it than in drama, for the playwright always had his finger on the public pulse. Until the development of the novel, the theater alone mirrored social manners and history.

There are many general French studies of witchcraft of...

...the greatest value, among which we may name such standard works as Antoine-Louis Daugis’s *Treatise on Magic, Sorcery, Possessions, Obsessions, and Evil Spells* <note>original: "Traité sur la magie, le sortilège, les possessions, obsessions et maléfices"</note>, 1732; Jules Garinet’s *History of Magic in France from the beginning of the monarchy to the present day* <note>original: "Histoire de la Magie en France depuis le commencement de la monarchie jusqu’à nos jours"</note>, 1818; Michelet’s famous *The Witch* <note>original: "La Sorcière"</note>; Alfred Maury’s *Magic and Astrology* <note>original: "La Magie et l’Astrologie"</note>, 3rd edition, 1868; L’Abbé Lecanu’s *History of Satan* <note>original: "Histoire de Satan"</note>; Jules Baissac’s *The Great Days of Witchcraft* <note>original: "Les grands Jours de la Sorcellerie"</note>, 1890; Theodore de Cauzons’s *Magic and Witchcraft in France* <note>original: "La Magie et la Sorcellerie en France"</note>, 4 vols., 1910, etc.

In German we have Eberhard Hauber’s *Library of Magic* <note>original: "Bibliotheca Magica"</note>; Roskoff’s *History of the Devil* <note>original: "Geschichte des Teufels"</note>, 1869; Soldan’s *History of the Witch Trials* <note>original: "Geschichte der Hexenprozesse"</note> (newly edited by Dr. Heinrich Heppe), 1880; Friedrich Leitschuch’s *Contributions to the History of Witchcraft in Franconia* <note>original: "Beitræge zur Geschichte des Hexenwesens in Franken"</note>, 1883; Johan Dieffenbach’s *The Witch-Delusion before and after the Reformation in Germany* <note>original: "Der Hexenwahn vor und nach der Glaubensspaltung in Deutschland"; "Glaubensspaltung" literally translates to "faith-splitting"</note>, 1886; Schreiber’s *The Witch Trials in Breisgau* <note>original: "Die Hexenprozesse im Breisgau"</note>; Ludwig Rapp’s *The Witch Trials and their Opponents in Tyrol* <note>original: "Die Hexenprozesse und ihre Gegner aus Tirol"</note>; Joseph Hansen’s *Sources and Investigations into the History of the Witch-Delusion* <note>original: "Quellen und Untersuchungen zur Geschichte des Hexenwahns"</note>, 1901; and very many more admirably documented studies.

In England, the best of the older books must be recommended with necessary reservations. Thomas Wright’s *Narratives of Sorcery and Magic*, 2 vols., 1851, is to be commended as the work of a learned antiquarian <note>A scholar who studies or collects objects and manuscripts from the past.</note> who often referred to original sources. However, it is nonetheless sketchy and can hardly satisfy the careful scholar. Some exceptionally good writing and sound, clear thinking are to be met with in Dr. F. G. Lee’s *The Other World*, 2 vols., 1875; *More Glimpses of the World Unseen*, 1878; *Glimpses in the Twilight*, 1885; and *Sight and Shadows*, 1894. All of these deserve to be far more widely known, since they well repay an unhurried and repeated reading.

Quite recent work is represented by Professor Wallace Notestein’s *History of Witchcraft in England from 1558 to 1718*, published in 1911. This detailed study of a century and a half concentrates, as its title tells, upon England alone. It is supplied with ample and useful appendixes. In respect to the orderly organizing of his facts, gathered from the trials and other sources—no small labor—Professor Notestein deserves a generous measure of praise; his interpretation

...of the facts and his deductions may not unfairly be criticized. Although his disbelief must surely be shaken now and then by the cumulative force of repeated and corroborating evidence, he nevertheless refuses to admit even the possibility that persons who claimed supernatural powers held secret meetings after nightfall in remote and lonely places for their own purposes and plots. If human testimony is worth anything at all—unless we are to be more skeptical <note>original: "Pyrrhonian," referring to the extreme skepticism of the philosopher Pyrrho</note> than the famous Dr. Marphurius himself (a character who would never say, "I have come," but rather, "It seems to me that I have come" <note>original: "Je suis venu ; mais ; Il me semble que je suis venu"</note>)—we must consider the events of 1612. In that year, when the magistrate Roger Nowell had raided the Lancashire coven and carried off Elizabeth Demdike and three other elderly women <note>original: "beldames"</note> to imprisonment <note>original: "durance vile"</note> in Lancaster Castle, Elizabeth Device summoned the whole Pendle gang to her home at Malking Tower. They met to discuss the situation and plot the rescue of the prisoners. As soon as they had gathered, they all sat down to dinner and had a traditional north-country spread of beef, bacon, and roast mutton. Surely there is nothing very remarkable in this; and the evidence as given in Thomas Potts’ famous narrative, *The Wonderful Discovery of Witches in the County of Lancaster* (London, 1613), bears the very mark of truth:

> "The aforementioned persons had for their dinners beef, bacon, and roasted mutton. This mutton (as the witness's <term>examinate</term> brother said) was from a ram <term>wether</term> belonging to Christopher Swyers of Barley. This ram was brought the night before into the house of the witness's mother by the said James Device, the witness's brother, and was killed and eaten in the witness's sight."

But Professor Notestein will have none of it. He writes:

> "The concurring evidence in the Malking Tower story is of no more compelling character than that to be found in a multitude of Continental stories of witch gatherings, which have been shown to be the outcome of physical or mental pressure and of leading questions. It seems unnecessary to accept even a foundation <note>original: "substratum"</note> of fact" (p. 124).

In the face of such sweeping and dogmatic assertion, mere evidence is of no use at all. For we know that the Continental stories of witch gatherings are, with very few exceptions, the chronicle of actual fact. It must be confessed that such weak skepticism, which repeatedly spoils his summary of the witch trials, is a serious...

<summary>This page critiques Professor Notestein's dismissal of the Malking Tower meeting, arguing that the mundane details of the feast (beef, bacon, and stolen mutton) recorded in the 1612 Lancashire trials point to the event's historical reality rather than being a fabricated myth.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION

...blemish in Professor Notestein's work and, considering his hard work, it is very regrettable.

Miss M. A. Murray does not for a moment support such a brief dismissal or uncritical rejection of evidence. Her careful reading of authors who wrote about witchcraft has rightly convinced her that their statements must be accepted. Sharp minds and clever investigators—such as Pope Gregory XV, Jean Bodin, Francesco Maria Guazzo, Pierre de Lancre, Jean D'Espagnet, Nicholas de la Reynie, Robert Boyle, Sir Matthew Hale, and Joseph Glanvill—were neither liars nor fools. The evidence must be taken seriously. However, because Miss Murray cannot accept the logical conclusions of this evidence, she quickly retreats with the unfounded claim that "the statements do not mean what people think they mean." In her book *The Witch-Cult in Western Europe* (1921), she goes on to develop a very clever but—as I demonstrate—completely unsupportable theory. <note>Miss Murray proposed that witchcraft was not "magic" but a surviving pre-Christian pagan religion; this "Murrayite theory" was influential for decades but is now largely rejected by historians.</note> Therefore, it is no surprise that many of the details Miss Murray collected through her hard work are (likely unconsciously) forced to fit her pre-existing theory. Although my perspective differs greatly from Miss Murray's—and I believe our disagreement is neither minor nor shallow—I must still praise her honest and brave handling of many essential details. These facts are too often hidden, which frequently results in a false and distorted historical picture.

# INTRODUCTION

...monographs <note>A monograph is a detailed written study on a single specialized subject.</note> which treat every phase of the question from all points of view, but also from correspondence and discussion with ardent devotees of the cult—and, not least, from the admissions and warnings of those who have abandoned these dangerous practices. These revelations were made in such circumstances, however, as to completely prevent even a hint regarding their definite meaning and scope.

The history of witchcraft is of great interest to the theologian, the psychologist, and the historian, and it cannot be ignored. But it presents a very dark and terrible side, the details of which have been almost universally unrecorded in the few English studies that claim serious attention; indeed, they have been deliberately suppressed <note>original: "burked"</note> and avoided. Such treatment is unscholarly to an extreme degree, as well as reprehensible and dishonest.

The work of Professor Notestein, for example, is seriously flawed <note>original: "vitiated"</note>, because he has completely ignored the sexual indecency <note>original: "immodesty"</note> of the witch-cult and has thus downplayed its evil. He is, indeed, so uncritical—I would even venture to say so unscholarly—as to naively remark (page 300): "No one who has not read for himself can have any notion of the vile character of the charges and confessions embodied in the witch pamphlets <note>Cheaply printed booklets from the 16th and 17th centuries that provided sensationalized accounts of witch trials for the public.</note>. It is an aspect of the question which has not been discussed in these pages." Such a confession is amazing. One cannot write in polite <note>original: "dainty"</note> phrases about Satanists and the Witches' Sabbath <note>original: "Sabbat"</note>. However disgusting the disease, the doctor must not hesitate to diagnose and to probe. This "ostrich-like" policy is moral cowardice. None of the Church Fathers and great writers of the Church were so blamefully prudish. When Saint Epiphanius had to discuss the Gnostics <note>A diverse group of early religious movements that the mainstream Church often accused of secret, immoral rituals.</note>, he described their abominations in detail and aptly remarked: "Why should I shrink from speaking of the things you do not fear to do? By speaking thus, I hope to fill you with horror of the depravities <note>original: "turpitudes"</note> you commit." And Saint Clement of Alexandria says: "I am not ashamed to name the parts of the body where the fetus is formed and nourished; and why, indeed, should I be, since God was not ashamed to create them?"

A few authors have painted the medieval witch in pretty colors, as if on satin. In their accounts, she has become a somewhat eccentric but kindly old lady—shrewd and observant, with a knowledge of healing herbs and medicinal plants <note>original: "simples"</note>, ready to advise and aid her...

...neighbors who are less intelligent than she is, and not refusing in return a simple gift of a side of bacon <note>original: "flitch"</note>, flour, a young chicken <note>original: "poult"</note>, or eggs from the farmyard. And so, for no clear reason, she became an easy victim for fanatical judges and greedy <note>original: "ravening"</note> inquisitors—who were famously the most ignorant and stupid of people—who caught her, threw her in a river to see if she would float <note>original: "swum her"; the "swimming test" was a common ordeal where it was believed that water, a pure element, would reject a witch and cause her to float.</note>, tried her, tortured her, and finally burned her at the stake. Many modern writers, even more skeptical, simply dismiss the witch to the world of nursery tales and holiday plays <note>original: "Christmas pantomime"</note>; they believe she never had any real existence, other than as Cinderella’s fairy godmother or Madame Merluche from the stories of the Countess d’Aulnoy <note>Marie-Catherine d'Aulnoy was a 17th-century French author known for her fairy tales.</note>.

I have even heard it publicly claimed from a lecture platform by a professional student of the Elizabethan period that the Elizabethans did not, of course, actually believe in witchcraft. He argued it would be impossible to imagine that men of the intellectual caliber of Shakespeare, Ford, Jonson, or Fletcher could have believed in such a useless illusion <note>original: "chimæra"; a mythical monster, used here to mean a wild or unrealistic fantasy.</note> born of diseased imaginations and hysteria. His audience agreed with great self-satisfaction, pleased to think that the famous names of the past had been cleared of the shame <note>original: "stigma"</note> of such a degrading and disgusting superstition. According to this view, a few uneducated peasants here and there may have been dark and ignorant enough to imagine witches, and the poets used these old women and hags effectively in songs and plays. But as for actually believing such fantasies, our great Elizabethans were certainly more enlightened than that! Indeed, witchcraft is a part of seventeenth-century culture that some people seem to have silently agreed to ignore.

All this is very unhistorical and very unscientific. In the following pages, I have tried to show the witch as she truly was: a person of evil life; a social nuisance and parasite; a follower of a disgusting and offensive religion <note>original: "creed"</note>; an expert at poisoning, blackmail, and other sneaky crimes; a member of a powerful secret organization hostile <note>original: "inimical"</note> to the Church and the government; someone who cursed God in words and actions; controlling the villagers through fear and superstition; sometimes a fraud and a fake doctor; a madam <note>original: "bawd"; a woman who manages a brothel.</note>; an abortionist; the sinister advisor to immoral court ladies and unfaithful gentlemen; a servant to vice and unimaginable corruption, thriving <note>original: "battening"</note> on the filth and the worst passions of the era.

# INTRODUCTION

My current work is the result of more than thirty years of close attention to the subject of witchcraft. During this period, I have made a systematic and intensive study of the older demonologists <note>A demonologist is a scholar who studies beliefs regarding demons and evil spirits.</note>, as I am convinced that their first-hand evidence is of prime importance and value. However, because their writings are so voluminous and extremely rare <note>original: "of the last rarity"</note>, they have been universally neglected and allowed to accumulate thick dust undisturbed. They are, moreover, often difficult to read due to technicalities of phrase and vocabulary. Among the most authoritative, I may cite a few names: Sprenger (*The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: *Malleus Maleficarum*, the most famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note>); Guazzo; Bartolomeo Spina, Order of Preachers <note>original: "O.P."; the Dominicans.</note>; John Nider, Order of Preachers; Grilland; Jerome Mengo; Binsfeld; Gerson; Ulrich Molitor; Basin; Murner; Crespet; Anania; Henri Boguet; Bodin; Martin Delrio, Society of Jesus <note>original: "S.J."; the Jesuits.</note>; Pierre le Loyer; Ludwig Elich; Godelmann; Nicolas Remy; Salerini; Leonard Vair; De Lancre; Alfonso de Castro; Sebastian Michaelis, Order of Preachers; Sinistrari; Perreaud; Dom Calmet; and Sylvester Mazzolini, Order of Preachers (also known as Prierias). 

When we supplement these with judicial records and legal codes, we have an immense body of material. In all that I have written, I have gone to original sources, and it has been my endeavor to fairly weigh and balance the evidence, to judge without passion <note>original: "heat"</note> or prejudice, and to present the facts and the commentary on them with candor, sincerity, and truth. At the same time, I am very well aware that several great scholars—for whom I have the sincerest personal regard and whose achievements I view with profound respect—will differ from me in many details.

I am conscious that the rough list of books which I have compiled does not deserve the dignified title of a Bibliography. It is sadly incomplete; yet, however inadequate it may be, should it prove helpful in even the smallest way, it will have justified its inclusion. I may add that my Biblical quotations, unless expressly noted otherwise, are from the Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> or its English translation commonly called the Douai Version <note>A translation of the Bible from the Latin Vulgate into English, favored by the Catholic Church at the time.</note>.

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

## CHAPTER I

### THE WITCH: HERETIC AND ANARCHIST

"A sorcerer is one who, by diabolical means, knowingly strives to achieve something." <note>original: "SORCIER est celuy qui par moyens Diaboliques sciemment s'efforce de paruenir à quel que chose."</note> With these words, the deeply learned legal expert <term>jurisconsult: a specialist in international or civil law</term> Jean Bodin—one of the sharpest and most strictly impartial minds of his age—opens his famous *The Demon-mania of Sorcerers* (*De la Demonomanie des Sorciers*),¹ and it would be, I imagine, hardly possible to find a more concise, exact, comprehensive, and intelligent definition of a Witch.

The entire massive subject of Witchcraft has, it would seem, seldom if ever been honestly and fairly examined in recent times. This is especially true regarding its many remarkable appearances throughout every district of Southern and Western Europe from the middle of the thirteenth until the start of the eighteenth century.²

The only reliable sources of information are the records from that time: the extremely detailed legal reports of the actual trials; the vast collection of pamphlets providing eyewitness accounts of individual witches and reproducing evidence word for word <note>original: "uerbatim"</note> as it was told in court; and, above all, the massive and highly technical works of the Inquisitors and demonologists <note>scholars who studied the activities of demons and their influence on humanity</note>. These authors were holy and respected clergymen, doctors of both civil and canon law <note>original: "utriusque iuris"</note>, and practical, steady, and serious lawyers. They were learned men, scholars with philosophical minds, and held the most honorable names in the universities of Europe. They stood at the forefront of literature, science, politics, and culture. They were monks who served as the spiritual advisors to kings and popes; men whose word would...

<meta>This page continues the introduction's argument that previous studies of witchcraft have been insufficient, transitioning from a discussion of the authors' credentials to the various biased ways the subject has been historically treated.</meta>

...set Europe aflame and bring an emperor to his knees at their gate.

It is true that witchcraft has been the subject of a significant amount of literature. However, one will find that researchers have mostly approached this eternal and terrible chapter in human history from biased and completely different points of view. As a result, it is often necessary to thoroughly sift through their one-sided presentations, disregard their unsupported commentaries and illogical conclusions, and finally reach the solid bedrock of fact.

In the first place, we have those writings and interests that can be described as merely "antiquarian" <note>concerned with the study of old and rare objects or customs as a hobby rather than a living reality</note>. In these works, witchcraft is treated as a curious side-path of history—a superstition that died out long ago, having no existence in or impact on the affairs of the present day. It is treated as a field for folklore, where one might gather strange flowers and poisonous weeds.

On the other hand, we often see the "romantic" treatment of witchcraft. It is the Eve of St. George, a dark and wild night; the pale moon can only struggle thinly through the thick, gathering clouds. The witches are out, hurtling quickly through the air like a hideous flock of birds, carried headlong by the shrieking wind. In delirious tones, they yell foul, mysterious words as they go: "Har! Har! Har! Altri! Altri!" <note>Traditional ritual chants recorded in historical witch trials</note>. They hasten to some peak of the Brocken <note>the highest peak of the Harz Mountains in Germany, traditionally associated with witches</note> or the lonely Cévennes mountains to participate in the orgies of the <term>Sabbat: a midnight assembly of witches to renew their oaths to the Devil</term>. There, they perform infernal sacraments and the dance of Acheron <note>Acheron is a river in the Greek underworld; here it refers to a hellish dance</note>—a sweet and fearful fantasy of evil, "toward impure debaucheries and foul kisses" <note>original French: "Vers les stupres impurs et les baisers immondes," a quote from the poet Pierre de Ronsard or similar decadent literature</note>. Hell seems to vomit its foulest dregs upon the shrinking earth. A loathsome shape of obscene horror squats huge and monstrous upon an ebony throne; the stifling air reeks with filth and blasphemy. Faster and faster whirls the witches’ lewd <term>lavolta: a lively, leaping dance for couples</term>; shriller and shriller the <term>cornemuse: a type of traditional bagpipe</term> screams. And then, a pale gray light flickers in the eastern sky. A moment later, the loud wake-up call of some village <term>chanticleer: a rooster</term> sounds. As quick as thought, the vile, shifting scene of imaginary images vanishes and is gone; all is quiet and still in the peaceful dawn.

But both the antiquarian and the romantic views of witchcraft may be considered irrelevant and trivial as far as the current research is concerned, no matter how entertaining and picturesque such treatments might be to many readers.

...providing quite a few pleasant hours, from which they are able to draw highly dramatic and brilliantly colored pictures of old-time sorceries. These are not meant to be taken too seriously, for the authors believe these things never were and never could have been.⁴

The rationalist historian and the skeptic, when inevitably confronted with the subject of Witchcraft, chose a charmingly easy way to deal with these intensely complex and intricate problems: a flat denial of all statements that did not fit, or could not somehow be forced to fit, their own narrow prejudice. What does the most irrefutable <note>original: "irrefragable"</note> evidence matter—evidence which, in the case of any other accusation, would have been unhesitatingly accepted as final? What does the logical and reasoned belief of centuries, held by the most cultured peoples and the highest intellects of Europe, matter? Any appeal to authority is, of course, useless, as the skeptic rejects all authority—except his own. Such things simply could not be. We must argue from that starting point, and therefore anything that is impossible to explain away as hallucination, hysteria, auto-suggestion, or any other vague buzzword that happens to be fashionable at the moment, must be uncompromisingly rejected. A tone of superior pity, used to sweeten <note>original: "candy"</note> their smooth yet crushingly decisive judgment, has proved very useful on more than one occasion. Why examine the evidence? It is really useless and a waste of time because we already "know" that the allegations are all idle and ridiculous. The "facts" sworn to by countless witnesses—which are repeated in unchanging detail century after century in every country and every town—simply did not take place. The skeptic fails to tell us how the absolute and total falsity of these facts can be proven; nonetheless, we are expected to blindly accept his infallible authority over reason, evidence, and truth.

Yet, suppose that with clear and open minds we carefully investigate this accumulated evidence. If we look into the circumstances of a number of typical cases and compare the trials of the fifteenth century in France with the trials of the seventeenth century in England, will we not find a very solid foundation <note>original: "substratum"; an underlying layer or basis</note> of a permanent and unchanging nature that can be clearly traced throughout the whole? In all fairness, this cannot be denied, and here we

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

...is where we find the core and the enduring reality of witchcraft and the witch-cult throughout the ages.

There were some gross superstitions; there were some unbridled imaginations; there was deception, there was sleight of hand <note>original: "legerdemain"</note>; there was fantasy; there was fraud. Henri Boguet <note>A famous French judge and demonologist (c. 1550–1619) known for his severity in witch trials.</note> seems, perhaps, a trifle credulous, a little too eager to explain obscure practices by an instant appeal to the supernatural. Brother Jetzer, the Dominican friar <note>original: "Jacobin of Berne." Hans Jetzer was a 16th-century monk involved in a famous religious fraud case in Switzerland.</note> of Bern, can only have been either the tool of his superiors or a cunning impostor. Matthew Hopkins <note>The self-styled "Witchfinder General" who was responsible for the execution of hundreds of people in East Anglia during the 1640s.</note> was an unmitigated scoundrel who preyed upon the fears of the Essex freeholders <note>original: "franklins"</note> while he emptied their pockets. Lord Torphichen’s son was an idle, mischievous boy whose pranks not only deluded both his father and the Reverend Mr. John Wilkins, but caused considerable confusion and amazement throughout the whole region of Calder. Anne Robinson (Mrs. Golding’s maid) and the two servant girls of Baldarroch were magicians <note>original: "prestidigitators"</note> of no common skill. 

All these examples of ignorance, gullibility, malice, trickery, and imposture might easily be multiplied twenty times over—and twenty times again. Yet, when every allowance has been made and every possible explanation exhausted, there remains a collection <note>original: "congeries"</note> of solid, proven facts which cannot be ignored, except by the short-sighted <note>original: "purblind"</note> prejudice of the rationalist. These facts cannot be accounted for unless we recognize that there were, and are, individuals and organizations deliberately, and even enthusiastically, devoted to the service of evil, greedy for the emotions, experiences, and rewards that the slavery <note>original: "thraldom"</note> of wickedness may bring.

The skeptic notoriously refuses to believe in witchcraft, but a sanely critical examination of the evidence at the witch trials will show that a vast amount of modern, common incredulity is founded upon a complete misconception of the facts. It may be well worth while to quite briefly review and correct some of the more common objections that are so loosely and so repeatedly maintained. There are many points which are urged as proving the foolish absurdity and demonstrable impossibility of the whole system, and yet there is not one of these phenomena which is not capable of a satisfactory, and often a simple, explanation <note>original: "elucidation"</note>. Perhaps the first thought of a witch that will occur to the average person <note>original: "man in the street"</note> is that of a hag on a broomstick flying up the chimney—

...through the air. This has often been vividly pictured in the public imagination, not only by woodcuts and illustrations traditionally found in books, but by the work of great painters. Examples include Quevedo's *The Departure for the Sabbath* <note>original French title: "Le Départ au Sabbat"</note>, David Teniers's *The Departure for the Sabbath* <note>original French title: "Le Départ pour le Sabbat"</note>, and Goya's midnight fantasies.

The famous Australian artist, Norman Lindsay, has a picture called *To The Sabbath*<sup>5</sup> <note>The "Sabbath" or "Sabbat" refers to the secret midnight gatherings where witches were believed to meet with the Devil.</note> where witches are depicted wildly rushing through the air on the backs of deformed pigs and hideous goats.

Shakespeare, too, expanded on this idea, and his line:
> "Hover through the fog and filthy air" <note>From the opening scene of William Shakespeare's *Macbeth* (1606).</note>
has firmly fixed itself in the English imagination.

But let us descend from the artistic realms of painting and poetry to the hard ground of reality. Throughout the entire historical record, there are very few instances where a witness definitely asserted that they had seen a witch carried through the air mounted upon a broom or stick of any kind. On every such occasion, there is obvious exaggeration intended to create a dramatic effect.

Sometimes the witches themselves boasted of this means of transport to impress their listeners. Henri Boguet <note>A famous French judge and demonologist (c. 1550–1619) known for his severity in witch trials.</note> records the case of Claudine Boban, a young girl whose head was turned by obsessive vanity. She was clearly an obsessive <note>original: "monomaniac"</note> who felt she must at all costs be the center of the stage and the focus of public attention. She confessed that she had been to the Sabbath, and this was undoubtedly true. however, walking or riding on horseback to the Sabbath were far too ordinary methods of travel for her; melodrama and the marvelous had to have their place in her account, and so she claimed:
> "that both she and her mother used to mount on a broom, and by exiting through the chimney in this fashion, they flew through the air to the Sabbath."<sup>6</sup>

In 1664, Julian Cox said that one evening when she was in the fields about a mile away from the house:
> "there came riding towards her three persons upon three broomsticks <note>original: "Broom-staves"</note>, held up about a yard and a half from the ground."<sup>7</sup>

There is obvious exaggeration here; she likely saw two men and one woman straddling brooms and leaping high into the air. They were, in fact, performing a magic rite—a specific movement of a dance.

Similarly, it is recorded of the Arab hags that:
> "In the time of the Munqidhites <note>original: "Munkidh," referring to the Banu Munqidh, a medieval Arab dynasty.</note> the witches rode about naked on a stick between the graves of the cemetery of Shaizar <note>A town and fortress in northern Syria.</note>."<sup>8</sup>

No one can deny that the witches straddled sticks and poles and, in their rituals, skipped and leaped to and fro in this manner.

This action is quite bizarre, but certainly not impossible. This strange ritual—of which there is frequent evidence that makes no mention of flying through the air—has been exaggerated and transformed into the popular superstition that sorcerers are carried aloft and transported from place to place. This was a wonder that they were all too ready to use as proof of their magical powers. And yet, it is not impossible that there were actual instances of levitation. For, outside the lives of the Saints, spiritualist seances provide us with examples of this supernatural phenomenon which, if human testimony is worth anything at all, are proven beyond all question.

As for the ointments <note>original: unguents</note> with which the sorcerers anointed themselves, we have the actual formulas for these mixtures. Professor A. J. Clark, who has examined these, considers it possible that a strong application of such lotions might produce unusual excitement and even delirium. But long ago, the great demonologists <note>Scholars who specialized in the study of demons and witchcraft.</note> recognized and stated that the ointments themselves possessed no such properties as the witches supposed. “The ointment and lotion are of no use at all to witches to aid their journey to the Sabbath <note>original: Sabbat</note>,” is the well-considered opinion of Boguet, who, speaking with confident precision and finality, is on this point in entire agreement with the most skeptical of later rationalists.

The transformation of witches into animals and the extraordinary appearance at their gatherings <note>original: orgies</note> of “the Devil” in many hideously unnatural shapes are two points which have been repeatedly mocked as obvious impossibilities. They are often cited as conclusive proof that the evidence is untrustworthy and the whole system is unbelievable. However, both can be easily and fairly interpreted in a way that offers a complete and convincing explanation for these wonders. The first—metamorphosis—is mentioned and fully explained in the *Penitential Book* <note>original Latin: *Liber Pœnitentialis*</note> of Saint Theodore, the seventh Archbishop of Canterbury (668–690). There is ample proof that "the Devil" of the Sabbath was very frequently a human being—the Grand Master of the district—and since his officers and immediate attendants were also termed "Devils" by the witches, some confusion has occasionally occurred. In a few cases where sufficient details are given, it is possible to actually identify "the Devil" by name. Thus, among a list of suspected persons in the reign of Elizabeth, we have "Old Birtles, the great devil, Roger Birtles and his wife, and Anne Birtles."¹² The evil William, Lord Soulis, of Hermitage Castle—often known as "Red Cap"—was "the Devil" of a coven of sorcerers.

Very seldom was "the Devil" a woman. In May 1569, the Regent of Scotland was present at St. Andrews "where a notable sorceress named Nicniven was condemned to death and burnt" <note>original Scots: "quhair a notabill sorceres callit Nicniven was condemnit to the death and burnt"</note>. Now, Nicniven is the Queen of Elphin <note>A folkloric figure in Scottish mythology, often associated with the Queen of Fairies or a goddess of witches.</note>, the Mistress of the Sabbath, and this office had evidently been filled by this witch whose real name is not recorded.

On November 8, 1576, Elizabeth or Bessy Dunlop, of Lyne, in the Barony of Dalry, Ayrshire, was tried for sorcery. She confessed that a certain mysterious Thom Reid had met her and demanded that she should renounce Christianity and her baptism, and apparently worship him. There can be little doubt that he was "the Devil" of a coven, for the original details, which are very full, all point to this. He seems to have played his part with some forethought and skill; when the accused stated that she often saw him in the churchyard of Dalry, as also in the streets of Edinburgh—where he walked back and forth among other people and handled goods that were exposed for sale on stalls <term>bulks: shop stalls or counters projecting from the front of a building</term> without attracting any special notice—she was asked why she did not speak to him. She replied that he had forbidden her to recognize him on any such occasion unless he made a sign or first actually spoke to her. She was "convicted and burnt."¹³ In the case of Alison Peirson, tried May 28, 1588, "the Devil" was actually her kinsman, William Sympson, and she "was convicted of the use of Sorcery and Witchcraft" <note>original: "wes conuict of the vsing of Sorcerie and Witchcraft"</note>.

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

Sampson <note>Refers to Agnes Sampson, a central figure in the North Berwick witch trials of 1590</note>. I have no doubt that the drawing for the masque <note>a form of festive courtly entertainment that involved music, dancing, and acting</note> was actually made in the theatre. Although this kind of costly and decorative entertainment was almost always designed for the royal court or a great nobleman’s house, we know that the play *The World Tost at Tennis* was produced with considerable success on the public stage by the "Prince's Servants" <note>original: "Prince his Seruants," a prominent acting company in the 17th century</note>. The dress of "the Devil" at the Sabbats <note>clandestine midnight meetings of witches</note>, then, seems frequently to have been an elaborate theatrical costume. Such a costume might have been found in the stock wardrobe of a wealthy London playhouse, but it would have had no such theatrical associations for country people or even simpler peasants.

From time to time, skeptics have pointed to the many recorded cases of a victim’s sickness or death following a witch's curse, and have incredulously asked if it is possible that a malediction <term>malediction: a magical word or phrase uttered with the intention of bringing about evil; a curse</term> could have such consequences. While frankly stating that I personally believe there is power for evil and even for destruction in such a curse—that a deadly anathema <term>anathema: a formal curse or denunciation</term> launched with concentrated hate and all the energy of one’s will may bring unhappiness and death in its wake—I will answer their objections using other reasoning, since they will not accept my first point. 

When some person who had in any way annoyed the witch was to be harmed or killed, it was obviously convenient, when possible, to follow up the symbolism of the solemn curse—or perhaps the melting of a wax image riddled with pins—with a dose of subtly administered poison. This would bring about the desired result, whether sickness or death. From the evidence concerning the witches' victims, who so frequently wasted away from a lingering disease, it seems more than probable that deadly drugs were continually employed. As Professor A. J. Clark records, "the society of witches had a very respectable knowledge of the art of poisoning,"¹⁸ and they are known to have freely used aconite, deadly nightshade (belladonna), and hemlock.

Therefore, far from the confessions of the witches being mere hysteria and hallucination, they are proved—even by the most material interpretation—to be, for the most part, hideous and horrible facts.

From the middle of the thirteenth to the beginning of the eighteenth century was the period when the diabolic cult reached its height, when it spread like a blight and a scourge throughout Europe and showed its most terrifying proportions. But it must not for a moment be supposed, as has often been superficially believed, that witchcraft was a product of the Middle Ages, and that only then did authorities adopt measures of repression and legislate against the warlock and the sorceress. If attention has been concentrated upon that period, it is because during those and the succeeding centuries, witchcraft blazed forth with unexampled virulence and ferocity, threatening the peace—and even, in some degree, the salvation—of mankind. 

But even pagan emperors had issued edicts absolutely forbidding <term>goetic theurgy</term> <note>original: "goetic theurgy"; black magic or the invocation of evil spirits</note>, confiscating <term>grimoires</term> <note>original: "grimoires"; textbooks of magic and spells</note> (books of prophecy <note>original: "fatidici libri"</note>), and punishing necromancers with death. In 33 B.C. <note>original: "A.U.C. 721"; refers to the year 721 from the founding of the city of Rome</note>, during the triumvirate of Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus, all astrologers and charmers were banished.<sup>19</sup> Maecenas called upon Augustus to punish sorcerers, and plainly stated that those who devote themselves to magic are despisers of the gods.<sup>20</sup> More than two thousand popular books of spells, written in both Greek and Latin, were discovered in Rome and publicly burned.<sup>21</sup> In the reign of Tiberius, a decree of the Senate exiled all traffickers in the occult arts; Lucius Pituanius, a notorious wizard, was thrown from the Tarpeian rock, and another, Publius Martius, was executed in the ancient fashion <note>original: "more prisco"</note> outside the Esquiline gate.<sup>22</sup>

Under Claudius, the Senate reiterated the sentence of banishment: "A decree of the Senate was passed regarding the expulsion of astrologers from Italy; it was severe but ineffective," says Tacitus <note>original: "De mathematicis Italia pellendis factum Senatus consultum, atrox et irritum"</note>.<sup>23</sup> During the few months he was emperor, Vitellius proceeded with implacable severity against all soothsayers and diviners; many of whom, when accused, he ordered for instant execution, not even granting them the simplest formality of a trial.<sup>24</sup> Vespasian, his successor, also refused to permit <term>scryers</term> <note>original: "scryers"; people who use crystal balls or other reflective objects to see the future</note> and enchanters to set foot in Italy, strictly enforcing the existing statutes.<sup>25</sup> It is clear from all these stringent laws—and the list of examples might be greatly extended—that although under the Caesars omens were respected, oracles were consulted, the augurs <note>official Roman diviners who interpreted the will of the gods from the flight of birds</note> honored, and <term>haruspices</term> <note>original: "haruspices"; priests who practiced divination by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</note> revered, the dark influences and foul criminality of the...

M. de Cauzons expressed himself quite forcefully when speaking of writers who trace the origins of witchcraft to the Middle Ages: "It is either a bad joke or a blatant falsehood," <note>original: "C’est une mauvaise plaisanterie... ou une contrevérité flagrante"</note> he remarks,<sup>26</sup> "to claim that witchcraft was born in the Middle Ages, or to attribute its existence to the influence or the beliefs of the Catholic Church."

An even more erroneous claim is the charge—not infrequently but far too emphatically brought forward by biased and poorly-documented historians—that the European crusade against witches, with its intense prosecutions and the ultimate penalty of death at the stake, is entirely due to the <term>Papal Bull</term> <note>a formal public decree or charter issued by a Pope</note> *Summis desiderantes affectibus* (issued December 5, 1484) by Pope Innocent VIII. ## THE WITCH: HERETIC AND ANARCHIST

To emphasize the point further, it is worth stressing that the <term>Bull</term> <note>a formal decree issued by a Pope</note> of Innocent VIII was only one of a long series of Papal ordinances dealing with the suppression of a monstrous and almost universal evil.<sup>31</sup>

The first Papal Bull directly launched against the dark arts and those who practiced them was that of Alexander IV, issued on December 13, 1258, and addressed to the Franciscan inquisitors. It is worthwhile here to examine exactly what the terms "inquisitor" and "inquisition" originally meant—terms that are so often misunderstood today. Our brief research will shed a great deal of light on the subject of witchcraft. Furthermore, it will help explain why writers who claim witchcraft began in the Middle Ages—though they are definitely and demonstrably wrong—were so easily misled. This is because it was during the Middle Ages that sorcery was violently unmasked. At that time, the entire horrific practice was officially exposed in its darkest and most repulsive forms—forms that had existed from the start but had been carefully hidden and kept secret.

Today, the term "Inquisition" (from the Latin word meaning "to look into" <note>original: "inquirere"</note>) is generally understood to be a specific church institution for fighting or suppressing heresy. The Inquisitors are the officials of that institution, specifically judges appointed to investigate charges of heresy and to try the individuals brought before them. During the first twelve hundred years, the Church was reluctant to deal with heretics except through argument and persuasion. Stubborn and admitted heretics were, of course, excluded from the Church community. In an age characterized by faith, such an expulsion naturally caused them many significant difficulties. Saint Augustine,<sup>32</sup> Saint John Chrysostom,<sup>33</sup> and Saint Isidore of Seville<sup>34</sup> in the seventh century, along with many other Church Doctors and Fathers, believed that the Church should never shed blood for any reason. 

On the other hand, the Roman Emperors who succeeded Constantine rightly felt they were responsible for the Church's physical well-being on earth. They believed that heresy is always unavoidably and permanently linked to attacks on social order, and that it is always both anarchic and political. Even the pagan persecutor Diocletian recognized this fact, which heretics, until they obtain the—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the early history of how religious dissent and sorcery were handled by the state and the Church. In 287 AD, less than two years after his accession to the throne, the Emperor Diocletian sent the leaders of the Manicheans <note>original: "Manichees"; a dualistic religious sect that saw the world as a battleground between good and evil</note> to the stake to be burned. The majority of their followers were beheaded, and a few who were deemed less guilty were sent to permanent forced labor in the government mines. Again in 296 AD, he ordered their total extermination (to be "rooted out and cut away" <note>original: *stirpitus amputari*</note>) as a filthy, wicked, and impure sect. 

Similarly, the Christian Emperors, persuaded that the protection of orthodox faith was their sacred duty, began to issue decrees for the suppression of heretics, viewing them as traitors and anti-social revolutionaries.^35 But the Church protested against this. When Priscillian, the Bishop of Avila, was found guilty of heresy and sorcery^36 and condemned to death by the Emperor Maximus at Trier in 384 AD, Saint Martin of Tours addressed the Emperor in such plain terms that he was solemnly promised the sentence would not be carried out. However, the promise was broken. Saint Martin’s indignation was so great that for a long while he refused to take communion with those who had been in any way responsible for the execution. Saint Ambrose also strongly condemned the act as a hateful crime.^37 The words of Pope Saint Siricius were even more crushing; Maximus was forced to humble himself in lowly repentance, and the Pope actually excommunicated Bishop Felix of Trier for his part in the deed.

From time to time, heretics were put to death under the civil law to which they were subject, as in 556 AD when a band of Manicheans was executed at Ravenna. Pope Pelagius I, who was consecrated that very year, took a milder approach when Paulinus of Fossombrone rejected his authority and openly stirred up division and revolt; the Pope merely sent the defiant bishop to a monastery. Saint Caesarius of Arles, who died in 547 AD, wrote^38 of the punishment to be given to those who stubbornly continue in open paganism. He recommended that they should first be reasoned with and reprimanded, so that they might, if possible, be persuaded of their errors. If they persisted, however, he suggested certain physical punishments. In extreme cases, a course of domestic discipline might be adopted, such as cutting the hair short as a mark of disgrace and confining them indoors under restraint. At this time, there was no hint of anything more than...

In the days of Charlemagne, the elderly Elipandus, Archbishop of Toledo, taught an offshoot of the Nestorian heresy <note>original: "Nestorian heresy"; a doctrine that suggested Jesus existed as two separate persons, one human and one divine</note> known as Adoptionism <note>original: "Adoptionism"; the belief that Jesus was born a mere man and was later "adopted" by God</note>. This was a subtle but deadly error, through which he won over the slippery expert in logic <note>original: "dialectician"</note>, Felix of Urgel. As a Frankish high official of the church <note>original: "prelate"</note>, Felix was summoned to Aix-la-Chapelle <note>modern: Aachen, Germany</note>. A church council <note>original: "synod"</note> condemned his doctrine, and he took back his words, only to later retract that statement and repeat his blasphemies. He was condemned again, and again he recanted. But he proved deceptive and cunning to the last. After his death, Agobard of Lyons found a scroll among his papers asserting that he was fully persuaded of this heresy, despite any contradictions he might have hypocritically signed. Yet, Felix only suffered a short period of detention at Rome, while no measures seem to have been taken against Elipandus, who died still believing his errors. It was presumably considered that the truth of the faith could be sufficiently defended and proven by the enthusiasm of such great men as Beatus, Abbot of Libana; Etherius, Bishop of Osma; Saint Benedict of Aniane; and the famous Alcuin.^39

Some forty years later, around the middle of the ninth century, Gottschalk <note>original: "Gothescalch"</note>, a monk of Fulda, caused a great scandal by stubbornly and shamelessly maintaining that Christ had not died for all mankind—a preview of the later Calvinist heresy. He was condemned at the Synods of Mainz in 848 AD and of Quierzy <note>original: "Kiersey-sur-Oise"</note> in 849 AD. He was sentenced to flogging and imprisonment, punishments which were then common in monasteries for various violations of the rule. In this case, because it was particularly shocking, it was Hincmar <note>original: "Hinemar"</note>, Archbishop of Rheims—a church leader notorious for his severity—who sentenced the culprit to be locked away. But Gottschalk had, through his harmful doctrines, been the cause of serious disturbances; his inflammatory speeches had incited riots, rebellion, and unrest, bringing hatred upon the monk's robes <note>original: "sacred habit"</note>. The sentence of the Quierzy Synod ran:

> “Brother Gottschalk... because you have dared to disturb both church and civil affairs, contrary to the purpose and name of a monk, and have presumed to violate church laws, we decree by our authority as bishops that you be punished <note>original: "castigari"</note> with the harshest floggings and, according to church rules, be confined in a prison <note>original: "ergastulo"</note>.” <note>original Latin: "Frater Goteschalc . . . quia et ecclesiastica et ciuilia negotia contra propositum et nomen monachi conturbare iura ecclesiastica præsumpsisti, durissimis uerberibus te cagistari et secundum ecclesiasticas regulas ergastulo retrudi, auctoritate episcopali decernimus."</note>

Around the year 1000, however, the poison of Manichaeism <note>original: "Manichæism"; an ancient dualistic religion that viewed the world as a struggle between a good spirit world and an evil material world</note> gained a new foothold in the West, where it had died out early in the sixth century. Between 1030 and 1040, an important Manichaean community was discovered at the Castle of Monteforte, near Asti, in the Piedmont region of Italy. Some of the members were arrested by the Bishop of Asti and a number of local noblemen; upon their refusal to renounce their beliefs, the government <note>original: "civil arm"</note> burned them. Others, by order of the Archbishop of Milan, Ariberto, were brought to that city because he hoped to convert them. They responded to his efforts by trying to win converts <note>original: "proselytes"</note> of their own. Consequently, Lanzano, a prominent noble and leader of the common people's party, caused the magistrates to intervene; once they had been taken into state custody, they were executed without further delay.

It had reached northwards to Germany, where it was completely organized, and was not unknown in England; as early as 1159, thirty foreign Manichaeans had secretly settled here. They were discovered in 1166 and handed over to the legal authorities <note>original: "secular authorities"</note> by the bishops of the Council of Oxford. In a great rage, King Henry II ordered them to be whipped, branded on the forehead, and cast out into the cold...

Pope Innocent III did not add anything fundamentally new to these regulations, but he gave them broader application and clearer definitions. In his *Decretals* <note>original: "Decretals"; collections of papal decrees that formed the basis of church law</note>, he speaks specifically about accusation, denunciation, and inquisition. It is clear that these measures were necessary to confront a massive secret society that aimed to destroy the established social order. All the cult members <note>original: "sectaries"</note> were busy with intense propaganda, and their followers had spread like a network across most of Europe. The members called each other "brother" and "sister" and used secret words and signs so they could recognize fellow initiates without exposing themselves to outsiders.⁴¹ Ivan de Narbonne, who had left this heresy, wrote in a letter to Giraldus, the Archbishop of Bordeaux (as quoted by the historian Matthew of Paris), that he was able to identify himself using these signs in every city he visited.⁴²

Local bishops needed help with the difficult task of tracking down heretics. Therefore, the Papacy <note>original: "Holy See"</note> turned to legates <note>original: "legates"; personal representatives of the Pope sent on special missions</note> who were given extraordinary powers to handle such a complicated situation. In 1177, acting as the representative of Pope Alexander III, Peter, Cardinal of San Crisogono, visited the Toulouse area at the specific request of Count Raymond V to stop the growing influence of Cathar <note>original: "Catharist"</note> beliefs.⁴³ In 1181, Henry, the Abbot of Clairvaux (who had been part of the previous group and was now the Cardinal of Albano), acted as a representative for the same Pope. He accepted the surrender of various heretical leaders and—since his powers were so extensive—officially removed the Archbishops of Lyons and Narbonne from their positions.

In 1203, Peter of Castelnau and Raoul were working in Toulouse on behalf of Innocent III, apparently with full authority <note>original: "plenipotentiary authority"; the power to act fully on the Pope's behalf</note>. The following year, Arnauld Amaury, the Abbot of Citeaux, joined them to create a three-person court <note>original: "triple tribunal"</note> with absolute power to judge heretics in the regions of Aix, Arles, Narbonne, and nearby dioceses. By the time Innocent III died in 1216, a system existed to hunt for heretics. This included church courts <note>original: "episcopal tribunals"</note> that often included an assistant—the future "inquisitor"—to monitor the trial, and most importantly, the papal legate to whom reports were made. Because of his high rank, the legate was usually a high-ranking church official <note>original: "prelate"</note> who was busy with many urgent matters. For instance, Arnauld Amaury was away for a considerable time...

This was a special but permanent judge acting in the name of the Pope, by whom he was granted the right and the duty to deal legally with offenses against the Faith. At this same time, two new religious orders were founded: the Dominicans and Franciscans. Because of their theological training and the very nature of their vows, their members seemed perfectly suited to carry out the work of the Inquisition with complete success. They were seen as being entirely uninfluenced by any worldly motives. Therefore, it is natural that the new officials were selected from these orders, especially from the highly educated ranks of the Dominicans, due to the importance that order placed on the study of divinity.

It is very obvious why the Papacy <note>original: "Holy See"</note> so wisely preferred to assign the prosecution of heretics—a matter of the highest importance—to a special tribunal <note>original: "extraordinary tribunal"; a court outside the normal judicial system</note> rather than leave the trials in the hands of the local bishops. Aside from the fact that these new duties would have seriously distracted from, if not completely consumed, a bishop’s time and energy, the high-ranking clergy who ruled most dioceses were often subjects of a monarch. They might have come into conflict with their king on many sensitive issues that could easily arise. The results of such disagreements would have led to endless political difficulties and internal problems. A court of religious monks or friars, responsible to the Pope alone, would act more fairly and more freely, without fear or favoritism. 

For example, the immoral Philip I of France, during his long, worthless, and dishonored reign (1060–1108), brought the condemnation of the Church upon himself through his wicked behavior. In response, he banished the Bishop of Beauvais and overturned the decisions of the church courts.⁴⁴ In a letter⁴⁵ to William, Count of Poitiers, Pope Saint Gregory VII forcefully declared that if the King did not stop harassing the bishops and interfering with their legal authority, a sentence of excommunication <note>original: "excommunication"; a punishment that cuts a person off from the sacraments and membership in the Church</note> would be issued. In another letter, the same Pope complained about the disrespect shown to the church tribunals, and addressing the French bishops he cried out:

The words "<term>Inquisition</term>" and "<term>Inquisitors</term>" began to acquire their modern meanings more clearly in the first half of the thirteenth century. For example, in 1235, Gregory IX wrote to the Archbishop of Sens:
> "Know then that we have charged the Provincial of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note> in this same realm to nominate certain of his brothers, who are best fitted for such important business, as <term>Inquisitors</term>. > "those brothers who have been sent abroad to preach the Mystery of the Cross of Christ, or to seek out and take measures against the plague-sore of heresy."<sup>48</sup>

All the heresies and the secret societies of heretics that infested Europe during the Middle Ages were <term>Gnostic</term> and, even more specifically, <term>Manichæan</term> <note>a dualistic religious system that saw the world as a struggle between a good spiritual world and an evil material world</note> in character. The <term>Gnostics</term> emerged almost at the same time as Christianity as a school or schools that explained the teachings of Christ by blending them with the doctrines of pagan dreamers. They claimed to have a higher and wider knowledge—the <note>original: "Γνῶσις" (Gnosis)</note> Knowledge—the first proponent of which was unquestionably Simon Magus <note>a first-century figure often considered the first heretic</note>.

"Two problems borrowed from heathen philosophy," says Mansel,<sup>49</sup> "were forced by <term>Gnosticism</term> onto the Christian revelation: the problem of absolute existence, and the problem of the Origin of Evil."

The <term>Gnostics</term> denied the existence of <term>free will</term>. Therefore, they believed that evil was not the result of man's voluntary sin, but must have come from the Creator Himself. Arguing along these lines, the majority asserted that the Creator must have been a malignant power, the Lord of the Kingdom of Darkness.

...opposed to the supreme and <term>ineffable</term> <note>original: "ineffable"; too great or sacred to be expressed in words</note> God. This doctrine was taught by the Gnostic sects of Persia, which became deeply influenced by the religion of Zoroaster, who believed in the existence of two original and independent Powers: one of Good and one of Evil. Each of these Powers is of equal strength and supreme in his own territory, while a constant war is fought between the two. 

This doctrine was particularly held by the Syrian Gnostics, including the Ophites, the Naasseni, the Peratae, and the Sethians, among whom the serpent was the primary symbol. Because they believed the Creator of the physical world was evil, they viewed the Tempter—the Serpent—as the benefactor of humanity. In fact, in some of their creeds, the serpent was identified with the <term>Word of God</term> <note>original: "Logos"</note>. 

The Cainites carried these Ophite doctrines to their most logical conclusion. Since they believed the Creator (the God of the Old Testament) was evil, they argued that everything praised by the Scriptures must actually be evil, and conversely, everything condemned by the Scriptures must be good. In their view, Cain, Korah, and other biblical rebels were to be imitated and admired. They even claimed that the only true Apostle was Judas Iscariot. This cult is very clearly visible in the Middle Ages among the Luciferians, and these "Cainite" ceremonies eventually found a place in the rituals of the witches' <term>Sabbat</term> <note>original: "Sabbat"; a secret midnight assembly of witches, believed by medieval authorities to involve devil worship</note>.<sup>50</sup>

All this Gnostic teaching was eventually summarized in the gospel of the Persian Mani. When he was a young man of only twenty-six, he first proclaimed his message in the streets and marketplaces of Seleucia-Ctesiphon on Sunday, March 20, 242—the coronation festival of Shapur I. He did not find immediate success in his own country, but his ideas took deep root in various places. However, in 276–277, he was captured and crucified by Bahram I, the grandson of Shapur, and his disciples were relentlessly hunted. 

Whenever Manicheans <note>original: "Manichees"</note> were discovered, they were brought to swift justice, executed, and held up to universal hatred and contempt. Muslims <note>original: "Moslems"</note> considered them not merely as unbelievers or followers of a false impostor, but as unnatural and anti-social threats to the State. It was for no small reason that the Manichean was loathed and abhorred by both faithful Christians and by those who proclaimed Mohammed as the true prophet of Allah. Yet, despite this, Manichaeism later spread in every direction to an extraordinary degree. This was perhaps because it functioned as a synthesis of various Gnostic philosophies, placing a heavy emphasis on the theory of two eternal principles: Good and Evil.

Moreover, the historical Jesus, "the Jewish Messiah <note>original: "Messias"</note>, whom the Jews crucified," was viewed by some as "a devil, who was justly punished for interfering in the work of the Aeon <term>Aeon</term> <note>original: "Æon"; in Gnostic belief, an emanation or power radiating from the supreme God</note> Jesus," who was neither born nor suffered death. A sub-sect known as the Messalians or Euchites taught that divine honors must be paid to Satan, who was further to be <term>propitiated</term> <note>original: "propitiated"; won over or appeased</note> by means of every possible outrage committed against Christ. Carpocrates even went so far as to intensify the teaching of the Cainites; he made the performance of every kind of sin forbidden in the Old Testament a solemn duty. He believed this was the most complete way of showing defiance to the "Evil Creator" and Ruler of the World. This doctrine was entirely consistent with that of medieval witches and is still boasted of by modern Satanists. 

Although the Manichees claimed to practice the greatest purity, it is quite certain that they did not oppose <term>unchastity</term> <note>original: "unchastity"; sexual immorality</note>, but rather the act of procreation itself. The Messalians, in particular, boasted of a treatise titled *The Ascetic* <note>original: "Asceticus"</note>, which was condemned by the Third General Council of Ephesus in the year 431 as "that filthy book of this heresy." In Armenia during the fifth century, special edicts were passed to restrain their immoralities, to the point that their very name became a synonym for "lewdness." The Messalians survived into the Middle Ages as the Bogomiles.

Attention has already been drawn to the striking fact that even the Roman Emperor Diocletian legislated with great vigor against the Manichees. When we find Valentinian I and his son Gratian passing laws of equal severity in the year 372—despite being tolerant of other groups—we feel that such a prohibition is especially significant. In a statute from 381, Theodosius I declared Manichees to be without civil rights and incapable of inheriting property. In the following year, he condemned them to death, and in 389, he sternly directed the rigorous enforcement of these penalties to the letter.

Valentinian II confiscated their goods, annulled their wills, and sent them into exile. Theodosius II (in 423) again repeated this legislation, while Valentinian III passed new laws in 425 and 445. Around 660, the Paulicians arose. This was a Manichaean sect that rejected the Old Testament, the Sacraments, and the priesthood. In 835, it was realized that the leadership of this group was political and aimed at revolution and total anarchy <note>original: "red anarchy"; a term implying extreme or violent social disorder</note>. The only result, however, was that the heretics were driven westward and spread rapidly through France and Italy.

The Bogomils were also Manichaeans. They openly worshipped Satan, rejecting the Holy Mass and the Passion of Christ. They replaced Holy Baptism with a corrupted ceremony of their own and used a strange version of the Gospel of St. John. Known as the Cathars <note>original: "Cathari"; from the Greek word for "pure ones"</note>, these people had their center in France at Toulouse and in Germany at Cologne. In Italy, their main gathering points were Milan, Florence, Orvieto, and Viterbo. Their meetings were often held in the open air, on mountains, or in the depths of some lonely valley. Their rituals were very secret, but we know that at night they celebrated their version of the Eucharist, known as the *Consolamentum* <term>Consolamentum</term> <note>original: "Consolamentum"; Latin for "The Consolation," the unique spiritual baptism and central rite of the Cathars</note>. During this rite, everyone stood in a circle around a table covered with a white cloth, and many torches were lit. The service ended with the reading of the first seventeen verses of their altered <note>original: "transfigured"</note> version of the Gospel. Bread was broken, but tradition states that the words of consecration were not spoken according to the Christian formula; in some cases, they were left out entirely.

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

It is true that when these heresies came into sharp conflict with the Catholic Church, they developed in ways that shed various non-essential additions <note>original: "accretions"</note> and the complex Eastern intellectual flourishes of their earlier thought. However, the underlying motive of Manichaean doctrines and of Witchcraft is one and the same, and the punishment for both Manicheans and witches was the same: death at the stake. The fact that these heretics were viewed as sorcerers explains, better than anything else, the severity of the laws against them—laws targeting what was seen as extraordinary wickedness. By the early eleventh century, "Manichean" and "warlock" <note>original: "warlock"; an archaic term for a male witch or sorcerer</note> were considered synonymous.

The sorcery of the Middle Ages, says Carl Haas (a learned and impartial authority), was born from the heresies of earlier eras; just as Christian authorities had dealt with heresy, so they dealt with its offspring, witchcraft. Both are the results of doubt, lack of faith, a disordered imagination, pride, and intellectual arrogance. Both are "sick fantasies" that grow and flourish quickly in shadow and sin until correct reasoning—and sometimes beneficial <note>original: "salutary"</note> force—are used to stop them. The authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "Hammer of Witches"; a famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches</note> clearly identify heresy and witchcraft as one and the same. When John George II Fuchs von Dornheim, the Prince-Bishop of Bamberg (reigned 1623–1633), built a massive prison specifically for sorcerers called the *Drudenhaus* <note>German: "Witches' House"</note>, he placed a statue of Justice over the main door. # THE WITCH: HERETIC AND ANARCHIST

The prosecution of witches, from the standpoint of Christian authority, whose representatives justly and logically regarded sorcery as being essentially heresy, was to be suppressed by the same measures and punished with the same penalties.

In connection with the close correlation between witchcraft and heresy, there is a very remarkable fact, the significance of which—as far as I am aware—has never been noted. The full fury of prosecution broke out in England during the first half of the seventeenth century; that is to say, shortly after the era of a great religious upheaval, when the work of restoration and recovery so nobly begun by Queen Mary I <note>Mary I (reigned 1553–1558) attempted to restore Catholicism in England.</note> had been wrecked owing to the pride, lust, and baseness of her sister <note>Queen Elizabeth I (reigned 1558–1603), whom the author views unfavorably.</note>. In Scotland, poisoned to the core with the teachings of Calvin and Knox, the fire and the hanging-rope <note>original: "fire and cord"</note> were seldom at rest. It is clear that heresy had quickly brought witchcraft in its wake. Ireland has always been singularly free from witchcraft prosecutions, and with the rarest exceptions—chiefly, if not solely, the famous case of Dame Alice Kyteler in 1324—the few trials recorded are from the seventeenth century and were engineered by the Protestant party. The reason for this exemption is plain: until the foreigner <note>original: "stranger"; referring to English and Protestant settlers.</note> forced his way into Ireland, heresy had no foothold there. We know that the Irish firmly believed in witches, but the Devil’s power <note>original: "claws"</note> was significantly restricted <note>original: "finely clipped"</note>.

They then begin to sing the names of various demons, as though they were chanting a litany, until suddenly they perceive that the Devil has appeared in the midst of them in the shape of some animal or other.
