We still occasionally hear echoes of this error, such as when Mrs. Grenside wrote that the Albigensians were "a sect of the 14th century which, because of their secret doctrine, endured much church persecution."⁵⁸ The impression left—and it was one that was not uncommon about seventy years ago—is that the Albigensian was a stern old Protestant forefather, Bible and sword in hand, who defended his home and family against lawless bandits driven to attack him by the schemes of priests. 

Nothing, of course, could be further from the truth. The Albigensian was a Satanist, a worshipper of the powers of evil, and he would have been given very little mercy—likely facing execution by fire and the stake—in Puritan England under Cromwell, or in Calvinistic Scotland, had his actual practices been even slightly suspected by the Church. As Dr. Arendzen well says⁵⁹: "Albigensianism was not really a heresy against Christianity and the Catholic Church; it was a revolt against nature, a plague-like perversion of human instinct."

It is said that this church still has a number of unfortunate followers. These Neo-Gnostics believe that the world was created by Satan, who is a powerful rival to the all-powerful God. They also preach a dangerous form of communism, deceptively masked under titles such as the "Brotherhood of Man" or the "Brotherhood of Nations."

The original founder of this sect, Valentinus, was, according to Saint Epiphanius (*Heresies* <note>original: *Hæresis*</note> XXXI), born in Egypt and educated at Alexandria. The **Christology** <term>the branch of theology relating to the person, nature, and role of Christ</term> of Valentinus is especially confused. He seems to have supposed the existence of three redeemers, but he believed that Christ, the Son of Mary, did not have a real body and did not suffer. Even his more prominent disciples—Heracleon, Ptolemy, Marcos, and Bardesanes—widely differed from their master as well as from one another. Many of the writings of these Gnostics, and a large number of excerpts from Valentinus’s own works, survive even now.

One or two writers of the nineteenth century remarked that there seemed to be some connection between certain points of the **Sabbat** <term>the secret midnight meeting of witches</term> ceremonial and the rites of various pagan deities, which is, of course, a perfectly correct observation. For we have seen that Witchcraft, as it existed in Europe from the eleventh century, was mainly the offspring of Gnostic heresy, and heresy by its very nature embraced and absorbed much of paganism. In some sense, Witchcraft was a descendant of the old pre-Christian magic, but it soon assumed a slightly different form; or rather, at the advent of Christianity, it was exposed and shown in its real, foul essence as the worship of the Evil Principle, the Enemy of Mankind: Satan.

While seeking to spread her doctrines within Greco-Roman civilization, the Church had adopted a completely unknown language for its interactions with the people and had systematically rejected everything that until then had served to express religious feelings.

Within the limits of different races and cultures, there are only so many ways to express the emotions of the heart. It was natural for the new religion to adopt and include everything good from rituals that simply needed to be correctly understood and guided to become the language of the Christian soul reaching for the one True God. Specific postures for prayer and reverence, the use of incense and lamps burning day and night in the sanctuary, and the offering of votive gifts <term>votive offerings (ex-votos) are items given to a deity in gratitude for a prayer answered or a favor received</term> as testimony of help received—all of these are natural human expressions of piety and gratitude toward a divine power. It would be strange if similar practices were not found in all religions.

Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), a Roman statesman and orator</note> tells us that in Agrigentum <note>a city on the coast of Sicily</note> there was a highly revered statue of Hercules, whose mouth and chin were worn down by the many worshippers who pressed their lips against it.⁶¹ The bronze foot of the statue of the first Pope, St. Peter, in Rome has fared no better against the pious kisses of the faithful. Yet only a fool would imagine that modern Christians learned this behavior from the Sicilian contemporaries of Verres <note>Gaius Verres (c. 120–43 BC), a Roman magistrate known for his corruption and theft of public art</note>. The truth is that the same thought, under similar circumstances, has found natural expression through identical actions and attitudes even after centuries have passed.

Among the Greeks, heroes—who were believed to be the mortal sons of a god—were specifically honored in the cities where they were born or that they had helped. After death, they became the patrons and protectors of these towns. Every region—indeed, almost every village—had such local divinities. Monuments were raised to them, and people called upon them in prayer. The center of this devotion was usually the hero's tomb, often built in the middle of the *agora* <term>the central public space or marketplace in ancient Greek city-states</term>, the heart of public life. Usually, these tombs were sheltered by a building, a type of chapel known as a *heroon* <note>original: ἡρῷον</note>. Famous temples were also frequently adorned with

The similarity between these ancient practices and Christianity can be taken even further. Just as in our own churches, objects that belonged to the Saints are displayed for the veneration of the faithful, so in the old temples visitors were shown various curiosities whose connection with a god or a hero commanded their respect. At Minihi Tréguier, we may revere a fragment of the prayer book <note>original: "Breviary"</note> of St. Yves; at Sens, the stole of St. Thomas of Canterbury; at Bayeux, the priestly robe <note>original: "chasuble"</note> of St. Regnobert; and in St. Mary Major <note>original: "S. Similarly, in various locations in Greece, the kithara <note>original: "cittara," a stringed instrument similar to a lyre</note> of Paris, the lyre of Orpheus, and portions of the ships of Agamemnon and Aeneas were exhibited. Is anything else needed to prove that the veneration of holy relics is merely a survival of paganism?

On the surface, this theory seems believable enough, and yet it cannot withstand historical scrutiny for even a moment. The worship of the Saints and their relics is not a result of ancient hero-worship, but of reverence for the Martyrs, and this can be proven beyond any doubt. Here we have two very striking parallels, each starting from a similar point—two cults that naturally developed along logical and similar lines, but without any direct influence on each other. Needless to say, the careless folklorist, who is generally poorly equipped for such research, has jumped to conclusions with his theories—to his own complete failure. Similarly, regarding witchcraft, there appear to be ceremonies in the rituals of the Sabbath <note>original: "Sabbat"</note> and other hellish superstitions that seem directly derived from heathendom; however, this is actually far from the case. *The Witch-Cult in Western Europe* [note: footnote 65], although constructed with considerable skill and a great deal of documentation, is fundamentally and completely mistaken. Miss Murray actually claims that "underlying the Christian religion was a cult practiced by many classes of the community" which "can be traced back to pre-Christian times, and appears to be the ancient religion of Western Europe." We are given a full account of the chief festivals of this imaginary cult, its hierarchy, its organization, and many other details. The feasts and dances—the obscene horrors of the Sabbat <note>The Sabbat was the secret midnight meeting of witches, often involving rituals and dancing</note>—"show that it was a joyous religion"! It is impossible to imagine a more astonishing statement. Miss Murray continues by saying that "as such it must have been quite incomprehensible to the gloomy Inquisitors and Reformers who suppressed it." 

The Reformers, despite their stern severity, perfectly understood what they were dealing with. The Inquisitors—the spiritual sons of St. Dominic (who was boundless in his charity) and St. Francis (whose very name evokes Christ-like love for all creation)—were men of the most profound knowledge and deepest compassion. Their primary duty was to eliminate the infection of witchcraft before the whole of society could be corrupted and damned. Miss Murray does not seem to suspect that witchcraft was, in truth, a foul and harmful heresy: the "poison" of the Manichees <note>original: "Manichees"; the Manicheans were followers of a dualistic religion that believed in a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness, often viewed as a dangerous heresy by the Church</note>. Her "Dianic cult"—the name she gives to this "ancient religion" supposed to have survived until the Middle Ages and even later as a formidable rival to Christianity—is nothing other than black heresy and the worship of Satan. It is not a primitive belief with pre-agricultural rituals that was later persecuted and misunderstood. It is true that in the Middle Ages Christianity had not a rival, but a foe: the eternal enemy of the Church Militant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the Christians on Earth who are struggling against sin and the devil</note> against whom she still contends today—the dark Lord of that city which is set opposite to the City of God <note>A reference to St. Augustine’s "City of God," contrasting the community of the faithful with the earthly or demonic world</note>, the terrible shadow of destruction and despair.

Miss Murray, with tireless industry, has collected a vast number of details to build up and support her imaginative theory. However, even those details that show the cult of evil adopting the most hideous heathen practices—both of lust and cruelty, which were common among primitive or declining peoples—provide no evidence whatsoever of a continuous, earlier religion. The majority of the facts she quotes are distorted—no doubt unconsciously—and sharply twisted so they might seem to support the meaning she attempts to read into them. Miss Murray <note>Margaret Murray (1863–1963) was an English anthropologist whose theory that witchcraft was a surviving pre-Christian pagan religion was popular for decades but is now largely rejected by historians.</note> speaks, for example, of witches "who, like the early Christian martyrs, rushed headlong to their fate, determined to die for their faith and their God."^66 Later, discussing the "Sacrifice of the God"—a theme which folklorists have elaborated in a highly imaginative way, though it is worth noting that they base these theories on the scantiest and most contradictory evidence—she tells us that the burning of witches by the public executioner was a "sacrifice of the incarnate deity."^67 One might suppose that the condemned went cheerfully and voluntarily to this most cruel and torturing punishment, as the phrase "self-devotion to death" is used in this connection.

On the contrary, we repeatedly find in the witch trials that the guilty, as was natural, sought to escape their doom by every possible means: by flight, as in the case of Gilles de Sillé and Roger de Bricqueville, companions of Gilles de Rais <note>Gilles de Rais was a 15th-century French knight and companion-in-arms of Joan of Arc who was later executed for the abduction, rape, and murder of scores of children; he was also accused of practicing alchemy and demonology.</note>; by long and drawn-out legal defenses, such as that of Agnes Fynnie, who was executed in Edinburgh in 1644; by threats and the blackmailing of influential patrons, through which "Old Bettie" Laing of Pittenweem <note>original: "Pittenween"</note> escaped punishment in 1718; by claiming pregnancy at the trial, as did Mother Samuel, the Warboys <note>original: "Warbois"; the "Witches of Warboys" case (1593) was one of the most famous trials in English history.</note> witch who was hanged on April 7, 1593; or by suicide, as in the case of the notorious warlock <note>warlock: a male witch</note> John Reid, who hanged himself in prison at Paisley in 1697.

It will be seen that Miss Murray’s <note>Margaret Murray (1863–1963) was a folklorist who famously, though controversially, argued that witchcraft was a surviving pre-Christian pagan religion.</note> citation is incorrect and therefore irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent"</note>. The heart of the whole matter lies elsewhere. Death at the stake was the punishment reserved for heretics. As we have already noticed, the Roman Emperor Diocletian ruthlessly burned the Manichees <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that the Roman state and later the Church viewed as a dangerous heresy.</note>: 
> “We order then that the professors and teachers be punished with the utmost penalties, which is to say they are to be burned with fire together with all their loathsome <note>original: "execrable"</note> books and writings.”⁷²

The Visigoth code condemned pagans or heretics who had committed sacrilege to the flames, and it grouped all Manichees together with them:
> “It is known that many Proconsuls have thrown blasphemers to the beasts, and have even burned some alive.”⁷³

The Visigoth code of Rekeswinth (reigned 652–672) punishes those practicing Jewish rites <note>original: "Judaizers"</note> with death: "Let them be stoned or burned with fire." <note>original: "aut lapide puniatur, aut igne cremetur"</note> But it was actually in the eleventh century that civil governments first generally established the penalty of the stake for heretics. These heretics, it must always be remembered, were seen as extremist anarchists attempting to destroy all social order, authority, and decency. 
> “In Italy many adherents of this plague-like <note>original: "pestilential"</note> belief were found, and these wretches were killed with the sword or burned at the stake,”⁷⁴

writes Adhémar de Chabannes, a monk of Angoulême, about the middle of the eleventh century. In a letter from Wazon, Bishop of Liège, there is a reference to similar punishments being carried out in Flanders.

A striking example of the heretical anarchists who troubled Europe about the beginning of the twelfth century may be seen in Tanchelin⁷⁵ <note>A heretical preacher in the Low Countries who claimed to be God and was eventually killed by a priest.</note> and his followers. This fanatic, who...

Tanchelin <note>Tanchelm of Antwerp (died c. 1115) was a charismatic heretic leader who traveled through the Low Countries, attacking the institutional Church.</note> was originally a native of Zealand and journeyed throughout Flanders, preaching his monstrous doctrines everywhere he could find listeners, especially concentrating on the city of Antwerp. In 1108 and 1109, he appeared at Arras and Cambrai, persuading many evil and ignorant persons to accept his abominable tenets. The seeds of heresy <note>original: "tares"—a biblical reference to weeds sown among wheat.</note> were thickly sown, and it is terribly significant that some three centuries later, about 1469, there was a fearful epidemic of sorcery throughout the whole district of Artois. Regarding this, the anonymous author—probably an Inquisitor—of a contemporary work entitled *The Errors of the Gazarians, or of those proven to ride on a broom or a stick* <note>original: "Erreurs des Gazariens ou de ceux que l’on prouve chevaucher sur un balai ou un bâton"</note> expressly identified such heretics as the Gazarians (who are Cathars <note>The Cathars were a dualist Christian sect that flourished in the 12th–14th centuries and were suppressed by the Church.</note>) and the Vaudois <note>The Waldensians, a movement of "Poor Men" often associated with early Protestant-style beliefs.</note> (Poor Lombards) with warlocks and sorcerers. In 1112 Tanchelin, who had actually visited Rome itself, was arrested upon his return and thrown into prison at Cologne. However, he managed to escape and was accompanied by an apostate priest named Everwacher and a Jew named Manasses, who had formerly been a blacksmith. At the head of a formidable band of three thousand ruffians, outlaws, failed gamblers, brigands, murderers, beggars, and thieves—the vomit <note>original: "parbreak"</note> of every slum and brothel district <note>original: "stew"</note>—he terrorized the whole countryside. The people were afraid, and the bishops and secular princes seemed unable to resist him.

The teaching of Tanchelin was, as might be expected, largely incoherent and illogical—the ravings of a frantic brain—but nonetheless dangerous and wholly abominable. The Church was, of course, directly attacked and blasphemed. With abuse and foul language, which was extraordinarily like the language used by the so-called Reformers in the sixteenth century, the hierarchy and all ecclesiastical order were repudiated and scorned. Priests and those in religious orders, in particular, were to be persecuted and exterminated since he claimed the priesthood was a fiction and a snare. He taught that the Sacrifice of the Holy Mass was a mockery, and all Sacraments were void and empty forms, useless for salvation.⁷⁶ He even claimed that the churches themselves should be considered brothels <note>original: "bawdy-houses"</note> and markets of shame. "This very spawn of Satan and black angel of woe declared that the churches, dedicated to God's worship, were brothels. He claimed that at Holy Mass there was no Sacrifice at the hands of the priest, and the Service of the Altar was filth, not a Sacrament."⁷⁷

Tanchelin declared himself to be the Messiah, God, the Son of God, the Perfect Man, and the sum of all divine emanations in one system. He claimed that the <term>pleroma</term> <note>From the Greek word for "fullness"; in Gnostic belief, it refers to the totality of divine powers.</note> of the Holy Spirit had descended upon him and lived within him. “This miserable wretch advanced from one evil to another, and at length reached such an extreme of unheard-of wickedness that he claimed to be God. He asserted that if Christ is God because the Holy Spirit dwelt in Him, then he himself was no less than and of the same nature as God, since he enjoyed the fullness of the Holy Spirit.” <note>original: A likely translation of a Latin chronicle, such as the *Vita Norberti*.</note> Here, the <term>Gnostic</term> <note>A variety of ancient religious movements that claimed salvation came through secret, mystical knowledge (gnosis) rather than faith or traditional authority.</note> character of his teaching is very apparent. He even had a temple built in his honor where he was worshipped with sacrifices and hymns. His followers, indeed, regarded this lunatic wretch with such excessive devotion that the dirty water from his bath was actually collected in vials and solemnly distributed among them; they drank this as if it were a sacrament.

It must be kept in mind that Tanchelin’s program did not only consist of a denial of Christian doctrine. We find such denials in most of the reformers at the time of the so-called Reformation. However, his ultimate aim was to bring about a social revolution, to overturn the existing order of things, and to create communistic chaos with himself as the supreme leader and dictator. The way for anarchy could only have been prepared by the destruction of the Church—the highest representative of authority and order in the world. Accordingly, it was against the Church that this "superman" launched his fiercest verbal attacks. To further his goals, he encouraged—even commanded—the open practice of the foulest vices. Incest, adultery, and sexual immorality were declared to be works of spiritual benefit. Unmentionable abominations were performed openly in broad daylight; virtue became a crime. Men were driven to vice and lawlessness, and soon they gradually sank into a state of infamy and total, spineless degradation.

The unfortunate town of Antwerp came directly under Tanchelin’s influence. Here he reigned as king, surrounded by vile and fawning followers who crushed the wretched citizens into the dust and filled every street and corner with orgies of lust and violence. There is a strange and striking parallel between the details of his foul career and the Russian tyranny today <note>The author, writing in the 1920s, is comparing medieval anarchy to the Bolshevik Revolution and the early Soviet Union.</note>. The other arguments brought forward by Miss Murray <note>Margaret Murray (1863–1963), an influential but controversial folklorist who argued that witchcraft was a surviving ancient pagan religion.</note> to support her theory <note>original: "thesis"</note> of the continuity of a primitive religion are mainly "the persistence of the number thirteen in the covens, the narrow geographical range of the domestic familiar, the avoidance of certain forms in the animal transformations, the limited number of personal names among the women-witches, and the survival of the names of some of the early gods."<sup>83</sup> Even if these details could be proven completely and shown to be relevant, the evidence would not be convincing. "The 'fixed number' among the witches of Great Britain," Miss Murray notes, "seems to have been thirteen,"<sup>84</sup> and certainly in many cases among the English trials, the coven appears to have consisted of thirteen members. However, it should be kept in mind that very probably there were often other associates who were not identified or caught, and thus escaped justice. Yet Miss Murray does not explain why the number thirteen should form any link with an earlier ritual and worship. On the other hand, the demonologists <note>Those who study demons and beliefs about them.</note> never tire of insisting that Satan mimics <note>original: "is the ape of"</note> God in all things, and that the worshippers of evil delight to parody every divine law and institution. The explanation is simple: the number thirteen was adopted by the witches for their covens in mockery of Our Lord and His Twelve Apostles.

"The narrow geographical range of the domestic familiar" <note>A demonic spirit or "imp" supposed to attend and obey a witch, often taking the form of a small animal like a cat or toad.</note> is not at all apparent, and it would be pointless to base any assumption upon such a weak line of argument. The avoidance of "certain forms in animal transformation" is, upon a general view of witchcraft, found to be nothing other than the absence of the lamb and the dove. These two were abhorred by sorcerers, seeing as Christ is the Lamb of God <note>original: "Agnus Dei"</note>, while the Dove is the manifestation of the Holy Ghost. ⁸⁵ There is one instance—the trial of Agnes Wobster at Aberdeen in 1597—when the Devil is said to have appeared to the witch "in the likeness of a lamb, whom you call your God, and bleated at you, and thereafter spoke to you." ⁸⁶ But this rare exception must be understood to be a black and deformed lamb, not the snow-white Lamb of God. In pictures of the Doctors of the Church, particularly perhaps St. Gregory the Great and St. Alphonsus de Liguori, the Dove is seen breathing divine inspiration into the ear of the Saint who writes the heavenly message, thus directly given by God the Holy Ghost. Similarly, in a Franco-German miniature of the eleventh century in the *Garden of Delights* <note>original: "Hortus Deliciarum," a medieval manuscript compiled by Herrad of Landsberg</note>, we see a black, hideous bird breathing evil and dark thoughts into the ear of a magician. This cloudy and sombre spirit, violent in its attitude and lean in body, stretches its meager throat towards the ear of the wicked man, who, seated at a desk, transcribes upon a parchment the malevolent and baleful charms which it dictates. It is, in fact, the Devil. ⁸⁷

With reference to the argument based upon "the limited number of personal names among the women-witches," this simply boils down to the fact that in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, there were in general use (particularly among the peasantry) far fewer personal names than have been employed in more recent years. To assert "that the name *Christian* clearly indicates the presence of another religion" ⁸⁸ is simple nonsense. It may be noticed, too, how many of the names which Miss Murray has catalogued in such conscientious and, alas, irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent"</note> detail are those of well-known Saints whose devotion <note>original: "cult"</note> was universal throughout Europe: Agnes, Alice, Anne, Barbara, Christopher, Collette, Elizabeth, Giles, Isabel, James, John, Katherine, Lawrence, Margaret, Mary, Michael, Patrick, Thomas, Ursula—and the list might be almost indefinitely prolonged.

"The survival of the names of some of the early gods" is also asserted. In connection with witchcraft, however, very few examples of this can be traced even by the most careful...

Thus, in a spell used by the witches of the Basses-Pyrénées <note>a region in southwest France</note> and cited by Pierre de Lancre (1609), we find a mention of the old Basque deity Janicot: "In the name of the father, Peter of Arague, Janicot of the Castle, kiss the horse's backside" <note>original: "In nomine patrica, Aragueaco Petrica, Gastellaco Ianicot, Equidæ ipordian pot"</note>. Jean Bodin <note>a 16th-century French jurist and writer on demonology</note> provides a dance-jingle: "Ha, ha, devil, devil, jump here, jump there, play here, play there" <note>original: "Har, har, diable, diable, saute icy, saute là, ioüe icy, ioüe là"</note>, to which the chorus was "sabbath, sabbath." Miss Murray tells us that the version from Guernsey, "which is currently reported to be used at the present day," runs: "Ha, ha, Hon, Hon, dance here" <note>original: "Har, har, Hon, Hon, danse ici"</note>. ⁸⁹ Hon was an old Breton god, and there are still remote districts whose local names recall and may be combined with the name of this ancient deity. It is significant that in one case we have a Basque deity and in the other a Breton one, for the Basque and Breton cultures are nearly—if obscurely—related. Such traces are interesting enough, indeed, since they can be so widely found. However, it would be pointless to build any detailed argument concerning the continuity of a fully organized cult based only upon slight and unrelated survivals in local dialects and the mere rhythmic nonsense of a peasant song.

There is, in particular, one statement put forward by Miss Murray which shows how completely she is unconsciously shaping her material to fit her theory. She writes:

"There is at present nothing to show how much of the Witches’ Mass (in which the bread, the wine, and the candles were black) derived from the Christian ritual and how much belonged to the Dianic cult [the name she gives to this hypothetical but universal ancient religion]; it is, however, possible that the witches’ service was the earlier form and influenced the Christian ritual." ⁹⁰

This last sentence is truly an amazing assertion. A more glaring case of reversing the natural order of things <note>original: *hysteron-proteron*, a Greek term for a logical fallacy where the "cart is put before the horse"</note> is hardly imaginable. The absurdity is so self-evident that it refutes itself. One can only suppose that these words remained in the text because they were overlooked during the revision of a long and difficult study—an excusable oversight. Every prayer and every gesture of the Holy Mass, since the first Mass was celebrated on the first Maundy Thursday, has been studied in the smallest detail by generations of liturgiologists <note>scholars of religious worship</note> and specialists in ritual. Their library of research is almost infinite in its size and scope, from the simplest...

...pamphlets to the largest volumes <note>original: "folios"</note>. We can trace each development: when a specific early phrase was added, or when a sacred sign was first made at certain words in a prayer <note>original: "orison"</note>. The witches' service is a hideous parody <note>original: "burlesque"</note> of Holy Mass; and, briefly, what Miss Murray <note>Margaret Murray (1863–1963), a prominent folklorist who argued that witchcraft was a surviving pagan religion</note> suggests is that the parody may have existed before the thing it parodied. It is true that some illogical <note>original: "topsy-turvy"</note> writers have actually proclaimed that magic preceded religion, but this view is generally discredited by the authorities of all schools. Sir James Frazer <note>author of the influential anthropological study "The Golden Bough"</note>, Sir A. L. Lyall, and Mr. F. B. Jevons, for example, recognize "a fundamental distinction and even opposition of principle between magic and religion."⁹¹

In short, upon an honest examination of this theory of the continuity of some primitive religion—which allegedly existed as an underlying organization manifested in witchcraft and sorcery, serving as a serious rival feared and hated by the Church—we find that nothing of the sort ever survived, and that there was no connection between sorcery and an imaginary "Dianic cult." To write that "in the fifteenth century open war was declared against the last remains of paganism <note>original: "heathenism"</note> in the famous Bull <note>a formal public decree issued by a Pope</note> of Innocent VIII"⁹² is to ignore history. As has been emphasized above, the Bull *Desiring with supreme ardor* <note>original: "Summis desiderantes affectibus"</note> of 1484 was only one of a long series of Papal decrees <note>original: "ordinances"</note> directed against an intolerable evil—not paganism indeed, but heresy. For heresy, sorcery, and anarchy were almost interchangeable words, and the first Bull launched directly against the dark arts was that of Alexander IV in 1258, two hundred and twenty-six years earlier.

It is common knowledge that various old, harmless customs and festivities lingered here and there, descending from pre-Christian times. The Church allowed these—indeed, it even sanctified them by directing them toward their right source—such as Maypole dances and the Midsummer bonfires which now honor St. John the Baptist. But this is not the continuation of a pagan cult.

From the first centuries of the Christian era, throughout the Middle Ages, and continuously to the present day, there has invariably been an open confession of intentional evil-doing by the followers of the witch-cult; the more mischief they did, the more they pleased their lord and master. Their revels were loathsome, lecherous, and abominable—a Sabbath...

...where every circumstance of horror and wickedness <note>original: "iniquity"</note> was expressed. This in itself is an argument against Miss Murray’s theory, as none of the earlier religions existed for the express purpose of committing evil for evil’s sake. We only have to read the eloquent and beautiful <note>original: "exquisite"</note> description of the Eleusinian Mysteries by that accomplished Greek scholar Father Cyril Martindale, S.J. <note>Cyril Martindale (1879–1963) was a prominent English Jesuit priest and author</note>,⁹³ to catch a true and clear glimpse of the indescribable <note>original: "ineffable"</note> longing for beauty, for purity, and for holiness which filled the hearts of the worshippers of the goddess Persephone <note>original: "Persephoneia"</note>. Her stately and impressive ritual—which required fasting, bathing in the sea, self-discipline, self-denial, and self-restraint—reached its peak in the Hall of Initiation. This place was made holy by the Earth-Mother, Demeter, where the symbolic drama of life, death, and resurrection was shown by the <term>Hierophant</term> <note>a high priest who interprets sacred mysteries</note> to those who had struggled, endured, and were judged worthy. What a beautiful foreshadowing this was—though it was always and only a shadow—of the undying and eternal realities to come! How different these Mysteries were from the disgusting orgies of witches, the Sabbat, the Black Mass, and the worship of hell.

In truth, it was not against paganism <note>original: "heathenism"</note> that Innocent VIII declared war, but against heresy. There was a secret <note>original: "clandestine"</note> organization hated by the Church, and this was not sorcery or some cult of witches reviving ancient rites and pagan creeds. Instead, it was a witch-cult that identified itself with and was constantly shown in the closest connection with Gnosticism <note>an early system of belief that the Church condemned as heresy</note> in its most degraded and vilest forms.

There is a curious little piece of symbolism that has passed into the local dialect <note>original: "patois"</note> of the Pyrenees. Wizards are commonly known as *poudouès* and witches as *poudouèros*; both words are derived from the Latin word meaning "to stink" <note>original: "putere"</note>. The writers on demons <note>original: "demonologists"</note> report, and it was commonly believed, that sorcerers could often be detected by their foul and stinking <note>original: "fetid"</note> odor. Biographers of saints <note>original: "Hagiographers"</note> tell that Saint Philip Neri could distinguish heretics by their smell, and he was often obliged to turn away his head when meeting them in the street. The same is recorded of many other Saints, and this tradition is interesting as it serves to show the close connection that people believed existed between magic and heresy.⁹⁴ Saint Pachomius, the <term>cenobite</term> <note>a monk who lives in a communal religious center</note>, could distinguish heretics by...

...their unbearable <note>original: "insupportable"</note> stench; the abbot Eugendus <note>Eugendus (c. 449–510) was the fourth abbot of Condat in France</note> could tell the virtues and vices of those whom he met by their perfume or their stink. On the other hand, the Saints themselves have given off the sweetest fragrances, and actually "the odor of sanctity" is more than just a mere phrase. One day in 1566, when he had entered the church at Somasca <note>original: "Somascha"</note>, a secluded hamlet between Milan and Bergamo, Saint Charles Borromeo exclaimed: "I know by the heavenly fragrance in this sanctuary that a great Servant of God lies buried here!" The church, in fact, contained the body of Saint Jerome Emiliani, who died in 1537. Saint Herman Joseph could be tracked through the corridors of Steinfeld by the rare perfumes he scattered as he walked. The same was the case with that marvelous mystic Saint Joseph of Cupertino. Saint Thomas Aquinas smelled of pure frankincense <note>original: "male frankincense," referring to the highest quality of incense collected in large, round "masculine" drops</note>. I myself have known a priest of fervent faith who at times gave off the odor of incense. Maria-Vittoria of Genoa, Ida of Louvain, Saint Colette, and Saint Humiliana were as fragrant as sweet flowers. Saint Francis of Paola and Venturino of Bergamo scattered heavenly aromas when they offered the Holy Sacrifice <note>the Mass</note>. Even the discharge <note>original: "pus"</note> from the sores of Saint John of the Cross gave off a strong scent of lilies.

Miss Murray <note>Margaret Murray (1863–1963), an Anglo-Indian archaeologist and folklorist</note> has worked out her thesis with considerable cleverness <note>original: "ingenuity"</note>, but when the details are considered, historically examined, and set in their proper proportions, it must be concluded that the theory of the continuity of an ancient religion is baseless. Her book is called *A Study in Anthropology*, and here we can, I think, immediately point out the fundamental mistake. Anthropology alone offers no explanation of witchcraft. Only a trained theologian can adequately treat this subject. An amount of interesting...

# CHAPTER II

## THE WORSHIP OF THE WITCH

To clearly understand and fully realize the shuddering horror and heart-sick dismay that any kind of interaction between human beings and evil spirits—the very core and kernel of witchcraft—aroused throughout all of Christendom, we must look deeper. We must appreciate why volume after volume was written on the subject by Europe’s most learned authors; why the holiest popes <note>original: "pontiffs"</note> and wisest judges, serious philosophers and careful scholars, kings and peasants, indifferent nobles and earnest clergymen <note>original: "divines"</note> were all of one mind in the prosecution of sorcery.

Whether in Catholic Spain or Puritan Scotland, in cold Geneva or pleasant <note>original: "genial"</note> Rome, people unhesitatingly and persistently sought to stamp out this "plague" with the most terrible of all penalties: the "cautery of fire" <note>This refers to execution by burning at the stake</note>. To ensure that we do not misread history and foolishly think that monks and magistrates, laypeople and lawyers were merely bloodthirsty tigers or mad fanatics—as they have too often been portrayed and slandered <note>original: "traduced"</note>—it is relevant to briefly summarize the orthodox doctrine regarding the Powers of Darkness. These facts are today often forgotten or ignored, but to the sharp medieval mind, they were always fearfully and prominently in view.

And here, as with many other beliefs, we will find a small amount of official dogma; certain points that can hardly be denied without being considered reckless <note>original: "temerity"</note>; and many details about which nothing definite can be known and upon which no official statement will be made.

In the first place, the name "Devil" is commonly given to the fallen angels, who are also called demons. The exact technical distinction between these two terms in church <note>original: "ecclesiastical"</note> usage can be seen in the phrase used in the decree of the Fourth Lateran Council (1215)¹: "For the Devil and the other demons" <note>original Latin: "Diabolus enim et alii dæmones"</note>. This implies that all are demons, and—

->THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT<-

The chief of the demons is called the Devil. This distinction is preserved in the Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> New Testament, where the Latin *diabolus* <note>original: *diabolus*</note> represents the Greek *diabolos* <note>original: διάβολος</note>, and in almost every instance refers to Satan himself. Meanwhile, his subordinate angels are described, following the Greek, as *demons* or *demonia* <note>original: *dæmones* or *dæmonia*</note>. But except in some highly specialized contexts where meticulous accuracy is required, we now use the words "devil" and "demon" interchangeably, and we use the definite article to denote Lucifer (Satan), the chief of the devils: *The* Devil. So, in Matthew 25:41, it is written "the devil and his angels." The Greek word *diabolos* <note>original: διάβολος</note> means a slanderer or an accuser, and it is in this sense that it is applied to him of whom it is said, "the accuser <note>original: ὁ κατήγορος - ho katēgoros</note> of our brethren is cast forth, who accused them before our God day and night" (Revelation 12:10 <note>original: Apocalypse xii. 10</note>). Thus, it corresponds to the Hebrew name Satan, which signifies an adversary or an accuser.

The Devil is mentioned in many passages in both the Old and New Testaments, but much is left in obscurity. The full Scriptural teaching on the legions of evil can best be determined by combining these scattered notices and reading them in the light of the writings of the Church Fathers <note>original: "patristic"</note> and theological tradition. The authoritative teaching of the Church is declared in the Decrees of the Fourth Lateran Council (Chapter 1, *We firmly believe* <note>original: *Firmiter credimus*</note>). In this decree, after explaining that God in the beginning had created two types of creatures—the spiritual and the physical; that is to say, the angelic and the earthly—and lastly man, who was made of both spirit and body, the Council continues: "For the Devil and the other demons were created by God naturally good; but they themselves, of their own doing, became evil." The dogma is clearly established here: the Devil and the other demons are spiritual or angelic creatures created by God in a state of innocence, and they became evil by their own free act. It is added that man sinned by the suggestion of the Devil, and that in the next world the rejected <note>original: "reprobate"</note> and unrepentant will suffer punishment with him.

This, then, is the actual dogma—the "dry bones" of the doctrine, so to speak. But later theologians have added a great deal to this—the authoritative "Exceptional Doctor" <note>original: *Doctor Eximius*</note>, Francisco Suarez, S.J., in his work *On the Angels* <note>original: *De Angelis*, VII</note>, is especially valuable—and much of what they conclude cannot be disputed without...

It is remarkable that for an account of the Fall of the angels—which happened before the creation of the world—we must turn to the last book in the Bible, the Revelation <note>original: Apocalypse</note> of St. John. For although the vision of Patmos blends images of the past with prophecies of what shall happen in the future, we must undoubtedly regard it in this way.

> “And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought back. To this may be added the words of St. Jude:

> “And the angels who did not keep their position of authority <note>original: principality</note>, but abandoned their own proper home, he has reserved in darkness in everlasting chains until the judgment of the great day.”

To these references should be added a striking passage from the prophet Isaiah:

> “How you are fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning! How you are fallen to the earth, you who wounded the nations! And you said in your heart: 'I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.' But yet you shall be brought down to hell, into the depths of the pit” (Isaiah 14:12-15).

The words of the prophet may, in one sense—perhaps primarily—be directed against Merodach-baladan, the King of Babylon. However, all the early Church Fathers and later commentators agree in understanding the passage as applying with deeper significance to the fall of the rebel angel. This interpretation is confirmed by the words of Our Lord to His disciples:

> “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven.” <note>original: "Uidebam Satanam sicut fulgur de coelo cadentem."</note> (St. Luke 10:18).

An obvious question which arises next, and which has been discussed at length by theologians, is: what was the nature of the sin of the rebel angels? This point presents some difficulty, for theology has logically formed the highest...

Sins of the flesh are certainly impossible for angels, and they would seem to be equally barred from many sins that are purely spiritual and intellectual. The great offense of Lucifer appears to have been the desire for independence from God and equality with God.

It is theologically certain that Lucifer held a very high rank in the celestial hierarchy, and it is evident that he maintains some kind of sovereignty over those who followed him in his rebellion: "But if Satan also is divided against himself, how shall his kingdom stand?" <note>original: “Si autem, et Satanas in seipsum diuisus est quomodo stabit regnum eius?”</note> says Our Lord. And St. Paul speaks of, "The Prince of the power of this air, who now works in the children of disobedience" <note>original: “Principem potestatis æris huius, qui nunc operatur in filios diffidentiæ.”</note> (Ephesians 2:2). It may seem strange that those rebellious spirits who rose against their Maker should be subordinate to and obey one of their fellows who led them to destruction, but this in itself is a proof that Lucifer is a superior intelligence. The knowledge of the angels would show them that they can cause more mischief and evil by cooperation and organization—even though their unifying principle is the bond of hate—than by anarchy and division. There can be little doubt that among their ranks are many mean and petty spirits⁵—relatively speaking—but even these can influence and betray foolish and arrogant men. We are on safe ground if we follow the opinion of Suárez <note>Francisco Suárez (1548–1617) was a highly influential Spanish Jesuit priest, philosopher, and theologian, often regarded as one of the greatest scholastics after Thomas Aquinas.</note>, who would allow Lucifer to have been the highest of all angels negatively—that is, that no one was higher—although many (and among these the three great Archangels, St. Michael, St. Gabriel, and St. Raphael) may have been his equals.

It has been argued that the highest of the angels, because of their greater intellectual illumination, must have entirely realized the utter impossibility of attaining equality with God. So St. Anselm <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher who served as Archbishop of Canterbury.</note>, in *The Fall of the Devil* <note>original: De Casu Diaboli</note> (IV), says: "For the devil was surely not so dull-witted that he did not know it was impossible to conceive of anything else similar to God?" <note>original: “Non enim ita obtusæ mentis [diabolus] erat, ut nihil aliud simile Deo cogitari posse nesciret?”</note> And St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a Dominican friar and immensely influential philosopher and theologian in the Catholic tradition.</note>...

He writes, in answer to the question of whether the Devil desired to be "as God," that "if by this we mean equality with God, then the Devil would not desire it, since he knew this to be impossible." But as the Venerable Duns Scotus—known as the "Subtle Doctor" <term>Doctor subtilis: a title given to Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308) in recognition of his extremely complex and nuanced theological arguments</term>—admirably points out, we must distinguish between an "efficacious volition" (a will that intends to achieve a result) and a "volition of complaisance" (a mere wish or desire for something). In the same way, he shows that although a creature cannot directly will its own destruction, it may do this as a consequence <note>original: "consequenter"</note>; that is, it can desire something from which its destruction would inevitably follow.

And although humans must realize they cannot be God, there have been men who have caused themselves to be hailed and even worshipped as God. One such man was Herod Agrippa I. On a festival day at Caesarea, he wore a garment made entirely of silver and entered the crowded theater early in the morning. His robe shone in the sun's rays with a dazzling light, and the superstitious crowd, prompted by his flatterers, cried out that he was a god. Cavalier escaped to England²⁸, from where he returned in 1709 and attempted to spark a revolt in Vivarais. On March 8, 1715, through a proclamation and commemorative medals, Louis XIV announced that these demon-possessed rebels were entirely extinct.

A number of these prophets fled to England, where they caused great disturbances. Voltaire, in *The Age of Louis XIV* <note>original: Siècle de Louis XIV</note>, chapter 36, tells us that one of the leading refugees and notorious rebels, Elie Marion, became so offensive because of his "prophetic warnings" <note>original: avertissements prophétiques</note> and fake miracles that he was deported from the country as a public nuisance.²⁹

As rare as such a connection may be, it is, at least, possible. It is this connection, along with its consequences, conditions, and attendant circumstances, that is known as witchcraft. The learned Sprenger <note>Jakob Sprenger (c. 1436–1495), a Dominican friar and co-author of the *Malleus Maleficarum*.</note> in the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: *Malleus Maleficarum* (1486), the most famous treatise on witchcraft.</note> expressly declares that, in his opinion, a denial of the possibility of witchcraft is heresy. That eminent lawyer Blackstone, in his *Commentaries* (1765), IV, 4, asserts: "To deny the possibility—nay, the actual existence—of witchcraft and sorcery, is at once flatly to contradict the revealed Word of God in various passages both of the Old and New Testament; and the thing itself is a truth to which every nation in the world has in its turn borne testimony, either by examples seemingly well-attested, or by prohibitory laws, which at least suppose the possibility of commerce with evil spirits." Even the ultra-cautious—I had almost said skeptical—Father Thurston <note>Herbert Thurston (1856–1939), a Jesuit priest and scholar known for his critical investigations of the paranormal.</note> acknowledges: "In the face of Holy Scripture and the teaching of the Church Fathers and theologians, the abstract possibility of a pact with the Devil and of a diabolical interference in human affairs can hardly be denied." 

Imposture, trickery, self-deception, hypnotism, and a morbid imagination have, no doubt, all played an important part in legends of this kind. It is not enough to sincerely claim to have magical powers to actually possess them in reality. Plainly, a man who not only firmly believes in a power of evil, but also believes that this power can and does meddle with and ruin human affections and human destinies, may invoke and dedicate himself to this power. He may surrender his will to it and ask this power to accomplish his wishes and ends, and so succeed in persuading himself that he has entered into a mysterious contract with evil, whose slave and servant he has become.³¹ Moreover, as we should expect, the records are full of instances of common charlatanry, of cunning villainies and crimes masquerading under the cloak of superstition, of clever fraud, and of what was clearly play-acting and performance to impress the ignorant and common people. They also show instances of diseased vanity, hungry for notoriety, that craved the name and reputation of a witch, and of quackery and deception that proved lucrative and comfortable enough.

<header>THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT</header>

<page-num>64</page-num>

But even when we have made every possible allowance, and as we examine the long and bloody history of witchcraft in detail, we must recognize the fearful fanaticism and the horrific excesses of the "witch mania." Today, with our broader understanding of both psychology and medicine, we can explain many details and accidents that would have inevitably led a person to the stake without mercy or relief in the past. We can clarify case after case: one might involve a person suffering from hysteria, catalepsy, or epilepsy, or someone with an obscure nervous disorder that remains difficult to diagnose even today. Another might be a person denounced by the malice of personal enemies, perhaps for political reasons. A third might be some senile elderly woman <note>original: "doting beldame"</note> who was a victim of idle superstition or mere spite. A fourth might be accused for the sake of profit by a disappointed blackmailer or a thief. Others were simply eccentric or mentally unstable. An even greater number of victims were incriminated by poor wretches raving in the agonies of the rack and the "boots" <note>The "boots" was a torture device used to crush the legs and feet.</note>. Nevertheless, even after we have frankly discounted every possible circumstance and fully realized the world-wide frenzy of persecution that swept through those centuries of terror, we cannot help but recognize that there remain many important cases which cannot be explained by any ordinary means and which fall into no normal category.

As one highly impartial writer has well said: “The underlying and provocative phenomena had really been present in a huge number of cases.”³² There is no other way to account for these except by acknowledging the reality of witchcraft and contracts with the Devil. It must be steadily remembered that the most brilliant minds, the keenest intelligences, the most learned scholars, and the noblest men—individuals who had heard the evidence first-hand—all firmly believed in witchcraft. Among them are such supreme authorities as St. Augustine, “a philosophical and theological genius of the first order, who towers like a pyramid over antiquity and the succeeding ages”³³; Blessed Albertus Magnus, known as the “Universal Doctor” <note>original: *Doctor Universalis*</note> for his encyclopedic knowledge; St. Thomas Aquinas, the “Angelic Doctor” <note>original: *Doctor Angelicus*</note>, one of the profoundest intellects the world has ever seen; the "Seraphic" St. Bonaventura <note>original: *Doctor Seraphicus*</note>, the most loving of mystics; and several Popes, including Alexander IV—the friend of the Franciscans, who was prudent, kindly, deeply religious, and “constant in prayer and strict in self-denial”³⁴—and John XXII,

Initiation into these mysteries usually occurred through a secret society. At an assembly <note>OCR correction: "asseblym" to "assembly"</note> of this society, the new initiate <note>original: "neophyte"</note> bound himself to the service of evil with terrifying <note>original: "terrific"</note> oaths and blasphemy. However, there are cases that can only be explained by the physical manifestation of a dark intelligence who actually received a written bond from the worshiper. These instances are, of course, extremely rare, but occasionally judges were able to examine such parchments and deeds.

In 1453, Guillaume Edelin, the Prior of Saint-Germain-en-Laye, signed a compact with the Devil; this document was later found on his person. Pierre de Lancre <note>A famous French judge and demonologist (1553–1631).</note> relates that the witch Stevenote de Audebert, who was burned in January 1619, showed him "the pact and agreement which she had made with the Devil, written in menstrual blood, and so horrible that one was terrified even to look at it."<sup>39</sup> <note>original French: "le pacte & conuention qu'elle auoit faict auec le Diable, escrite en sang de menstrues, & si horrible qu'on auoit horreur de la regarder."</note> In the library at Upsala, the contract is preserved by which Daniel Salthenius—who in later life became a Professor of Hebrew at Königsberg—sold himself to Satan.

In the archives of the Holy Office <note>The Roman Inquisition.</note> is preserved a picture of the Crucifixion, regarding which the following account is given: A young man of notoriously wicked life and extreme impiety had squandered his fortune. Being in desperate need, he resolved to sell his body and soul to Lucifer on the condition that he should be supplied with enough money to indulge in all the luxuries and lusts he desired. 

It is said the demon assumed a visible form and required him to write down a formal deed of "self-donation" to hell. The youth consented to do this on one condition <note>original: "proviso"</note>. He asked the demon if he had been present at Calvary <note>The hill where Jesus was crucified.</note>. When the demon answered that he had, the young man insisted that Lucifer should draw him an exact representation of the Crucifixion; only then would he hand over the completed document. After much hesitation, the fiend consented and shortly produced a picture. 

But at the sight of the tortured and bleeding Body stretched on the Cross, the youth was seized with such remorse <note>original: "contrition"</note> that, falling upon his knees, he invoked the help of God. His companion disappeared, leaving behind both the fatal contract and the picture. In order to gain absolution for such a terrible <note>original: "heinous"</note> guilt, the penitent was obliged to appeal to the Cardinal Penitentiary <note>A high-ranking official in the Roman Catholic Church who deals with matters of conscience and the forgiveness of sins.</note>, and the picture was taken into the charge of the Holy Office. Prince Barberini later obtained permission to have an exact copy made of it, which he eventually presented to the Capuchin monks at the church of Santa Maria della Concezione <note>A famous church in Rome known for its crypt decorated with human bones.</note>.

A contract with Satan was said always to be signed in the blood of the signer. "The signature is almost invariably written with the writer’s own blood. . . . Thus at Augsburg, Joseph Egmund Schultz declared that on May 15, 1671, toward midnight—when it was between eleven and twelve o'clock—he threw down an illuminated parchment where three crossroads met. It was written throughout in his own blood and wrapped up in a fine handkerchief <note>original: "fair kerchief"</note>, and thus he sealed the compact . . . Widmann also tells us how that unhappy wretch Faust slightly cut his thumb and, with the drops of blood which trickled from it, devoted himself in writing, body and soul, to the Devil, utterly repudiating God’s claim on him."⁴⁰ From the earliest times and in many nations, we find human blood used as an unbreakable <note>original: "inviolably"</note> way to ratify a pledged word.⁴¹ Rochholz (Volume I, page 52) relates that it is a custom of German University freshmen (<term>Burschen</term> <note>German: members of a student association or fraternity</note>) for the parties to write "mutually with their own blood on leaves in each other’s albums." The parchment is still said to be in existence on which Maximilian, the great and devout Bavarian elector, religiously dedicated himself to the Most Holy Mother of God with his own blood. Blood was the most sacred and irrevocable of seals, as may be seen in the custom of blood-brotherhood when friendship was sworn and alliances concluded. Either the blood itself was drunk, or wine was mixed with blood. Herodotus (Book IV, 70) tells us that the Scythians were accustomed to conclude agreements by pouring wine into an earthen vessel, into which the contracting parties, having cut their arms with a knife, let their blood flow and mingle. Afterward, both they and the most distinguished of their followers drank from it. Pomponius Mela, in *Concerning the Geography of the World* <note>original Latin: *De Situ Orbis*</note> (Book II, 1), records the same custom as still existing among them in his day: “Not even their alliances are made without shedding blood: the partners in the compact wound themselves, and when the blood gushes out, they mingle the stream and taste it when it is mixed. This they consider to be the most assured pledge of eternal loyalty and trust.”⁴² Gyraldus, in *The Topography of Ireland* <note>original Latin: *Topographia Hibernorum*</note> (XXII, p. 743), says: “When the Irish <note>original: "Ireni"</note> conclude treaties, each drinks the blood of the other, which is shed voluntarily for this purpose.” In July 1891, a band of brigands <note>meaning: outlaws or bandits</note> which had existed for three years was discovered and broken up in South Italy. In several grimoires <term>grimoire</term> <note>a textbook of magic, typically including instructions on how to create magical objects and cast spells</note> and books of magic, such as *The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts*, *The Key of Solomon the King*, and *The Holy Kingdom* <note>original: "Sanctum Regnum"</note>, one may find goetic rituals <term>goetic</term> <note>relating to goetia, a type of magic involving the invocation of demons</note> as well as summons. Toward the end of the eighteenth century, a man named Juan Perez was reduced to extreme poverty and vowed his body and soul to Satan if he could have revenge on those he suspected of harming him. He consulted several magicians and witches and tried more than one magical ceremony <note>original: "theurgic ceremonial"</note>, but it was all in vain. Hell was deaf to his appeal. Because of this, he openly declared his disbelief in the supernatural and the existence of devils; he mocked Holy Scripture as a fairy tale or a nursery story. Naturally, this behavior brought him before the Tribunal of the Holy Office <note>The Inquisition</note>. During his first questioning, he confessed the whole story and declared himself ready to submit to any punishment <note>original: "penance"</note> they chose to impose.

His feast day is observed on May 14.

Satan promises to give his devotees <note>original: "votaries"</note> all they desire: knowledge, wealth, honors, pleasure, and vengeance upon their enemies; yet all he can give is disappointment, poverty, misery, hate, and the power to hurt and destroy. He is ever holding elusive hopes before their eyes, and they are so infatuated <note>original: "besotted"</note> that they trust him and confide in him until all is lost. Sometimes, in the case of those who are young, the pact is for a short while, but he always renews it. So at Lille in 1661, the pupils of Antoinette Bourignon <note>a Flemish mystic and influential religious figure whose orphanage became the center of a witchcraft scandal</note> confessed: "The Devil gives them a mark, which they renew as often as those persons have any desire to quit him. The Devil reproves them more severely and obliges them to make new promises, also giving them new marks as an assurance or pledge that those persons should continue faithful to him."⁵³

The Devil’s Mark referenced here—or the Witch’s Mark, as it is sometimes called—was regarded as perhaps the most important point in identifying a witch. It was seen as the very sign and seal of Satan upon the actual flesh of his servant, and any person who bore such a mark was considered convicted and proven, beyond any shadow of a doubt, to be in league with and devoted to the service of the fiend. This mark was said to be entirely unable to feel pain <note>original: "insensible to pain"</note>, and when pricked, however deeply, it did not bleed. In his tract *The Trial of Witchcraft; or Witchcraft Arraigned and Condemned*, published early in the eighteenth century, the author explains: "The witch mark is sometimes like a blue spot, or a small teat <note>original: "tate"</note>, or red spots like flea bites. This mark is placed in secret places, such as among the hair of the head, the eyebrows, inside the lips, under the armpits, and in the most private parts of the body." Robert Kirk <note>The OCR reads "Hink," but this refers to Robert Kirk (1644–1692), author of The Secret Commonwealth.</note>, a minister at Aberfoyle, writes in his *Secret Commonwealth* (1691): "I have seen a spot like a small mole, horny and brown-colored. When a large pin was thrust through this mark—both in the buttock, nose, and roof of the mouth—until the pin bent and became crooked, the witches (both men and women) neither felt pain nor bled. Nor did they know the exact time this was being done to them, as their eyes were covered." This mark was sometimes the complete shape of a toad or a bat; or, as Delrio <note>Martin Delrio (1551–1608) was a Jesuit theologian and influential demonologist.</note> says, the track of a hare <note>original: "slot of a hare"</note>, the foot of a frog, a spider, a deformed puppy <note>original: "whelp"</note>, or a mouse.⁵⁴ The same great authority informs us on what part of the body it was usually imprinted: "In men it may often be seen under the eyelids, under the lips, under the armpits, on the shoulders, or on the anus <note>original: "fundament"</note>; in women, moreover, it is found on the breast or on the genitals <note>original: "pudenda"</note>."⁵⁵

In his profound treatise *On Demonality* <note>original: "De Dæmonialitate"</note>, that most learned Franciscan Ludovico Maria Sinistrari writes: "[Witches or Wizards] are marked by some Demon with a certain sign <note>original: "charactere"</note>, especially those whose loyalty <note>original: "constantia"</note> he doubts. It is imprinted on the most hidden parts of the body: in men, sometimes under the eyelids, or the armpits, or the lips, on the shoulder, the anus <note>original: "sede ima"</note>, or elsewhere. In women, however, it is usually on the breasts or the female parts. ...body we observed three little marks, which were not very different in color from his natural skin. The first is on his right thigh, about the middle toward the lower part. When we pierced this with a needle to the depth of two fingers' breadth, he felt no pain, nor did any blood or other bodily fluid <note>original: "humour"</note> seep from the incision.

"The second mark is in the region of the lower back <note>original: "loins"</note>, toward the right, about an inch from the spine and some four fingers' breadth above the thigh muscles <note>original: "femoral muscles"</note>. Here, we drove the needle in to a depth of three fingers' breadth, leaving it fixed in this spot for some time, as we had already done in the first instance. Yet all the while, the said Gaufridy <note>Louis Gaufridy (c. 1572–1611) was a French priest executed for sorcery after a famous case of demonic possession in Aix-en-Provence.</note> felt no pain, nor was there any flow <note>original: "effluxion"</note> of blood or any other kind of bodily fluid.

"The third mark is around the region of the heart. At first, the needle was introduced without any sensation being felt, just as in the previous instances. But when the place was probed with some force, he said he felt pain; even so, no moisture dripped <note>original: "distilled"</note> from this wound <note>original: "laceration"</note>. Early the next morning we visited him again and found that the parts which had been probed were neither swollen nor red. In our judgment, such hardened <note>original: "callous"</note> marks, which release no moisture when pierced, cannot be caused by any old skin condition <note>original: "ancient affection of the skin"</note>. In accordance with this opinion, we submit our report on this tenth day of March, 1611.

->*Fontaine, Grassy, Doctors;*<-
->*Mérindol, Bontemps, Surgeons.*" <note>The names represent the medical panel that examined Gaufridy.</note>

On April 26, 1634, during the famous Loudun trials <note>The Loudun possessions involved a convent of Ursuline nuns who accused the priest Urbain Grandier of witchcraft.</note>, the accused Urbain Grandier was examined in order to discover the witch-mark. He was stripped naked, blindfolded, and searched in the presence of officials. René Mannoury, one of the leading physicians of the town, conducted the search. Two marks were discovered—one on the shoulder blade and the other on the thigh—both of which proved to be numb <note>original: "insensible"</note> even when pierced with a sharp silver pin.

Because the discovery of the "devil-mark" was regarded as one of the most convincing indications—if not, indeed, absolute proof—that the accused was guilty, since he bore Satan’s own signature <note>original: "sign-manual"</note> permanently branded upon his flesh, it is easy to see how searching for, identifying, and probing such marks actually grew into a profession.

<summary>This page details the medical examinations used to identify "witch-marks" on Louis Gaufridy and Urbain Grandier, highlighting the use of needles to test for pain and bleeding. These examinations were considered legal proof of a pact with the Devil, leading to the rise of professional witch-finders.</summary>

...in which quite a few clever individuals became recognized as experts and practical authorities. In Scotland, especially, the "prickers," as they were called, formed a regular guild <note>original: "gild"</note>. They received a good fee for every witch they discovered, and, as might be expected, they did not fail to reap a golden harvest. At the trial of Janet Peaston in 1646, the magistrates of Dalkeith "ordered John Kincaid of Tranent, the common pricker, to exercise his craft upon her. He found two marks of the Devil's making; for she could not feel the pin when it was put into either of the said marks, nor did the marks bleed when the pin was taken out again. When she was asked where she thought the pins were inserted into her, she pointed to a part of her body far from the actual place. They were pins three inches in length."⁶⁰ Another notorious pricker was John Bain, upon whose unsupported evidence a large number of unfortunate wretches were sentenced to death. About 1634, John Balfour of Corhouse was feared throughout the countryside for his exploits; while twenty years later, one John Dick proved a rival to Kincaid himself. The regular trade of these "common prickers" became a serious nuisance and admittedly opened the door to all sorts of roguery. The following extraordinary incident shows how dangerous and villainous these examinations could become in the hands of swindlers <note>original: "mountebank"</note>—examinations which, if conducted at all, should at least have been safeguarded by every precaution and only entrusted to skilled physicians, who would report the results to serious and learned divines.

> "There came then to Inverness one Mr. Paterson, who had traveled across the kingdom for the trial of witches and was usually called the 'Pricker,' because his method of trial was with a long brass pin. After stripping them naked, he claimed <note>original: "alleged"</note> that the 'spell spot' <note>A supposed insensitive mark on a witch's body where the Devil was said to have touched them.</note> was seen and discovered. After rubbing their entire bodies with his palms, he would slip in the pin; it seems that because they were overwhelmed <note>original: "dashed"</note> with shame and fear, they did not feel it. He left the pin in the flesh, deep to its head, and asked them to find and remove it. It is certain that some witches were discovered, but many honest men and women were slandered <note>original: "blotted"</note> and ruined <note>original: "break"</note> by this trick. In Elgin, two were killed; in Forres, two; and one Margaret Duff, a notorious <note>original: "rank"</note> witch, was burned in Inverness. This Paterson came to the Church of Wardlaw and, within the church, pricked fourteen women and one man who were brought there by the Chisholm of <note>The "Chisholm" refers to the chief of Clan Chisholm.</note>..."

<summary>This page describes the rise of "prickers" in 17th-century Scotland—professional witch-finders paid to identify "Devil's marks" by piercing the skin with long pins. It highlights the fraudulent methods used by men like John Kincaid and Mr. Paterson, which led to the execution of many innocent people.</summary>

...from Commer, and four others brought by Andrew Fraser, the chamberlain <note>original: "chamerlan"</note> of Ferrintosh. He first shaved <note>original: "polled"</note> all their heads and gathered the heap of hair together, hiding it in a stone ditch, and then proceeded to pricking.⁶¹ Several of these women died in prison without ever being brought to a confession. This villain gained a great deal of money, having two servants; at last, he was discovered to be a woman disguised in men's clothes. Such cruelty and rigor were endured at the hands of a vile, low-life <note>original: "varlet"</note> impostor.”⁶² 

No doubt in many—indeed, in the majority of instances—these witch-marks were natural malformations of the skin, thickened tissue, birthmarks (I myself have known a person who, by a prenatal accident, was stamped upon the upper part of the arm with the complete figure of a rat), moles, calloused warts, or spots of some kind. But this explanation will not cover all cases, and even the skeptical Miss Murray <note>Margaret Murray (1863–1963), an anthropologist known for her "witch-cult" theory</note>, who writes:

> “Local anesthesia <note>numbness or loss of sensation</note> is supported by much of the evidence, which suggests that there is a foundation of truth in these statements,” is bound candidly to confess, “but I can at present offer no solution to this problem.”⁶³

Moreover, as previously noticed, this mark was frequently branded upon the novice at their admission, often by the "Witch-Master" who presided over the assembly <note>original: "rout"</note>, though sometimes—it must be admitted—by non-human agency.

The “little teat or pap,” so often found on the body of the wizard or witch and said to secrete milk which nourished the "familiar" <note>a supernatural entity or spirit-animal supposed to assist a witch</note>, must be carefully distinguished from the insensitive devil-mark. This phenomenon, for no explainable reason, seems to occur only in the records of England and New England, where, however, it is an exceedingly frequent occurrence. It is worth remarking that in the last act of Thomas Shadwell’s play, *The Lancashire Witches* (1681), the witches are searched by a woman who reports, “they have all great biggs <term>an archaic or dialect word for teats or nipples</term> and teats in many parts, except Mother Madge, and hers are but small ones.” Shadwell, who in his voluminous notes includes citations from nearly fifty authors, writes on this point:

> “The possession of biggs and teats is affirmed by all modern witch-hunters <note>original: "Witch-mongers"</note> in England.”⁶⁴

In 1597, at the trial of an old woman <note>original: "beldame"</note>, Elizabeth Wright of Stapenhill, near Burton-on-Trent:

> “They stripped the old woman and found behind her right shoulder a thing much like the udder of a female sheep <note>original: "ewe"</note> that gives suck, with two teats, like two great warts.”

<summary>This page discusses the physical "marks" associated with witchcraft, specifically the fraudulent "pricker" Mr. Paterson (who was actually a woman in disguise) and the distinction between insensitive devil-marks and the "teats" used to feed familiars.</summary>

...one behind under her armpit <note>original: "armehole"</note>, the other a hand's breadth away toward the top of her shoulder. Being asked how long she had those teats, she answered she was born that way.”⁶⁵ In the case of the Witch of Edmonton, Elizabeth Sawyer—who was searched upon the express order of the judges <note>original: "the Bench"</note> despite her resistance—it was found by Margaret Weaver, a widow of honest reputation, and two other serious <note>original: "grave"</note> matrons who performed this duty, that there was upon her body “a thing like a teat the size <note>original: "bignesse"</note> of the little finger and half a finger long, which was branched at the top like a teat, and looked as if someone had sucked it.”⁶⁶ John Palmer of St. Albans (1649) confessed that “upon his pact with the Devil, he received a mark branded into his flesh <note>original: "flesh brand"</note> on his side, which gave milk to two familiars <note>supernatural entities believed to assist witches, often appearing as small animals</note>.”⁶⁷ The Kentish witch, Mary Read of Lenham (1652), “had a visible teat under her tongue and showed it to many.”⁶⁸ At St. Albans around 1660, there was a wizard who “had something like a breast on his side.”⁶⁹ In the same year at Kidderminster, a widow, her two daughters, and a man were accused; “the man had five teats, the mother three, and the eldest daughter one.”⁷⁰ In 1692, Bridget Bishop, one of the Salem witches, was brought to trial: “A jury of women found a supernatural <note>original: "preternatural"</note> teat on her body; but upon a second search, within three or four hours, no such thing could be seen.”⁷¹ There is similar evidence presented in the accounts of Rose Cullender and Amy Duny, two Suffolk witches executed in 1664; Elizabeth Horner, a Devon witch (1696); Widow Coman, an Essex witch who died in her bed (1699); and, indeed, innumerable other examples might be quoted, providing a whole chain <note>original: "catena"</note> of relevant illustrations. 

No doubt many of these are explained by cases of polymastia (extra breasts <note>original: *mammæ erraticæ*</note>) and polythelia (extra nipples), of which there are continuous records in recent medical works. It must be freely admitted that these anatomical variations <note>original: "divagations"</note> are more common than is generally supposed; frequently they are so slight that they may pass almost unnoticed; doubtless there is exaggeration in many of the inaccurately observed seventeenth-century narratives. However, it must be said, as before, that when every most generous allowance is made, the facts that remain—and the details are very extensive—cannot be explained away as mere physical peculiarities or malformations.

The author acknowledges that while many cases could be explained by medical conditions like extra nipples, he argues that the sheer volume and detail of the evidence suggest something beyond mere physical malformation.</summary>

^59 We, the undersigned doctors and surgeons, following the command given to us by Master Anthoine de Thoron, Lord of Thoron and Counselor to the King in his court of parliament, have examined Master Louis Gaufridy <note>A French priest executed for witchcraft in 1611</note>. On his body, we noticed three small marks, little different in color from the rest of his skin. Into the first, on his left thigh toward the middle and lower part, we thrust a needle about two fingers' breadth; he felt no pain, and no blood or other moisture came from the spot.

The second is in the region of the lower back on the right side, an inch near the spine and four fingers above the buttock muscles. We thrust the needle three fingers' breadth into this, leaving it there for some time as we had done with the first, yet the said Gaufridy felt no pain, and no blood or fluid of any kind came out.

The third is near the region of the heart. When we first inserted the needle, it appeared like the others, without feeling; but as we thrust it in deeper, he said he felt some pain. However, no moisture came out. Having examined him again the next morning, we recognized neither swelling nor redness in the pricked parts. Because of this, we say such marks—being insensible and yielding no fluid when pricked—cannot be caused by any preceding skin disease. We make our report this 10th of March, 1611. *Fontaine, Grassy, doctors; Mérindol, Bontemps, surgeons.*

So great was the importance attached to the discovery of a witch-mark upon the body of the accused that when the above medico-legal report was read in court, Father Sebastian Michaëlis, a learned Dominican who was acting as a consultant in the case, was horror-struck and involuntarily exclaimed: "In truth, were we at Avignon this man would be executed tomorrow!" Gaufridi confessed: "I admit that the said marks are made as a protestation that one will always be a good and faithful servant of the devil all the..."
