# CHAPTER III

## DEMONS AND FAMILIARS

ONE of the most authoritative of the older writers upon witchcraft, Francesco-Maria Guazzo—a member of the Congregation of Saint Ambrose of the Grove <note>original: "S. Ambrose ad Nemus" — a religious order based in Milan</note>¹—in his encyclopedic *Compendium of Witches* <note>original: "Compendium Maleficarum," first published at Milan, 1608</note>, has drawn up under eleven heads those articles in which a solemn and complete profession of witchcraft was then held to consist:

*First:* The candidates have to conclude with the Devil, or some other wizard or magician acting in the Devil’s place, an express contract <note>original: "compact"</note> by which, in the presence of witnesses, they devote themselves to the service of evil, while he gives them in exchange his pledge for riches, luxury, and such things as they desire.

*Secondly:* They reject <note>original: "abjure"</note> the Catholic Faith, explicitly withdraw from their obedience to God, renounce Christ and in a particular manner the patronage and protection of the Virgin Mary <note>original: "Our Lady"</note>, curse all saints, and renounce <note>original: "forswear"</note> the Sacraments. In Guernsey, in 1617, Isabel Becquet went to Rocquaine Castle, "the usual place where the Devil kept his Sabbat <note>original: "Sabbath" — the secret midnight meeting of witches</note>: no sooner had she arrived there than the Devil came to her in the form of a dog, with two great horns sticking up; and with one of his paws (which seemed to her like hands) took her by the hand; and calling her by her name told her that she was welcome. Then immediately the Devil made her kneel down while he himself stood up on his hind legs; he then made her express hatred for the Eternal God <note>original: "detestation of the Eternal"</note> in these words: *I renounce God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost;* and then caused her to worship and pray to him."² Pierre de Lancre <note>A famous French judge and witch-hunter active in the early 17th century</note> tells us that Jeannette d’Abadie, a girl of sixteen, confessed that she was made to "renounce and deny her Creator, the Holy Virgin, the saints, baptism, father, mother, relations, heaven, earth, and all that the world contains."³

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

In a very full confession made by Louis Gaufridi <note>A French priest executed for witchcraft in 1611 following the "Aix-en-Provence possessions."</note> on the second of April, 1611, to two Capuchin friars, Father Ange and Father Antoine, he revealed the wording of his renunciation <note>original: "abjuration"</note> of the Catholic faith. It ran as follows:

> “I, Louis Gaufridi, renounce all good, both spiritual as well as worldly <note>original: "temporal"</note>, which may be given to me by God, the Blessed Virgin Mary, all the Saints of Heaven, especially my patron Saint John the Baptist, as also Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Francis; and I give myself body and soul to Lucifer, before whom I stand, together with every good thing that I may ever possess (excepting always the validity of the sacraments for those who receive them) <note>Gaufridi, as a priest, specifies that the sacraments he administers remain valid for the faithful despite his own apostasy.</note>. And according to the terms of these words, I have signed and sealed this.” $^4$

Madeleine de la Palud, one of his victims, used a longer and more detailed declaration in which the following terrible blasphemies occurred:

> “With all my heart and most sincerely <note>original: "unfeignedly"</note> and with all my will most deliberately, I wholly renounce God—Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; the most Holy Mother of God; all the Angels and especially my Guardian Angel; the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ, His Precious Blood and the merits gained by it; my place <note>original: "lot"</note> in Heaven <note>original: "Paradise"</note>; all the good inspirations which God may give me in the future; and all prayers which are made or may be made for me.” $^5$

*Thirdly:* They throw away with scorn the most Holy Rosary, delivered by Our Lady to Saint Dominic; $^6$ the Cord of Saint Francis; the belt <note>original: "cincture"</note> of Saint Augustine; and the Carmelite scapular <note>A garment worn over the shoulders as a sign of devotion.</note> bestowed upon Saint Simon Stock. They throw upon the ground and trample under their feet in the mud the Cross, Holy Medals, and the *Lamb of God* <note>original: "Agnus Dei" — a small wax disc blessed by the Pope, bearing the image of a lamb and used as a sacred object</note>, $^7$ should they possess such things or carry them on their persons. Saint Francis tied a rough rope around his waist in memory of the ropes with which Christ was bound during His Passion, and a white belt with three knots has since formed part of the Franciscan habit. Sixtus IV, by his papal decree <note>original: "Bull"</note> *Of the supreme disposition* <note>original: "Exsupernæ dispositionis"</note>, established the Archconfraternity <note>A large religious society or brotherhood.</note> of the Cord of Saint Francis in the basilica of the Sacred Convent at Assisi, enriching it with many indulgences <note>Remissions of temporal punishment for sins.</note>—favors which have been confirmed by pope after pope. These Archconfraternities are established not only in Franciscan churches but in many others and are linked to the center at Assisi. The Archconfraternity of Our Lady of Consolation, or of the Black Leather Belt of Saint Monica...

# DEMONS AND FAMILIARS 83

Saint Augustine and Saint Nicholas of Tolentino took their inspiration from a vision of Saint Monica, who received a black leather belt from the Virgin Mary. Saint Augustine, Saint Ambrose, and Saint Simplicianus all wore such a girdle, which became a distinguishing feature of the clothing of the <term>Augustinian Eremites</term> <note>original: "Augustinian Eremites"; members of the Order of Saint Augustine, often called 'hermits.'</note>. After the canonization of Saint Nicholas of Tolentino, it came into general use as a devotional item, and Pope Eugenius IV established the aforementioned Archconfraternity in 1439. A Papal Bull issued by Gregory XIII titled *Ad ea* <note>original: "Ad ea"; Latin for "To those things" or "Regarding those matters."</note> on July 15, 1575, confirmed this and added various privileges and <term>Indulgences</term> <note>In Catholic theology, the remission of temporal punishment for sins.</note>. This Archconfraternity is established in Augustinian sanctuaries; permission for it to be extended to other churches must be obtained from the General of that Order.

Fourthly: All witches vow obedience and subjection to the Devil; they pay him homage and <term>vassalage</term> <note>A formal pledge of loyalty and service, similar to that of a knight to his lord.</note> (often through obscene ceremonies) and lay their hands upon a large black book presented to them. They bind themselves by blasphemous oaths never to return to the true faith, to observe no divine commandments, and to perform no good works, but instead to obey only the Demon and to attend the nightly <term>conventicles</term> <note>original: "conventicles"; secret or illegal religious meetings, here used to describe witch gatherings.</note> without fail. They pledge themselves to attend these midnight assemblies.⁸ These conventicles or **covens**⁹ (from the Latin *conventus* <note>An assembly, gathering, or meeting.</note>) were groups or companies of witches made up of both men and women. They were apparently under the discipline of an officer, and for the sake of convenience, all members belonged to the same district. According to evidence from trials, those who belonged to a coven were required to attend the weekly **Esbat** <note>A smaller, regular meeting of a local coven, as opposed to the larger, less frequent Sabbats.</note>. The arrest of one coven member generally led to the naming and arrest of the others. Cotton Mather remarked, "The witches are organized like Congregational Churches."

Fifthly: The witches promise to strive with all their power and use every incentive and effort to draw other men and women into their detestable practices and the worship of Satan.

The witches were filled with a missionary spirit, which made them doubly damnable in the eyes of the clergy and doubly guilty in the eyes of the law. For example, in the case of Janet Breadheid of Auldearne, we find that her husband "enticed her into that craft."¹⁰ A girl named Bellot, from Madame Bourignon’s academy, confessed that her mother had taken her to the **Sabbat** <note>A large, secret gathering of witches for rituals.</note> when she was quite a child. Another girl alleged that all worshippers of the Devil "are"

Elizabeth Francis of Chelmsford, a witch tried in 1566, was only about twelve years old when her grandmother first taught her the art of <term>sorcery</term> <note>The use of magic, especially involving the assistance of evil spirits.</note>.<sup>11</sup> The famous Pendle <term>beldame</term> <note>original: "beldame"; an old woman, often used to describe a hag or a witch.</note>, Elizabeth Demdike, "brought up her own children, instructed her grandchildren, and took great care and effort to bring them to be witches."<sup>12</sup> At Salem, George Burroughs, a minister, was accused by a large number of women as "the person who had seduced and compelled them into the snares of witchcraft."

*Sixthly*: The Devil performs a kind of sacrilegious baptism for witches. After renouncing the godfathers and godmothers of their Christian Baptism and Confirmation, they are assigned new sponsors—so to speak—whose duty is to instruct them in sorcery. They drop their former name and exchange it for another, which is usually a vulgar and grotesque nickname.

In 1609, Jeanette d'Abadie, a witch of the Basses-Pyrénées, confessed "that she often saw children baptized at the <term>Sabbat</term> <note>original: "Sabbat"; a secret midnight assembly of witches.</note>, and she informed us these were the offspring of sorcerers and not of other people—specifically, of witches who are accustomed to have their sons and daughters baptized at the Sabbat rather than at the <term>Font</term> <note>The stone basin used for Christian baptism in a church.</note>."<sup>13</sup> On June 20, 1614, at Orleans, Silvain Nevillon, among other crimes, acknowledged that he had frequented assemblies of witches, and "that they baptize babies at the Sabbat with <term>chrism</term> <note>original: "Chrism"; a mixture of oil and balsam, consecrated and used for anointing in church rites.</note>. . . . Then they anoint the child's head with it, muttering certain Latin phrases."<sup>14</sup> Gentien le Clerc, who was tried at the same time, "said that his mother, as he had been told, presented him at the Sabbat when he was only three years old to a monstrous goat, whom they called <term>the Asp</term> <note>original: "l'Aspic"; likely referring to the venomous snake, a symbol of the Devil.</note>. He said that he was baptized at the Sabbat, at Carrior d'Olivet, with fourteen or fifteen other children. . . ."<sup>15</sup>

Among the confessions made by Louis Gaufridi at Aix in March 1611, were: 

> "I confess that baptism is performed at the Sabbat, and that every sorcerer, devoting himself to the Devil, binds himself by a particular vow that he will have all his children baptized at the Sabbat, if this can be achieved by any possible means. Every child who is thus baptized at the Sabbat receives a name that is completely different from his own name. I confess that at this baptism water [is used]..."

A number of Swedish witches (1669) were baptized: “they added, that he caused them to be baptized too by such priests as he had there, and made them confirm their baptism with dreadful oaths and <term>imprecations</term> <note>Spoken curses or invocations of evil.</note>.”¹⁷

The giving of a new name seems to have been very general. Thus in May 1569, at St. Andrews, “a notable sorceress called <term>Nicniven</term> <note>Nicnevin is a figure in Scottish folklore often identified as the Queen of the Witches or a mother-witch figure.</note> was condemned to death and burned.” Her Christian name is not given, merely her witch’s name bestowed by the demon. In the famous Fian case, it was stated that when at the meeting in North Berwick church <note>original: "kirk"</note>, Robert Grierson was named, great confusion ensued for the witches and warlocks; “all ran <term>hirdie-girdie</term> <note>original: "hirdie-girdie"; a Scottish term meaning in a state of confusion or topsy-turvy.</note> and were angry, for it was promised that he should be called Robert the Comptroller, for the <note>original: "expriming"; meaning the pronouncing or expressing.</note> expressing of his name.”¹⁸ Euphemia McCalyan of the same <term>coven</term> was called Cane, and Barbara Napier [was called] Naip. *Seventhly:* The witches cut off a piece of their own garments and, as a token of homage, offer <note>original: "tender"</note> it to the Devil, who takes it away and keeps it.

*Eighthly:* The Devil draws a circle on the ground wherein stand the novices, wizards, and witches, and there they confirm all their aforesaid promises by oath. This has a mystical significance. “They take this oath to the Demon standing in a circle described upon the ground, perhaps because a circle is the symbol of Divinity, and the earth is God’s footstool; and thus he assuredly wishes them to believe that he is the lord of Heaven and earth.”¹⁹

...witnessing their first homage, and they are inscribed in this book by the Devil’s claw.

These books or rolls were kept with great secrecy by the chief officer of the <term>coven</term> <note>A group or gathering of witches.</note> or even the Grand Master of a district. They would have been guarded as carefully as life itself, seeing that they contained the damning evidence of a full list of the witches of a province or county. In addition to this, they seem to have included a number of magic formulae <note>original: "formulæ"</note>, spells, charms, and probably, from time to time, a record of the doings of the various witches. The signing of such a book is continually referred to in the New England trials. For example, when Deliverance Hobbs had made a full confession of her sorceries, "She now testified that this Bishop [Bridget Bishop, condemned and executed as a long-practicing witch] tempted her to sign the *Book* again, and to deny what she had confessed." The enemies of the notorious Matthew Hopkins <note>Matthew Hopkins (c. 1620–1647) was an English witch-hunter whose career flourished during the English Civil War.</note> took great advantage of the story that, by some trick of sorcery, he had obtained one of these Devil’s memorandum books. It was said he copied a list of witches from it, and this was what enabled him to be so accurate in his "scent" for finding them. The Witch-Finder General struggled to defend himself from this accusation and became quite pitiful in his whining assertions <note>original: "asseverations"</note> of innocence. There is a somewhat vague story, with no dates provided, that a Devil’s book was carried off by Mr. Williamson of Cardrona (Peebles), who stole it from the witches while they were dancing on Minchmoor. But the whole coven immediately gave chase, and he was glad to abandon it and escape alive.

Sometimes the list of witches was written on a separate parchment, and the book was only used to record charms and spells. Such a volume was the Red Book of Appin, which was known to have actually been in existence a hundred years ago. Tradition said it was stolen from the Devil by a trick. It was a manuscript and contained a large number of magic runes and incantations for the cure of cattle diseases, the increase of flocks, and the fertility of fields. This document, which must be of immense importance and interest, was (I believe) last heard of in the possession of the now-extinct Stewarts of Invernahyle. The *Book of Penance* <note>original: *Liber Pœnitentialis*</note> of St. Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury (668–690)—the earliest ecclesiastical law of England—contains clauses condemning those who invoke fiends and thus cause the weather to change, "if anyone has been a sender of storms" <note>original: *si quis emissor tempestatis fuerit*</note>. All persons found guilty of employing such arts were to be executed immediately upon conviction. Innocent VIII, in his celebrated Bull, *Desiring with supreme fervor* <note>original: *Summis desiderantes affectibus*</note>, dated December 5, 1484, charges sorcerers in detail with precisely the same foul practices. 

The most celebrated occasion when witches supposedly raised a storm was that which played so important a part in the trial of Dr. Fian and his coven (1590–1). In that case, the witches—in order to drown King James and Queen Anne on their voyage from Denmark—"took a cat and christened it," and after they had bound a dismembered corpse to the animal, "in the night following, the said cat was conveyed into the midst of the sea by all these witches, sailing in their sieves <note>original: "riddles or cives"</note>. . . this done, there arose such a tempest in the sea that a greater has not been seen."²⁵ The bewitching of cattle is alleged from the earliest times; and at Dornoch in Sutherland as late as 1722, an old woman was burned for having cast spells upon the pigs and sheep of her neighbors, the sentence being pronounced by the sheriff-depute, Captain David Ross of Little Dean. This was the last execution of a witch in Scotland.

It is clear that there is no question here of animal familiars, but rather of evil spirits who were believed to be able to take on physical bodies. This entire issue is perhaps one of the darkest and most difficult topics related to witchcraft and magic. The details of these hideous encounters are so extreme—for just as the saints reach for the purity of angels, those enslaved to Satan defile themselves with every kind of lust <note>original: "lewdness"</note>—that many writers, out of excessive hesitation and modesty, have dismissed the subject too briefly for the serious researcher to be satisfied.

First, we can freely admit that many of these lewd acts <note>original: "lubricities"</note> can be attributed to hysteria, hallucinations, nightmares, or the delusions of disease. However, even after making these allowances—and admitting that in many cases the incubus <note>A male demon believed to have sexual relations with sleeping women.</note> or succubus <note>A female demon believed to have sexual relations with sleeping men.</note> was simply a human being acting as an agent for the local Grand Master <note>The leader of a witch coven or district.</note>—enough evidence remains from trial records to convince an open mind that there was a significant basis of fact in the confessions of the accused. As Canon Ribet stated in his comprehensive work *Divine Mysticism* <note>original: *La Mystique Divine*</note>, a book highly praised by the brilliant Pope Leo XIII:

> “After what we have learned from records and personal confessions, we can scarcely have any more doubts. It is our plain duty to oppose—even if only by a simple statement—those numerous writers who, through arrogance or recklessness, treat these horrors as idle talk or mere hallucination.”²⁹

Bizouard also writes about the incubus and succubus in his authoritative work, *Reports on Man’s Relationship with the Demon* <note>original: *Rapports de l’homme avec le démon*</note>:

> “These relationships, far from being untrue, bear the strongest marks of authenticity possible. They come from official legal proceedings, which were regulated and approved with all the caution and judgment shown by enlightened and conscientious judges. Throughout history, these magistrates have been in a position to test clear facts.”³⁰

It seems to me that if reliable evidence means anything at all, and if the authority of the smartest and sharpest minds from all ages and countries is not to be dismissed as mere nonsense <note>original: "vapourings"</note> or fairy tales, then the possibility of these demonic connections cannot be denied. I have quoted many great names: men of science, men of learning, and men of authority to whom the world still looks with admiration—even with reverence and love. This is because today it is difficult, and in most cases almost inconceivable, for the modern mind to believe in the possibility of these dark deeds of devilry and these foul lusts of male and female demons.⁶⁶ They seem like a sick and loathsome fantasy from the dim Medieval days, shrieked out on the rack by some poor soul crazed with agony and fear, then written down in long-forgotten books by fanatics who were childishly gullible and more ignorant than savages. "Even if such horrors could have taken place in the 'Dark Ages'"—those vague Dark Ages!—men say, "they would never be permitted now." 

But the priest sitting in the grated confessional, into whose ears are poured the filth and folly of the world for shriving <note>The act of hearing a confession and granting absolution for sins.</note>, sighs to himself, "I wish to God that were actually true!" The skeptics are happier in their simple-mindedness, glad that they do not and will not realize the monstrous things that lie just beneath the surface of our cracking civilization.

It is appropriate <note>original: "not impertinently"</note> to ask how demons or evil intelligences—since they are purely spiritual beings—can not only take on human flesh but also perform the specifically physical act of sexual intercourse <note>original: "coition"</note>. Sinistrari <note>Ludovico Maria Sinistrari (1622–1701) was a Franciscan friar and author of a famous treatise on demons.</note>, following the opinion of Guazzo <note>Francesco Maria Guazzo was an Italian priest who wrote the Compendium Maleficarum in 1608.</note>, says that either the evil intelligence is able to animate the corpse of a human being (male or female, as the case may be), or that he fashions a body for himself from a mixture of other materials. This body is endowed with motion, and through it, the demon is joined to the human being: “from a mixture of other materials he fashions for himself a body, which he moves, and by means of which he is joined to a human” <note>original Latin: "ex mixtione aliarum materiarum effingit sibi corpus, quod mouet, et mediante quo homini unitur."</note>.⁶⁷ 

In the first instance, advantage might no doubt be taken of a person in a mediumistic trance or hypnotic sleep. But the second explanation seems far more probable. Can we not look to the phenomena observed in connection with **ectoplasm** <note>In spiritualism, a physical substance supposed to emanate from a medium's body during a séance to form spirits.</note> as an adequate explanation of this? It must be admitted that this explanation is certainly supported by the phenomena of the **materializing séance**, where physical forms that can be touched and handled are built up and then disintegrated again.

Council after council forbade the use of the *fascinum*, and their very insistence on prohibition shows how deeply these abominations had taken root. ...common in pagan antiquity, have been shamelessly practiced throughout all the ages, as indeed they are at the present day, and they have been repeatedly banned and condemned by the voice of the Church. This very fact would recommend them to the favor of the Satanists, and there can be no doubt that amid the dark debaucheries which celebrated the Sabbats <note>A secret gathering of witches to worship the Devil.</note>, such practice was almost universal. The animal familiar was quite distinct from the familiar in human shape. In England particularly, there is an abundance of evidence concerning them. Even today, who pictures a witch with "nut-cracker" jaws <note>A description of a face where the nose and chin nearly meet due to tooth loss, a common stereotype for the elderly and alleged witches.</note>, a pointed steeple hat, and a red cloak, hobbling along on her crutch, without her big black cat beside her? It is worth noting that in other countries the domestic animal familiar is rare, and Bishop Francis Hutchinson even says: "I find little mention of imps <note>Small demonic entities often taking animal form, believed to assist a witch.</note> in any country but ours, where the Law makes the feeding, suckling, or rewarding of them to be a felony."<sup>89</sup> <margin>Bishop Francis Hutchinson</margin> Curiously enough, this familiar is most frequently encountered in Essex, Suffolk, and the Eastern counties. We find that animals of all kinds were regarded as familiars: dogs, cats, ferrets, weasels, toads, rats, mice, birds, hedgehogs, hares, and even wasps, moths, bees, and flies. 

It is heartbreaking to think that in many cases some miserable person who—shunned and detested by her neighbors—sought friendship in the love of a cat or a dog, whom she petted and lovingly fed with the best choice morsels she could give, was dragged to the gallows or the stake on the strength of this affection alone. But very frequently, the witch actually did keep some small animal which she nourished on a diet of milk, bread, and her own blood in order that she might perform divination <note>original: "divine"; the practice of "augury" or foretelling the future.</note> by its means. The details of this particular method of divination <note>original: "augury"</note> are by no means clear. Probably the witch observed the gait of the animal, its actions, or the tones of its voice, which were easily interpreted to have some imaginary meaning; no doubt a dog, or a bird such as a raven or a jackdaw <note>original: "daw"</note>, could be taught tricks to impress the simple-mindedness of those seeking answers.

<page-num>102</page-num>
<header>THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT</header>

The immense importance of blood to life has undoubtedly been clear to humans since the earliest times. Man experienced a feeling of weakness after the loss of blood; therefore, blood was seen as strength—life itself. Throughout the ages, blood has been considered to be of the greatest therapeutic and the deepest magical value. The few drops of blood the witch gave her familiar were not only a reward or a renewal of strength, but they also established a closer connection between herself and the dog, cat, or bird, as the case might be. Blood formed a psychic bond <note>original: "copula," a term for a connecting link</note>.

At the trial of Elizabeth Francis in Chelmsford in 1556, the accused confessed that her familiar—given to her by her grandmother, a notorious witch—was "in the likeness of a white spotted cat." Her grandmother "taught her to feed the said cat with bread and milk, and she did so; she also taught her to call it by the name of Satan <note>original: "Sattan"</note> and to keep it in a basket. Furthermore, every time that he did anything for her, she said that he required a drop of blood, which she gave him by pricking herself, sometimes in one place and then in another."⁹⁰ It is unnecessary to provide more examples; in the witch trials of Essex—particularly while Matthew Hopkins and his associate <note>original: "satellite"</note> John Stearne were busy at work from 1645 to 1647—the animal familiar is mentioned again and again in the records. As late as 1694 at Bury St. Edmunds, when old Mother Munnings of Hartis, in Suffolk, was hauled before Lord Chief Justice Holt, it was asserted that she had an imp like a polecat <note>A small, carnivorous mammal related to the weasel and ferret.</note>. But the judge dismissed the evidence of a pack of thick-headed peasants <note>original: "clodpate rustics"</note> and directed the jury to bring a verdict of Not Guilty.⁹¹ "Upon particular inquiry," says Hutchinson, "of several people in or near the town, I find most are satisfied it was a very correct judgment." In 1712, the familiar of Jane Wenham, the witch of Walkern in Hertfordshire, was stated at her trial to be a cat.

In Ford and Dekker’s play *The Witch of Edmonton*, the familiar appears on the stage as a dog. This, of course, is directly taken from Henry Goodcole’s pamphlet *The Wonderful Discovery of Elizabeth Sawyer* (London, 1621), where in answer to this question, the witch confesses that the Devil came to her in the shape of a dog of two colors, sometimes black and sometimes white. The witnesses informed the Court that they had seen her feeding imps—specifically two white ferrets—with white bread and milk, but she firmly denied this. In Goethe’s *Faust*, Part I, Scene 2, Mephistopheles first appears to Faust outside the city gates as a black poodle and accompanies him back to his study, snarling and yelping when the words "In the beginning" <note>original: "In Principio"; these are the opening words of the Gospel of John, often used in exorcisms</note> are read. This is part of the old legend. Manlius (1590), in the report of his conversation with Melanchthon, quotes the latter as having said: “He [Faust] had a dog with him, which was the devil.” Paolo Jovio relates⁹² that the famous Cornelius Agrippa always kept a demon attendant with him in the shape of a black dog. However, Johann Weyer <note>original: "John Weye"</note>, in his well-known work *On the Illusions of Demons* <note>original: "De Præstigiis Dæmonum"</note>,⁹³ informs us that he had lived for years in daily attendance upon Agrippa and that the black dog, *Monsieur*, about whom such strange stories were spread, was a perfectly innocent animal which he had often led around on a leash himself. Agrippa was much attached to his dog, which used to eat at the table with him and sleep in his bed at night. Since he was a profound scholar and a great recluse, he never bothered to contradict the idle gossip his neighbors chattered about at every window and door. It is hardly surprising, considering the hermetic <note>Hermetic works are texts concerning alchemy, astrology, and magic</note> writings that carry Agrippa’s name, that even in his own lifetime this great man acquired the reputation of a mighty magician.

Grotesque names were generally given to the familiar: Lizabet; Verd-Joli; Master Parsley <note>original: "Maître Persil"</note>; Verdelet; Martinet; Abrahel (a succubus <note>a demon in female form intended to seduce men</note>); and to animal familiars in England, Tissy; Grissell; Greedigut; Blackman; Jezebel (a succubus); Ilemanzar; Jarmara; and Pyewackett.

The familiar in human shape often associated with the witch and was visible to clairvoyants. Thus, in 1324, one of the accusations brought against Lady Alice Kyteler was that a demon came to her "sometimes in the form of a certain black man with two companions" <note>original: "quandoque in specie cuiusdam æthiopis cum duobus sociis"</note>. The company met at Sabbats <note>the secret midnight gatherings of witches</note> is not as easily shaken off as one might wish.

**43** The word *bestiality* <note>original: "bestialitas"</note> has theologically a far wider meaning than the modern word. Evans remarks: “It seems rather odd that the Christian lawgivers should have adopted the Jewish code against sexual intercourse with beasts, and then enlarged it so as to include the Jews themselves. The question was gravely discussed by jurists whether cohabitation of a Christian with a Jewish woman, or vice versa, constitutes sodomy. Damhouder (*Practice of Criminal Matters*, chapter 96, number 48) is of the opinion that it does, and Nicolaus Boer (*Decisions*, 136, number 5) cites the case of a certain Johannes Alardus, or Jean Alard, who kept a Jewish woman in his house in Paris and had several children by her: he was convicted of sodomy on account of this relation and burned, together with his lover, ‘since sexual intercourse with a Jewish woman is precisely the same as if a man should copulate with a dog’ <note>original Latin: "since coition with a Jewess is precisely the same as if a man should copulate with a dog"</note> (*Double Theater* volume 2, page 157). Damhouder includes Turks and Saracens in the same category.” *The Criminal Prosecution and Capital Punishment of Animals*, page 152. London, 1906.

**51** All theologians speak of sexual meeting with a demon appearing in the form of a man, a woman, or some beast, or as present represented through the imagination; they say that such a sin is to be referred to the category of bestiality and has a special malice to be declared in confession—namely, the superstition consisting in a pact with the demon. In this crime, therefore, two malices are necessarily found: one against chastity, and the other against the virtue of religion. If anyone approaches a demon appearing under the likeness of a man with sodomitic intent, there is a third type of sin, as is clear. Likewise, if it is feigned to appear under the likeness of a relative or a married woman, the type of incest or adultery is present; if under the likeness of a beast, bestiality is present. <note>original: "Omnes theologi loquuntur de congressu cum dæmone in forma uiri, mulieris aut alicuius bestiæ apparente, uel ut præsente per imaginationem repræsentato, dicuntque tale peccatum ad genus bestialitatis reuocandum esse, et specialem habere malitiam in confessione declarandam, scilicet superstitionem in pacto cum dæmone consistentem. In hoc igitur scelere duæ necessario reperiuntur malitiæ, una contra castitatem, et altera contra uirtutem religionis. Si quis ad dæmonem sub specie uiri apparentem affectu sodomitico accedat, tertia est species peccati, ut patet. Item si sub specie consanguineæ aut mulieris conjugatæ fingatur apparere, adest species incestus uel adulterii ; si sub specie bestiæ, adest bestialitas."</note>

## CHAPTER IV

### THE SABBAT

The assemblies of the witches differed greatly from each other in an almost infinite number of ways. On certain ancient anniversaries, the meeting was always particularly solemn, with as large an attendance as possible. Everyone who belonged to the infernal cult was required to attend, and punishment was handed out to those who proved lazy or slow to arrive. At other times, these gatherings were occasional, attended by the members who lived within a specific local area; it might be just one coven of thirteen, or perhaps a few more, as the opportunity arose. There were also, as is to be expected, variations unique to each country and a seemingly endless number of local peculiarities. 

There does not appear to be any clear or consistent order in the ceremonies throughout, nor should we look for one, seeing that the liturgy of darkness is, by its very nature, opposed to the proper worship of God. In God's worship, as the Apostle <note>St. Paul, referencing 1 Corinthians 14:40: "Let all things be done decently and in order."</note> commands, all things are to be done "decently and in order." The ceremonial of hell, which is quite complex, obscure, and obscene, is made even more confusing in the witches’ accounts by many additional circumstances that are often contradictory or even mutually exclusive. Therefore, although we can piece together a very complete picture of their orgies, some details must still remain unexplained, incomprehensible, and perhaps entirely irrational and absurd. "The ridiculous is mixed with the horrible, and childishness with abominations." <note>original French: "Le burlesque s’y mêle à l’horrible, et les puérilités aux abominations."</note> (Ribet, *Divine Mysticism* <note>original French title: "La Mystique Divine"</note>, III. 2. *Diabolical Parodies* <note>original French title: "Les Parodies Diaboliques"</note>.) 

In the smaller assemblies, much undoubtedly depended on the fickle whims and unhealthy impulses of the officer or president in charge at the moment. The conduct of the more important assemblies was, to a certain extent...

...regularized and followed more or less traditional lines. The name Sabbat may be considered to cover every kind of gathering,² though it must always be kept in mind that a Sabbat ranges from the relatively simple—a secret rendezvous of half a dozen miserable people devoted to the Devil—to a large and crowded assembly presided over by incarnate evil spirits. Such a mob exceeds even the demons in their malice, blasphemy, and rebellion, appearing as the true face of hellish chaos on earth.

The origin of the word "Sabbat" does not seem to be clearly established. It is perhaps unnecessary to point out that it has nothing to do with the number seven and is entirely unrelated to the Jewish festival <note>The Jewish Sabbath</note>. Sainte-Croix and Alfred Maury³ agree that the word derives from the degraded Bacchanalia <note>The Bacchanalia were ancient Roman festivals of Bacchus, famous for wild and drunken revelry.</note>. Sabazius <note>original Greek: Σαβάζιος</note> was a Phrygian god, sometimes identified with Zeus and sometimes with Dionysus, but who was generally regarded as the patron of lust and worshipped with frantic debauchery. He is a patron of the crude old Syrian eunuch in the writings of Apuleius: "The almighty and all-parent Syrian Goddess, and holy Sabazius, and Bellona, and the Idaean Mother, and Lady Venus with her Adonis"⁴ <note>original Latin: "omnipotens et omniparens Dea Syria et sanctus Sabadius et Bellona et Mater Idaea (ac) cum suo Adone Venus domina"</note> are the deities whom Philebus invokes to take revenge on the mocking crier. The term "to celebrate the rites of Sabazius" <note>original Greek: Σαβαζεῖν</note> is found in the commentary on Aristophanes (*Birds, 874*), and "*Sabai*" <note>original Greek: σαβαῖ</note>, a Bacchic shout, occurs in a fragment of the *Baptae* by Eupolis; the fuller phrase "*Euoi Saboi*" <note>original Greek: εὐοῖ Σαβοῖ</note> is reported by the geographer Strabo. Modern Greeks still call a madman *zabos* <note>original Greek: ζαβός</note>. However, the lexicographer Littré completely rejects such an easy etymology: "Attempts have been made to trace the origin of the 'Sabbat' (the witches' assembly) from Sabazius; but the way the word is formed does not allow for this. Furthermore, what did people in the Middle Ages even know about Sabazius?"⁵

The times of the year for the main assemblies also vary from country to country. Throughout most of Western Europe, one of the primary dates was the eve of May Day, April 30;⁶ in Germany⁷ this is famous as Walpurgis Night <note>original German: Die Walpurgis-Nacht</note>. Saint Walburga (also known as Walpurgis, Waltpurde, Gauburge in Perche, or Vaubourg and Falbourg in other parts of France) was born in Devonshire around <note>original Latin: circa</note> 710 AD. She was the daughter of Saint Richard, one of the sub-kings of the West Saxons, who had married a sister of Saint Boniface. In 748 AD, Walburga, who was...

After a life of extraordinary holiness, she died at Heidenheim on February 25, 777. her <term>cultus</term> <note>The formal system of religious veneration and devotion directed toward a particular saint.</note> began immediately, and about 870 her relics were <term>translated</term> <note>The ceremonial transfer of a saint's body or remains from one location to another.</note> to Eichstätt, where the Benedictine convent that maintains the sacred shrine still flourishes today. St. Walburga was formerly one of the most popular saints in England, as well as in Germany and the Netherlands <note>original: "Low Countries"</note>. She is the patroness of Eichstätt, Oudenaarde, Furnes, Groningen, Weilburg, Zutphen, and Antwerp, where—until the standard Roman Liturgy <note>original: "Roman office"</note> was adopted—they celebrated her feast four times a year. In the Roman Martyrology, she is commemorated on May 1, but in the Monastic Calendar on February 25. The first of May was the ancient festival of the Druids, when they offered sacrifices upon their sacred mountains and lit their "May-fires." These magical observances were appropriately continued by the witches of a later date. According to peasant belief, there was not a hilltop in Finland that was not crowded with demons and sorcerers at midnight on the last day of April.

The second witches’ festival was the Eve of St. John the Baptist, June 23. This was when the St. John’s fires were lit, a custom still practiced in certain regions. In olden times, the Feast was distinguished—like Christmas—with three Masses: the first at midnight recalled his mission as the <term>Forerunner</term> <note>original: "Precursor"</note>, the second at dawn commemorated the baptism he performed, and the third honored his sanctity.

Other Major Sabbat days, particularly in Belgium and Germany, were St. Thomas’ Day (December 21) and a date—which seems to have been flexible—shortly after Christmas. In Britain, we also find Candlemas (February 2), Halloween (October 31), and Lammas (August 1) mentioned in the trials. Wright, in *Narratives of Sorcery and Magic* (Volume I, page 141), further specifies St. Bartholomew’s Eve (August 23), but although a Sabbat may have been held on this day, it would seem to be an exceptional or purely local custom.

...were usually held at Zugarramurdi and Berroscoberro in the Basque districts, and the days were fixed as the vigils <note>The eve or the night before a religious festival.</note> of the "nine principal feasts of the year." These were: Easter, Epiphany, Ascension Day, the Purification and Nativity of Our Lady, the Assumption, Corpus Christi, All Saints, and the major festival of St. John the Baptist (June 24). It is certainly curious to find no mention of Christmas and Pentecost in this list, but throughout the entire trial, not one of the accused—and we have their evidence in the fullest detail—named either of these two solemn celebrations as being chosen for the infernal rendezvous.⁹

Satan is, as Boguet <note>Henry Boguet (c. 1550–1619), a French judge and demonologist.</note> aptly says, "God's ape in everything,"¹⁰ <note>original: "Singe de Dieu en tout"</note> and it became common to hold a General Sabbat around the time of the high Christian festivals in evil mockery of these holy ceremonies. He specifically asserts that the Sabbat "is still held on the most solemn festivals of the year."¹¹ <note>original: "se tient encor aux festes les plus solemnelles de l’année."</note> To support this, he records the confession of Antide Colas (1598), who "had been at the Sabbat on every holy day of the year, such as Christmas, Easter, and Corpus Christi." <note>original: "auoit esté au Sabbat à vn chacun bon iour de l’an, comme à Noel, à Pasques, à la feste de Dieu." Note: "feste de Dieu" refers to the Feast of God, or Corpus Christi.</note> The Lancashire witches met on Good Friday, and in a second instance (1633) on All Saints' Day. The witches of Kinross (1662) held an assembly on the feast of Scotland’s Patron, St. Andrew, November 30—termed "St. Andrew’s Day at Yule" to distinguish it from the secondary Feast of the Translation of St. Andrew on May 9. The New England witches were known to celebrate their chief Sabbat at Christmas. In many parts of Europe where the Feast of St. George is celebrated with high honor and a holiday, the vigil (April 22) is the Great Sabbat of the year. The Hutsuls <note>original: "Huzulo"</note> of the Carpathians believe that at this time every evil thing has power and witches are most dangerous. In response, every Bulgarian or Romanian farmer closes each door and fastens every window at nightfall. They place sharp thornbushes and brambles on the lintels and new turf on the windowsills so that no demon or hag may find entry there.

The Grand Sabbats were naturally held in a great variety of places, while the lesser Sabbats could be easily assembled in an even larger number of spots. These locations were chosen for the convenience of the local <term>coven</term> <note>A gathering or group of witches, traditionally numbering thirteen.</note> and might include a field near a village, a wood, a <term>tor</term> <note>A rocky peak or hill.</note>, a valley, or an open wasteland beneath a withered <note>original: "blasted"</note> oak.

It was recommended that the chosen location be remote and deserted to avoid any chance of spying or accidental interruption. In many regions, some wild, unlucky ravine or lonely hilltop was fearfully identified as the notorious haunt of witches and their demons. Pierre de Lancre <note>A French judge and demonologist (1553–1631) who conducted massive witch-hunts in the Labourd region.</note> says that the Grand Sabbat must be held near a stream, lake, or water of some kind,¹² and Jean Bodin <note>A famous French jurist and writer on demonology (1530–1596).</note> adds: "The places where sorcerers meet are notable and generally distinguished by certain trees, or even a cross."¹³ These ancient cromlechs <note>A tomb made of large upright stones; a megalithic structure.</note> and granite dolmens <note>A single-chamber megalithic tomb.</note>, the stones of the Marais de Dol, the standing stone that lies between Seny and Ellemelle (in the Condroz region), and even the market crosses of sleepy old towns and English villages were among the favorite meeting places of the sorcerers <note>original: "pythons and warlocks"; "python" here refers to a person possessed by a spirit or a diviner.</note> of an entire countryside. On one occasion, which seems exceptional, a Sabbat was held in the very heart of the city of Bordeaux. Throughout Germany, the Blocksburg or the Brocken—the highest peak of the Harz Mountains—was the great meeting place of the witches; it was said that some came from as far as Lapland and Norway to gather there. However, local "Blocksburgs" existed, or rather hills called by that name, especially in Pomerania, which boasted two or three such crags. The sorcerers of Corrières held their Sabbat at a deserted spot, turning off the highway near Combes; the witches of La Mouille met in a tumbledown house which had once belonged to a religious order <note>original: "religious"; referring to monks or nuns.</note>; and the Gandillons and their coven, who were brought to justice in June 1598, met at Fontenelles, a forsaken and haunted spot near the village of Nezar.

Dr. Fian and his associates (1591) assembled at "the church of North Berwick in Lothian" <note>original: "the kirke of North-Berrick in Lowthian"</note> on "the night of Halloween" <note>original: "Allhollen-Even"</note>. Silvain Nevillon, who was executed at Orléans on February 4, 1615, confessed "that the Sabbat was held in a house," <note>original: "que le Sabbat se tenoit dans vne maison"</note> and the full details he provided show this to have been a large château—no doubt the home of some wealthy local aristocrat—where over two hundred persons could assemble. Isobel Young, Christian Grinton, and two or three other witches entertained the Devil in Young’s house in 1629. Alexander Hamilton, a "known warlock" executed at Edinburgh in 1630, confessed that "the accused" <note>original: "the pannel"; a Scots legal term for the defendant on trial.</note>...

It is true that the hysterical and obscene ravings of Maria de Sains—a witness involved in the trial of Louis Gaufridi who was examined on May 17–19, 1614—asserted that the Sabbat was held every day of the week. She claimed Wednesday and Friday were the Sabbats of blasphemy and the "black ass" <note>A symbolic representation of the Devil in bestial form.</note>. To the other days, the most hideous abominations of which humanity is capable were assigned. The woman was obviously mentally and sexually disturbed, suffering from a mania for blasphemy <note>original: "mania blasphematoria"</note> and a compulsive use of obscene language <note>original: "coprolalia"</note>.

Night was almost always the time for the Sabbat, although as Martin Delrio <note>Martin Delrio (1551–1608) was a Jesuit scholar whose "Disquisitionum Magicarum Libri Sex" became a standard work on witchcraft.</note> says, there is no actual reason why these evil rites should not be performed at noon. The time at which these Sabbats began was generally at the stroke of midnight. Thomas Leyis, Issobell Coky, Helen Fraser, Bessie Thorn, and the rest of the Aberdeen witches—thirteen of whom were executed in 1597, and seven more banished—generally met "between twelve and one o’clock at night." <note>original Scots: "betuixt tuell & ane houris at nycht"</note>²⁴ Boguet <note>Henry Boguet (1550–1619) was a French judge and author of a famous treatise on witchcraft.</note> notes that in 1598 the witch Françoise Secretain "added that she always went to the Sabbat around midnight, and many other witches whom I have handled have said the same." <note>original French: "adioustoit qu’elle alloit tousjours au Sabbat enuiron la minuit, & beaucoup d’autres sorciers, que i’ay eu en main, ont dit le mesme."</note> In 1600, Anna Mauczin of Tübingen confessed that she had taken part in witch gatherings which she dubbed *Hochzeiten* <note>German for "weddings."</note>. A Scottish witch, Marie Lamont, "a young woman of the age of eighteen years, dwelling in the parish of Innerkip," on March 4, 1662, confessed most ingenuously "that when she had been at a meeting since Yule <note>original: "Zowle"</note> last, with other witches, in the night, the devil escorted <note>original: "convoyed"</note> her home at dawn <note>original: "dawing"</note>."²⁵

The Sabbat lasted until cock-crow, before which time none of the assembly was allowed to withdraw. The confession of Louis Gaufridi, executed at Aix in 1610, seems somewhat unusual: "I was conveyed to the place where the Sabbat was to be held, and I remained there sometimes one, two, three, or four hours, for the most part just as I felt inclined."²⁶ That the crowing of a cock dissolves enchantments is a tradition of extreme antiquity. The Jews believed that the flapping of a cock’s wings would make the power of demons ineffectual and break magic spells. So Prudentius <note>Aurelius Prudentius Clemens (c. 348–413 AD) was a Roman Christian poet.</note> sang: "They say that the night-wandering demons, who rejoice in the darkest shades, at the crowing of the cock tremble and scatter in great fear."²⁷ The rites of Satan ceased because the Holy Office of the Church began. In the time of St. Benedict, Matins and Lauds <note>The earliest morning prayer services in the Catholic Church.</note> were recited at dawn and were actually often known as *Gallicinium* <note>Latin: "cock-crowing."</note>. In the exquisite poetry of St. Ambrose, which is chanted at Sunday Lauds, the praises of the cock are beautifully sung:

->With days dividing night from night!<-
->Loud crows the dawn’s shrill harbinger,<-

A witch named Latoma confessed to the judge Nicolas Remy that roosters were most hateful to all sorcerers. That bird is the herald of dawn; he awakens men to the worship of God, and many a vile sin shrouded by darkness will be revealed in the light of the coming day. At the hour of the Nativity <note>The birth of Christ (Christmas).</note>, that most blessed time, the roosters crowed all night long. A rooster crowed vigorously at the Resurrection. For this reason, the rooster is placed upon the steeples of churches. The ancient authors Pliny and Ælian tell us that even a lion fears the rooster; likewise, the Devil—the "roaring lion" <note>original Latin: "leo rugiens"</note>—flees at the cock-crow.

"The rooster," says the judge Pierre de Lancre, "is sometimes heard at the Sabbats sounding the retreat for the sorcerers." <note>original French: "Le coq... s'oyt par fois es Sabbats sonnāt la retraicte aux Sorciers."</note>²⁹

The witch traveled to the Sabbat in various ways. If it were a matter of attending a local assembly where, at most, a mile or two had to be traveled, the group would go on foot. Very often the distance was even less. It should be remembered that in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries—and indeed, until quite recently—once a traveler had gone a few steps outside the gates of a town or beyond the last house in a village, he was enfolded in darkness. He was entirely solitary, remote, and distant <note>original: "eloined"</note>. Madrid,³⁰ how black with shadows, dangerous, and utterly lonely was the pathless countryside! Witches often had to carry lanterns to light their way on the journey to the Sabbat. The learned Bartolomeo de Spina, of the Dominican Order <note>original: "O.P." (Order of Preachers)</note>,³¹ in his *Treatise on Sorceresses and Witches* <note>original Latin: "Tractatus de Strigibus et Lamiis"</note> (Venice, 1533), writes that a certain peasant living in Clavica Malaguzzi, in the district of Mirandola, had to rise very early one morning to drive to a neighboring village. At three o'clock, before daybreak, he found himself crossing a large stretch of wasteland that lay between him and his destination.

In the distance, he suddenly caught sight of what seemed to be numerous fires flickering back and forth. As he drew nearer, he saw that these were actually large lanterns held by a group of people who were moving here and there in the patterns of a bizarre dance, while others—as if at a country picnic—were seated eating delicacies and drinking mugs <note>original: "stoups"</note> of wine. At the same time, a harsh music, like the drone of a bagpipe <note>original: "cornemuse"</note>, filled the air. Strangely, no word was spoken; the company whirled and spun, ate and drank, in a bizarre and meaningful silence. 

Noticing that many people were shamelessly surrendering to the wildest debauchery and publicly performing sexual acts in the most indecent ways, the horrified onlooker realized he was witnessing the revels of the Sabbat. Crossing himself fervently and saying a prayer, he drove as fast as possible away from the accursed spot. However, before he left, he recognized some of the crowd as notorious wrongdoers and local residents who were already under grave suspicion of sorcery. The witches must have noticed his presence, but they seemed to ignore him and did not even attempt to chase him.

Very often, when going to a local Sabbat, the coven of witches used to meet just beyond the village and make their way to the appointed spot in a group for mutual help and security. This is pointed out by Bernard of Como <note>Bernardo Rategno da Como (c. 1450–1513), a Dominican inquisitor and author of a famous manual on witchcraft</note>, a famous scholar, who says:

The fact that these dark initiates walked to the Sabbat is frequently mentioned in the trials. Boguet <note>Henry Boguet (1550–1619), a French judge and demonologist</note>, who is most exact in detail, writes:

When Catharine Oswald of Niddrie (1625) one night took Alexander Hamilton, “a known warlock,” “to a den between Niddrie and Edmiston, where the Devil had arranged to meet her <note>original: "trysted hir"</note>,” it is obvious that the couple walked there together.

On one occasion, a truly subtle point was raised: whether those who walked to the Sabbat were as guilty as those who were carried there by the Devil. But De Lancre <note>Pierre de Lancre (1553–1631), a French judge who conducted a massive witch-hunt in Labourd</note> decided: 

> “It is truly as criminal and abominable for a sorcerer to go to the Sabbat on foot as to be voluntarily conveyed there by the Devil.”³⁵

Major Weir <note>Thomas Weir (1599–1670), a Covenanter executed for witchcraft and other crimes in Edinburgh</note> and his sister seem to have gone to a meeting with the Devil in a coach and six horses when they drove from Edinburgh to Musselburgh and back again on September 7, 1648. The woman confessed this in prison and added “that she and her brother had made a compact with the Devil.”³⁶

In the popular imagination, the witch is always associated with the broomstick, which she used to fly wildly through the air. This belief seems almost universal across all times and regions. The broomstick is, of course, closely connected to the magic wand or staff, which was considered just as useful for riding <note>original: "equitation"</note>. The wood it was made from often came from the hazel tree or witch-hazel, although in the days of Pierre de Lancre <note>De Lancre (1553–1631) was a French judge who conducted a famous witch-hunt in the Labourd region.</note>, the sorcerers of Southern France favored the "Souhandourra"—*Cornus sanguinea*, or dogwood. Amid hurricanes and tempests, in the very heart of the dark storm, the group of witches, straddling their broomsticks, sped swiftly along to the Sabbat. Their yells and hideous laughter sounded louder than the crashing elements, mingling in terrifying discord with the frantic howling of the wind.

There is a very important reference to these beliefs from the pen of the famous and learned Benedictine Abbot, Regino of Prüm (A.D. 906), who wrote in his influential work *Concerning Ecclesiastical Disciplines* <note>original: "De ecclesiasticis disciplinis"</note>:

> "This also must by no means be overlooked: certain utterly wicked women, turning aside to follow Satan and seduced by the illusions and ghostly visions of demons, firmly believe and openly claim that in the dead of night they ride upon certain beasts along with the pagan goddess Diana and a countless horde of women. They believe that in those silent hours, they fly over vast stretches of country and obey her as their mistress, while on certain other nights they are summoned to pay her honor and serve her."³⁹ 

Witches sometimes rode upon a broom <note>original: "besom"</note> or a stick, and sometimes upon an animal. This journey through the air was generally preceded by anointing themselves <note>original: "unction"</note> with a magic ointment. Various recipes are given for this ointment...

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

And it is interesting to note that they contain deadly poisons: aconite, belladonna, and hemlock.⁴⁰ Although these ointments <note>original: "unguents"</note> may in certain circumstances be capable of producing definite physiological results, it is Delrio <note>Martín del Río (1544–1608) was a Jesuit theologian and author of a highly influential book on magic and witchcraft.</note> who best sums up the reasons for their use:

> "The Demon is able to carry them to the Sabbat without the use of any ointment, and often he does so. But for several reasons, he prefers that they should anoint themselves. Sometimes, when the witches seem afraid, it serves to encourage them. When they are young and tender, they will thus be better able to bear the hateful embrace of Satan, who has assumed the shape of a man. For by this horrid anointing, he dulls their senses and persuades these deluded wretches that there is some great virtue in the sticky <note>original: "viscid"</note> lubricant. Sometimes, too, he does this in hateful mockery of God’s holy Sacraments, and so that through these mysterious ceremonies he may infuse, as it were, something of a ritual and liturgical nature into his beastly orgies."⁴¹

Although the witch is universally credited with the power to fly through the air⁴² to the Sabbat mounted upon a broomstick <note>original: "besom"</note> or some kind of stick, it is remarkable, given popular belief, to find that the confessions admitting this actual mode of aerial transport are extraordinarily few. Paul Grilland, in his treatise *On Sorceries* <note>original: "De Sortilegiis"</note> (Lyons, 1533), speaks of a witch in Rome during whose trial, seven years before, it was asserted she flew in the air after she had anointed her limbs with a magic liniment. Perhaps the most detailed accounts of this feat are to be found in Boguet <note>Henri Boguet (c. 1550–1619) was a French judge known for his severe prosecutions of witches.</note>, who meticulously reports the lengthy and rambling evidence of witches—evidence he laboriously gathered during the notorious trials throughout Franche-Comté <note>A historical province in eastern France.</note> in the summer of 1598. He records quite plainly such statements as:

> "Françoise Secretain said that in order to go to the Sabbat, she placed a white stick between her legs and then pronounced certain words, and from then on she was carried through the air to the sorcerers’ assembly." <note>original: "Françoise Secretain disoit, que pour aller au Sabbat, elle mettoit un baston blanc entre ses iambes & puis prononçait certaines paroles & dés lors elle estoit portée par l’air iusques en l’assemblée des Sorciers."</note>

## THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

Certain of the Aberdeen witches (1597) “danced a devilish dance, riding on trees for a long time.” In an old representation of Dr. Fian and his company swiftly pacing around North Berwick church counter-clockwise <note>original: "withershins," meaning to move in a direction opposite to the sun's path, considered unlucky or diabolical</note>, the witches are depicted running and leaping in the air, some mounted on broomsticks, others carrying their brooms <note>original: "besoms"</note> in their hands.

There was discovered in the closet of Dame Alice Kyteler of Kilkenny—who was arrested in 1324 upon accusations of nightly meetings with a familiar spirit named Artisson and numerous charges of sorcery—a pipe of ointment with which she greased a staff “upon which she ambled <note>original: "ambolled"</note> and galloped through thick and thin, whenever and in whatever manner she pleased.”⁴⁶ In the trial of Martha Carrier, a notorious witch and “rampant hag” at the Court of Oyer and Terminer <note>original: "Oyer and Terminer," a legal commission to "hear and determine" criminal cases</note> held by adjournment at Salem on August 2, 1692, the eighth article of the indictment ran: “One Foster, who confessed her own share in the witchcraft for which the prisoner stood indicted, affirmed that she had seen the prisoner at some of their witch-meetings, and that it was this *Carrier* who persuaded her to be a witch. She confessed that the Devil carried them on a pole to a witch-meeting; but the pole broke, and she, hanging about *Carrier’s* neck, they both fell down, and she then received an injury from the fall, from which she had not yet recovered by this time.”⁴⁷

In many of these instances, it is plain that no actual flight through the air is implied; although there is a "riding a-cock-horse" on brooms or sticks, it is, in fact, a piece of symbolic ritual.

It is very relevant, however, to notice in this connection the actual levitation of human beings. Although perhaps an unusual phenomenon, it is by no means unknown in the séances of modern spiritualism <note>original: "spiritism"</note>, where both the levitation of persons (with which we are solely concerned) and the rising of tables or chairs off the ground without contact with any individual or by any human agency have occurred again and again. These have happened under conditions which cannot possibly allow for sleight of hand <note>original: "legerdemain"</note>, illusion, or trickery. From a mass of irrefutable evidence, we may select some striking words by Sir William Crookes, a Fellow of the Royal Society, regarding levitation. “This has occurred,” he writes, “in my presence on four occasions in darkness; but . . . I will only mention cases in which deduc-

This mark is as near as may be six feet from the floor. . . . From the position of the mark on the wall, it is clear that my head must have been close to the ceiling. . . . I was simply levitated and lowered to my old place.”⁵⁰

Above all, St. Joseph of Cupertino (1603–1663), one of the most extraordinary mystics of the seventeenth century, whose whole life seemed to be one long series of unbroken raptures and ecstasies, was frequently lifted on high to remain suspended in mid-air. So much attention was drawn by this marvel that his superiors moved him from one lonely house of Capuchins or Conventual Franciscans <note>original: "Conventuals"</note> to another; he eventually died at the small hill town of Osimo, where his remains are still venerated today. For many years, he was obliged to say Mass at a private altar because the ecstasies that came upon him during the Sacrifice of the Mass were so inevitable. I believe there are few sanctuaries more sweet and fragrant with holiness than this convent at Osimo. During a most happy visit to the shrine of St. Joseph, I was deeply touched by the many memorials of the Saint and by the kindness of the Fathers, who are his modern-day brethren. It is well known that in a certain London church, a holy member of a religious order <note>original: "religious"</note> was frequently <note>original: "not unseldom"</note> levitated from the altar platform <note>original: "predella"</note> while saying Mass. But, as Görres <note>Joseph von Görres (1776–1848) was a German writer and scholar of Christian mysticism.</note> very appropriately remarks,⁵⁵ although many examples can be cited of Saints who have levitated while in a spiritual trance <note>original: "ecstasy"</note>, and although it is not impossible for evil powers to imitate this phenomenon—as indeed they certainly do in the cases of spiritualist mediums—we find nowhere in the biographies of the saints <note>original: "hagiography"</note> that a large number of Saints were raised from the earth together as a group or carried through the air to meet at an appointed spot. Is it likely, then, that demons would be permitted to appear to surpass, through their own power, such an extraordinary and exceptional divine miracle? It must also be remembered that, except in very rare and unique instances such as that of St. Joseph of Cupertino, levitation usually only reaches a height of a foot or about eighteen inches, and even this rarely happens except during moments of great solemnity and intense mental focus <note>original: "psychic concentration"</note>.

A question that is widely discussed by demonologists <note>scholars who study demons and the supernatural</note> then arises: Do witches actually attend the Sabbat <note>the secret gathering of witches</note> in person, or is their journey and presence there merely a diabolical illusion? Giovanni Francesco Ponzinibio, in his work *On Witches* <note>original: "De Lamiis"</note>,⁵⁶ completely leans toward the latter view. However, this is superficial reasoning, and the celebrated expert in church law <note>original: "canonist"</note> Francisco Peña rightly takes him very severely to task for his boldness. Peña’s profound work, *Notes on the "Lantern of Inquisitors" by the Dominican Bernard of Como and his treatise on witches* <note>original: "In Bernardi Comensis Dominicani Lucernam inquisitorum notæ et eiusdem tractatum de strigibus"</note>,⁵⁷ which is a valuable collection of highly scholarly commentaries <note>original: "erudite glosses"</note>, entirely refutes Ponzinibio’s arguments and presents the case with weighty authority.

Sprenger, in the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Malleus Maleficarum"</note>, Part I, had already considered “How witches are bodily transported from one place to another,” and he concludes, “It is proven, then, that sorcerers can be bodily transported.”⁵⁸ Paul Grilland asks: “Whether magicians and witches or Satanists are...”

...whether they are bodily and actually transported back and forth by the Devil, or whether this is merely imaginary?" In his *Compendium of Witches* <note>original: *Compendium Maleficarum*</note>, Francesco Maria Guazzo discusses (Book 1, Chapter 13) "Whether witches are actually and physically transported from place to place to attend their Sabbats" <note>The Sabbat was the term used for the secret nocturnal gathering of witches.</note>; and he states:

> "The opinion held by many followers of Luther and Melanchthon <note>Leaders of the Protestant Reformation.</note> is that witches only attend these assemblies in their imagination, and that they are deceived <note>original: "choused"</note> by some trick of the devil. In support of this argument, those who object assert that witches have very often been seen lying in one spot without moving. Moreover, the story related in the life of Saint Germain is relevant here: specifically, when certain women declared that they had been present at a banquet, and yet all the while they slumbered and slept, as several witnesses confirmed. It is certain that women of this kind are very often deceived in such a way; but it is by no means certain that they are *always* so deceived. . . . The alternative opinion, which I personally hold most strongly, is that sometimes, at any rate, witches are actually transported from one place to another by the Devil. He carries them himself while in the bodily form of a goat or some other unclean and monstrous animal, and they are truly and indeed present at their foul midnight Sabbats. This is the opinion generally held by the authoritative theologians and expert legal scholars <note>original: "Master Jurisprudists"</note> of Italy and Spain, as well as by Catholic divines and lawyers. Indeed, the majority of writers promote this view—for example, Torquemada in his commentary on Grilland; Remy; Saint Peter Damian; Silvester of Abula; Tommaso de Vio Gaetani <note>Also known as Cardinal Cajetan.</note>; Alfonso de Castro; Sixtus of Siena, of the Order of Preachers <note>original: "O.P." (Dominicans)</note>; Father <note>original: "Père"</note> Crespet; Bartolomeo Spina in his explanations <note>original: "glosses"</note> of Ponzinibio; Lorenzo Anania; and a vast number of others, whose names I omit here for the sake of brevity."⁶¹

This seems to sum up the whole matter perfectly. In the encyclopedic treatise *On Witches* <note>original: *De Strigibus*</note>⁶² by an earlier authority, Bernard of Como, the following remarkable passage occurs: “These abominable wretches attend these assemblies—or rather, orgies—while they are actually awake and in full possession of their normal senses. When they are going to a nearby location, they travel there on foot, conversing cheerfully as they walk. However, if they are to meet in a distant place, they are carried by the Devil. Regardless of how they travel—whether on foot or carried by the Devil—it is certain that their journey is real and physical, and not imaginary. They are not suffering from any delusion when they renounce the Catholic faith, worship and adore the Devil, trample on the Cross of Christ, desecrate the Most Blessed Sacrament, and surrender themselves to filthy and unhallowed sexual acts. They commit fornication with the Devil himself, who appears to them in human form—acting as a *succubus* <note>original: "succubus"; a demon in female form believed to have sex with men.</note> for the men and as an *incubus* <note>original: "incubus"; a demon in male form believed to have sex with women.</note> for the women.”⁶³

The conclusion, then, is clear and proven. Witches do actually and individually attend the Sabbat, an orgy of blasphemy and obscenity. Whether they travel there on foot, on horseback, or by some other means is a minor detail that varies according to different and infinitely varied circumstances.

It is not denied that hallucination and self-deception played a large part in some cases, but such examples are relatively few in number. Furthermore, these cases were carefully investigated and usually identified by the judges and theologians <note>original: "divines".</note>. For example, in the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: *Malleus Maleficarum*, the famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note>, Sprenger tells of a woman who voluntarily turned herself in to be examined as a witch. She confessed to the Dominican friars that she attended the Sabbat every night and that no locks or bars could stop her from flying to those hellish celebrations. Consequently, she was locked securely in a room from which escape was impossible, while sharp-eyed <note>original: "lynx-eyed".</note> officers watched her through a secret vent <note>original: "soupirail"; an air hole or small window, often used for observation.</note>. They reported that as soon as the door was closed, she threw herself onto the bed, where she immediately became perfectly rigid in every limb. In the celebrated cases investigated by Henri Boguet in June 1598, young George Gandillon confessed to having walked to the Sabbat at a deserted spot called Fontenelles, near the village of Nezar, and also to having ridden to the Sabbat. Moreover, in his indictment, the following occurs:

> “George Gandillon, on one Good Friday night, lay in his bed, rigid as a corpse, for the space of three hours, and then suddenly came to himself. He has since been burned alive here with his father and his sister.” ⁶⁴

# THE SABBAT

**12. Satan is always the imitator <note>original: "Ape"</note> of God in everything.**

As the procedure in the various Sabbats <note>A secret midnight assembly of witches and sorcerers to worship the Devil.</note> differed very greatly according to the century, decade, country, and district—and even according to the social status and the very temperaments of those assembled—it is only possible to outline in a general way some of the most remarkable ceremonies which took place during these infernal congregations. An intimate and intensive study of the Sabbat would require a large volume, for it is quite possible to reconstruct the rites in every particular, although the precise order of the ritual was not always and everywhere the same.

Dom Calmet <note>Antoine Augustin Calmet (1672–1757), a French Benedictine monk and scholar famous for his works on the Bible and his "Treatise on Apparitions."</note>, it is true, has very mistakenly said: “To attempt to give a description of the Sabbat is to attempt a description of what does not exist, and what has never existed except in the fantastic and disordered imagination of warlocks and witches; the pictures which have been drawn of these assemblies are merely the fantasy of those who dreamed that they had actually been carried, body and soul, through the air to the Sabbat.”⁶⁶ What a happy skeptic! But unfortunately, the Sabbat did—and does—take place; formerly in deserted wastes, on the hillside, and in secluded spots, and now, as often as not, in the privacy of vaults and cellars, and in those lone empty houses innocently marked with "To be Sold" signs.

The President of the Sabbat was, in purely local gatherings, often the leader <note>original: "Officer"</note> of the district; in the more formal assemblies convened from a wider area, it was the Grand Master, whose dignity would be proportionate to the numbers of the company and the extent of his province. In any case, the President was officially known as the “Devil,” and it would seem that his immediate attendants and followers <note>original: "satellites"</note> were also somewhat loosely termed “devils.” This formal naming system has given rise to considerable confusion and quite a bit of mystery in the reports of witch trials and the confessions of offenders. But in many instances it is certain—and traditional religious belief <note>original: "orthodoxy"</note> forbids us to doubt the possibility—that the Principle of Evil, made flesh <note>original: "incarnate"</note>, was present for the hideous adoration of his foolish <note>original: "besotted"</note> worshippers. Such is the opinion of the Church Fathers <note>The influential early Christian theologians whose writings established the intellectual and doctrinal foundations of Christianity.</note>,

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

Such is the conclusion of the theologians who have dealt with these dark abominations. Metaphysically it is possible; historically it is indisputable.

When a human being—a man—occupied the chief position at these meetings and directed the performance of the rites, he would sometimes appear in a hideous and grotesque disguise, and sometimes without any attempt at concealment. This masquerade generally took the shape of an animal and had its origin in paganism <note>original: "heathendom"</note>, from which it passed through the ceremonies of heretics to the sorcerer and the witch. As early as the *Penitential Book* <note>original: *Liber Pœnitentialis*</note> of St. Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury (668–690), we have a distinct prohibition of this foul mummery. Chapter 27 <note>original: "Capitulum xxvii"</note> denounces the man who "goes about as a little stag or a heifer during the Kalends of January" <note>original Latin: "in Kalendas Ianuarii in ceruulo et in uitula uadit"</note>. It states: "If anyone at the Kalends <note>The first day of the month in the Roman calendar, often associated with New Year celebrations</note> of January goes about as a stag or a bull—that is, making himself into a wild animal, dressing in the skin of a herd animal, and putting on the heads of beasts—those who transform themselves into the appearance of a wild animal in such a way shall perform penance for three years because this is devilish."

Among the many animal forms which the leader of the Sabbat (the "Devil") assumed in masquerade, the most common are the bull, the cat, and above all the goat. Thus the Basque term for the Sabbat is "*Akhelarre*," which means "goat pasture." Sometimes the leader is simply said to have shown himself in the shape of a beast, which possibly points to the traditional disguise of a black hairy skin, horns, hoofs, claws, and a tail—in fact, the same costume a demon wore upon the stage.⁶⁷ In an old German ballad, *The Witch's Gazette* <note>original: *Druten Zeitung*</note>, printed at Schmalkalden in 1627, "to be sung to the tune of *Dorothea*," it is said that the judges, anxious to extract a confession from a witch, sent down into her dim dungeon the common hangman dressed in a bear’s skin with horns, hoofs, and tail complete. The miserable prisoner, thinking that Lucifer had indeed visited her, at once appealed to him for help:

> -> Whom they had dressed up properly, <-
> -> In a bear’s skin, <-
> -> As if he were the Devil; <-
> -> When the witch <note>original German: "Drut"</note> looked at him, <-
