### THE SABBAT

Here we have a curious and perhaps unique example of the "demoniac masquerade" being subtly used to obtain evidence of guilt through a trick. The Aberdeen witch Jonet Lucas (1597) said that the Devil was at the Sabbat "being in the likeness of a beast." However, Agnes Wobster, a member of the same company, declared that "Satan appeared to them in the likeness of a calf," so it is possible that two different disguises were used. Gabriel Pellé (1608) confessed that he attended a Sabbat presided over by the Devil, and "the Devil was in the form of a black cow" <note>original French: "le Diable estoit en vache noire"</note>.⁶⁸ Françoise Secretain, who was tried in August 1598, saw the Devil "sometimes in the form of a cat" <note>original French: "tantost en forme de chat"</note>. Rolande de Vernois acknowledged that "the Devil presented himself then at the Sabbat in the form of a large black cat" <note>original French: "Le Diable se presenta pour lors au Sabbat en forme d’vn groz chat noir"</note>.⁶⁹

There are innumerable allusions to the goat. In the Basses-Pyrénées (1609): "The Devil was in the form of a goat, having a tail, and underneath it was the face of a black man" <note>original French: "Le Diable estoit en forme de bouc ayant vne queue & audessous vn visage d’homme noir"</note>. Iohannis d’Aguerre said that the Devil was "in the form of a goat" <note>original French: "en forme de bouc"</note>.⁷⁰ Marie d’Aguerre said that "there was in the midst of the ring an immense pitcher from which the Devil issued in the form of a goat." Gentien le Clerc, who was tried at Orleans in 1614, "said that, as he was told, his mother presented him at the Sabbat to a goat when he was three years old; they saluted the goat as 'the Asp'" <note>original French: "l’Aspic"</note>.⁷¹ "On the throne," writes Görres, "is seated a goat, or at least the form of a goat, for the demon cannot hide what he is" <note>original French: "Sur le trône est assis un bouc, ou du moins la forme d’un bouc, car le démon ne peut cacher ce qu’il est"</note>.⁷²

In 1630, Elizabeth Stevenson, also known as Toppock, of Niddrie, confessed to her judges that she went to a "den between Niddrie and Edmiston" where the Devil had arranged to meet her. She was accompanied by Catharine Oswald—who was tried for being a witch *by habit and reputation*—and Alexander Hamilton, a "known warlock." She claimed the Devil "appeared first to them like a foal, and then like a man, and appointed a new meeting <term>dyet: a scheduled date or meeting, often for legal or formal purposes</term> at Salcott Moor." When one of Catharine Oswald’s associates, Alexander Hunter (also known as Hamilton or Hattaraick), a "Warlock Churl" <note>original Scots: "Warlok Cairle"; a 'cairle' or 'carline' is a term for a peasant or a person of low birth, often used dismissively</note> who "deceived the country for a long time,"⁷³ was arrested at Dunbar, he confessed that the Devil would meet him riding upon a black horse, or in the shape of a raven <note>original: "corbie"</note>, a cat, or a dog. He was burned upon Castle Hill, Edinburgh, in 1631.

In the second half of the 18th century, the territory of Limburg <note>A region now divided between the Netherlands and Belgium.</note> was terrorized by a mysterious society known as "**The Goats**." These wretches met at night in a secret chapel, and after the most hideous orgies—which included paying divine honors to Satan and other foul blasphemies of the Sabbat—they put on masks made to look like goats' heads, draped themselves in long disguising cloaks, and went out in bands to plunder and destroy. Between 1772 and 1774 alone, the tribunal of Foquemont condemned 400 "Goats" to the gallows. However, the organization was not completely wiped out until about the year 1780, following a period of the most repressive measures and constant vigilance.

Among certain tribes living in the regions of the Congo, there exists a secret association of Egbo worshippers. **Egbo** (or **Ekpé**) is the evil spirit or Satan. His rituals are **Obeah** <note>original: "Obeeyahism"</note>—the adoration of **Obi**, or the Devil. # THE SABBAT

The first ceremony of the Sabbat was the worship of, and the paying of homage to, the Devil. It would seem that sometimes this was preceded by a roll-call of the evil devotees. Agnes Sampson <note>A central figure in the North Berwick witch trials of 1590 in Scotland.</note> confessed that at the meeting in North Berwick, when the whole assembly had entered the church, “The *Devil* started up himself in the pulpit like a large <note>original: "mickle"</note> black man, and calling the roll <note>original: "Row"</note>, every one answered *‘Here.’* When *Mr. Robert Grierson* was named, they all ran in confusion <note>original: "hirdie girdie"</note> and were angry, for it had been promised he should be called *Robert the Comptroller*, or *Rob the Rower*, instead of using his real name <note>original: "expriming of his name"</note>. The first thing he demanded was whether they had been good servants, and what they had done since the last time they had convened.”

The witches adored Satan, or the Master of the Sabbat who presided in place of Satan, through prostrations, kneeling, gestures, and bows. In mockery of solemn bows and polite courtesies, the worshippers of the Demon approach him awkwardly, with grotesque and obscene grimaces <note>original: "mops and mows"</note>, sometimes straddling sideways, sometimes walking backwards, as Guazzo <note>Francesco Maria Guazzo, author of the *Compendium Maleficarum* (1608).</note> says: "When they approach the demons to worship them, they turn their backs and, as they are about to make their supplication, they walk backward like crabs, placing their hands behind them with the palms reversed." <note>original Latin: *Cum accedunt ad dæmones eos ueneraturi terga obuertunt & cessim eum cancrorum more supplicaturi manus inuersas retro applicant*.</note> But their chief act of homage was the reverential kiss, the "shameful kiss" <note>original Latin: *osculum infame*</note>. This impious and lewd ritual is mentioned in detail by most authorities and is to be found in all lands and centuries. 

So Delrio <note>Martin Delrio, a Jesuit theologian and author of *Disquisitionum Magicarum Libri Sex* (1599).</note> writes: “The Sabbat is presided over by a Demon, the Lord of the Sabbat, who appears in some monstrous form, most generally as a goat or some hound of hell, seated upon a haughty throne. The witches who resort to the Sabbat approach the throne with their backs turned, and worship him . . . and then, as a sign of their homage, they kiss his fundament <note>The buttocks or anus.</note>.” Guazzo notes: “As a sign of homage, witches kiss the Devil’s fundament.” And Ludwig Elich <note>A German legal scholar and author of *Daemonomagia* (1607).</note> says: “Then as a token of their homage—with reverence be it spoken—they kiss the fundament of the Devil.” “And at the time they kiss him under the tail, he releases a flatulence of a very horrible odor,” <note>original Spanish: *Y al tiempo que le besan debajo de la cola, da una ventosidad de muy horrible olor*</note> adds the Spanish *Relacion* <note>An official account or report of a trial, likely the Logroño trial of 1610.</note>, “fetid, foul, and filthy.”

To cite other authorities would be merely to quote the same words. Thomas Cooper, indeed, seems to regard this ceremony as a part of the rite of admission, but to confine it to this occasion alone is clearly incorrect, for there is a continual record of its observance at frequent Sabbats by witches of many years' standing. "Secondly," he remarks, "when this acknowledgment is made, in testimony of this subjection, Satan offers his back-parts to be kissed by his vassal."<note>Thomas Cooper (c. 1569–1626) was an English clergyman and author of *The Mystery of Witchcraft* (1617).</note> But in the indictment <note>original: "dittay"</note> of the North Berwick witches, all of whom had long been notorious for their malpractices, "Item, the said Agnes Sampson confessed that the devil, being then at North Berwick Kirk, awaiting their arrival in the form or likeness of a man, and seeing that they tarried too long, at their arrival commanded them all to a penance; which was, that they should kiss his buttocks in sign of duty to him, which being put bare over the pulpit, everyone did as he had commanded them."<note>The North Berwick witch trials (1590) were a series of famous Scottish trials involving King James VI.</note>

One of the principal charges which was repeatedly brought against the Knights Templars during the lengthy ecclesiastical and judicial processes (1307–1314) was that of the *shameful kiss* <note>original: "osculum infame"</note> given by the juniors to their superiors <note>original: "preceptors"</note>. Even so prejudiced a writer as Lea <note>Henry Charles Lea (1825–1909), an American historian known for his critical works on the Inquisition.</note> cannot help but admit the truth of this accusation. In this case, however, it has nothing to do with sorcery but must be connected with the homosexuality which the Order universally practiced.

There are some very important details recounted in a Papal Bull dated June 8, 1303, from the noble but slandered <note>original: "calumniated"</note> Boniface VIII, with reference to the case of Walter Langton, Bishop of Lichfield and Coventry (1296–1322) and treasurer to Edward I. This high-ranking clergyman was accused of sorcery and paying homage to Satan: "For some time past it has come to our ears that our Venerable Brother Walter, Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield, has been commonly defamed and accused, both in the realm of England and elsewhere, of paying homage to the Devil by kissing his posterior, and that he has had frequent conversations <note>original: "colloquies"</note> with evil spirits." The Bishop cleared himself of these charges with his character witnesses <note>original: "compurgators"</note>. Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and demonologist.</note> refers to Guillaume Edeline, who was executed in 1453 as a wizard. He was a doctor of the Sorbonne and prior of Saint-Germain-en-Laye: "The aforesaid Lord Guillaume..."

...confessed that he had done homage to the aforementioned Satan, who appeared in the shape of a ram, by kissing his buttocks as a token of reverence and homage. (Note 83). A very rare pamphlet <note>original: "tract"</note> from the fourteenth century directed against the Waldenses <note>The Waldenses were a medieval Christian movement that was declared heretical and often accused by the Church of practicing witchcraft.</note> among other charges brings the following: "Also, in some other regions, the Devil appears to them in the form and shape of a cat, which they kiss one by one under its tail." <note>original: "Item, in aliquibus aliis partibus apparet eis dæmon sub specie et figura cati, quem sub cauda sigillatim osculantur."</note> (Note 84).

Barthélemy Minguet of Brécy, a young man of twenty-five who was tried in 1616, said that at the Sabbat "he often saw [the Devil] in the shape of a man who held a horse by its bridle, and that they went forward to worship him, each one holding a pitch candle of black wax in their hands." (Note 85). These candles, as Guazzo <note>Francesco Maria Guazzo (c. 1570–1640) was an Italian priest and author of the influential witch-hunting manual *Compendium Maleficarum* (1608).</note> tells us, were symbolic and required by the ritual of the Sabbat, not merely used for the purpose of giving light: "Then they made an offering of pitch-black candles, and as a sign of homage kissed his backside." (Note 86). The candles were ordinarily black, and one taper, larger than the rest, was frequently carried by the Devil himself. At the North Berwick meeting when the witches were all to assemble in the church, "John Fian <note>original: "Iohn Fein"</note> blew open the church doors and blew in the lights, which were like large <note>original: "Mickl"</note> black candles sticking all around the pulpit." (Note 87). Boguet <note>Henry Boguet (1550–1619) was a French judge known for his severe prosecutions of witches.</note> relates that the witches whom he tried confessed that the Sabbat commenced with the adoration of Satan, "who appeared, sometimes in the shape of a tall dark man, sometimes in the shape of a goat; and to express their worship and homage, they made him an offering of candles, which burned with a blue light." (Note 88). John Fian, also, when doing homage to the Devil, "thought he saw the light of a candle... which appeared as a blue flame <note>original: "blue lowe"</note>." This, of course, was on account of the sulfurous material from which these candles were specially made. De Lancre <note>Pierre de Lancre (1553–1631) was a French judge who conducted a massive witch hunt in the Basque region of Labourd.</note> expressly states that the candles or torches <note>original: "flambeaux"</note> used at the Sabbat were made of pitch.

An important feature of the greater Sabbats was the ritual dance, for the dance was an act of devotion which has descended to us from the earliest times and is to be found in every age and country. Dancing is a natural movement, a primitive expression of emotion and ideals. In the ancient world, there can have been few things more beautiful than that rhythmic thanksgiving of flexible limbs and sweet voices...

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

...which Athens loved, and for many a century the memory of that day was preserved when the young Sophocles led the choir in celebration of the victory of Salamis. <note>The Battle of Salamis (480 BCE) was a major naval victory for the Greeks against the Persian Empire.</note> The Mystae <note>original: "Mystæ"; these were the initiated members of the ancient Greek mystery religions.</note> in the meadows of Elysium <note>In Greek mythology, the dwelling place of the blessed after death.</note> danced their rounds with the silver clash of cymbals and with madly twinkling snow-white feet. At the solemn procession of the Ark from Kiriath-Jearim <note>original: "Cariathiarim"</note>, King David "danced with all his might before the Lord... dancing and leaping before the Lord." Saint Basil urges his disciples to dance on earth in order to fit themselves for what may be one of the occupations of the angels in heaven. 

As late as the seventeenth century, the ceremonial dance in church was not uncommon. In 1683, it was the duty of the senior canon to lead a dance of choirboys in the Paris cathedral. Among the Abyssinian <note>Ethiopian</note> Christians, dancing forms a significant part of worship. Year by year on Whit Tuesday <note>The Tuesday following Pentecost, a Christian feast day.</note>, hundreds of pilgrims dance through the streets of Echternach (Luxembourg) to the shrine of Saint Willibrord in Saint Peter’s Church. Formerly, the devotees danced three times around the great Abbey Courtyard before proceeding to the sanctuary. 

But beyond all these, the dance still has its own place in the ritual of the Holy Church even today. Three times a year in Seville Cathedral—on Holy Thursday, upon Corpus Christi, and the feast of the Immaculate Conception—"The Sixes" <note>original: "Los Seises"; a traditional dance performed by choirboys in Seville Cathedral.</note> dance before a specially constructed altar, exquisitely adorned with flowers and lights, erected near the outer door of the grand western entrance of the cathedral. This ceremony in all probability dates from the thirteenth century.

The dresses of the boys, who dance before the improvised altar at Benediction on Corpus Christi, are from the period of Philip III <note>King of Spain from 1598 to 1621.</note> and consist of short trousers and jackets that hang from one shoulder; the doublets <note>A man's snug-fitting buttoned jacket.</note> are made of red satin with rich embroidery. Plumed white hats with feathers are worn, along with shoes featuring large, sparkling buckles. On Holy Thursday, the costume is also red and white, while it is blue and white for "the day of the Virgin."

The eight boy choristers—with eight others as attendants—dance with castanets in their hands to a soft organ accompaniment <note>original: "obbligato"</note>, advancing slowly and gracefully down the center of the cathedral to the decorated altar. Here they remain for about a quarter of an hour, singing a hymn and accompanying it (like the carols of olden times <note>Originally, a "carol" referred to a dance in a ring accompanied by singing, not just a Christmas song.</note>) with dance and castanets.

# THE SABBAT

They sing a two-part hymn in front of the altar, forming into two groups of eight, facing each other, with the clergy kneeling in a semi-circle around them.

I certainly cannot do better than to quote Mr. Arthur Symons’ judgment of this dance as he saw it a few years ago in Seville:

> “And, yes, I found it perfectly dignified, perfectly religious, without a suspicion of levity or indecorum. This consecration of the dance, this turning of a possible vice into a means of devotion, this bringing of the people’s art, the people’s passion—which in Seville is dancing—into the church and finding a place for it there, is precisely one of those acts of divine worldly wisdom which the Church has so often practiced in her conquest of the world.”

It is not too far-fetched for a writer to suggest that the High Mass itself, in some sense, preserves a survival of the ancient religious dance—that stately, magnificent series of slow movements which surely can express devotion of the most solemn and reverent kind, just as much as the color of a vestment or sanctuary, or the sounds of music.

Because the dance is so fundamentally religious, it must inevitably be mocked and parodied by the "ape of God" <note>original: "God's ape"; a traditional name for the Devil, who was said to mockingly imitate God's sacred rites.</note>. For the dance of the witches is degraded, awkward, foul, and unclean. These very movements are counter-clockwise <note>original: "withershins"; moving in a direction opposite to the sun's path, considered unlucky or diabolical.</note>, as Guazzo points out: “Then follow the round dances in which, however, they always tread the measure to the left.”⁹⁰ “The sorcerers,” says Boguet, “dance a country dance with their backs turned to one another.”⁹¹ This, of course, is the exact reverse of a natural country dance. “Sometimes, although seldom,” he adds, “they dance in couples, and sometimes one partner is here and another there, for everything is always in confusion.”⁹² De Lancre writes of witches’ revels: “They only dance three kinds of bransles <note>original: "brawls"; a type of French Renaissance dance.</note>. . . . The first is in the Gypsy style <note>original: "*à la Bohémienne*"</note> . . . the second with quick trippings: these are round dances.”⁹³ In the third Sabbat dance, the dancers were placed one behind another in a straight line.

An old Basque legend reported by Estefanella Hirigaray describes how the witches were accustomed to meet near an old lime kiln to dance their rounds, a ceremony regarded throughout that district as an essential feature of the Sabbat. De Lancre notes the Gypsy-style dances <note>original: "brawls *à la Bohémienne*"</note> as especially favored by sorcerers in Labourd <note>A historical Basque province in France.</note>. # THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio (1460–1523), Master of the Sacred Palace and the great champion of orthodoxy against the leader of the heretics <term>heresiarch</term> Luther, in his learned work *Concerning the Magic of Witches* <note>original: "De Strigimagia"</note>⁹⁴ relates that in Como and Brescia, a number of children between eight and twelve years old who had attended the Sabbat, but had been fortunately converted by the tireless patience of the Inquisitors, gave demonstrations of these dances at the request of their superiors. They showed such extraordinary cleverness and skill in performing the most complicated and strange patterns that it was clear they had been taught by more than just human instruction. Marco de Viqueria, the Dominican Prior of the Brussels monastery, investigated the matter thoroughly. He was a clergyman known for such sharp insight and exceptional integrity that his testimony soon convinced many high-ranking officials in Rome who were inclined to suspect some trickery or clever deception. In Belgium, this Sabbat dance was known as the *Pavane* <note>original: "Pauana"; a slow, processional dance common in Europe.</note>.

In the Fian trial, Agnes Sampson confessed that “They danced through the churchyard <note>original: "Kirk-yeard"</note>, while Geillis Duncan played on a trump <note>original: "Trump"; a small mouth instrument also known as a jaw harp or Jew’s harp.</note>, and John Fian, who was hooded <note>original: "mussiled"; meaning masked or blindfolded</note>, led the ring dance. Agnes and her daughter followed next. Besides these, there were Kate Gray, George Noilis’s wife, . . . with the rest of their associates <term>cummers</term> numbering over a hundred people.”⁹⁵ She further added “that this Geillis Duncan went before them, playing this reel or dance on a small trump, called a Jew’s trump, until they entered the North Berwick church.”⁹⁶ “These confessions filled the King [James I, then James VI of Scotland] with wonderful amazement, and he sent for the said Geillis Duncan, who played the same dance on a similar trump before His Majesty.”

Music generally accompanied the dancers, and there is plenty of evidence that various instruments were played: violins, flutes, tambourines, citterns <note>original: "citterns"; a stringed instrument similar to a guitar</note>, oboes <note>original: "hautboys"</note>, and, in Scotland, the bagpipes. Those witches who had any skill were the performers, and they often entertained the group for a while with favorite popular songs; however, the concert always ended in the most hideous discord and animalistic noise; the rules of harmony and decency were both crudely broken. In August 1590, a man named Nicolas Laghernhard, while traveling to Assencauria, was passing through the edge of a forest when he saw through the trees a number of men and women...

Madeleine de la Palud declared that she had never seen salt, olives, or oil at the Devil's feasts.¹⁰⁹

These are all forms that have been used by heretical sects, and it may be that the Templars <note>The Knights Templar were a Catholic military order accused of heresy and devil-worship in the early 14th century.</note> used one of these. But it is far more probable that the words were purposely omitted; the Templars were corrupted by Gnostic doctrines and held the heresies of the Mandaeans or Johannites, who were filled with an insane hatred of Christ in much the same way as witches and demon-worshipers. They followed the tenets of the Ophites <term>Ophites</term> <note>a Gnostic sect that revered the serpent of Genesis as a bringer of knowledge</note>, who worshiped the Serpent and prayed to him for protection against the Creator. They adored and offered sacrifice before an idol—a Head—which, as Professor Prutz holds, represented the lower god whom Gnostic groups worshiped: Satan. At his trial in Tuscany, the knight Bernard of Parma confessed that the Order firmly believed this idol had the power to save and to enrich; in short, it was pure diabolism. The secret mass of the Templars may have parodied an Eastern liturgy rather than the Western rite, but it was nonetheless the essential worship of the principle of evil.

In 1336, a priest who had been imprisoned by the Count of Foix, Gaston III Phoebus, on a charge of celebrating a Satanic mass, was sent to Avignon and examined by Pope Benedict XII in person. The next year, the same pope appointed his trusted official Guillaume Lombard to preside at the trial of Pierre du Chesne, a priest from the diocese of Tarbes who was accused of desecrating the Host.

Gilles de Sillé, a priest of the diocese of St. Malo, and the Florentine Antonio Francesco Prelati (formerly of the diocese of Arezzo) were accustomed to officiating at the black masses of Tiffauges and Machecoul. These were the castles of Gilles de Rais <note>Gilles de Rais (c. 1405–1440) was a French nobleman and former comrade of Joan of Arc who was executed for the serial murder of children and practicing the occult.</note>, who was executed in 1440.

In the sixteenth century, a priest named Benedictus caused a great scandal when it was discovered that he had assisted in secret and unholy rites. In Paris, a friar named Séchelle was burned at the stake in the Place de Grève <note>A public square in Paris famous for hosting historical executions.</note> after being found guilty of participating in similar profane rituals. In 1597, the Parliament of Paris <note>A high court of justice under the French monarchy.</note> sentenced Jean Belon, the priest <note>original: "curé"</note> of Saint-Pierre-des-Lampes in the diocese of Bourges, to be hanged and his body burned for desecrating the Sacrament and repeatedly performing abominable ceremonies.$^{114}$ In 1598, the Parliament of Bordeaux condemned Pierre Aupetit, the priest of Pageas, near Châlus in the Limousin region, to be burned at the stake. In 1609, the Parliament of Bordeaux sent the judges Pierre De Lancre and d'Espagnet to Labourd in the Bayonne district to eliminate the practitioners of witchcraft who plagued that region. No fewer than seven priests were arrested on charges of celebrating "Satan's Mass" at the Sabbat. Two of them—Migalena, a seventy-year-old man, and Pierre Bocal, aged twenty-seven—were executed. However, the Bishop of Bayonne intervened, claiming the other five for his own ecclesiastical court, and managed to arrange their escape from prison. Three other priests who were being held were immediately released and wisely left the country. 

A year later, the city of Aix and the entire surrounding countryside echoed with the confessions of Madeleine de la Palud, who "[She] also said that this wretched Louis, a magician . . . was the first to devise the saying of Mass at the Sabbat, and to truly consecrate and present the sacrifice to Lucifer."$^{116}$ <note>original: "Dit aussi que ce malheureux Loys magicien . . . a controuvé le premier de dire la messe au sabatt et consacrer Véritablement et présenter le sacrifice à Lucifer."</note> It was, of course, simply ignorance on her part to believe that "that accursed Magician Louis [Gaufridi] was the first to invent the saying of Mass at the Sabbaths," although Gaufridi may have told her this to impress her with a sense of his importance and power within the hierarchy of evil. Certainly, in her testimony, the details of Sabbat worship are exceptionally thorough and complete.

These accounts are, however, fully matched—if not surpassed—by the narrative of Madeleine Bavent, a Franciscan sister of the Third Order attached to the convent of Saints Louis and Elizabeth at Louviers. Her confessions, which she wrote at length under the direction of her confessor, des Marets (a member of the Oratorian order), describe scenes of the most hideous nature in meticulous detail.

The missal <note>a book containing the texts used in the Mass</note> used at the Black Mass was obviously a manuscript, although it is said that in later times these grimoires <note>books of magic spells and invocations</note> of hideous profanity have actually been printed. The black mass of the Sabbat varied slightly in form according to circumstances. In the modern liturgy of the Satanists, it would appear that a significant feature is the burning of certain heavy and noxious weeds, known as the "Devil’s incense." In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the use of incense was very rare at the Sabbat, although Silvain Nevillon stated that he had seen at the Sabbat "both holy water and incense. This latter smelled foul, not fragrant like the incense burned in church."¹³⁵

Today, the person leading the ceremony <note>original: "officiant"</note> consecrates a host and the chalice using the actual sacred words of Holy Mass, but then instead of kneeling, he turns his back upon the altar,¹³⁶ and a few moments later—pardon the words! <note>original: *sit uenia uerbis!*</note>—he cuts and stabs the Host with a knife, throwing it to the ground, treading upon it, and spurning it. A part, at least, of the contents of the chalice is also spilled in a fearful act of desecration. Not infrequently, there is also provided a ciborium <term>A covered container used to hold the consecrated bread or Hosts for the Eucharist.</term> of consecrated Hosts, all stolen from churches¹³⁷ or carried away in their mouths during Communion by wretches who are unafraid to provoke the sudden judgment of an outraged God. These the "black priest"—for so the celebrant is called by the Devil-worshipers—scatters over the pavement to be struggled and fought for by his congregation in their madness to seize and outrage the Body of Christ.

Closely connected with the black mass of the Satanists, and a clear survival from the Middle Ages, is that grim superstition of the Gascon peasant, the Mass of Saint Sécaire.¹³⁸ Few priests know the awful ritual, and of those who are learned in such dark lore, even fewer yet would dare to perform the monstrous ceremonies and utter the prayer of blasphemy. No confessor, no bishop, not even the Archbishop of Auch, may grant absolution to <note>original: "shrive"</note> the celebrant; he can only be forgiven at Rome by the Holy Father <note>The Pope</note> himself. The mass is said upon a broken and desecrated altar in some ruined or deserted church where owls hoot and sit gloomily, and bats flit through the crumbling windows—where toads spit their venom upon the sacred stone. The priest must make his way there late, attended only by an assistant <note>original: "acolyte"</note> of impure and evil life. At the first stroke of eleven, he begins; the liturgy of hell is mumbled backward, and the canon <term>The most solemn part of the Mass, which includes the consecration of the bread and wine.</term> is said with a grimace <note>original: "mow"</note> and a sneer; he ends just as midnight tolls. The presence of toads at the Sabbat is mentioned in many witch trials. They seem to have been associated with sorcerers because of the disgust <note>original: "repugnance"</note> they generally provoke, and in some districts, it is a common superstition that those at whom they stare fixedly will be seized with heart palpitations, spasms, convulsions, and fainting fits <note>original: "swoons"</note>. It is hardly surprising that we find the toad as a close companion of the witch. Pierre de Lancre <note>A French judge and demonologist (1553–1631) who conducted massive witch trials in Labourd.</note> says that demons often appeared in that form. Jeannette d’Abadie, a witch of the Basses-Pyrénées whom he prosecuted and who confessed in detail, declared that she saw many toads brought to the <term>Sabbat</term> <note>the secret midnight assembly of witches</note> dressed in black or scarlet velvet, with little bells attached to their coats. In November 1610, a man walking through the fields near Bazas noticed that his dog had scratched a large hole in a bank and unearthed two pots, covered with cloth and closely tied. When opened, they were found to be packed with bran, and in the middle of each was a large toad wrapped in green silk gauze <note>original: "tiffany"</note>. These had undoubtedly been placed there by a person who believed in sympathetic magic and was attempting a harmful <note>original: "malefic"</note> spell. No doubt toads were captured and taken to the <term>Sabbat</term>, and the reason is not hard to find. Owing to their legendary venom, they served as a primary ingredient in poisons and potions; they were also used for telling fortunes, since witches often practiced divination using their toad <term>familiars</term> <note>supernatural entities believed to assist witches, often taking the form of animals</note>. Juvenal <note>A Roman poet known for his Satires.</note> alludes to this when he writes:

> "I neither will, nor can, predict
> The fate of the young, eager heir’s father,
> Nor have I pried into the entrails of a toad."¹⁵⁶

Upon which passage Thomas Farnabie, the celebrated English scholar (1575–1647), comments <note>original: "glosses"</note> thus: "He refers to the office of the <term>Haruspex</term> <note>a priest in ancient Rome who practiced divination by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</note> who used to inspect entrails and intestines. Pliny says: The entrails of the toad (the bramble toad, or *Rana rubeta*), that is to say the tongue, tiny bones, gall, and heart, have rare qualities, for they are used in many medicines and salves. Perhaps he means the common toad <note>original: "puddock"</note> or hop-toad, thus demonstrating that these animals are not poisonous, and their entrails are completely ineffective for making <note>original: "confecting"</note> poisons."¹⁵⁷ 

In 1610, Juan de Echalar, a sorcerer of Navarre, confessed at his trial before the Alcantarine inquisitor Don Alonso Becerra Holguin that he and his coven collected toads for the <term>Sabbat</term>. He claimed that when they presented these animals to the Devil, he blessed them with his left hand, after which they were killed and cooked in a stewpot with human bones and pieces of corpses robbed from new-made graves. From this filthy mixture <note>original: "hotch-potch"</note> were brewed poisons and ointments <note>original: "unguents"</note> that the Devil distributed to all present with directions on how to use them. With this liquid, it was supposed they could blight a standing field and also destroy flowers and fruit. A few drops let fall upon a person’s garments was believed to ensure death, and a smear upon a shed or sty effectively infected cattle. From these crude superstitions, the fantastic stories of dancing toads, toads dressed like horsemen <note>original: "en cavalier"</note>, and demon toads at the <term>Sabbat</term> <note>the secret midnight assembly of witches</note> were easily developed.

There is ample and continuous evidence that children—usually tender infants who were as yet unbaptized—were sacrificed at the Sabbat. These were often the witches’ own offspring; since a witch was not infrequently the midwife or "wise-woman" of a village, she had exceptional opportunities for killing a child at birth as a victim for Satan outside of the Sabbat ritual. "No persons can do more cunning harm to the Catholic faith than midwives," says the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "Nemo fidei catholicæ amplius nocet quam obstetrices"</note>, Part I, Question 11 <note>A famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note>. The classic examples of child sacrifice are those of Gilles de Rais (1440) <note>A French knight and companion-in-arms of Joan of Arc who was later executed for serial murder and occultism.</note> and the Abbé Guibourg (1680) <note>A French priest involved in the "Affair of the Poisons," a major scandal involving murder and witchcraft under Louis XIV.</note>. In the legal proceedings against the former, 140 children are explicitly named; some authorities accept as many as 800 victims. Their blood, brains, and bones were used to brew magic potions <note>original: "decoct magic philtres"</note>. 

In the days of Guibourg, the sacrifice of a baby at the impious mass was so common that he generally paid no more than a crown-piece for his victim. "He had bought the child who was sacrificed at this mass for a crown" <note>original: "Il avait acheté un écu l’enfant qui fut sacrifié à cette messe"</note>. These abominable ceremonies were frequently performed at the request of Madame de Montespan <note>The influential mistress of King Louis XIV of France.</note> so that Louis XIV would always remain faithful to her, reject all other mistresses, repudiate his queen, and ultimately raise her to the throne.¹⁵⁸ 

The most common method was to cut the child's throat; the blood was drained into the chalice and allowed to fall upon the naked flesh of the person seeking the spell <note>original: "the inquirer"</note>, who lay stretched across the altar. La Voisin <note>Catherine Monvoisin, a famous French fortune-teller and professional poisoner.</note> asserted that a toll of 1,500 infants had been murdered in this way. This is not impossible, as a vast number of people—including a crowd of clergymen—were involved. Many of the most prominent families in France had assisted at these orgies of blasphemy. The belief that corpses and body parts constitute a powerful cure and a primary ingredient in magical elixirs is a universal idea of great antiquity. The power to directly cure diseases and offer protection has long been attributed to a corpse <note>original: "cadaver"</note>. Tumors, skin eruptions, and gout were thought to be dispelled if the affected limb was stroked with a dead person's hand.<sup>159</sup> Toothaches were supposedly charmed away if the face was touched with the finger of a dead child.<sup>160</sup> Birthmarks were said to vanish under the same treatment.<sup>161</sup> Burns, carbuncles <note>A cluster of painful, pus-filled boils.</note>, herpes, and other skin complaints—which were fearfully common in the Middle Ages—could supposedly be cured by contact with some part of a corpse. In Pomerania <note>A historical region on the southern coast of the Baltic Sea, split between modern-day Germany and Poland.</note>, the "cold hand of a corpse" is considered a protection against fire,<sup>162</sup> and Russian peasants believed that a dead hand protects one from bullet wounds and blades.<sup>163</sup> For a long time, ignorant country folk believed that the doctors at the hospital in Graz, Austria, enjoyed the privilege of being allowed to sacrifice one human life every year for medicinal purposes. The story went that some young man who went there for a toothache or some other minor ailment would be seized, hung up by his feet, and tickled to death! Skilled pharmacists then supposedly boiled the body into a paste and used this, along with the fat and charred bones, in their medicine shop. ->THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT<-

This tradition is, perhaps, not unconnected with the alleged ritual sacrifices of Saint William of Norwich (1144); Harold of Gloucester (1168); William of Paris (1177); Robert of Bury Saint Edmunds (1181); Saint Werner of Oberwesel (1286); Saint Rudolph of Berne (1294); Saint Andreas of Rinn (1462); Saint Simon of Trent, an infant of two and a half years old (1473); Simon Abeles, whose body lies in the Teyn Church <note>original: "Teyn Kirche" in Prague</note> at Prague, murdered for the sake of Christ on February 21, 1694, by Lazarus and Levi Kurtzhandel; The Holy Child of La Guardia <note>original: "El santo Niño de la Guardia"</note>, near Toledo (1490), and many more.<sup>165</sup>

The riots which have broken out so continually during three centuries in China against Europeans—and particularly against Catholic asylums for the sick, orphanages <note>original: "foundling hospitals"</note>, and schools—are almost always stirred up by a group of intellectuals who begin by issuing fiery appeals to the public: “Down with the missionaries! Kill the foreigners! They steal or buy our children and slaughter them in order to prepare magical remedies and medicines out of their eyes, hearts, and other parts of their dead bodies.” Baron Hübner, in his *A Journey Around the World* <note>original: "Promenade autour du monde"</note>, Volume II (Paris, 1873), tells the story of the massacre at Tientsin on June 21, 1870, and relates that it was engineered on these very lines. In 1891, similar uprisings against Europeans living in China were found to be due to the same cause. Toward the end of 1891, a charge was brought in Madagascar against the French that they devoured human hearts and, for this purpose, kidnapped and killed native children. Harsh legislation was actually found necessary to check the spread of these accusations.<sup>166</sup>

In the witch trials of Navarre in 1610, Juan de Echelar confessed that a candle had been used that was made from the arm of an infant strangled before baptism. The ends of the fingers had been lit and burned with a clear flame; this was, in fact, a “Hand of Glory” <note>term: A charm made from the dried and pickled hand of a hanged man, or sometimes an infant, believed to have magical properties such as making the user invisible or causing those who see it to fall into a trance.</note>. At Forfar, in 1661, Helen Guthrie and four other witches dug up the body of an unbaptized infant and made portions of it into a pie, which they ate. They believed that by this means, no threat or torture could force them to confess their sorceries. This, of course, is clearly sympathetic magic <note>term: A type of magic based on the principle that "like affects like." Here, because the infant's tongue had never spoken, eating it was believed to prevent the witches' own tongues from speaking a confession.</note>. The tongue of the infant had never spoken articulate words, and so the tongues of the witches would be unable to speak.

THE SABBAT 163

It is a fact rarely understood, but nonetheless of the deepest significance, that almost every detail of the old witch trials can be exactly matched in Africa today. For example, there exists among the Bantu people a society called the "Witchcraft Company." Its members hold secret meetings at midnight in the depths of the forest to plot sickness and death against their enemies by means of incantations and spells. The owl is their sacred bird, and their signal call is an imitation of its hoot. They claim to leave their physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> bodies asleep in their huts, and it is only their spirit-bodies that attend the magic gathering <note>original: "rendezvous"</note>, passing through walls and over the tree-tops with instant speed. At the meeting, they have visible, audible, and physical communication with spirits. They hold feasts at which the "heart-life" of some human being is eaten; through the loss of his heart, this person falls sick and—unless "the heart" is later restored—eventually dies. 

The first crow of the cock is the warning for them to scatter, since they fear the appearance of the morning star. If the sun were to rise upon them before they reached their physical bodies, all their plans would not merely fail but backfire <note>original: "recoil"</note> upon them, and they would waste away and suffer miserably. This hideous society was introduced by enslaved Africans to the West Indies—to Jamaica and Haiti <note>original: "Hayti"</note>—and also to the Southern United States as Voodoo worship. Authentic records are easily obtained which prove that midnight meetings were held in Haiti as late as 1888, where human beings, especially kidnapped children, were killed and eaten at these mysterious and evil banquets. European governments in Africa have largely suppressed the practice of the dark magic <note>original: "black art"</note>, but this foul belief still secretly persists. Dr. Norris <note>likely Edwin Norris (1801–1872), a British philologist and ethnographer</note> is of the opinion that if European influence were withdrawn, it would soon hold power as strongly as in the past.

A honest consideration will show that for every detail of the Sabbat <note>a secret midnight assembly of witches</note>—however fantastically presented and exaggerated in the witch trials of so many centuries—there is ample support and undeniable <note>original: "unimpeachable"</note> evidence. There is some hallucination, no doubt; there is a vivid imagination and vanity which paints the details thick; but there is a solid layer <note>original: "stratum"</note> of fact, and very terrible fact, throughout.

# THE SABBAT

It is certain, but it is not proved to always happen this way. . . . The other opinion, which I consider to be the truest, is that sometimes witches are truly transported by a Demon from place to place, usually on a goat or another phantom animal carrying them together physically, and they take part in the wicked assembly. This is the much more common opinion of theologians, and even of the legal experts of Italy, Spain, and Germany among Catholics; many others hold this same view. Turrecremata in his work on Grillandus,^1 Remigius,^2 Petrus Damianus,^3 Silvester of Avila,^4 Caietanus,^5 Alfonso de Castro,^6 Sixtus of Siena,^7 Crespet,^8 Spina^9 against Ponzinibio, Ananias,^10 and many others whom I omit for the sake of brevity. <note>original Latin: "certum est, sed semper ita fieri non probatur... hæc sententia est multo communior Theologorum..."</note> *Compiled by Brother Francesco Maria Guazzo of the Order of St. Ambrose at the Grove of Milan. Milan. From the Ambrosian College Printing House. 1626.*

62 *On Witches* <note>original: "De Strigibus"</note>, II. I have used the reprint of 1669, which is included in the valuable collection appended to the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Malleus Maleficarum"</note> of that date, 4 volumes, quarto.

63 To which gathering or "game" <note>original Latin: "ludum" – a common term for the Sabbat</note> the aforementioned plague-ridden persons go physically and while awake, and with their own senses. When they go to nearby places, they go on foot, inviting one another. If, however, they are to gather in some distant place, they are then carried by the devil. Regardless of how they travel to said place—whether on their own feet or carried by the devil—it is true that they really and truly (and not through fantasy or illusion) renounce the Catholic faith, worship the devil, trample upon the cross, and commit many most wicked outrages against the most holy Body of Christ <note>the Eucharist</note>. They also perpetrate many other most filthy acts with the devil himself, who appears to them in human form, presenting himself as a succubus <note>a demon in female form</note> to men and an incubus <note>a demon in male form</note> to women.

64 George Gandillon, on the night of a Maundy Thursday, remained in his bed like a dead man for the space of three hours, and then came to himself with a start. <header>THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT</header>

### Chapter XIX.

1. *Witches go to the Sabbat around midnight.*
2. *The reason why the Sabbat is usually held at night.*
3. *Satan delights in darkness and the color black, whereas whiteness is pleasing to God.*
4. *Witches dance back-to-back at the Sabbat, and most of them wear masks.*
5, 8. *When the rooster crows, the Sabbat immediately disappears, and the reason for this.*
6. *The voice of the rooster is fatal to Satan, just as it is to the lion and the serpent.*
7. *The Demon, according to some, is afraid of a naked sword.*

### Chapter XX. *On the Day of the Sabbat.*

1. *The Sabbat is held on every day of the week, but primarily on Thursday.*
2. *It is also held on the most solemn feast days of the year.*

### Chapter XXI. *On the Location of the Sabbat.*

1. *The location of the Sabbat is marked, according to some, by certain trees or even certain crosses; and the author's opinion on this subject.*
2. *A remarkable thing regarding a place alleged to be used for the Sabbat.*
3. *Water is required at the place where the Sabbat is held, and the reason why.*
4. *Witches, for lack of water, urinate into a hole they make in the ground.*

### Chapter XXII. *On What Is Done at the Sabbat.*

1. *Witches worship Satan there, who appears <gloss>estant</gloss> in the form of a black man or a goat; they offer him candles and kiss him on his shameful hindparts.*
2. *They dance there, and details about their dances.*
3. *They indulge in all sorts of lewdness, and how Satan acts as an Incubus and Succubus.*
4. *Incest and execrable lewdness <note>original French: "paillardises"</note> of the Euchites and Gnostics.*
5. *Witches banquet at the Sabbat with their food and drink, and the way they bless the table and give thanks.*
6. *However, they get no taste from the food and usually leave the meal hungry.*
7. *When the meal is finished, they give an account of their actions to Satan.*
8. *They once again renounce God, the Chrism <term>holy oil used in baptism and confirmation</term>, etc., and how Satan urges them to do evil.*
9. *They create hail there.*
10. *They celebrate Mass there, and details about their copes <term>liturgical cloaks</term> and holy water.*
11. *Satan finally consumes himself in fire and turns to ash, which all the witches take, and for what purpose.*
12. *Satan is the Ape of God <note>original: "Singe de Dieu" — a theological concept that the Devil mimics God’s rituals in a perverted way</note> in everything.*

<header>THE SABBAT</header>

⁷⁸ Those brought to the assembly are accustomed to worship the demon presiding over the meeting, who sits on a throne in a terrifying form—usually that of a goat or a dog—approaching him with their backs turned... and then, as a sign of homage, they kiss him on the buttocks <note>original Latin: "osculari eum in podice"</note>."¹ Guazzo notes: "As a sign of homage, they kiss the demon on the buttocks."² And Ludwig Elich says: "Then, as a sign of homage (if I may say so without offending your ears), they must give kisses to the demon’s buttocks."³

# CHAPTER V

## THE WITCH IN HOLY WRIT

In the course of the Holy Scriptures, there occur a great number of words and expressions which are employed in connection with witchcraft, divination, and demonology, and of these more than one authority has made detailed and particular study. Some terms are of general import—one might even venture to say vague and not exactly defined—while some are directly specific. Concerning some phrases, the meaning is plain and accepted; regarding others, scholars are still undecided and differ more or less widely among themselves. Yet it is noteworthy that from the very earliest period, the attitude of the inspired writers toward magic and related practices is almost wholly condemnatory and uncompromisingly hostile. The vehement and repeated denunciations launched against the <term>professors</term><note>In this context, "professors" refers to those who claim to possess or who openly practice these arts.</note> of occult sciences and those initiated in foreign esoteric mysteries do not, moreover, seem to be based upon any supposition of fraud, but rather upon the "abomination" of the magic itself, which is recognized as potent for evil and able to cause harm to life and limb. 

It is obvious, for example, that the opponents of Moses, the sorcerers<gloss>1</gloss> Jannes and Mambres, were masters of no mean learning and power. When, in the presence of Pharaoh, Aaron’s rod became a live serpent, they and their mob of disciples "did in like manner by Egyptian incantations and certain secrets" <note>original Latin: "fecerunt per incantationes Ægyptiacas et arcana quædam similiter"</note>, casting down their rods, which were changed into a mass of writhing snakes. They were able also to bring up frogs upon the land, but it was beyond their power to drive them away. We have here, however, a clear acknowledgment of the reality of magic and its dark possibilities, while at the same time prominence is given to the fact that when it contests with the miraculous power divinely bestowed upon Moses, it fails hopelessly and completely. The serpent, which was Aaron’s rod, swallows all...

<summary>This page introduces the biblical perspective on witchcraft, arguing that the Bible treats magic as a real and dangerous power rather than a fraud, though it is ultimately inferior to divine miracles.</summary>
<keywords>Bible, Holy Writ, witchcraft, divination, demonology, Moses, Jannes and Mambres, Pharaoh, Aaron's rod, Egyptian magic, occult sciences</keywords>

--- Page 204 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of biblical magic and sorcery, moving from the failure of Pharaoh's magicians to replicate the plagues of Egypt to the story of the seer Balaam in the Book of Numbers.</meta>

the other serpents. The swarms of mosquitoes and gadflies which Aaron caused to rise in myriads from the dust, the native <term>warlocks</term><note>A term used here for the Egyptian magicians or sorcerers.</note> could not produce; indeed, they were constrained to cry out, "This is the finger of God" <note>original Latin: "Digitus Dei est hic"</note>; while a little later, they were unable to protect even their own bodies from the pest of boils <note>original: "blains"</note> and swelling sores. Nonetheless, a supernatural power was possessed by Jannes and Mambres <note>According to tradition, these were the names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses.</note> as truly as by Moses, although not to the same extent, and it was derived from another—in fact, from an opposite and antagonistic—source.

Even more striking is the episode of Balaam, who dwelt at Pethor, a city of Mesopotamia (the *Pitru* of the cuneiform texts), and who was summoned from there by Balak, King of Moab, to lay a withering curse upon the Israelites, who were encamped after their victory over the Amorites at the very borders of his territory. The royal messengers come to Balaam "with the rewards of divination in their hand," a most illuminating detail, for it shows that already the practice of magical arts is rewarded with gifts of great value.² In fact, when Balaam refuses, although with reluctance, to accompany the first embassy, princes of the highest rank are then sent to him with instructions to offer him rank and wealth or whatever he may care to ask. "I will promote you to very great honor, and I will do whatever you say to me; come, therefore, and curse this people," are the king’s actual words. After great difficulties—for Balaam is, at first, forbidden to go and only wins his way on condition that he undertakes to do what he is commanded and to speak no more than he is inspired to say—the seer commences his journey and is met by the king at a frontier town. He is taken by the king "unto the high places of Baal," to the sacred groves upon the hill-tops, where seven mystic altars are built, and a bullock and a ram offered upon each. Balaam then senses the imminent presence of God, and withdraws swiftly apart to some secret place where "God met" him. He returns to the scene of sacrifice and forthwith blesses the Israelites. Balak, in consternation and dismay, hurries him to the crest of Pisgah (Phasga), and the same ceremonies are performed. ### THE WITCH IN HOLY WRIT

This location was the center of the local cult of Baal Peor <note>A local Moabite deity whose worship was often associated with immoral rites.</note>, whose ancient worship included a ritual of extremely crude obscenity.<sup>3</sup> Once again, a sevenfold sacrifice is offered upon seven altars, and this time Balaam deliberately resists divine control—a vain effort, since he falls into a trance and speaks words of profound blessing. He gazes down the long paths of the future to the glorious vision of the Madonna, the Star of Jacob <note>original Latin: Stella Jacob</note>, and her Son, the Scepter of Israel. Beating his clenched hands together in a fit of uncontrollable rage, the cheated <note>original: "choused"</note> and frustrated king immediately dismisses his guest.

It must be noted that throughout this entire narrative—the details of which are as interesting as they are significant—the writer completely recognizes the claims made by Balaam, which were so fully acknowledged and valued by Balak. Balaam was a famous sorcerer and one, moreover, who knew and could speak the mystic "Word of Power" with deadly effect. Among the early Arabs, as among the Israelites, the magic spell—whether a Word of Blessing or a Curse—played a prominent role. In war, a poet who cursed the enemy with rhythmic spells <note>original: "runes"</note> rendered services equal to the heroism of the warrior himself. Similarly, the Jews of Medina used to bring images of their hated enemy *Malik b. al-Aglam* into their synagogues; they would hurl curses at these effigies every time they met. The reality of Balaam's power is clearly the keynote of the Biblical account. Otherwise, why would his services be sought for the cause of Israel? Balak's greeting to the seer is no empty compliment but a vital truth:

> "I know <note>original: "wot"</note> that he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed."

Relevant <note>original: "not impertinent"</note> to this is the bitter condemnation in the song of Deborah, Judges 5:23:

> "Curse Meroz, said the angel of the Lord, curse its inhabitants bitterly; because they did not come to help the Lord, to help the Lord against the mighty!" (Authorized Version)

Belief in the power of the spoken word has existed at all times and in all places, and it continues to exist everywhere today.

Although Balaam prophesied, it must be kept in mind that he was not a prophet in the Scriptural sense of the term; he was a soothsayer or a wizard. The Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> uses the term *hariolus* <note>meaning "soothsayer" or "diviner"</note>,<sup>4</sup> which is derived from the Sanskrit *hira*, meaning "entrails" <note>This refers to extispicy, the practice of divining the future by inspecting the internal organs of sacrificed animals.</note>, and

equivalent to a <term>haruspex</term> <note>original: *haruspex*; an Etruscan diviner who interpreted the "will of the gods" by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</note>. This term originally denoted an Etruscan diviner who foretold future events by an inspection of the entrails of sacrificial victims. It was from the Etruscans that this practice was introduced to the Romans. It is probable that Balaam employed the seven bullocks and rams in this way, using the technical <term>extispicium</term> <note>original: *extispicium*; the practice of using animal organs for prophecy</note>, a method of inquiry and forecasting which seems to have been almost universal, although the exact manner in which the omens were read differed among various peoples and at different times. It persisted, nonetheless, until very late, and indeed it is resorted to, so it has been said, by certain occultists even at the present day. It is known to have been practiced by Catherine de' Medici <note>1519–1589; Queen of France known for her interest in astrology and the occult</note>, and it is closely connected with the dark Voodoo worship of Jamaica and Haiti. St. Thomas Aquinas, it is true, has spoken of Balaam as a prophet, but the holy doctor hastens to add "a prophet of the devil." The learned Cornelius à Lapide <note>A 17th-century Jesuit priest known for his comprehensive Bible commentaries</note>, commenting <note>original: "glossing"</note> upon Numbers 22 and 23 writes: "It is clear that Balaam was a prophet, not of God, but of the Devil. . . . He was a magician, and he sought for a conference with his demon to take counsel with him."<gloss>5</gloss> He is of the opinion that the seven altars were erected in honor of the Lords of the Seven Planets. Seven is, of course, the perfect number, the mystic number, even as three; and all magic must be done by odd numbers. The woman in Virgil who tries to call back her estranged lover Daphnis by potent incantations cries: "God delights in odd numbers" <note>original Latin: *numero deus impare gaudet*</note>. (*Eclogue* 8. 75, titled *The Sorceress* <note>original Latin: *Pharmaceutria*</note>). St. Augustine, St. Ambrose, and Theodoret consider that when Balaam on the first occasion withdrew hastily saying "Perhaps the Lord will come to meet me," he expected to meet a demon, his familiar spirit. But "God met Balaam." The very haste and disorder seem to point to the design of the sorcerer; for just as in the Divine Liturgy all is done with due dignity, grace, and beauty <note>original: "comeliness"</note>, so in the rituals of black magic all is hurried, ugly, and terrible.

...overwhelming forces of the ruthless foe. To add to his panic, when he consulted the Divine Oracles, no answer was returned, "neither by dreams, nor by Urim <note>Sacred objects used by ancient Hebrew priests to discern the divine will</note>, nor by prophets." And although he had, in the earlier years of his reign, shown himself a determined suppressor of witchcraft, in his dire extremity he catches at any straw and bids his servants seek out some woman "who has a familiar spirit." His servants said to him, "Behold, there is a woman who has a familiar spirit at Endor," which is a miserable hamlet on the northern slope of a hill, lying somewhat south of Mount Tabor.

The phrase used here, rendered by the Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> as "a spirit of divination" (Seek for me a woman having a spirit of divination <note>original: *Quærite mihi mulierem habentem pythonem*</note>) and by the Authorized Version as "familiar spirit," is in the original Hebrew *’ôbh*<gloss>6</gloss>. This term signifies the departed spirit that is called up, and it also came to stand for the person controlling such a spirit and divining by its aid. The Witch of Endor is described as the possessor of an *’ôbh*. The Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates this word as "ventriloquist" <note>original: *ἐγγαστράμυθος*</note>, which literally means one who speaks from the belly. This translation was chosen either because the observers thought the magician’s alleged communication with the spirit was a mere deception to fool the inquirer—a trick where the voice is "thrown" into the ground and given a strange quality (a view which strongly appeals to Lenormant<gloss>7</gloss> and the skeptical Renan<gloss>8</gloss> but which is quite unsustainable)—or rather because of the belief common in antiquity that ventriloquism was not a natural faculty, but was due to a spirit temporarily possessing the medium. 

In this connection, the prophet Isaiah <note>original: Isaias</note> has a remarkable passage: "Seek from the spirits of divination, and from the diviners who chirp in their incantations" <note>original: *Quærite a pythonibus, et a diuinis qui strident in incantationibus suis*</note>. ("Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep and that mutter," according to the Authorized Version.) Many Greek and Latin poets attribute a peculiar and distinctive sound to the voices of spirits. Homer, in the *Iliad* (Book 23, line 101) and the *Odyssey* (Book 24, lines 5 and 9), uses the verb "to chirp" <note>original: *τρίζειν*</note>, which is elsewhere found describing the shrill cry or chirping of partridges, young swallows, locusts, mice, and bats<gloss>9</gloss>. It is also used for sounds such as the creaking of a door or the sharp crackling of something burning in a fire. Virgil <note>original: *Vergil*</note>, in the *Aeneid* (Book 3, line 39), speaks of the cry of Polydorus from his grave as a "tearful groan" <note>original: *gemitus lacrimabilis*</note>, and the clamor of the spirits in Hades as a "feeble voice" <note>original: *uox exigua*</note>. When Saul had been informed of this witch, he completely removed his royal robes and insignia. In a close disguise, accompanied only by two of his most trusted followers who were similarly muffled in cloaks, he painfully made his way at the dead of night to her remote and filthy hut. He eagerly requested that she exercise her powers and raise the spirit of the person he would name. At first she refused, since some years earlier the laws had been strictly enforced and the penalty of death awaited all sorcerers and magicians. She reasonably feared that these mysterious strangers might be laying a trap to endanger her life. 

But the hidden king persuaded her, binding himself with a solemn oath that she would come to no harm. Consequently, she agreed to summon the soul of the prophet Samuel, as he desired. The ritual began, and after the vision of various spirits—the woman said, "I saw gods ascending out of the earth" <note>original: *Deos uidi ascendentes de terra*</note>—and Saint Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century theologian and Church Father</note> explains these as demons, "the phantoms" <note>original: *τὰ φαντάσματα*</note>—Samuel appeared in a scene of great terror and awe. In that same moment, the sibyl <note>term: A woman able to communicate with the spirit world; here referring to the witch</note> recognized the identity of her visitor (though we are not told how).

Feeling that he was facing no earthly figure—he could not see the ghost himself, although he sensed a presence from beyond the grave—he asked, "What is his form?" "...covered with a mantle," Saul at once recognized Samuel and fell prostrate upon the ground, while the apparition spoke of his swiftly approaching doom.

<margin><unclear>✓</unclear></margin>
Here we have a detailed scene of proper necromancy <term>necromancy: the practice of communicating with the dead to predict the future</term>. There are, it is true, some remarkable and perhaps unusual features: the witch alone sees the phantom, but Saul instantly knows who it is from her description; he directly addresses Samuel, and he hears the prediction of the dead prophet. The whole narrative undoubtedly carries the mark of reality and truth.

<margin><unclear>20</unclear></margin>
There are several interpretations of these incidents. In the first place, some writers have denied the reality of the vision, claiming that the witch deceived Saul through skillful trickery. This hardly seems possible. It is not likely that she would have taken such a grave risk—as the exercise, or pretended exercise, of magical arts must entail—if she were a mere fraud. An accomplice of remarkably quick wit and invention would have been necessary to carry out the details of the plot; it is surely incredible that they should have ventured upon such an uncompromising condemnation of the king and foretold so evil an end for his royal house. In fact, the whole tone of the story conflicts with this explanation, which is not accepted by the Church Fathers <term>Church Fathers: the influential early theologians of the Christian Church whose writings established orthodoxy</term>. Theodoret, it is true, leans toward the idea that some deception was practiced, but he hesitates to maintain a firm opinion on the matter. In his *Questions on 1 Kings Chapter 28* <note>original: *Quæstiones in I Regum Cap. xxviii*</note>, he asks, "How should the events concerning the woman with the familiar spirit be understood?" <note>original: *πῶς τὰ κατὰ τὴν ἐγγαστρίμυθον νοητέον ;*</note> and says that some think the witch actually summoned Samuel, while others believe the Devil took the likeness of the prophet. He characterizes the first opinion as impious and the second as foolish.

<margin><unclear>to the ... ... the ...</unclear></margin>
St. Jerome, whose authority would, of course, be entirely conclusive, does not perhaps pronounce a definitive judgment; but his comments sufficiently show, I think, that he regarded the apparition as truly being Samuel. In his treatise *On Isaiah* <note>original: *In Esaiam*</note>, Book III, chapter vii, he writes: "Most authors think that a clear sign was given to Saul from the earth itself and from the very depths of Hades when he saw Samuel summoned by incantations and magic spells." And again, in *On Ezekiel* <note>original: *In Ezechielem*</note>, Book IV, chapter xiii, the holy doctor, speaking of witches, says: "they are inspired by an evil spirit. The Hebrews say that they are well-versed in baleful crafts, necromancy, and soothsaying..."

"...such as was the witch <note>original: "hag"</note> who seemed to raise up the soul of Samuel."¹³

<margin>⌜</margin>Some authors directly attribute this appearance of Samuel to an evil spirit, who took the form of the prophet in order to discourage Saul and tempt him to despair. For instance, St. Gregory of Nyssa, in his letter *On the Witch, to Theodosius* <note>original: "De pythonissa ad Theodosium"</note>,¹⁴ says that the Devil deceived the witch, who then in her turn <margin>⌜</margin>deceived the king. St. Basil expressly states in his *Commentary on Isaiah* <note>original: "In Esaiam"</note> (VIII. 218): "They were demons who assumed the appearance of Samuel."¹⁵ He suggests that because the condemnation of Saul was accurate in every detail, the demons—having heard the sentence previously delivered by God—simply reported it. Among the Latin-speaking fathers, Tertullian had written more than a century earlier: "And I believe that evil spirits can deceive many by their lies; for a lying spirit was allowed to pretend to be the ghost <note>original: "shade"</note> of Samuel."¹⁶

<margin>✓</margin>The majority of opinion, however, is decidedly in favor of a literal and exact understanding of the event: that it was, in fact, Samuel himself who appeared to the guilty monarch and predicted his death. Origen argues along these lines, basing his reasons on the plain statements of Holy Scripture: "But it is distinctly stated that Saul knew it was Samuel."¹⁷ Later he adds: "The Scripture cannot lie. And the words of Scripture are: 'And the woman saw Samuel.'"¹⁸ Elsewhere, when treating the subject of evil spirits, he precisely states: "And I have made known to you that souls have a place where they remain from the calling forth <note>original: "evocation"</note> of Samuel by the witch, when Saul requested her to divine."¹⁹ St. Ambrose also says: "Even after his death, Samuel, as Holy Scripture informs us, prophesied of what was to come."²⁰ We also have the powerful testimony of St. Augustine, who discusses the question at length in more than one place; he concludes that the phantom called up by the sibyl <term>sibyl: a woman in ancient times believed to utter the oracles and prophecies of a god</term> was really and truly the soul of the prophet Samuel. Thus, in that important treatise *On Christian Doctrine* <note>original: "De Doctrina Christiana"</note>, begun in 397 and finally revised for publication in 427, he writes: "The ghost of Samuel, long since dead, truly foretold what was to come to King Saul."²¹ Meanwhile, a passage in the even more famous and influential work *On Care for the Dead* <note>original: "De Cura pro mortuis gerenda"</note>, written in 421, asserts: "For the prophet Samuel, who was dead, revealed the future to King Saul, who was still alive."²²

Josephus believed the ghost <note>original: "apparition"</note> to have been summoned by the witch’s powers of necromancy, for in his *Jewish Antiquities* (Book 6, chapter 14, section 2), when dealing with the story of Endor, he records: “[Saul] ordered her to bring up to him the soul of Samuel. She, not knowing who Samuel was, called him out of the underworld <note>original: "Hades"</note>,”²³ which is a remarkable testimony.

Throughout the whole of the Old Testament, the sin of necromancy <note>original: "necromancy," the practice of communicating with the spirits of the dead</note> is condemned in the strongest terms. However, the very repetition of this ban shows that the summoning of the dead was nevertheless practiced extensively and continuously, although in the most hidden and secret manner. The Law of Moses <note>original: "Mosaic law"</note> denounces such arts again and again: “Do not turn to wizards, nor seek out soothsayers <note>original: "soothsayers," those who predict the future</note>, to be defiled by them: I am the Lord your God” (Leviticus 19:31); “The person who turns to magicians and soothsayers, and commits spiritual adultery <note>original: "fornication"</note> with them, I will set my face against that person and destroy them from among their people” (Leviticus 20:6). Even more explicit in its details is the following prohibition: “Neither let there be found among you anyone . . . who consults soothsayers, or pays attention to dreams and omens, nor let there be any wizard, nor charmer, nor anyone who consults <term>pythonic spirits</term>, or fortune tellers, or who seeks the truth from the dead. For the Lord detests all these things” (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). 

<margin>⌜</margin> <term>pythonic spirits</term> — derived from the "Python" or oracle of Delphi; in a biblical context, this refers to spirits of divination or the mediums who channel them.

Therefore, it is obvious that the essential evil of the sin lay in the fact that it was treason <note>original: "*lèse-majesté*," a crime against a sovereign or the state</note> against God, just as is the sin of heresy.²⁴ This is, moreover, clearly demonstrated by the fact that the worldly penalty was death. “A man or woman in whom there is a pythonic or divining spirit, let them die” (Leviticus 20:27). And the famous statute in Exodus 22:18 expressly says: “You shall not allow a wizard <note>original: "Wizards," often translated as "sorceress" or "witch"</note> to live.” 

Nevertheless, necromancy persisted, and on occasion—such as during the reign of Manasses, the thirteenth king of Judah (692–638 B.C.)²⁵—it no longer lurked in dark corners and foul hiding places, but displayed its disgusting practices openly in the courts of the palace and in broad daylight before the eyes of the superstitious capital. In the days of this monarch, divination was used openly, omens were observed, "pythons" <note>mediums or spirits</note> were publicly appointed, and soothsayers multiplied “to do evil before the Lord, and to provoke Him” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 21:6). ...before the Hijra <note>original: "Hejira," the migration of the Prophet Muhammad from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD</note>, there was a statue of a man made of agate that held seven arrows in one hand, similar to those the pagan Arabs used for divination. This figure, which is said to have anciently represented the patriarch Abraham, was regarded with special awe and reverence.

The arrows used by the early Arabs for magical practices were generally only three in number. These were carefully preserved in the temple of an idol, having been consecrated before that idol's shrine. One of them was inscribed with the words, "My Lord has commanded me"; another said, "My Lord has forbidden me"; and the third was left blank. If the first arrow was drawn, the seeker viewed it as a favorable omen promising success in their task. If the second was drawn, he predicted failure. If the third was drawn, all three arrows were mixed together again and another attempt was made. These divining arrows seem to have been consulted by the Arabs before they started any important undertaking—for example, when a man was about to set out on a specific journey, to marry, or to begin some significant business.

In certain cases and in many countries, rods were used instead of arrows. Small sticks were marked with occult signs, thrown into a vessel, and then drawn out. Alternatively, they might be cast into the air, with the direction they took and the position in which they fell being carefully noted. This practice is known as <term>rhabdomancy</term> <note>divination by means of rods or wands</note>. Indeed, the Septuagint <note>original: "LXX," the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament</note> in Ezekiel 21:21 uses the term *divination by rods* <note>original Greek: ῥαβδομαντεία, rhabdomanteia</note> rather than *divination by arrows* <note>original Greek: βελομαντεία, belomanteia</note>. Rhabdomancy is also mentioned by Saint Cyril of Alexandria.

In the Koran, chapter V, titled "The Table" or "The Chapter of Contracts," "divining arrows" are described as "an abomination of the work of Satan," and the command is given, "therefore avoid them so that you may prosper."

It is notable that in the early Biblical narrative, one form of divination is mentioned—if not with approval, then at least without direct criticism. During the second journey of Jacob’s sons to Egypt to buy grain <note>original: "corn," which in historical English referred to any cereal crop like wheat or barley</note> during the famine, Joseph ordered that their sacks be filled with food and that each man’s money be placed in the opening of his sack. However, in Benjamin’s sack, he also ordered the concealment of "the cup, the silver cup." The next morning, when they had set out toward home and had traveled only a short distance from the city, they were overtaken by a group...
