The Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> has: “The cup which you have stolen is the one in which my lord drinks and in which he is accustomed to practice divination <note>original: augurari solet</note>: you have done a very evil thing” (Genesis 44:5). And later, when they are brought back in custody and led into the presence of Joseph, he asks them: “Do you not know that such a man as I can certainly practice divination?” Vulgate: “Do you not know that there is no one like me in the <term>science of divination</term> <note>original: augurandi scientia</note>?”

In the first place, it cannot be for a moment supposed that Joseph’s claim—which he states here so publicly and so emphatically—to be a diviner of no ordinary powers was a mere trick for the occasion. From the prominence given to the cup in the story, it is clear that his steward regarded it as a vessel of special value and importance, endowed <note>original: "dight"</note> with mysterious properties.

This cup was used for that species of divination known as <term>hydromantia</term> <note>hydromancy: divination by means of water</note>, a practice almost universal in antiquity and common enough even today. The seer, or in some cases the seeker, by gazing fixedly into a pool or basin of still water, will see reflected there, as if in a mirror, a picture of the knowledge they seek. Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and philosopher, c. 64 BC–24 AD</note>, in Book 16, section 2, paragraph 39, writing of the Persians, says: “Among the Persians there are the Magi and the necromancers <note>original: νεκυομάντεις</note>, and also those called bowl-diviners <note>original: λεκανομάντεις</note> and water-diviners <note>original: ὑδρομάντεις</note>.” King Numa, according to one very ancient tradition, practiced divination by seeing gods in a clear stream.

> “For Numa himself, not being instructed by any prophet or Angel of God, was forced to resort to <term>hydromancy</term>: making his gods (or rather his demons) appear in water to instruct him in his religious institutions. This kind of divination, says Varro <note>A celebrated Roman scholar, 116–27 BC</note>, came from Persia and was used by Numa and later by Pythagoras; in it they also used blood and called forth spirits of the underworld. The Greeks call it <term>necromancy</term> <note>divination through communication with the dead</note>, but whether you prefer to call it necromancy or hydromancy, it is there that the dead seem to speak” (*St. Augustine, The City of God*, Book 7, Chapter 35).²⁷

Apuleius in his *On Magic* <note>original: *De Magia*</note>,²⁸ quoting from Varro, says: “When the people of Tralles were consulting by magical inquiry about the outcome of the Mithridatic War, a boy [gazing] into the water [saw] the image of Mercury [who] con- <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "con-", likely "contemplated" or "confirmed". Original Latin: "Trallibus de euentu Mithridatici belli magica percontatione consultantibus puerum in aqua simulacrum Mercuri con-"</note>

In Egypt today, the Magic Mirror is frequently consulted. A boy is hired to gaze into a splash of water, or perhaps ink or some other dark liquid poured into the palm of the hand; there, he will certainly see answers to the questions put to him revealed in pictures. When a theft has been committed, the Magic Mirror is always questioned in this way. In Scandinavia, country people who had lost anything would go to a diviner on a Thursday night to see in a pail of water who had robbed them. This belief prevails all over the world: in Tahiti and among the Hawaiians, in the Malay Peninsula, in New Guinea, and among the Eskimos.

Similar forms of divination involve dropping objects into a liquid. A precious stone or a costly amulet is cast into a cup, and the rings formed on the surface of the liquid were believed to predict the future. In other cases, warm wax or molten lead is poured into a vessel of cold water, and significant letters of the alphabet may be spelled out or objects identified from the shapes the wax or lead takes. Similarly, an empty tea cup is tilted, and prognostications are made from the size, shape, and position of the remaining leaves. This is common in England, Scotland, Ireland, Sweden, and Lithuania, while in Macedonia, coffee grounds are used in the same manner.

But whether the seer is a Hebrew patriarch or a Roman king, and whether the divination is dignified by some occult name—such as <term>Ceromancy</term> (the melting of wax), <term>Lecanomancy</term> (using basins of water), or <term>Oinomancy</term> (using the dregs of wine)—or whether it is practiced by some old grandmother in a plaid shawl peering at tea leaves by her cottage fire, the object has been the same throughout the ages. All systems of divination are merely various methods of obscuring the outer physical vision so that the inner spiritual vision may be opened.

As was inevitable, <term>hydromancy</term> <note>original: hydromantia</note> lent itself to much trickery. Hippolytus of Rome, a priest and "antipope" who died around 236 AD <note>original: ob. circa A.D. 236</note>, explains in detail how people were elaborately fooled by "pseudo-magicians" in his important work against heretics, the *Philosophumena*. Folklore held that the white poplar was sacred to Hercules,$^{31}$ and as it grew on the banks of the river Acheron in Epirus, it was connected with Acheron, the "waters of woe" in the underworld—a confused tradition which is undoubtedly of very early origin. Leah indeed conceives, and in due time she bore Issachar. Leah ate of the mandrake as a charm to induce pregnancy, and the biblical text expresses no disapproval of such use.

Mandrakes and mallows were potent in all forms of enchantment, and a whole library of legend has grown up around the mandrake in particular, which would require much time and space to investigate thoroughly. Western lore is mainly of a somewhat grim character, but not entirely, and by Eastern cultures, the mandrake is regarded as a powerful aphrodisiac. The Shakespearean allusions have made this aspect familiar to everyone.

The Arabs and ancient Germans thought that a powerful spirit inhabited the plant, an idea derived, perhaps, from the imagined resemblance of the root to the human form. Ducagne <note>Charles du Fresne, sieur du Cange, a 17th-century philologist.</note> records under the entry for Mandragore:

> "A type of fruit mentioned in Genesis 30:14, known to our people under the name *Mandragores*, which they dream is suitable for acquiring wealth for themselves if kept close to the chest." <note>original Latin: Pomi genus cuius mentio fit, Gen. xxx. 14. nostris etiam notis sub nomine Mandragores, quod pectore asseruatum sibi diuitiis acquirendis idoneum somniabunt.</note>

The teraphim that Rachel stole from her father Laban (Genesis 31:19, and 31–35), and which she concealed by a clever trick when he was in pursuit, were used for purposes of <term>divination</term> <note>the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means</note>. From the account of the incident, it is obvious that they were regarded as immensely valuable—he who had taken them away was to be put to death if found—and they were imbued with a mysterious sanctity. Centuries later, during a period of radical religious reform, King Josiah (639–608 B.C.) would no longer tolerate them:
> “Moreover, Josiah removed those who consulted mediums, the wizards, the household idols [teraphim], the idols, and all the abominations that were seen in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem” (2 Kings 23:24, Authorized Version).

> “But Josiah also took away the mediums, the soothsayers, the figures of idols, the uncleanness, and the abominations that had been in the land of Judah and Jerusalem.” <note>original Latin: “Sed et pythones, et hariolos, et figuras idolorum, et immunditias, et abominationes, quæ fuerant in terra Juda et Jerusalem, abstulit Josias.”</note>

> “For the children of Israel shall remain many days without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice, and without an altar, and without an ephod <note>a ceremonial garment worn by high priests</note>, and without teraphim.” <note>original Latin: “Dies multos sedebunt filii Israel sine rege, et sine principe, et sine sacrificio, et sine altari, et sine ephod, et sine teraphim.”</note>

The learned Cornelius à Lapide <note>A Flemish Jesuit priest and scholar (1567–1637) known for his Bible commentaries</note>, writing on Genesis 31, notes: “Idols, or teraphim, which mean human statues or figures having human forms, as is evident in 1 Kings 19.” <note>original Latin: “Idola, teraphim quod significat statuæ humanæ siue humaneas formas habentes ut patet, I. In the Book of Tobit <note>referred to here as the Book of Tobias; a book of scripture found in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles</note>, we find a detailed and important account of <term>exorcism</term> <note>the religious practice of evicting demons or other spiritual entities from a person or area</note>, which clarifies the demonology of that era. Tobias, the son of Tobit, is sent under the guidance of the undercover Archangel Raphael to a man named Gabelus in the city of Rages in Media to retrieve ten talents of silver left in bond by his father. The heart and liver are intended to stop a demon from attacking him—the same demon who had killed the seven previous husbands of Sarah, the beautiful daughter of Raguel. 

When they arrive at Raguel's house, Tobias asks to marry Sarah. However, she is so desired by the demon Asmodeus that he had murdered seven men on their wedding nights, before the marriages could be consummated. Through the act of exorcism—specifically using the odor from the burning fish liver—and with the help of Saint Raphael, Tobias drives Asmodeus away: "Then the Angel Raphael took the Devil and bound him in the desert of upper Egypt." This story, which the author presents as a factual narrative, was originally written during the Babylonian exile in the early 7th century B.C. It clearly demonstrates that demons were believed to be capable of sexual love, similar to the "sons of God" who loved the "daughters of men" recorded in Genesis 6:2. This concept is comparable to the stories of the *Jinns* <note>supernatural spirits in Arabian folklore, often called genies</note> in Arabian lore. Asmodeus is perhaps the same as the Persian *Aëshma daêva*, who in the *Avesta* <note>the primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism</note> is second only to Angra Mainyu, the chief of evil spirits. Among the Persians, a certain power over evil spirits was justly attributed to the faithful dog.

The New Testament evidence for the reality of magic and divination is such that it cannot be disregarded by anyone who accepts the Christian revelation.

In the Gospels, we continually encounter possession by demons <note>original: "devils"</note>. These include: the miracle performed in the country of the Gerasenes (or Gergesenes) (Saint Matthew 8:28-34); the mute <note>original: "dumb"</note> man possessed by a demon (Saint Matthew 9:32-34); the healing of the boy who was <term>obsessed</term> <note>In traditional demonology, "obsession" refers to a demon attacking a person from the outside, whereas "possession" involves the demon controlling the person from within</note> (Saint Matthew 17:14-21); the <term>exorcism</term> <note>the religious act of expelling evil spirits</note> of the unclean spirit (Saint Mark 1:23-27); the casting out of demons whom Christ would not allow to speak (Saint Mark 1:32-34); the exorcism performed in the name of Jesus (Saint Mark 9:38); the demons who fled from our Lord's presence, crying out, "You are Christ, the Son of God" (Saint Luke 4:41); the healing of those troubled <note>original: "vexed"</note> by unclean spirits (Saint Luke 6:18); and many more instances.

Very early in the Apostolic ministry, one of the most famous figures in the entire history of witchcraft appears: Simon, known as **Simon Magus** <note>Simon the Sorcerer</note>, a sorcerer and <term>heresiarch</term> <note>the founder or leader of a heretical sect</note>. At the beginning of the persecution of the Christian community in Jerusalem (around 37 A.D.) <note>original Latin: circa</note>, which began with the martyrdom of Saint Stephen, Philip the Deacon went down to Samaria. Simon, a native of Gitta, was living in that city at the time. By his magic arts and by his mysterious doctrine—in which he announced himself as "the great power of God"—he had made a name for himself and gained many followers. He listened to Philip's sermons and was greatly impressed by them; he watched with wonder the miracles of healing and the exorcisms of unclean spirits. Like many of his countrymen, he was baptized and joined the community of believers in Christ. But it is obvious that he only took this step in order to gain, as he hoped, greater magical power and thus increase his influence. For when the Apostles Saint Peter and Saint John came to Samaria to bestow the outpouring of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note>—which was accompanied by heavenly manifestations—upon those who had been baptized by Philip, Simon offered...

Saint Peter immediately <note>original: "forthwith"</note> sharply rebuked the unholy neophyte <note>a new convert or beginner</note>, who, alarmed at this denunciation, implored the Apostles to pray for him.

Simon is not mentioned again in the New Testament, but the first Christian writers have much to say concerning him. Saint Justin Martyr, in his first *Apology* <note>original: *Apologia*</note> (AD 153–155) and in his dialogue *Against Trypho* <note>original: *Contra Tryphonem*</note> (before AD 161), describes Simon as a warlock who, at the instigation of demons, claimed to be a god. During the reign of the Emperor Claudius, Simon came to Rome, and by his sorceries won many followers who paid him divine honors <note>original: "honours"</note>. He was accompanied by an immoral <note>original: "lewd"</note> concubine from Tyre named Helena, whom he claimed was "Heavenly Intelligence" <note>This refers to the Gnostic concept of Ennoia, the first thought of God</note>, set free from bondage by himself, the “Great Power.”

In the *Pseudo-Clementine Homilies* (probably second century), Simon appears as the chief antagonist of Saint Peter, by whom his devilish practices are exposed and his enchantments dissolved. The apocryphal *Acts of Saint Peter*, which are of great age <note>original: "high antiquity"</note>,<sup>35</sup> give in detail the well-known legend of the death of Simon Magus. By his spells, the warlock had almost won the Emperor Nero to himself, but he was continually being foiled and thwarted owing to the intercession of the Apostle. At last, when Caesar <note>original: "Cæsar"</note> demanded one final proof of the truth of his doctrines—some miracle that might be performed at midday in the face of all Rome—Simon offered to take his flight into the heavens (a diabolical parody of the Ascension) so that men might know his power was just as mighty as that of Him whom the Christians worshipped as God.

A mighty crowd <note>original: "concourse"</note> gathered in the Forum: Vestal Virgins, Senators, Knights <term>Equites</term> <note>the social class of horsemen or knights in ancient Rome</note>, their ladies, and a whole rabble of common people. In the forefront of a new Imperial box sat the Lord Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus; on one side his mother, Agrippina, and on the other, Octavia his wife. Magic staff in hand, the magician advanced into the middle of the arena. Muttering a spell, he commanded his staff to await his return, and it immediately <note>original: "forthwith"</note> stood upright, alone, upon the pavement. Then, with a deep bow <note>original: "obeisance"</note> to the ruler of the known world, Simon Magus stretched forth his arms, and a moment more with

But the fame of Simon Magus as a wizard has been swallowed up by his bad reputation as a heretic; so early do heresy and magic go hand in hand. He was the first Gnostic, whose disciples—the Simonians, an Antinomian <note>A sect believing that Christians are released by grace from the obligation of observing moral laws</note> sect of the second century—indulged in the most repulsive <note>original: "sickest"</note> fantasies. Menander, the successor of Simon, proclaimed himself the Messiah and asserted that through his baptism, immortality was granted to his followers. He also was regarded as a mighty magician, and the sect named after him, the Menandrians, seems to have lasted for a considerable time.

In his missionary journeys, St. Paul was continually fighting witchcraft. At Paphos, he was opposed by the sorcerer Elymas; in Philippi a medium, “a certain girl possessed with a spirit of divination,” <note>original: "*spiritum pythonem*," referring to the Pythian spirit of the Oracle at Delphi</note> followed him along the streets crying out and naming him as “a servant of the most high God,” until he exorcised the spirit. In Ephesus, also, a large number of wandering <note>original: "vagabond"</note> Jewish exorcists had gathered. The chief characteristic of a Jewish exorcism was the recitation of names believed to be effective <note>original: "efficacious"</note>, principally the names of good angels, which were used either alone or in combination with *El* (God). Indeed, a blind reliance upon the sound of mere names had long been a settled practice with these amateur sorcerers, who considered that the essence of their charms lay in the use of particular names declaimed in a particular order, which varied on different occasions.

It was this belief, no doubt, that induced the seven sons of Sceva, who had witnessed St. Paul’s exorcisms in the name of Jesus, to try the formula for themselves: “I command <note>original: "conjure"</note> you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches.” This was an experiment that proved disastrous to their reputation. For in one case, the possessed man <note>original: "patient"</note> cried out, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?” and leaped upon them with hellish <note>original: "infernal"</note> strength, beating and wounding them. They fled from the house for their safety, their limbs bruised and their garments torn, to the great scandal of the neighborhood.

The authority of Christ Himself plainly supports the reality of demonic possession; meanwhile, Witchcraft is explicitly ranked by St. Paul alongside murder, rebellion <note>original: "sedition"</note>, hatred, and heresy (Galatians 5:20–21). St. John also twice mentions sorcerers in a hideous list <note>original: "catalogue"</note> of sinners. There can be no doubt whatsoever that the reality of Witchcraft is definitely maintained by the New Testament writers, and any denial of this implicitly involves a rejection of the truth of the Christian revelation.

Among the Jews of a later period, and probably even today, various diseases are said to be caused by demons. # CHAPTER VI

## DIABOLIC POSSESSION AND MODERN SPIRITISM

The phenomenon of demonic possession—the mere possibility of which materialists and modernists have mostly denied in recent years—has, nevertheless, been a belief held by all peoples throughout every period of history. In truth, anyone who accepts the reality of the spiritual world must realize that an age-long struggle for dominion <note>original: "empery"</note> exists all around us. This is a conflict where disembodied evil constantly fights against the eternal, unconquerable powers of good, using a thousand cunning tricks and a myriad of sorceries. Nature itself bears witness to this contest; disease and death, cruelty and pain, ugliness and sin are all evidence of this epic conflict. It would be surprising if some were not wounded in the fray—for we cannot stand apart; as St. Ignatius says, every person must fight under one of the two standards <note>A reference to the *Spiritual Exercises* of St. Ignatius of Loyola, which depicts a choice between the "Standard of Christ" and the "Standard of Satan."</note>—and it is not surprising if some even fall.

The ancient Egyptians, whose extremely old religion is notable for its sincere devotion, purity, and lofty idealism, certainly believed that some diseases were caused by evil spirits or demons. They believed these entities had the power, in exceptional circumstances, to enter human bodies and torment them, depending on the opportunities—conscious or unconscious—provided to their malicious natures and influence. Furthermore, the Egyptians were considered uniquely gifted in the art of curing diseases caused by demonic possession. One noteworthy instance of this was inscribed upon a <term>stele</term> <note>An upright stone slab or pillar, often used as a monument or to commemorate events.</note> and set up in the temple of the god Khonsu at Thebes so that everyone might learn of his power and glory.^1 When King Rameses II was in Mesopotamia, various princes gave him many offerings of gold and gems, and among them came the Prince of Bekhten, who brought his daughter, the most beautiful maiden of that land. When the king saw her, he loved her and granted her the title of "Royal Spouse, Chief Lady."

“Ra-neferu” (meaning "the beauties of Ra," the sun god), and taking her back to Egypt, he married her with great pomp and sacred solemnity. In the fifteenth year of the king’s reign, an ambassador arrived at his court from the Prince of Bekhten. He brought rich gifts and pleaded on behalf of the lady Bentresh <note>original: "Bent-ent-resht"</note>, the younger sister of the queen, Ra-neferu. He explained that a terrible disease had taken hold of her body; “therefore,” the envoy said, “I beg your Majesty to send a physician <note>The original text includes a footnote marker here, likely referring to the Egyptian term for a healer-scribe.</note> to see her.” 

Rameses ordered the books of the “Double House of Life” <note>An ancient Egyptian institution of higher learning where sacred texts, medical scrolls, and magical papyri were kept and copied.</note> to be brought and commanded the wise men to choose one from their number to be sent to Bekhten. They selected the sage Tehuti-em-heb, who immediately set out on the journey with the ambassador. When they arrived, the Egyptian priest soon discovered that Lady Bentresh was possessed by a demon or spirit over which he was powerless. Nearly in despair, the Prince of Bekhten sent another message to the king, begging him to dispatch even a god to his aid.

When the ambassador arrived a second time, Rameses was worshipping in the Temple of Khonsu Nefer-hetep at Thebes. He immediately petitioned that deity to allow his counterpart, Khonsu <note>Specifically "Khonsu-the-Planmaker," a manifestation of the god specialized in healing and driving out spirits.</note>, to go to Bekhten and deliver the prince's daughter from the demon who possessed her. Khonsu Nefer-hetep granted the request, and a fourfold measure of magical power was bestowed upon the statue of the god that was to travel to Bekhten. 

The god, seated in his ceremonial boat <note>In Egypt, statues of gods were transported in portable shrines shaped like boats, known as barques.</note>, along with five other boats carrying figures of other gods and a noble escort of horses and chariots on both the right and the left, set out for Bekhten. In due time, they were received with great honor. The god Khonsu was brought to where the princess was staying, magical ceremonies were performed, and the demon immediately <note>original: "incontinently"</note> departed. Khonsu remained in Bekhten for three years, four months, and five days, being worshipped with the deepest reverence. One night, however, the Prince had a dream in which he saw a golden hawk emerge from the sacred shrine and fly toward Egypt. In the morning, the Egyptian priests interpreted his dream to mean that the god now wished to return home. Accordingly, he was escorted back in magnificent state, and grateful gifts were sent along with him.

The Greeks of the earlier civilization were generally inclined to attribute all sickness to the gods. These deities often used illness as a means of immediate revenge against those who had insulted their images, profaned their sanctuaries, or mocked their worship. For example, Pentheus, who resisted the introduction of the mysteries of Dionysus <note>The god of wine, fertility, and ritual madness.</note> into Thebes, was driven mad by the offended deity.³ The madness of Ajax and that of the daughters of Proetus⁴—who imagined they had been changed into cows—shows us that this belief dates back to heroic times. In later days, Demaratus and his brother Alopecos were driven insane (original: *paraphronēsan*) after finding a statue of Artemis Orthosia, and this was considered to be the work of the goddess.⁵ The frenzy that attacked Quintus Fulvius was regarded as a punishment—a possession by evil spirits—because of his sacrilege in stealing the marble roof from the temple of Juno Lacinia at Locri.⁶

Pythagoras taught that the ailments of both humans and animals are caused by demons who swarm in the regions of the air. This doctrine simply stated clearly what had been more or less vaguely believed since the dawn of human history. This is why Homer, in the *Odyssey*, speaks of a man racked by a painful disease and says that a "hateful demon" is tormenting him: "But a hateful demon gripped him fast" <note>original Greek: στυγερὸς δέ οἳ ἔχραε δαίμων, V, 396</note>. The word *kakodaimonia* <note>original: κακοδαιμονία</note>, meaning possession by an evil spirit, signifies "raving madness" in the works of Aristophanes. Furthermore, the verb *kakodaimonao* <note>original: κακοδαιμονάω</note>, meaning to be tormented by an evil spirit, is used by Xenophon, Demosthenes, Dinarchus, and Plutarch⁷ among other authors.

Many philosophers believed that every person has a protecting spirit or *daimon* who, in a sense, personifies their individuality. It followed that they believed lunatics and the delirious were afflicted with madness by these spirits who guided them. Accordingly, the Greek names for those who were distraught are highly significant: *energoumenoi* <note>original: ἐνεργούμενοι; in later Greek, persons possessed by an evil spirit</note>, *daimonioleptoi* <note>original: δαιμονιόληπτοι; influenced by devils</note>, *theoleptoi* <note>original: θεόληπτοι; seized by a god</note>, *theoblaves* <note>original: θεόβλαβες; stricken by God</note>, and *theomanes* <note>original: θεόμανες; maddened by the gods</note>. Following this, Euripides uses the phrases "god-sent madness" <note>original: λύσσα θεομανής</note> and a "god-maddened fate" <note>original: θεομανὴς πότμος</note>.⁸ Even the very name *mania* given by the Greeks to madness was derived from the root-word *man*,

Indeed, the Romans believed that a madman was tormented by the goddess <term>Mania</term>, the mother of the <term>Lares</term> <note>guardian spirits of the Roman household</note>; they viewed the hallucinations of the insane as specters that relentlessly pursued them.¹⁰ Consequently, a madman was described as being "full of ghosts" (<term>laruarum plenus</term>) or "ghost-possessed" (<term>laruatus</term>)¹¹—someone disturbed by phantoms. We see this in the works of the playwright Plautus, where a doctor asks: "What kind of disease is this? Explain. Tell me, old father, I say. Are you ghost-possessed (<term>laruatus</term>) or a lunatic? Tell me now."¹²

The frenzied state of religious ecstasy that gripped the <term>Galli</term> <note>the eunuch priests of the goddess Cybele</note> and the <term>Corybantes</term> <note>armed, dancing worshippers of the goddess Rhea</note> when they celebrated the <term>Dionysia</term> <note>festivals in honor of Dionysus, the god of wine and ritual madness</note> seems to have been epidemic. It was universally believed to be the result of divine possession. There are many historical references connecting the rites of the goddesses <term>Cybele</term> and <term>Rhea</term> to those of <term>Dionysus</term>. Apollodorus¹³ notes that Dionysus was purified of his madness by Rhea at the Phrygian Cybele; he was then initiated into her secret rites and adopted her style of dress. From there, he traveled into Thrace accompanied by a procession of <term>Bacchanals</term> <note>female worshippers of Dionysus</note> and <term>Satyrs</term> <note>nature spirits, half-man and half-goat</note>. On the other hand, the historian Strabo¹⁴ believes these rites were brought from Thrace to Phrygia by colonists. He even cites a fragment from the lost play *The Edonians* by Aeschylus¹⁵ to prove that the worship of Dionysus and Cybele was essentially the same. We find a similar sentiment in Euripides' play *The Bacchae* (line 58):

> Up, and wake the sweet old sound,
> The clang that I and mystic Rhea found,
> The Timbrel of the Mountains.¹⁶

It is interesting to note that Nicander of Claros,¹⁷ who was a physician, wrote in his *Treatise on Antidotes* <note>original: *Alexipharmaca* (᾿Αλεξιφάρμακα)</note> about a specific form of lunacy. He compares the screams of his patients to the cries of a priestess of Rhea on the ninth day of her rituals, when she makes everyone she meets in the street tremble at the "hideous howl of the Idaean Mother." He specifically uses the phrase "the vessel-bearing priestess who serves the altar of Rhea" <note>original Greek: κερνοφόρος ζάκορος βωμίστρια 'Ρείης</note>.¹⁸

In the play *Hippolytus* (lines 141 and following), the Chorus speaks to Phaedra, saying:

> Is this some spirit, O child of man?
> Does Hecate hold you perhaps, or Pan?
> Does She of the Mountains work her ban,
> Or the Dread Corybantes bind you?¹⁹

And in the play *Medea* (lines 1171–1172), we read: "She seemed, I think, to be someone frenzied, inspired with madness by Pan or some other of the gods."²⁰

Aretæus, the medical writer famous for his accurate diagnoses, describes <term>Corybantic frenzy</term> <note>a state of wild, rhythmic madness associated with the worshippers of the goddess Cybele</note> as a mental illness in his book *On the Signs of Chronic Diseases* <note>original: *De signis chronicorum morborum*</note>, Book VI. This appears to be the only example of <term>demonic possession</term> in the Old Testament. Although the Hebrew word for "spirit" (*rûah*) does not necessarily imply a literal person or entity, the historian Josephus²⁴ indicates that the Jews certainly interpreted the word that way in this specific passage.

At this point, it is helpful to clearly explain the difference between <term>possession</term> and <term>obsession</term>, two technical terms that are often confused. <term>Obsession</term> means that a demon attacks a person’s body from the outside;²⁵ <term>possession</term> means that the demon takes control of the body from within. For example, Saint Jerome describes the "obsessions" that tormented Saint Hilarion:

> "His temptations were many; day and night the demons changed and renewed their traps. . . . How often, when he lay down, did naked women surround him? When he was hungry, how often was a lavish feast spread before him?"²⁶

Saint Antony the Great was also attacked in a similar way:

> "The devil did not stop attacking him; at night, he took the form of a young woman and mimicked a woman’s movements to deceive Antony."²⁷

These painful experiences are common in the lives of the Saints. Many examples could be mentioned, but one will suffice: Saint Margaret of Cortona,²⁸ a member of the <term>Franciscan</term> order of penitents,²⁹ who was long and terribly tormented:

> "Following her back and forth through her humble cell while she wept and prayed, [the devil] sang the most filthy songs. He lewdly urged Christ's dear servant—who was tearfully entrusting herself to the Lord—to join him in singing dirty songs . . . but her prayers and tears finally defeated the foul spirit and drove him far away."³⁰

Theologians, however, warn us to be very cautious in dealing with so difficult a matter, and the supreme authority of St. Alphonsus Liguori advises us that by far the greater part of these obsessions are distressing hallucinations, nervous exhaustion <note>original: "neurasthenia"</note>, imagination, or hysteria—in a word, pathological. He states: "It is advisable always to be very suspicious of such diabolic attacks, for it cannot be denied that for the most part they are fancy, or the effect of imagination, or weakness, especially when women are concerned."³¹ Dom Dominic Schram presses home the same point with equal emphasis: "Very often what are supposed to be demonic obsessions are nothing else than natural ailments, or morbid imaginings, or even distractions or actual lunacy. Therefore, it is necessary to deal with these cases most carefully, until the peculiar symptoms clearly show that it is actual obsession."³²

Demonic possession is frequently presented to us in the New Testament, and we have the authority of Christ Himself as to its reality. The skeptical <note>original: "infidel"</note> argument is to deny the possibility of possession in any circumstances, either on the hypothesis that there are no evil spirits in existence, or that they are powerless to influence the human body in the manner described. But whatever view <term>Rationalists</term> <note>thinkers who rely on reason rather than religious faith or revelation</note> may adopt—and they are continually shifting their ground—no reader of the scriptural narrative can deny that Christ, by word and deed, showed His entire belief in possession by evil spirits. And if Christ were divine, how could He foster and encourage a delusion? Why did He not correct it? Only two answers can be imagined. Either He was ignorant of a religious truth, or He deliberately gave instructions that He knew to be false, frequently acting in a way which was something more than misleading. To a Christian, either of these explanations is, of course, unthinkable. The <term>theory of accommodation</term> <note>the idea that Christ adapted His teaching to fit the mistaken cultural beliefs of His time</note> formulated by Winer³³ may be accepted by <term>Modernists</term> <note>a movement seeking to reinterpret religious tradition in light of modern science and philosophy</note>, but will be instantly condemned by all others. Accommodation is understood as the toleration of harmless illusions of the day that have little or no connection with religion. Even if this offensive idea <note>original: "fine piece of profanity"</note> were allowed—which, of course, must not be the case—the argument could not be applied here. Indeed, it seems wholly inappropriate even regarding a saint, but entirely impossible in consideration of the divinity of Christ.

According to St. Matthew 10:1, our Lord gave special powers to the Apostles to exorcise <note>original: "exorcize"</note> demons: "And having called his twelve disciples together, he gave them power over unclean spirits to cast them out, and to heal all manner of diseases, and all manner of infirmities." Our Lord Himself directly appeals to His power over evil spirits as a proof of His status as the Messiah <note>original: "Messiahship"</note>: "If I by the finger of God cast out devils; doubtless the kingdom of God is come upon you"; for if I by the finger of God cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you <note>original Greek: "εἰ δὲ ἐν δακτύλῳ Θεοῦ ἐκβάλλω τὰ δαιμόνια, ἄρα ἔφθασεν ἐφ' ὑμᾶς ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note> (St. Luke 11:20).

While yet on earth, Christ empowered the Apostles to cast out demons in His Name, and in His last solemn charge He promised that the same delegated power should be continued <note>original: "perpetuated"</note>: "These signs shall follow them that believe: in my name they shall cast out devils"; and these signs will follow those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons <note>original Greek: "σημεῖα δὲ τοῖς πιστεύσασι ταῦτα παρακολουθήσει· ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου δαιμόνια ἐκβαλοῦσι"</note> (St. Mark 16:17). But the efficacy of exorcism was conditional, not absolute as in the case of our Lord Himself; for He explained, on an occasion when the Apostles seemed to fail, that certain spirits could only be expelled by prayer and fasting. Moreover, a perfect belief and complete command are necessary for the exorciser. Then the disciples, coming to Jesus privately, said, "Why were we not able to cast it out?" And Jesus says to them, "Because of your little faith... but this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting" <note>original Greek: "τότε προσέλθοντες οἱ μαθηταὶ τῷ Ἰησοῦ κατ ἰδίαν εἶπον, Διατί ἡμεῖς οὐκ ἠδυνήθημεν ἐκβαλεῖν αὐτό; ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς λέγει αὐτοῖς, Διὰ τὴν ὀλιγοπιστίαν ὑμῶν· . . . τοῦτο δὲ τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐκπορεύεται εἰ μὴ ἐν προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ"</note> (St. Matthew 17:19–21). St. Paul, and no doubt the other Apostles and disciples, regularly made use of this exorcising power. Thus, at Philippi, where the girl "having a <term>pythonical spirit</term> <note>term: A spirit of divination. The name "python" refers to the serpent of Delphi in Greek mythology; in the New Testament, it describes someone possessed by a spirit that allowed them to tell fortunes.</note>... who brought to her masters much gain by <term>divining</term> <note>term: fortune-telling or predicting the future through supernatural means</note>" (a certain slave girl having a spirit of divination... who provided much profit to her masters by fortune-telling) <note>original Greek: "παιδίσκην τινὰ ἔχουσαν πνεῦμα πύθωνα . . . ἥτις ἐργασίαν πολλὴν παρεῖχε τοῖς κυρίοις αὐτῆς μαντευομένῃ"</note><sup>34</sup> met St. Paul and St. Luke and proclaimed them as servants of the most high God, St. Paul "being grieved,"

Paul turned and said to the spirit: "I command you, in the name of Jesus Christ, to go out from her." And it went out that same hour (Acts 16:16–18). And at Ephesus, a center for magic and necromancy, "God worked unusual miracles through the hands of Paul. So that even handkerchiefs and aprons were carried from his body to the sick, and diseases left them, and the evil spirits went out of them" (Acts 19:11, 12). Those who do not believe that the powers Our Lord permanently granted to the Apostles and their followers suddenly ended with the final verse of the Acts of the Apostles, realize that the spiritual gift <note>original: "charisma"</note> of exorcism has continued through the ages. In truth, the Church has practiced it without interruption until the present day.

The Exorcist is ordained by the Bishop for this office; this ordination is the second of the four minor orders <note>In the historical hierarchy of the Western Church, "minor orders" were stages of clergy service below the rank of subdeacon, deacon, and priest.</note> of the Western Church. Pope Cornelius (251–252) mentions in his letter to Fabius that there were then forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers in the Roman Church. The establishment of these orders, along with the organization of their duties, seems to have been the work of Cornelius’s predecessor, Pope Saint Fabian the Martyr (236–251).

The rite for the Ordination of Exorcists, "On the Ordination of Exorcists" <note>original Latin: "De Ordinatione Exorcistarum"</note>, is as follows: First, the Book of Exorcisms (or the Pontifical or Missal in its place) must be ready at hand. The liturgical instruction <note>original: "rubric"</note> states: "A Book of Exorcisms must be prepared for those who are to be ordained Exorcists; however, the Pontifical or the Missal may be handed to them instead" <note>original Latin: "Pro Exorcistis ordinandis paretur liber exorcismorum, cuius loco dari potest Pontificale uel Missale"</note>. When the Readers <note>original: "Lectors"</note> have been ordained, the Bishop puts his mitre <note>A ceremonial tall, pointed headdress worn by bishops.</note> back on and takes his place upon his seat or faldstool <note>A portable folding chair used by a bishop during ceremonies.</note> at the Epistle side <note>The right-hand side of the altar when facing it.</note> of the altar. His assistants bring the Missal <note>A book containing the texts for the Mass.</note> and the bugia <note>A small hand-held candle used to help the bishop read.</note>, and he proceeds to read the Gradual, or—if it is within the eight-day celebration <note>original: "Octave"</note> of Pentecost—the *Alleluia*. Meanwhile, the choir sings the Gradual. When it is finished, he rises, removes his mitre, and turning to the altar, chants the third collect <note>A brief, formal prayer used in the liturgy.</note>. He then sits again, puts his mitre back on, and the third reading <note>original: "Lection"</note> is read. Two chaplains assist him with the candle and the book from which he reads the reading. It should be remarked that the Exorcist is specifically ordained "to cast out demons," and he receives "power to place his (your) hands upon the possessed, so that by the laying on of his (your) hands,<sup>39</sup> the grace of the Holy Ghost, and the words of exorcism, evil spirits are driven out from the bodies of the possessed." The very striking term *spiritual commander* <note>original: "spiritualis imperator"</note> is strictly applied to him, and God the Father is earnestly entreated to grant him the grace "to cast out demons from the bodies of the possessed with all their many tricks <note>original: "sleights"</note> of wickedness." Nothing could be plainer, nothing could be more solemn, and nothing could be more full of meaning and intention. The order and delegated power of Exorcists cannot be dismissed as unimportant; at least, to do so is completely contrary to the mind of the Church as emphatically expressed in her most authoritative rites. In actual practice, the office of Exorcist has almost wholly been taken over by clerics in major orders <note>Major orders include priests, deacons, and (formerly) subdeacons; minor orders were the lower ranks of the clergy.</note>, but this, of course, in no way affects the status and authority of the second of the four minor orders.

Every priest, and perhaps especially a parish priest, is liable to be called upon to perform his duty as an Exorcist. In doing so, he must carefully bear in mind and adhere to the instructions of the *Roman Ritual* <note>original: "Rituale Romanum," the official liturgical book containing the rites for sacraments and various blessings.</note>, and he will do well to respect the laws of provincial or diocesan synods, which for the most part require that the Bishop should be consulted and his authorization obtained before an exorcism is attempted.

The chief points of importance in the detailed instructions, organized under twenty-one sections prefixed to the rite in the *Ritual*, may be briefly summarized as follows: (1) The priest or exorcist should be of mature age, humble, of blameless life, courageous, experienced, and of well-attested prudence. The exorcist should prepare himself for his task by special acts of devotion and mortification <note>original: "mortification"; religious practices of self-discipline, such as fasting or abstinence, intended to strengthen the spirit</note>, by fervent prayer, and by fasting (Matthew 17:21). 

(2) He must be a person of scholarship and learning, a systematic student, and well-versed in the latest trends and developments of psychological science. 

(3) Possession is not to be easily assumed. Each case is to be carefully examined, and great caution must be used in distinguishing genuine possession from certain forms of disease. 

(4) He should advise the possessed person, as far as they are capable, to prepare themselves for the exorcism through prayer, fasting, confession, and Holy Communion. While the rite is in progress, the exorcist must foster in his heart a most lively faith in the goodness of God and a perfect surrender to the divine will. 

(5) The exorcism should take place in the Church or some other sacred place, if convenient, but no crowd of onlookers must be allowed to gather out of mere curiosity. There should, however, be a number of witnesses—serious and devout persons of standing, high respectability, and proven integrity—who are not prone to idle gossip but are discreet and silent. If the exorcism takes place in a private house due to sickness or some other legitimate reason, it is best for members of the family to be present. This is especially required as a measure of precaution if the subject is a woman. 

(6) If the patient seems to fall asleep or tries to hinder the exorcist in any way during the rite, he is to continue, if possible with even greater persistence, for such actions are likely a ruse to trick him. 

(7) Although the exorcist should be humble and place no reliance upon himself alone, he is to speak with command and authority. Should the patient be convulsed or tremble, let the exorcist be more fervent and more insistent; the prayers and adjurations <note>original: "adjurations"; solemn commands or appeals to a spirit or person to act</note> are to be recited with great faith and a full, assured consciousness of power. 

(8) Let the exorcist remember that he uses the words of Holy Scripture and the Holy Church, not his own words and phrases. 

(9) All idle and irrelevant questioning of the demon is to be avoided, nor should the evil spirit be allowed to speak at length without being stopped or rebuked. 

(10) The Blessed Sacrament <note>The consecrated bread (the Host) used in the Mass, believed by Catholics to be the literal Body of Christ</note> is not to be brought near the body of the obsessed <note>original: "obsessed"; in traditional theology, "obsession" refers to an external demonic attack, while "possession" refers to an internal one</note> during the exorcism for fear of possible disrespect. Relics of the Saints may be used, but in this case every care must be most scrupulously [observed...]

A shorter form of exorcism, which is more general and differs in its aim and use, was published by order of Pope Leo XIII and may be found in the later editions of the *Rituale Romanum* <note>The Roman Ritual, a liturgical book containing the rites for sacraments and other ceremonies.</note>, titled "Exorcism against Satan and the Apostate Angels."⁴¹ <note>original Latin: "Exorcismus in Satanam et Angelos apostaticos." Note: The OCR likely misread "apostaticos" as "apostalicos."</note> After the customary invocation "In the name [of the Father, etc.]..." <note>original: "In nomine . . ."</note> the rite begins with a prayer to St. Michael. A solemn adjuration <note>a formal, earnest command or oath</note> of some length follows with versicles <note>short sentences said by the priest</note> and responses, a second prayer is next recited, and the whole concludes with three petitions from the Litany:

> "From the deceits and crafts of the Devil; O Lord, deliver us. That it may please You to rule Your Church so it shall always serve You in lasting peace and true liberty; We beseech You, hear us. That You would deign to crush and subdue all the enemies of Your Holy Church; We beseech You, hear us."

The final rubric <note>liturgical instruction</note> states: "And the place is sprinkled with *Holy Water*."⁴²

It might perhaps be inappropriate to treat the Baptismal Exorcism and exorcisms such as those for water, salt,⁴³ and oil here. It may, however, be noticed that in the ceremony of the Blessing of the Waters⁴⁴ (approved by the Sacred Congregation of Rites <note>the Vatican department responsible for liturgy and sainthood</note>, December 6, 1890), performed on the Eve of the Epiphany, there occurs a solemn "Exorcism against Satan and the Apostate Angels," followed by "Exorcism of Salt" and "Exorcism of Water." <note>original Latin: "Exorcismus contra Satanam et Angelos apostalicos," "Exorcismus salis," and "Exorcismus aquæ."</note>

There are recorded throughout history innumerable examples of obsession and demoniacal possession, as well as of potent and successful exorcism. It is, of course, quite possible, and indeed probable, that many of these cases were due to natural causes, such as epilepsy, acute hysteria, early stages of insanity <note>original: "incipient lunacy"</note>, and the like. But, nonetheless, when every allowance has been made for incorrect diagnosis, for ill-informed descriptions of rare and obscure forms of both physical and mental maladies, for credulity, honest mistakes, and exaggerations of every kind, there will yet remain a very considerable portion which it seems impossible to account for and explain except as possession by some evil and hostile intelligence. But nobody is asked to accept all the instances of diabolic possession recorded in the history of the Church, nor even to form any definite opinion upon the historical evidence in favor of any particular case. That is primarily a matter for historical and medical science. And, perhaps, even at

At the present day and among civilized races, this phenomenon is not as rare as is popularly supposed.

The annals of <term>Bedlam</term> <note>The Bethlem Royal Hospital in London, a famous and ancient psychiatric hospital whose name became a synonym for madness and chaos.</note>, of many a private madhouse, and many an asylum could tell strange and hideous histories. And if we may judge from the accounts furnished by the pioneers of the Faith in missionary countries, the evidence of diabolic agency there is as clearly defined and unmistakable as it was in Galilee in the time of Christ.⁴⁵

Demoniacal possession is frequently described and alluded to by the early Church Fathers and apologists in matter-of-fact terms which leave no shadow of doubt as to their belief in this regard. Indeed, the success of Christian exorcism is often brought forward as an argument for the acceptance of the divinity of the founder of Christianity. It would be an easy, but a very lengthy process, to make a <term>catena</term> <note>original Latin: "catena" (chain); a sequence of connected citations or authorities used to prove a point.</note> of such passages from Greek and Latin authors alike.⁴⁶ St. Justin Martyr (*died around* A.D. 165) speaks of demons flying from "the touch and breathing of Christians" (*Apology*, II, 6), "as from a flame that burns them," adds St. Cyril of Jerusalem (*died* 385–386: *Catechesis*, XX, 3). Origen (*died* 253–254) mentions the laying on of hands to cast out devils, while St. Ambrose⁴⁷ (*died* 397), St. Ephrem the Syrian⁴⁸ (*died* 373), and others used this ceremony when exorcising. The holy sign of the Cross also is extolled by many Fathers for its efficacy against all kinds of diabolic molestation; thus Lactantius writes: "For now it is enough to explain the power of this sign [the Cross] and how much it prevails. Whoever sees how much of a terror this sign is to demons will know, for when they are commanded in the name of Christ, they flee from the bodies that they have possessed,"⁴⁹ <note>original Latin: "Nunc satis est, huius signi [Crucis] potentiam, quantum ualeat exponere. Quanto terrori sit dæmonibus hoc signum, sciet, qui uiderit, quatenus adiurati per Christum, de corporibus, quæ obsederint, fugiant."</note> *Divine Institutes*, IV, xxvii.⁵⁰ St. Athanasius (*died* 373), *On the Incarnation of the Word*, XLVII; St. Basil (*died* 379), *On Isaiah*, XI, 249; St. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis*, XIII; St. Gregory of Nazianzus (*died around* 389), *Poem Against Anger*, 415 sqq., all have passages of no little weight to the same effect. St. Cyril, *Introductory Catechesis*, IX; and St. Athanasius, *To Marcellus*, XXIII, recommend that the prayers of exorcism and the solemn command <note>original: "adjuration"</note> should as far as possible repeat the exact words of Holy Scripture.

...and relieved by the power and prayer of some Saint or holy servant of God.⁵¹

Thus in the life of Saint Benedict—that noble, calm, dignified, prudent, great-souled, and high-minded hero—there are recorded several occasions when he was confronted by extraordinary manifestations of evil spirits who resisted the building of his monastery on the crest of Monte Cassino, where Satanism had previously been practiced. It is not said that there were any visible appearances, except to Saint Benedict alone,⁵² but a succession of unfortunate accidents, abnormal occurrences, and constant alarms plainly showed that the Saint was contending against superhuman difficulties. More than once he found it necessary to <term>exorcize</term> <note>To drive out an evil spirit through ritual or prayer.</note> certain of his monks,⁵³ and his triumph over these malignant and destructive influences was so marked that he has always been venerated in the Church as a most powerful "chaser of demons" <note>original Latin: "effugator dæmonum"</note>, and he is confidently invoked in the hour of spiritual peril and deadly attack. Great faith is also placed in the Medal of Saint Benedict. This medal, which was originally a cross, is dedicated to the devotion in honor of the <term>Patriarch</term> <note>A title of honor for the founder of a religious order; here, Saint Benedict of Nursia, the founder of Western Monasticism.</note>. One side bears the figure of the Saint holding a cross in his right hand and the <term>Holy Rule</term> <note>The Rule of Saint Benedict, a foundational book of precepts written for monks living in community.</note> in his left. On the other side is a cross, together with the following letters arranged on and around it: C.S.P.B., *The Cross of the Holy Father Benedict* <note>original Latin: "Crux Sancti Patris Benedicti"</note>. C.S.S.M.L., *May the Holy Cross be my Light* <note>original Latin: "Crux Sacra Sit Mihi Lux"</note>. N.D.S.M.D., *Let not the Devil be my guide* <note>original Latin: "Non Draco Sit Mihi Dux"</note>.

> U.R.S. : N.S.M.U. : S.M.Q.L. : I.U.B. : *Begone, Satan; never suggest vain things to me. What you offer is evil; drink your own poison.* <note>original Latin: "Vade Retro Satana: Nunquam Suade Mihi Vana: Sunt Mala Quae Libas: Ipse Venena Bibas."</note>⁵⁴

The "Centenary" version of the medal (struck at Monte Cassino in 1880 to commemorate the 1,300th anniversary of the birth of Saint Benedict in 480) has the words "From Holy Monte Cassino, 1880" <note>original Latin: "Ex S.M. Cassino MDCCCLXXX"</note> under the figure. On the same side, around the edge, runs the inscription: "May we be protected by his presence at the hour of our death" <note>original Latin: "Eius in obitu nrõ præsentia muniamur"</note>, and the word PAX (Peace) appears above the cross.

<header>DIABOLIC POSSESSION</header>

At the abbey of Metten in Bavaria during the year 1647, several women accused of witchcraft testified that they had no power over Metten because it was under the particular protection of the cross. Upon investigation, a number of painted crosses surrounded by the letters which are now engraved upon Benedictine medals were found on the walls of the abbey, but their meaning <note>original: "signification"</note> had been wholly forgotten. At length, in an old manuscript written in 1415, a picture was discovered representing Saint Benedict holding a staff which ended in a cross in one hand, and a scroll in the other. On the staff and scroll were written in full the formulas for which the mysterious letters were the initials. Medals with the figure of Saint Benedict, a cross, and these letters then began to be manufactured <note>original: "struck"</note> and rapidly spread over Europe. The medals were first authoritatively approved by Pope Benedict XIV in his official documents <note>original: "briefs," referring to papal letters</note> of 23 December 1741, and 12 March 1742.

In the case of the possessed boys of Illfurt (Alsace), they exhibited the utmost horror and dread of a Medal of Saint Benedict.

These medals are hallowed with a specific rite⁵⁵ in which the command <note>original: "adjuration"</note> commences:

> “I exorcize you, medals, by God the Father ✠ Almighty. . . .” <note>original Latin: “Exorcizo uos, numismata, per Deum Patrem ✠ omnipotentem. . . .”</note> “May the power of the adversary, all the host of the Devil, every evil attack, and every spirit and illusion <note>original: "glamour," meaning a deceptive spell</note> of Satan be utterly put to flight and driven far away by the virtue of these medals. . . . ⁵⁶

The prayer runs:

> “O Lord Jesus Christ . . . by Your most Holy Passion, I humbly pray and beseech You that You would grant that whoever devoutly invokes Your Holy Name in this prayer and petition which You Yourself have taught us, may be delivered from every deceit of the Devil and from all his wiles; and that You would graciously grant <note>original: "vouchsafe"</note> to bring Your servant to the harbor of salvation. You who live and reign. . . .”⁵⁷

Saint Maurus also, the beloved disciple of Saint Benedict, was famous for the cures he performed <note>original: "wrought"</note> in cases of possession.⁵⁸ Visiting France in 543, he became the founder and superior of the abbey of Glanfeuil in Anjou, which was later known by his name, Saint-Maur-sur-Loire <note>original: "St. Maur-sur-Loise"</note>.⁵⁹ The relics of Saint Maurus, after various transfers <term>translations</term> <note>In hagiography, "translation" refers to the formal moving of a saint's remains from one location to another.</note>, were finally enshrined at Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Throughout the Middle Ages, the tomb of Saint Maur at Saint-Germain was a celebrated place of pilgrimage, and the possessed were brought here in large numbers to be healed.⁶¹

The Holy Winding Sheet of Besançon, likewise, was a place of great resort for the relief and cure of possession. This venerable relic, being one of the linen cloths used at the burial of Christ, was brought to Besançon in 1206 by Otto de la Roche, and the feast of its arrival (<term>The Reception</term> <note>original: *Susceptio*</note>) was ordered to be kept on 11 July. At present, it is celebrated as a "double of the first class" <note>a ranking in the Catholic liturgical calendar indicating a feast of the highest importance</note> in the cathedral, Saint Jean, and as a "double of the second class" throughout the diocese.

Novenas <note>a traditional Catholic practice of saying prayers or holding religious services over nine successive days</note> made in the church at Bonnet, near Nantes, were popularly supposed to be of especial efficacy in healing possession.

It is, of course, impossible even briefly to catalog the most important and striking of the numberless cases of possession recorded throughout the centuries in every country and every era. Of these, a great number are, no doubt, to be attributed to disease; very many to a mixture of hysteria and semi-conscious or, more frequently, unconscious fraud; some few to mere <term>trickery</term> <note>original: "chousing"</note>; and, if human evidence is worth anything at all, many actually to diabolic influence.

There were some curious episodes in England during Queen Elizabeth’s reign, when a third-rate Puritan minister, John Darrel, made a considerable stir owing to his attempts at <term>exorcism</term> <note>the religious rite of expelling evil spirits</note>. This idea seems to have been suggested to him by the <term>exorcisms</term> of the famous Jesuit missionary priest, William Weston, who after having been educated at Oxford, Paris, and Douai, entered the Society of Jesus <note>the Jesuit order</note> on 5 November 1575, at Rome. He then worked and taught in Spain until he was called to his native mission, actually arriving in England on 20 September 1584. In the course of his labors, which at that dangerous time were carried out in circumstances of extreme peril, he was required to perform the rite of <term>exorcism</term> upon several distressed persons, who were for the most part brought to him at the houses of two zealous Catholics, Sir George Peckham of Denham, near Uxbridge,

Although the rites—which several priests attended—were performed with the utmost secrecy, and every precaution was taken to prevent reports from spreading, someone gossiped. Within about a year, various exaggerated accounts were circulating, until the matter eventually came before the <term>Privy Council</term> <note>the monarch's body of advisors in England, who often dealt with matters of state security and religious dissent</note>. A violent flare-up of persecution followed immediately. Many of the exorcists were seized and killed because they were priests; the rest, including Weston, were thrown into jail in August 1586. A long period of imprisonment followed. In 1599, Weston was sent to the Tower of London, where he suffered such hardships that he nearly lost his sight. Finally, in 1603, he was banished. He spent the rest of his days at Seville and Valladolid in Spain. He was serving as the rector of the college in Valladolid at the time of his death on June 9, 1615.⁶²

In 1586, just as the Jesuit fathers' exorcisms had unfortunately attracted widespread attention and foolish commentary, John Darrel—though a Protestant and lacking both proper ordination and training—rashly decided to try to match their achievements. He was young, barely over twenty years old, foolhardy, and ignorant—three qualities that even today often win a person cheap notoriety. 

It appears he was first called in to cure a seventeen-year-old girl named Katherine Wright, who lived in Mansfield, Nottinghamshire. Darrel immediately declared that she was afflicted by an evil spirit. He prayed over her from four o'clock in the morning until noon, but without any result at all. He then claimed that the girl had been bewitched and that the demon had been sent by a woman named Margaret Roper, with whom the patient had recently quarreled. The girl supported his story, and the accused woman was immediately taken into custody by the constable. After having been harassed and even tortured, the wretched creature made some rambling and incoherent admissions of guilt, which were twisted into a connected story. By now, Darling had been ill for three months, and far from improving, he was getting worse.

At this juncture—at exactly the most dramatic moment—John Darrel, full of bluster and arrogance, appeared on the scene and immediately took charge of affairs. He was accused of having drawn magic circles upon the ground, and although he firmly denied the charge, he was convicted of felony and hanged at Lancaster.

It is possible that Darrel had some degree of hypnotic <note>original: "mesmeric"</note> control over Somers, whose performance was at the very least remarkable. It was reported that "he tore at himself; he foamed at the mouth; he rolled around; his face was twisted; his eyes stared, and his tongue hung out," along with a thousand other such animal-like <note>original: "apish"</note> antics that greatly impressed the onlookers. However, <term>obsession</term> <note>In the theology of the time, "obsession" referred to external harassment by a demon, whereas "possession" meant the demon was inside the body.</note> followed possession. The demon continued to attack him, and before long, young Master Somers accused thirteen women of causing his illnesses through their witchcraft. Darrel, the witch-finder, had by this time achieved a position of significant importance in the town, having been chosen as a preacher at St. Mary's Church, and he was prepared to support his pupil to the absolute limit. 

Yet even his influence failed for some reason, and all but two of the women involved were released from prison. Next, certain skeptical citizens had the "bad taste" to interfere. They took the main actor (Somers) to the house of correction, where he soon confessed that he was a fraud and had been carefully coached by Darrel. The matter now became a public scandal. Based on a report from the Archdeacon of Derby, the Archbishop of York appointed a commission to investigate the facts. When brought before these clergymen—none of whom had the means to make a sound judgment—Somers took back his confession. He claimed he had been pressured into slandering Darrel, and he then fell into such fits, foamings, and contortions that the ill-informed <note>original: "ignoramuses"</note> officials were convinced that his demonic possession was real.

It is obvious that Bancroft really controlled the examination from start to finish, and that he acted as both prosecutor and judge. Somers now told the Court how he had been in constant communication with Darrel, and how they had met secretly when Darrel taught him "to do all those tricks which Katherine Wright did" and later sent him to see and learn from the "boy of Burton" <note>Referring to Thomas Darling, another youth who had previously claimed to be possessed under Darrel's guidance.</note>. The cunning <note>original: "vulpine"</note> Puritan was finally caught. No doubt the Bishop of London may have been a bit harsh, but after all, he was dealing with a complete fraud. Darrel and More were removed from the ministry and sent to strict imprisonment.

The whole of this case is reported by Samuel Harsnett, chaplain to Bancroft, in a book of three hundred and twenty-four pages titled *A Discovery of the Fraudulent Practices of John Darrel, Bachelor of Arts. . . . It is probable that in his books, Harsnett is largely acting as the mouthpiece for the ideas of Richard Bancroft,<sup>65</sup> whose opinions must have carried significant weight, seeing as he became the Archbishop of Canterbury in 1604. But Harsnett himself was also a man who could stand on his own, a clergyman destined for the highest promotions. As the Master of Pembroke Hall at Cambridge, Vice-chancellor of that University, Bishop of Chichester, Bishop of Norwich, and finally, in 1628, the Archbishop of York,<sup>66</sup> he was certainly one of the most prominent men of his day. His views, therefore, are not only interesting but may be regarded as an expression of recognized Anglican authority. 

Bancroft, who was a harsh persecutor of Catholics, seems to have turned over a large amount of research material he had collected to Harsnett. In 1603, Harsnett published a bitter <note>original: "verjuiced"</note> attack upon the priesthood in particular and upon the supernatural in general under the title *A Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures*.<sup>67</sup> This violent and foolish argument <note>original: "polemic"</note>, with its heavy sentences of coarse ill-humour and scornful profanity, grates upon the reader like the harsh screeching of a spiteful person. It is true that it has a certain power due to the sheer vehemence and elaborate enthusiasm of the angry clergyman—the kind of force found in vulgar abuse <note>original: "Billingsgate"; named after a London fish market famous for the foul language of its traders.</note> and deafening insults shouted by someone with tireless lungs and a raspy tongue. As a sober argument or a reasoned contribution to debate, the work is worthless and has been completely forgotten. 

Nevertheless, historically, Harsnett and Bancroft are important. It was Bancroft who drew up (or at least inspired and pushed through the Church council) and immediately enforced the church laws generally known as the Canons of 1604. This article seems definitely intended to fix the official position of the Church of England.⁶⁸ The whole question of exorcism had, in common with every other point of Christian doctrine, caused the most bitter <note>original: "acrid"</note> disagreement. The Lutherans kept <note>original: "retained"</note> exorcism in the baptismal ceremony <note>original: "rite"</note> and were both immediate <note>original: "instant"</note> and persistent in their exorcisms of the possessed. Martin Luther himself had a most vivid awareness of and the firmest belief in the physical <note>original: "material"</note> opposition <note>original: "antagonism"</note> of evil. The black stain in the castle of Wartburg still marks the room where he threw his ink-pot <note>original: "ink-horn"</note> at the Devil. People with frail <note>original: "silly"</note> bodies, the blind, the mute <note>original: "dumb"</note>, and the mentally disabled <note>original: "idiot"</note>, were, as often as not, afflicted by demons; the raving madman was assuredly possessed. Doctors <note>original: "physicians"</note> might explain these evils as natural illnesses <note>original: "infirmity"</note>, but such doctors were ignorant men; they did not know the cunning <note>original: "craft"</note> and power of Satan. Many a poor soul who was generally supposed to have committed suicide had in truth been seized by the Fiend and strangled by him. The Devil could father <note>original: "beget"</note> children; had not Luther himself encountered <note>original: "come in contact with"</note> one of them?⁶⁹ 

At the close of the sixteenth century, however, an endless <note>original: "interminable"</note> and desperate struggle took place between the believers in exorcism and the Swiss and Silesian religious groups <note>original: "sectaries"</note> who entirely rejected <note>original: "discarded"</note> exorcism,⁷⁰ either declaring it to have belonged only to the earliest years of Christianity or else trying to explain away the Biblical examples on purely logical <note>original: "rationalistic"</note> grounds. In England, baptismal exorcism was kept in the First Prayer Book of 1549, but by 1552, owing to the influence <note>original: "authority"</note> of Martin Bucer, we find it entirely removed. Under Elizabeth, the ever-increasing influence of Zurich and Geneva, to which the most complete respect <note>original: "deference"</note> was paid, thoroughly discredited exorcisms of any kind, and this skeptical <note>original: "misbelieving"</note> attitude is repeatedly and fully made clear in the various “Apologies” and “Defenses” written by Bishop John Jewel and his followers.

A letter of Archbishop Parker in 1574⁷¹ regarding <note>original: "with reference to"</note> the proven frauds of two lazy girls <note>original: "idle wenches"</note>, Agnes Bridges and Rachel Pinder,⁷² shows that he was thoroughly skeptical as to the possibility of possession, and his successor, the strong <note>original: "stout"</note> old Calvinist Whitgift, was certainly of the same mind.

In 1603, five clergymen attempted an exorcism in the case of Mary Glover, the daughter of a merchant in Thames Street. She was said to be possessed due to the sorceries of a certain Elizabeth Jackson. John Swan, “a famous Minister of the Gospel,” took the lead in this business, which caused quite a stir <note>original: "made considerable noise"</note> at the time. The Puritans were naturally anxious to prove <note>original: "vindicate"</note> their power over the Devil, and they seem to have greedily <note>original: "avidly"</note> seized any such opportunity that arose. Swan did not fail to publicize his supposed triumph in *A True and Brief Report of Mary Glover’s Torment <note>original: "Vexation"</note> and of Her Deliverance by the Means of Fasting and Prayer, 1603*. Moreover, after her deliverance, he took her home to be his servant “lest Satan should assault her again.” 

Old Mother Jackson was indicted, committed by Sir John Crook, the Recorder of London, and actually sentenced by Sir Edmund Anderson, the Lord Chief Justice, to be placed in the pillory four times and be kept in prison for a year. Unfortunately for the would-be exorcists and their claims, King James—whose sharp <note>original: "shrewd"</note> suspicions were aroused—sent a physician, Dr. Edward Jorden, to examine the girl. Dr. Jorden detected her fraud <note>original: "imposture"</note>, in which I have no doubt she had been well coached by the Puritans. Dr. Jorden recounted the circumstances in his pamphlet *A Brief Discourse of a Disease Called the "Suffocation of the Mother," Written Upon the Occasion which has Lately Been Taken Thereby to Suspect Possession by an Evil Spirit* (London, 1603). <note>The "Suffocation of the Mother" was a contemporary medical term for hysteria, which was then believed to be caused by the womb—or "mother"—rising up in the body and suffocating the patient.</note> 

The ministers were extremely frustrated <note>original: "chagrined"</note>, and one Stephen Bradwell even defended them in a biting reply <note>original: "tart rejoinder"</note> to Jorden. This was ultimately pointless, as his laborious writings <note>original: "lucubrations"</note> remain unpublished. It is not improbable that this performance influenced Bishop Bancroft when he drew up Article 72 of the 1604 Canons. <note>The 1604 Canons were the laws of the Church of England; Article 72 prohibited clergy from performing exorcisms without the express permission of their Bishop.</note>

Francis Hutchinson, in his *Historical Essay on Witchcraft* (1718), doubts whether any Bishop of the Church of England ever granted a license for exorcism to any of his clergy. Indeed, the case provided by Dr. F. G. Lee—who relates how Bishop Seth Ward of Exeter assigned a ritual form under his own signature and seal in January 1665 to the Rev. ...belonging to the parish of Little Petherick <note>A village in Cornwall, England.</note>, an apparition was seen by a boy about sixteen years old, the son of a man named Mr. Bligh. At last, he confessed his fears to his family. They treated the matter with ridicule and scolded him harshly when they saw that jokes and mockery were of no use.

Eventually, Mr. Ruddle <note>John Ruddle (1637–1699), the Vicar of Launceston, known for his account of this exorcism.</note> was sent for to argue the boy out of his foolishness. The vicar, however, was quick to perceive that young Bligh was speaking the truth, and he immediately accompanied his pupil to the field, where they both unmistakably saw the phantom exactly as it had been described. After a little while, Mr. Ruddle visited Exeter to interview his bishop and obtain the necessary license for an exorcism. The Bishop, however, asked: “On what authority do you claim that I am entrusted with the power to do this? Our Church, as is well known, has renounced <note>original: "abjured"</note> certain branches of her ancient power because they were perverted and abused.”

Mr. Ruddle quoted the Canons of 1604 <note>The 1604 Canons of the Church of England; specifically, Canon 72 prohibited ministers from attempting to cast out devils without the express license of their Bishop.</note>, and this appears to have satisfied the prelate, who called in his secretary and authorized a form of service, so that the matter was completed immediately <note>original: "incontinently done"</note>. But the worthy vicar was not permitted to depart without a thoroughly characteristic warning: “Keep this secret, Mr. Ruddle—weak brethren! Weak brethren!” <note>A reference to "the weak," meaning those whose faith might be easily unsettled or who might be prone to superstition if they heard of such things.</note>

The manuscript diary gives some details of the manner in which the ghost was "laid" <note>Banished or put to rest.</note>, and it is significant to read that the practitioner described a circle and a pentacle <note>A five-pointed star symbol used in ritual magic.</note> upon the ground, while also making use of a rowan “crutch” or wand <note>Rowan wood was traditionally used in folk magic for protection against spirits.</note>. He mentions “a parchment scroll,” spoke in Syriac <note>An ancient Aramaic language often used in religious and magical texts.</note>, and proceeded to interrogate the spirit as the books advise; he “went through the proper forms of dismissal and fulfilled everything as it was set down and written in my notes,” and then “with certain fixed rites I did dismiss that troubled ghost.” It would be interesting to know what form and ceremonies the Bishop prescribed. It does not sound like the details of a Catholic exorcism, but rather some superstitious and magical ritual. From what is related, the form can hardly have been created just for that specific occasion <note>original: "for the nonce"</note>.

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

There are recorded instances where English country folk appealed for the services <note>original: "ministrations"</note> of a Catholic priest. In April 1815, Father Edward Peach of the Midland District <note>The Roman Catholic Apostolic Vicariate of the Midland District, which covered central England.</note> was implored to visit a young married woman named White in King’s Norton, Worcestershire. For two months, she had been suffering from an extraordinary kind of illness that doctors could neither identify nor cure. Her sister claimed that a young man of bad reputation, whose proposal of marriage had been rejected, had sworn revenge and employed a well-known wizard at Dudley to cause her harm. 

Whatever the cause may have been, the unhappy girl seemed to be at death’s door. She raved about being surrounded day and night by spirits who mocked and grimaced <note>original: "moped"</note> at her, threatening to carry her away body and soul, and suggesting suicide <note>original: "self-destruction"</note> as the only way to escape them. The parish clergyman visited and prayed with her, but no good resulted from all his efforts. 

It so happened that a nurse called to the house was a Catholic. Horrified by the patient’s hideous ravings, she obtained a bottle of holy water, which she sprinkled around the room and on the bed. When a few drops fell upon the sufferer, she uttered the most piercing cries and screamed, “You have scalded me! You have scalded me!” The seizure <note>original: "paroxysm"</note>, however, passed, and for the first time in many weeks, she fell into a sound sleep. 

After showing some slight improvement for forty-eight hours, she was attacked by violent convulsions. Her relatives, in great alarm, sent a special messenger on Tuesday in Rogation Week <note>May 2, 1815. Rogation Week is the period of prayer and fasting preceding Ascension Thursday in the Christian calendar.</note> to beg Father Peach to come immediately.

When the priest arrived, the girl was being held down in bed by two women who were forced to use all their strength. As soon as she saw him—even though he was a complete stranger to her and his sacred profession could not be recognized by his clothing—her struggles were so terrible that her husband was forced to help restrain her writhing limbs. Eventually, she fell into a state of complete exhaustion. Father Peach, dismissing the rest of the company, was able to talk to her for a long time and quite seriously. He seems to have been fully satisfied that it was a genuine case of diabolic possession.
