I have quoted this case at some length because of the prominence it was given in a popular and widely read newspaper. I see no reason at all to doubt that the facts are substantially true. It is an ordinary instance of obsession <term>obsession</term> <note>original: "obsession"; in this context, a theological term for the state of being besieged or attacked by an evil spirit from the outside, often distinguished from "possession" where the spirit is inside.</note>, and will be easily recognized as such by those priests whose duty has required them to study these distressing phenomena. However, I am very certain that the interpretation put upon some of these occurrences is utterly false. Engaging in clairvoyance is merely playing with fire—I might even say, with hellfire—by those who cannot understand what they are doing, or what forces they are thus blindly summoning. “Professor J.” and “the band of Indians,” and indeed all these “workers on the other side,” are nothing other than evil—or at the very least, gravely suspect—entities, masquerading as spirits of light and goodness. At Illfurt, five miles south of Mulhouse <note>original: Mulhausen</note> in Alsace, there is a monument consisting of a stone column thirty feet high, topped with a statue of the Immaculate Conception. Joseph Burner<gloss>77</gloss> and his wife, Anna Maria, were poor but intelligent people who were not merely respected but even looked up to for their honesty and hard work by their fellow villagers of Illfurt. The family consisted of five children: the eldest son, Thiébaut, was born on August 21, 1855, and the second, Joseph, on April 29, 1857. They were quiet boys of average ability who, when they were eight years old, were sent in the usual course to the local primary school. In the autumn of 1864, both were seized with a mysterious illness that would not respond to ordinary remedies. Dr. Levy of Altkirch, who was called in to examine the case, acknowledged himself completely baffled, and a number of other doctors who were consulted afterward declared themselves unable to diagnose such extraordinary symptoms. From September 25, 1865, the two boys displayed most abnormal phenomena. While lying on their backs, they suddenly spun around like whirling tops with the utmost rapidity. Convulsions seized them, twisting and distorting every limb with unparalleled flexibility; or again, their bodies would become absolutely rigid and motionless for hours together, so that no joint could be bent while they lay as still as logs or stones. A famous case is on record where a servant girl of meager education fell ill and, during a delirium, began to mutter and babble in a language that was recognized as Syriac. On the eve of his examinations, he used to walk up and down the stairs and pace his room, saying Syriac roots and words aloud to himself, which she thus often overheard and which became registered in her brain.

The priest <note>Monsieur Ignace Sp..., mentioned on the previous page</note> had made up his mind about the diabolic nature of these events. He was certain it was an undoubted case of possession, as there was no other way to explain what was happening. Accordingly, he sent a full account of these extraordinary and terrifying events to his bishop, Monsignor Andreas Räss (who served from 1842 to 1887). The Bishop, however, was far from convinced that these things could not be explained by natural causes. In fact, it was only after a delay of three or four years that, at the urging of the Dean of Altkirch, he decided to order a special church investigation. He finally appointed three astute theologians for this task: Monsignor Stumpf, the head of his major seminary at Strasburg; Monsignor Freyburger, the Vicar-General of the diocese; and Monsieur Sester, the rector of Mulhausen. These priests arrived unexpectedly at the Burners' house at ten o'clock on Tuesday morning, April 13, 1869. They found that Joseph Burner had already hidden himself, and it was only after a long search that he was dragged with great difficulty from under his bed, where he had taken refuge. Thiébaut pretended to be unaware of the strangers' presence. The inquiry lasted for more than two hours, and the investigators did not leave the house until after noon. During that time, they witnessed the most horrific scenes, and their minds were completely made up regarding the reality of the possession. They soon presented their report to the Bishop, who only then allowed himself to be convinced of the facts.

Even so, the cautious bishop ordered further precautions to be taken. At the beginning of September 1869, Thiébaut was taken, accompanied by his unhappy mother, to the orphanage of Saint Charles at Schiltigheim. He was to stay there while the case was investigated from the beginning <note>original Latin: "de nouo"</note> by Monsignor Rapp, Monsignor Stumpf, and Father Eicher, a Jesuit <note>original: "S.J.", abbreviation for the Society of Jesus</note> and Superior of the Jesuit house at Strasburg. At the same time, Father Hausser, the chaplain of Saint Charles, and Father Schrantzer, a well-known scholar and psychologist, were to keep the boy under the closest observation, systematically but in secret.

It was decided to proceed with an exorcism, and a priest of great reverence and experience, Father Souquat, was commissioned by the Bishop to perform the solemn rite. We have here the case of a woman who possessed the qualities of a medium and a clairvoyant <note>A clairvoyant is someone who claims to have a supernatural ability to perceive events in the future or beyond normal sensory contact.</note> to an almost unparalleled degree. Instead, they would regard them with caution and indeed shrink from any occult practice at all, lest they accidentally become the prey of "controls" and influences so cunning and so powerful for evil that they might consume both body and soul in untold miseries and shadows darker even than the bitterness of death.

The modern Spiritualist movement, which is so strongly supported by recent scientific statements, is increasingly affecting all classes and conditions of society. In every direction, it is beginning to undermine and actually take the place of the religious beliefs and convictions of thousands of earnest and serious people who are not very accurately informed or well-instructed. Consider the consolation and comfort such a doctrine holds for the bereaved: how eagerly and with what yearning mourners will embrace such teaching, and how perseveringly and with what tender agonies of hungry <note>original: "an hungered"</note> love they will devote themselves to the practices they imagine will place them in the closest connection <note>original: "con-nexion"</note> and communion with those whom they have lost for a time, but whose voices they ever long to hear and whose faces they long to see once again. 

It is a matter of common knowledge that during and since the Great War <note>The First World War (1914–1918), which saw a massive resurgence in spiritualism due to the high death toll.</note>, Spiritualism <note>original: "Spiritism"</note> has increased tenfold. Many who were once accustomed <note>original: "wont"</note> to laugh at it—who refused to listen to its claims and scorned it as useless nonsense—are now among its most enthusiastic followers <note>original: "devotees"</note>. In truth, there must be few of us who cannot appreciate the irresistible influence such beliefs will have upon the mind. Spiritualism is seemingly full of joy, hope, promise, and happiness. It claims it will wipe all tears of sorrow from poor human eyes; it is balm to the wounded heart, divine solace, and sympathy. Through it, the barriers of death are broken down, and mortality is robbed of its terrors.

Were it true—could we summon to our side the spirits of those whom we have so fondly cherished and converse with them of things holy and eternal; could we learn wisdom from their fuller knowledge; could we be assured in their own sweet accents of their undying <note>original: "fadeless"</note> love; could we now and again be comforted with a sight of their well-known faces and the touch of their hands upon ours; were it God’s will that this should be so—then assuredly Spiritualism would be a most blessed and sacred thing, a consolation to the afflicted, help <note>original: "succour"</note> to the distressed, a shining light upon earth’s dark ways, and a very ready help to us all.

In my own experience, I have personally seen these symptoms clearly displayed, not just once but repeatedly, in people whose only interest and goal in life seemed to be a constant attendance at séances <note>original: "séances"; meetings where people attempt to communicate with the dead</note>. Despite every effort I made to stop and discourage them, I have watched these traits develop with frightening speed in people who began to dabble in <term>Spiritism</term> (a belief system based on communication with the spirits of the dead). At first, they likely did so out of lightheartedness and reckless curiosity, but they soon became consumed by intense anxiety and a morbid obsession.

Some fifteen years ago, in a well-known English provincial town, a group of friends formed a "circle" to experiment with <term>table-turning</term> (the practice of attempting to communicate with spirits through the movements of a table), <term>psychometry</term> (the supposed ability to sense the history of an object through touch), the <term>planchette</term> (a heart-shaped board on wheels used for automatic writing), <term>ouija-boards</term>, crystal-gazing, and similar activities. They were, perhaps, a little tired of the usual routine of social engagements: dances, concerts, bridge <note>a popular card game</note>, the theater, dinner parties, and all those mildly pleasant activities that make up so much of life—or at least a large portion of life—for so many people. They wanted some new excitement, something a little out of the ordinary.

A lady, who had just returned home from a long visit to London, had apparently been taken to a Spiritistic meeting, and she was full of the wonders she had both witnessed and heard there. The sense of the eerie and the unknown added a touch of adventure as well. The earlier meetings were informal, held first at one house and then at another. They began by meeting infrequently, almost casually, at fairly long intervals. Next, a specific evening each week was set aside for these gatherings, which soon were fully attended by everyone involved. No member would willingly miss a single reunion. Before long, they were meeting twice or three times a week, and eventually every evening. Professional <term>mediums</term> (people who claim to act as a bridge between the living and the dead) were hired. These experts traveled down from London and other large cities, some from quite a distance, to give strange demonstrations of their powers. I personally met two of these experts, a man and a woman, both of whose names I have since seen advertised in Spiritistic journals of a very recent date. I must say that I was very unfavorably impressed by both of them. This is not because I thought they were frauds...

Arguments, pleas, rebukes, authority, and official warnings all proved useless; one could only stand by and watch the terrible process do its deadly work. Everyone in the group fell into a state of apathy; their former interests vanished, and they neglected the basic courtesies of social life. They let old friendships end for no reason at all. A complete and terrible change for the worse took place in their characters; a total deterioration occurred. Their physical health suffered: their faces became pale and haggard, and their eyes looked dull and glazed—except when <term>Spiritism</term> (the practice of communicating with the dead) was being discussed. Then, their eyes would light up with a disturbing, unholy intensity. There was secret gossip hinting at crude debauchery, blasphemous talk, lack of self-control, and moral degradation. 

Fortunately, through a series of providential events, the "circle" was broken up. External circumstances forced the main members to move away. Most importantly—and likely the most powerful factor—one or two members were suddenly brought to realize the extreme danger and the foolishness of what they were doing. It proved to be a very hard struggle to free themselves from the <term>controls</term> <note>in Spiritism, a "control" is a spirit that supposedly takes over a medium's body</note> to which they had so blindly and completely submitted. Their willpower was weakened and their health was damaged. More than once, they relapsed into the old danger zone, and more than once they were on the verge of giving up the fight in despair. But under guidance, and by using those <term>means of grace</term> <note>sacraments or religious practices believed to provide spiritual strength</note> that the Church so generously offers, they persevered and were finally healed.

That Spiritism opens the door to demonic <note>original: "demoniac"</note> possession—which is so often misclassified as insanity <note>original: "lunacy"</note>—is generally acknowledged by everyone except those who are prejudiced or superstitious. In 1850, an attack was made upon Margaretta Fox, who was staying in West Troy at the house of a Mr. Bouton. A violent mob surrounded the property, stones were thrown at the windows, and shots were fired, while both men and women shouted threats and curses against the “unholy witch-woman within.” At one of the séances, Dr. Kane, a famous Arctic explorer <note>Dr. Elisha Kent Kane (1820–1857) was a celebrated American explorer and medical officer.</note>, was present. He was so fascinated by Margaretta Fox’s beauty that he did not rest until he had removed her from her sordid and harmful surroundings. He had her educated in Philadelphia and finally—much to the annoyance of his relatives, who hated any connection with the Fox family—made her his wife.

Dr. Kane died soon after his marriage, but in the book published by his widow, there are several references to his hatred of Spiritism <note>original: "Spiritism"; a term often used interchangeably with Spiritualism, the belief that the living can communicate with the spirits of the dead.</note>. “Do avoid spirits,” he urges. “I cannot bear to think of you as engaged in a course of wickedness and deception.” For ten years, Mrs. Kane did indeed abandon the practice; in fact, in August 1858, she was baptized as a Catholic in New York. However, then,<sup>101</sup> perhaps due to the pressures of poverty, she again took up work as a medium and was welcomed back with cheers by the entire Spiritistic community. From that moment began her steady decline, both physically and morally.

Kate Fox—who had become Mrs. Jencken, the wife of a London barrister <note>A high-ranking lawyer in the British legal system.</note>—was the mother of a baby whom popular rumor credited with extraordinary mediumistic powers. The whole Spiritistic movement prophesied a brilliant future for the poor child; however, nothing is recorded of him except that he was sadly neglected by his miserable mother, who died of chronic alcoholism in June 1892. Mrs. Kane survived her sister by only nine months, a pitiable and hopeless wreck, craving only drink. The last few weeks of her life were spent in a run-down tenement house. “This wreck of womanhood has been a guest in palaces and courts. The mental powers that are now failing <note>original: "imbecile"; here used in the archaic sense to mean weakened or diminished by illness.</note> were once the wonder and the study of scientific men in America, Europe, and Australia. . . . The lips that now utter little more than profanity once proclaimed the doctrine of a new religion.”<sup>102</sup> It would indeed be difficult to imagine anything more sordid and more miserable than this sad and shocking story of utter degradation. In the earliest days of Spiritism, the subject was investigated by men such as Horace Greeley, William Lloyd Garrison, Robert Hare (a professor of chemistry at the University of Pennsylvania), and John Worth Edmonds (a judge of the New York State Supreme Court). Notable among the spiritists was Andrew Jackson Davis, whose work *The Principles of Nature* (1847) was dictated while he was in a trance. It contained theories of the universe that closely resembled those of the Swedenborgians <note>Followers of Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772), a Swedish scientist and theologian who claimed he could talk with spirits and angels.</note>. 

The movement spread from America to Europe. When two mediums, Mrs. Haydon and Mrs. Roberts, arrived in London in 1852, they attracted not only popular interest but also the serious attention of the leading scientists of the time. Robert Owen, the Socialist, openly accepted the Spiritistic explanation for the various phenomena. Meanwhile, the mathematician Professor De Morgan, in his account of a session <note>original: "sitting"</note> with Mrs. Haydon, declared himself convinced that “somebody or some spirit was reading his thoughts.” 

In the spring of 1855, Daniel Dunglas Home (pronounced Hume) traveled from America to England. Home—who was the son of the eleventh Lord Home and a chambermaid at the Queen’s Hotel in Southampton, but had been raised in America—was then a young man of twenty-two. In 1856, Home was received into the Catholic Church in Rome by Father John Etheridge, a Jesuit <note>original: "S.J."; an abbreviation for the Society of Jesus, a Catholic religious order.</note>. At that time, Home promised to stop using his powers as a medium. However, in less than a year, he broke his pledge and returned to his previous lifestyle. 

This famous medium is almost the only one who—as even the skeptic Frank Podmore admits—was never clearly caught committing fraud. The scientist Sir David Brewster and Dr. J. J. Garth Wilkinson—a highly respected scholar and leading homeopathic <note>A system of alternative medicine that was very popular in the 19th century.</note> physician—both admitted they were unable to explain the phenomena they witnessed through any natural laws. 

In 1855, the first English magazine dedicated entirely to the subject, *The Yorkshire Spiritual Telegraph*, was published in Keighley, Yorkshire. The Davenport brothers visited England in 1864, followed by Henry Slade in 1876. I still have the pieces of the beard and muslin that I cut off. It is well known that in Spiritistic séances and circles, fakery and swindling of every kind are common; that again and again mediums have been convicted of fraud; that not infrequently all kinds of props—stuffed gloves, gauzes, yards of transparent muslin, invisible wires, hooks, beards, and wigs—have been discovered. In France, Spiritism was first announced by a pamphlet by Guillard titled *The Dancing Table and the Answering Table* <note>original: *Table qui danse et Table qui répond*</note>. The way had long been prepared due to the general interest in the teachings of Emanuel Swedenborg <note>A Swedish scientist and theologian (1688–1772) who claimed to have conversations with spirits and angels.</note>. In 1835, Balzac had published his mystical hybrid novel *Séraphita* (*Séraphitus*), an imaginative yet interesting work containing many pages of <term>theosophical</term> <note>Relating to a philosophy that seeks direct knowledge of the divine through spiritual ecstasy or intuition.</note> philosophy. He may have intended these seriously, but it is impossible to view them as anything other than flights of romantic fiction. In 1848, Cohognet paved the way more directly for Guillard by publishing the first volume of his *Secrets of the Future Life Revealed* <note>original: *Arcanes de la vie future devoilées*</note> in Paris, which contains what are claimed to be communications from the dead.

By 1853, <term>séances</term> <note>Meetings where people attempt to communicate with the spirits of the dead.</note> were being held in Bourges, Strasbourg, and Paris, and a massive public sensation ensued. Nothing was discussed except the wonders of Spiritism. However, the movement soon encountered an opponent in Count Agénor de Gasparin, a Swiss Protestant. Gasparin carefully investigated <term>table-turning</term> <note>A type of séance where participants sit around a table, placing their hands on it, and wait for it to rotate or tilt, allegedly moved by spirits.</note> with a circle of his friends and concluded that the phenomena originated from some physical force within the human body. One must admit that his book *On Turning Tables* <note>original: *Des Tables Tournantes*</note> (Paris, 1854) is unconvincing and somewhat superficial, though perhaps more could hardly be expected from a pioneer in such a complex investigation. 

The Baron de Guldenstubbe, on the contrary, declared his firm belief in the reality of these phenomena and in spirit intervention in general. His work *The Reality of Spirits* <note>original: *La Réalité des Esprits*</note> (Paris, 1857) eloquently argued for his convictions. Meanwhile, *The Spirits' Book* <note>original: *Le Livre des Esprits*</note> (Paris, 1853) by M. Rivail (better known by his pseudonym Allan Kardec) became a worldwide textbook on the entire subject. 

During these early days, highly distinguished men used to meet on the Rue des Martyrs in Paris for séances. Tiedman Marthèse, the governor of Java; the scholar Saint-René-Taillandier; the playwright Victorien Sardou and his son; and the astronomer Camille Flammarion were all frequent visitors. The notorious medium Daniel Dunglas Home was reportedly expelled from France following a séance at the Tuileries Palace <note>The former royal residence in Paris.</note>. During this session, he allegedly touched the Empress’s arm with his bare foot, pretending it was the gentle touch of a small child’s hands just before the child fully <term>materialized</term> <note>The process of a spirit taking on a physical, visible form.</note>. This is not because she disbelieves in it, but because she believes in it so thoroughly—because she knows the real nature of the moving forces, no matter how skillfully they may disguise themselves, or how quick and subtle their shifts and turns: the spirits <note>original: "intelligences"</note> which inform and direct the whole thing. It is a painful subject since (I repeat) many good people, no doubt many thoughtful seekers after truth, have been fascinated and swept along by Spiritism. They are as yet conscious of neither physical nor moral harm, and it may be they have been playing with fire for years. Even more <note>original: "Nay more"</note>, Spiritism has been a sweet solace to many in their most painful hours of bitter sorrow and loss; for this reason, it is hallowed in their eyes by the most tender memories. They are woefully deceived. Hard as it may seem, we must get down to the bedrock of fact.

Spiritism has been specifically condemned on no less than four occasions by the Holy Office <note>Now known as the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, this is the Vatican department responsible for defending Catholic doctrine.</note>, whose decree on March 30, 1898, utterly forbids all Spiritistic practices even if communication with demons is strictly excluded and communication is sought with good spirits only. It forbids them to attend séances even out of idle curiosity, for some, at least, of the manifestations must necessarily be attributed to Satanic intervention, since they can be understood or explained in no other manner.

## CHAPTER VII

### THE WITCH IN DRAMATIC LITERATURE

The English theater, like every other form of drama in the world, had a religious—or more specifically, a liturgical—origin. Following the Norman Conquest <note>The Norman Conquest of 1066 brought French influence to English culture, language, and religion.</note>, as English monasteries began to be populated by educated French scholars, there is evidence that Latin dialogues and the legends of saints and martyrs found their way here. These were somewhat like the comedies of Hrotsvitha <note>Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim (c. 935–973) was a German canoness and playwright who wrote Latin dramas based on Christian themes to provide a moral alternative to Roman plays.</note>, which we do not believe to have been an isolated case. Moving from reciting these texts to performing them was an easy and inevitable step, as it is nearly impossible to deliver a speech without using appropriate gestures and actions. The Mystery Play <term>biblical plays performed by medieval craft guilds</term> grew directly out of the heart of the church's liturgy.

The way these early English guild plays were performed has been described many times and with great detail. I only want to point out one specific feature of the movable stage <note>original: "scaffold"</note> that traveled from place to place: the dark cave at the side of the last of the three stations <note>original: "sedes"; these were fixed locations or "mansions" on a medieval stage representing specific settings.</note> known as "Hell-mouth." No expense or effort was spared to make this as terrifying and realistic as possible. Demons with hideous heads emerged from it, while flickering flames frequently burst out and mournful cries were heard within. For example, the stage directions for the Digby *St. Mary Magdalen* play state: "a stage, and Hell underneath <note>original: "ondyrneth"</note> that stage." At Coventry, the guild of Cappers <note>The Cappers were the guild of hat-makers.</note> used a "hell-mouth" for the *Harrowing of Hell* <note>The Harrowing of Hell is the traditional Christian belief that Jesus descended into the underworld between his crucifixion and resurrection to free the souls of the righteous.</note>, and the Weavers' guild used another for their play about Doomsday. This set was equipped with fire, a winch, and a barrel to simulate an earthquake. In the stage directions for William Jordan’s Cornish play, *The Creation of the World*, Lucifer descends to hell "dressed hideously with fire around him," and the location is filled with "every level of devils made of leather and spirits hanging on cords." Among the "sets" <note>original: "establies"</note> required for the Rouen play of 1474 was "Hell made in the manner of a large mouth, closing and opening when there is need" <note>original: "Enfer fait en maniere d’une grande gueulle se cloant et ouvrant quant besoing en est."</note>. The final stage direction of the

->WITCH IN DRAMATIC LITERATURE 277<-

*Sponsus*, a liturgical play from Limoges—dated by scholars M. W. Cloetta and Gaston Paris to the first half of the twelfth century—deals with the story of the Wise and Foolish Virgins. It contains the following stage direction: "Now let the demons take them [the foolish virgins] and cast them into hell" <note>original Latin: "Modo accipiant eas [fatuas uirgines] dæmones et præcipitentur in infernum."</note>.

The Devil himself is one of the most prominent characters in these Mystery Plays <term>medieval dramas based on biblical stories</term>; he is the "villain of the piece." For example, the York cycle of plays begins with *The Creation and the Fall of Lucifer*. While the Angels are singing "Holy, Holy, Holy" before the throne of God, Satan appears, exulting in his pride, only to be quickly cast down into hell. From there, he howls his complaint, beginning: "Out, out! Help!" <note>original: "Owte, owte! harrowe!"—'Harrow' was a traditional medieval cry of distress or an appeal for help.</note>. There is also a curious incident in the episode concerning the dream of Pontius Pilate’s wife. While she sleeps, Satan whispers a vision into her ear to move her to try to stop the condemnation of Jesus—an act intended to thwart the redemption of mankind. The final play of the York cycle is the *Day of Judgment*.

Similarly, the Towneley cycle <note>A series of thirty-two mystery plays, also known as the Wakefield cycle, dating from the 15th century.</note> opens with *The Creation*, which includes the stage direction: "Here God withdraws from His throne and Lucifer shall sit in the same throne" <note>original Latin: "hic deus recedit à suo solio & lucifer sedebit in eodem solio"</note>. The scene soon shifts to hell, where we hear the demons reproaching Lucifer for his pride. Following the creation of Adam and Eve, we hear Lucifer’s lament. In the long episode of *Doomsday*, a number of demons appear and are kept extremely busy.

The Devil was represented as black, with goat’s horns, donkey’s ears, cloven hoofs, and an immense phallus. He is, in fact, the Satyr of the ancient Greek Dionysiac processions—a nature-spirit representing the essence of joyful freedom and unrestrained delight. He was shameless, perhaps, because the ancient Greeks did not associate these traits with shame. He is the same figure who danced light-heartedly across the stage in the plays of Aristophanes, completely nude in the broad midday sun,<sup>1</sup> physically animalistic, exuberant, and ecstatic. He cried aloud the primitive refrain: "Phales, companion of Bacchus, fellow-reveler, night-wanderer, adulterer, lover of boys" <note>original Greek: Φαλῆς, ἑταῖρε Βακχίου, ξύγκωμε, νυκτεροπλάνητε, μοιχε, παιδεραστά</note>. In short, he was Paganism incarnate, and Paganism was the Christian’s deadliest foe. Consequently, the Christians took this Bacchic reveller and blackened him from horn to hoof; yet he remained the Christian’s deadliest foe: the Devil.<sup>2</sup>

It was a long time before this phallic demon was banished from the stage, for strange as it may seem, positive evidence exists...

...that he was known there as late as Shakespeare’s day. In 1620, Edward Wright published in London *A Courtly Masque: The Device called, The World Tossed at Tennis*. The title page states it was: “As it has been several times presented to the satisfaction of many noble and worthy spectators by the Prince's servants.” It was “invented and written by Thomas Middleton, Gentleman, and William Rowley, Gentleman.” 

The title page presents a rough engraving of the various characters in this masque, undoubtedly based on a sketch made during an actual performance. Outside the main group stands a hideous black figure, “The Devil,” who appeared toward the end to take part in the final dance, equipped with horns, hoofs, talons, a tail, and a massive phallus <note>The phallus was often used in theater to emphasize the "bestial" or "animalistic" nature of demons and satyrs, linking them to sinful lust.</note>. It is worth noting that these horns are prominent on the goat-like head (clearly a satyr <term>a Greek mythological figure, half-man and half-goat, associated with indulgence and lust</term>) of the Devil in *Doctor Faustus*, as depicted on the title page of the quarto edition of Christopher Marlowe's play. 

A phallus, which is mentioned in the text, was also worn by the character dressed as the monkey (*Bavian*) <note>original: "Bavian"—derived from the Dutch word for baboon, a common character in May Day celebrations.</note> in the May-dance scene in Shakespeare and Fletcher’s *The Two Noble Kinsmen*, Act III, Scene 5 (1613). It is important to remember that groups of phallic demons were a standard feature of old German carnival comedies. Furthermore, several of the grotesque characters in the *Commedia dell’ arte* <term>a form of professional improvised Italian comedy</term> during the 1610s were traditionally equipped in the same way.³ The fact that the Devil was represented this way in the English theater is significant. It reveals the popular conception of the Prince of Evil and, incidentally, sheds light on much of the grotesque and obscene testimony found in contemporary witch trials.

In John Skelton’s lost play *The Necromancer* <note>original: "Nigramansir"</note>, one of the stage directions is said to have been: “Enter Beelzebub with a beard.” This was undoubtedly a black mask <term>vizard: a mask used in theater</term> with an immense goat-like beard, a familiar sight in early religious drama. Presumably, the main purpose of the Necromancer, who gives his name to this play, was simply to speak the prologue that summons the Devil, who then beats and kicks him for his efforts. However, we only know of the play through the historian Thomas Warton, who describes seeing it when the poet William Collins showed it to him in Chichester around 1759. Warton says: 

“It is *The Necromancer*, a moral interlude <term>a short play or entertainment</term> and a concise one, written by Master Skelton, Poet Laureate, and performed before the King and others...”

...the estates <note>the social ranks or nobility</note> at Woodstock on Palm Sunday. It was printed by Wynkyn de Worde <note>a famous early printer who worked with William Caxton</note> in a thin quarto volume in the year 1504. It must have been performed before King Henry VII at the royal manor or palace at Woodstock in Oxfordshire, which is now destroyed. The characters include a Necromancer (a conjurer), the Devil, a notary public, Simony <term>the illegal buying or selling of church offices</term>, and Philargyria (Avarice) <note>original: "Philargyria," from the Greek for "love of money"</note>. It is partly a satire on certain abuses in the Church. The story, or plot, is the trial of Simony and Avarice. Beyond what the historian Thomas Warton tells us, nothing further is known of the play. Joseph Ritson, in his *Bibliographia Poetica* (1802), declared: "It is utterly incredible that *The Necromancer* <note>original: "Nigramansir"</note> ever existed." It has also been shown that Warton is not infrequently unreliable as a literary historian, and E. G. Duff, in his *Hand Lists of English Printers*, could find no surviving copy of this "moral interlude."

In the English morality plays, the Devil plays an important part. Just as in their French originals or similar works, he is consistently hindering and opposing the moral purpose or lesson that these compositions are designed to enforce. In the later English plays, which developed with more regularity from these interludes, the Devil is always a popular character. He is generally accompanied by the "Vice," who—although a sort of servant or jester in the demon's employ—devotes his time to taunting, teasing, tormenting, and thwarting his master for the education and amusement of the audience. In the play *The Castle of Perseverance*, Lucifer appears shouting in the traditional fashion, "Out, harrow! I roar!" <note>original: "Out herowe I rore"; "Harrow" was a traditional medieval cry used to raise an alarm or express distress</note> just as he used to announce himself in the Mystery plays. He wears his "devil’s clothing" over the outfit of a "proud gallant" <note>a fashionable and often arrogant young man</note>. 

Richard Wever’s *Lusty Juventus* contains unmistakable traces of the unpleasantness of the troubled days of King Edward VI, in whose reign it was written. When the Devil calls Hypocrisy to his aid, we are prepared for a flood of empty but bitter abuse that embodies the sharp Puritan hatred against the Catholic Church. Toward the end, under the poorly chosen title *God’s Merciful Promises*, we encounter a tiresome old man who hypocritically explains the doctrine of Justification by Faith.

In the interlude to which John Payne Collier assigned the name *Mankind*, the character Mischief summons the demon Titivillus to her aid. Titivillus had previously appeared in the *Judgment* <note>original: "Judicium"</note> of the Towneley Mystery plays. Once known as the Devil’s record-keeper and tax collector, he is best known as...

“Master Lollard.” According to a foolish old superstition, Titivillus was an imp whose job was to pick up any words a priest might drop or omit while saying Mass.

As we move into the beginnings of professional drama, we find an extremely interesting play that features fortune-telling, if not actual magic: John Lyly’s *The Pleasant, Conceited Comedy of Mother Bombie*, performed by the Children of Paul’s <note>a troupe of boy actors recruited from the cathedral choir</note> and first printed in 1594. Although the plot is incredibly complex and artificial, it does not seem to be derived from any classical or ancient source, unlike most of Lyly’s stories. Instead, the "cunning woman" of Rochester <note>a "cunning woman" was a folk healer or fortune-teller</note> who provides the title actually has little to say or do, though her intervention helps untangle a messy web of incidents. When Selena says to the old woman, “They say you are a witch,” Mother Bombie quickly retorts, “They lie; I am a cunning woman”—a passage that is quite significant <note>at the time, a "cunning woman" was often seen as a helpful healer, whereas a "witch" was considered harmful and malevolent</note>.

On a completely different level from Lyly’s play stands Marlowe’s magnificent drama, *The Tragical History of Dr. Faustus*. The legend of a man who sells his soul to the Devil for infinite knowledge and absolute power seems to have taken shape around the sixth century, when the story of Theophilus was supposedly recounted in Greek by his pupil Eutychianus. Of course, every warlock had bartered his soul to Satan; throughout the entire Middle Ages, judicial records and the courts of the Inquisition—to say nothing of common knowledge—could have told of a thousand such cases. 

However, this particular legend captured the imagination of both Western and Eastern Christianity. It is found in many forms: it was included in the collections of Jacopo à Voragine <note>author of the *Golden Legend*, a famous medieval collection of saints' lives</note>; it entered the repertoire of minstrels through Rutebeuf, a French poet <note>original: "trouvère," a medieval poet-composer from northern France</note> of the thirteenth century; it reappeared in early English stories and in Low-German drama. Icelandic versions of the story have also been found. It was the subject of a poem by William Forrest, a priest and poet, in 1572, and it also provided the material for two seventeenth-century Jesuit “comedies.”

The original Faust was a real person, <gloss>4</gloss> a wandering conjurer and medical quack who was well known in the southwest of the German Empire as well as in Thuringia.

That he lived in Saxony and the adjoining countries somewhere between the years 1510–1540 is no longer a matter of serious doubt. Philip Begardi, a physician from Worms and author of an *Index of Health* <note>original: *Index Sanitatis*</note> (1539), mentions this fraud, many of whose victims he personally knew. He says that Faust was frequently seen at one time, although nothing had been heard of him in recent years. It has indeed been suggested that the entire legend originated in the strange history of Pope Saint Clement I and his father Faustus (or Faustinianus), as related in the *Recognitions* <note>a popular medieval religious romance</note>, which were immensely popular throughout the Middle Ages. 

However, the theologian Melanchthon knew a Johannes Faustus born at Knittlingen in Württemberg, not far from his own home, who studied magic at Kraków and afterwards "roamed about and talked of secret things" <note>referring to occult or forbidden knowledge</note>. There was also a Doctor Faustus in the early part of the sixteenth century who was a friend of Paracelsus and Cornelius Agrippa; he was a scholar who earned an infamous reputation for the practice of <term>necromancy</term> <note>the practice of communicating with the dead or using black magic</note>. 

In 1513, Conrad Mutt, the Humanist <note>a scholar of the Renaissance movement that revived classical learning</note>, encountered a vagabond magician at Erfurt named Georgius Faustus "the Half-god" <note>original: *Hermitheus*</note> of Heidelberg. In 1506, the abbot Trithemius met a "Faustus Junior" whose boast was that if all the works of Plato and Aristotle were burned, he could restore them from memory. It seems probable that the legend became finally and definitely attached to the Dr. Faustus who was the companion of Paracelsus and Cornelius Agrippa. 

The first literary version of the story was the *People's Book* <note>original: *Volksbuch*</note>, which was published by Johann Spies in 1587 at Frankfurt-on-the-Main. Spies tells us that he obtained the manuscript "from a good friend at Speyer." Soon after, it appeared in England as *The History of the Damnable Life and Deserved Death of Dr. John Faustus*, a <term>chap-book</term> <note>a cheap, popular pamphlet or booklet</note> which Marlowe mainly followed for the incidents in his play. 

The tragedy was carried back to Germany by the English actors who visited that country in the final years of the sixteenth and the earlier part of the seventeenth century. Thus, while the play was itself derived from a German source, it greatly influenced—and perhaps even gave rise to—the treatment of the same theme in German popular drama and puppet plays. These were seldom printed and were usually mostly improvised, while keeping more or less closely to the theme. Scheible, in his work *The Monastery* <note>original: *Kloster*</note> (1847), Volume V, gives—

...the excellent Ulm play, and there are puppet show <note>original: "marionette"</note> versions edited by W. Hamm (1850; English translation by T. C. H. Hedderwick, 1887), O. Schade (1856), K. Engel (1874), Bielschowsky (1882), and Kralik and Winter (1885).

Gotthold Ephraim Lessing planned two presentations of the story, and Friedrich Klinger worked the subject into a romance, *Faust’s Life, Deeds, and Journey to Hell* <note>original: *Fausts Leben, Thaten, und Höllenfahrt*</note> (1791; translated into English by George Borrow in 1826). A high-flown <note>original: "bombast"</note> tragedy was published by August Klingemann in 1815, while Nikolaus Lenau issued his epic-dramatic *Faust* in 1836. Heinrich Heine’s ballet *Doctor Faust, a Dance Poem* <note>original: *Der Doctor Faust, ein Tanzpoem*</note> appeared in 1851. The script <note>original: "libretto"</note> for Louis Spohr’s opera (1814) was written by Johann Karl Bernard.

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe’s masterpiece, planned as early as 1774, was given to the world in 1808, but the second part was delayed until 1831.

General evidence points to 1588 as the date of the first production of Christopher Marlowe’s *Doctor Faustus*, for it seems certain that the song <note>original: "ballad"</note> titled *The Life and Death of Doctor Faustus the Great Conjurer*, entered in the Stationers’ Register <note>the official record-book of the London Company of Stationers, used to claim copyright</note> in February 1589, did not precede the drama but was suggested by it. The first surviving printed edition <note>original: "extant quarto"</note> dates to 1604, but by then it had already been subjected to more than one revision. Upon the stage, *Doctor Faustus* remained popular for a long time; and in England, at least, however fragmented Marlowe’s tragedy may be, it has never been supplemented by any other literary handling of its theme. The writer William Prynne, in his book *The Actor's Scourge* <note>original: *Histriomastix* (1633), a famous Puritan attack on the theater</note>, recounts an absurd story to the effect that the Devil in person <note>original: *in propria persona*</note> "appeared on the stage at the Belle Sauvage Playhouse in Queen Elizabeth’s days" while the tragedy was being performed, "the truth of which I have heard from many now alive who well remember it." It was revived after the Restoration of the monarchy, and on Monday, May 26, 1662, the diarist Samuel Pepys and his wife witnessed the production at the Red Bull Theatre, "but it was so wretchedly and poorly done that we were sick of it." It was being performed at the Theatre Royal in the autumn of 1675, but no details of that performance are recorded. In 1685–1686, at the Dorset Garden Theatre, there appeared William Mountfort’s *The Life and Death of Doctor Faustus, Made into a Farce, with the Humors of Harlequin and Scaramouch*, a strange mixture of Marlowe’s scenes with the style of Italian improvisational comedy <note>original: *commedia dell’ arte*</note>. Harlequin was acted by the agile Thomas Jevon—the first English Harlequin—and Scaramouch by Antony Leigh.

*   F. C. Burnand’s ***Faust and Marguerite*** (July 9, 1864).

Of more recent English dramas that use the Faust legend as their theme, the most remarkable is undoubtedly the adaptation by W. G. Wills from the first part of Goethe’s tragedy. It was produced at the Lyceum Theatre on December 19, 1885, with H. H. Conway as Faust, George Alexander as Valentine, Mrs. Stirling as Martha, Ellen Terry as Margaret, and Henry Irving as Mephistopheles. When compared to the masterpieces of Marlowe and Goethe—or even the theatrical versions of the legend by much lesser men—the play itself was nothing; it was a superb spectacle, helped along by a "witches’ kitchen," a wild revelry <note>original: "bacchanalia"</note> of demons, and brightly colored visual effects <note>original: "chromo-lithographic effects"; referring to the vivid, often exaggerated color palettes used in 19th-century printing and stage design</note>. It relied on the stage mechanics and the paintings of artists like Telbin and Hawes Craven. However, the production was elevated to heights of greatness—even to awe and terror—by the genius of Henry Irving as the red-plumed Mephistopheles. He was a mocking, weary, and restless figure, horribly unreal yet disturbingly alert and alive, who dominated the entire performance.

To attempt a comparison between Marlowe and Goethe would be quite absurd, and it is unnecessary to speak at length <note>original: "expatiate"</note> upon the supreme merits of either masterpiece. In Goethe’s mighty and complex work, the story is essentially refined into a wealth of immortal philosophy. Marlowe, on the other hand, adheres quite simply to the incidents found in the original popular pamphlets <note>original: "chap-book"; small, inexpensive books sold by traveling peddlers</note>. Yet, in all secular <note>original: "profane"</note> literature, I hardly know of any words filled with more shuddering dread and total agony than those in Faust’s last great speech:

> Ah, Faustus,
> Now you have only one short hour to live,
> And then you must be damned forever!
<note>original: "Ah, Faustus, / Now hast thou but one bare hour to live. / And then thou must be damned perpetually!"</note>

The scene becomes unbearable. It is almost too painful to read, overflowing with hopeless darkness and despair.

It has been remarked that *King Henry VI, Part I* is defiled by the obscene caricature of St. Joan of Arc, which is surely the most foul and abominable irreverence that shames English literature. It is too loathsome for words, and I would only point out the list in one scene—where various familiars <term>familiars: supernatural spirits, often taking animal form, believed to assist witches</term> are introduced—of the most revolting details of contemporary witch-trials. To think of such horrors in connection with St. Joan revolts and sickens the imagination. <note>Shakespeare’s portrayal of Joan of Arc as a witch reflects the English prejudices of his time rather than historical reality.</note>

In *King Henry VI, Part II*, the Duchess of Gloucester employs John Hume and John Southwell, two priests; Bolingbroke, a conjurer; and Margery Jourdemain, a witch, to raise a spirit who will reveal the various destinies of the King and the Dukes of Suffolk and Somerset. The scene is written with extraordinary power and carries a great deal of awe and terror. Just as the demon is dismissed amid thunder and lightning, the Duke of York rushes in with his guards and arrests the sorcerers. Later, the two priests and Bolingbroke are condemned to the gallows, and the witch is "burned to ashes" in Smithfield, <note>Smithfield: an area in London famous for being a site of public executions and cattle markets.</note> while the Duchess of Gloucester, after three days of public penance, is banished for life to the Isle of Man.

The incidents as used by Shakespeare are fairly accurate to history. It is certain that the Duchess of Gloucester, an ambitious and licentious woman, called to her counsel Margery Jourdemain (commonly known as the Witch of Eye <note>Eye: a village formerly located near Westminster.</note>), Roger Bolingbroke (an astronomer and astrologer), Thomas Southwell (Canon of St. Stephen’s), a priest named Sir John Hume (or Hun), and a certain William Wodham. These persons frequently met in secret, and it was discovered that they had created, according to the usual method of sympathetic magic, a wax image of the King which they melted before a slow fire. <note>The melting of a wax image was a common practice in "maleficium" (harmful magic), believed to cause the victim to waste away as the wax melted.</note> Bolingbroke confessed, and Hume also turned informer. In 1441, Bolingbroke was placed on a high scaffold before Paul’s Cross <note>Paul’s Cross: an outdoor preaching cross in the grounds of Old St. Paul's Cathedral, London.</note> together with a chair—curiously carved and painted and found at his lodging—which was supposed to be an instrument of necromancy. <term>necromancy: the practice of communicating with the spirits of the dead to predict the future.</term> In the presence of Cardinal Beaufort of Winchester, Henry Chicheley, the Archbishop of Canterbury, and an imposing array of bishops, he was compelled to make an abjuration <note>original: abjuration (a formal renunciation or recanting under oath)</note> of his wicked arts. The Duchess of Gloucester, being refused sanctuary at Westminster, was arrested and confined in Leeds Castle, near Maidstone. She was brought to trial...

With her accomplices in October, sentence was passed upon her as has been related above. Margery Jourdemain perished at the stake as a witch and a relapsed heretic; Thomas Southwell died in prison; and Bolingbroke was hanged at Tyburn <note>Tyburn: The principal location for public executions in London for several centuries.</note> on November 18.

In *The Tempest*, Prospero is a philosopher rather than a wizard, and Ariel is a fairy, not a familiar <term>familiar: a supernatural spirit or demon supposed to attend and obey a witch</term>. Prospero’s magic is of the intellect, and throughout the play, Shakespeare is careful to emphasize a certain detachment from human passions and ambitions. His love for Miranda, indeed, is exquisitely portrayed, and once—at the base ingratitude of Caliban—his anger flashes forth. Nevertheless, even while overseeing the fortunes of those he watches over tenderly and utterly loathing the thought of revenge, he seems to stand apart like a divine Providence guiding events toward the desired outcome of reconciliation and forgiveness. Even so, the situation was delicate to present before an Elizabethan audience; notice how nobly and with what art Shakespeare touches upon Prospero’s “rough magic”! In Sycorax, we recognize the typical witch: wholly evil, vile, malignant, terrible in her mischief, and the consort and mistress of devils.

There are few scenes that have so captured the world’s imagination as the wild opening of *Macbeth*. In the storm and wilderness, we are suddenly brought face to face with three mysterious phantasms that ride on the wind and mingle with the mist in thunder, lightning, and rain. They are not merely agents of evil—they *are* evil; nameless, ghostly, and completely horrible. And then, after the briefest of intervals, they reappear to describe such exploits as killing swine and begging chestnuts from a sailor’s wife, or to brag of having obtained such charms as the thumb of a drowned pilot. These are the petty businesses of real-life accused witches like Mother Demdike <note>Mother Demdike: Elizabeth Southern, a key figure in the famous Lancashire Pendle witch trials of 1612.</note> or Anne Bishop of Wincanton, Somerset. 

Could this shift in tone have been intentional? I think not, and its very violence and suddenness are jarring to a degree. The meeting with Hecate <note>Hecate: In Greek mythology, the goddess of magic and witchcraft; she appears in "Macbeth" to scold the three witches.</note>, who is angry and scolds them as “hags <note>original: "beldames"</note> as you are, saucy and overbold,” does not improve matters. Furthermore, despite the horror when the apparitions are summoned, the ingredients of the cauldron—however offensive <note>original: "noisome"</note> and hideous—are too material and physical for what is called “a deed without a name.” There is a weakness here, and it says much for the genius of the tragedy that this weakness is not noticeably felt.

Nevertheless, actors seized upon this when they "wrote up" the incantation scenes for theatrical effect by inserting new material. In his openly operatic version of *Macbeth*, produced at Dorset Garden in February 1672–3, William Davenant also expanded the witch scenes to an incredible extent. By his ample borrowing <note>original: "conveyance"; here meaning the theft or unlicensed use of literary material.</note> from Thomas Middleton’s *The Witch*, along with added songs and dances, he was merely following established theatrical tradition.⁹

There seems to be no reasonable doubt that *The Witch* is a later play than *Macbeth*, but it is only fair to say that the exact date of *The Witch* is unknown—it was first printed in 1778 from a manuscript now held in the Bodleian Library—and the date of *Macbeth* (written before 1610, probably in 1606) is not demonstrably certain. *The Witch* is a good but not a distinguished play. Because of its incantation scenes and its connection with *Macbeth*, it has acquired an accidental interest and an enduring reputation. The witches themselves—Hecate and her crew—stand midway between the mystical Norns <note>Norns: In Norse mythology, these are the three Fates who rule the destinies of gods and men.</note> of the first scene in *Macbeth* and the miserable hag depicted by Dekker in *The Witch of Edmonton*. They are just a little below the Witches in *Macbeth* as they appear after the opening lines. There is a ghastly fantasy in their revels which is not diminished by the physical crudeness of Firestone the clown, Hecate’s son. They raise "jars, jealousies, strifes, and heart-burning disagreements, like a thick scurf over life," and although their figures are often grotesque, their power for evil is not to be despised. Much of their specialized language—their charms and awkward rituals—is taken word for word from Reginald Scot’s *The Discovery of Witchcraft* (London, 1584).

The village witch as she appeared to her contemporaries—a filthy, senile <note>original: "doting"</note> old woman, hunchbacked, ignorant, malicious, and hateful to both God and man—is shown with photographic detail in *The Witch of Edmonton; A Known True Story*. This play, written by William Rowley, Thomas Dekker, and John Ford, was produced at the Cockpit in Drury Lane during the autumn or winter of 1621. It seems to have been very popular at the time; it was not only applauded in the public theater but was also presented before King James I at Court. It did not, however, find its way into print until as late as 1658.

The trial and execution of Elizabeth Sawyer (April 19, 1621) attracted a great deal of public attention.

### WITCH IN DRAMATIC LITERATURE

A remarkable number of ballads and simple songs were written about the event, detailing her enchantments: how she had blighted standing corn, how a ferret and an owl constantly attended her, and how many demons and <term>familiars</term> <note>supernatural spirits or demons believed to assist a witch, often taking animal form</note> kept her company in prison. Not only were these songs sung aloud on the day of her execution, but many were published as broadsides and sold widely. Accordingly, the <term>Newgate Ordinary</term> <note>The chaplain of Newgate Prison, responsible for the spiritual welfare of condemned prisoners</note> hastened to write *The Wonderful Discovery of Elizabeth Sawyer, a Witch, Lately of Edmonton: Her Conviction, Condemnation, and Death; Together with the Account of the Devil's Access to Her and Their Conversations Together*, "Written by Henry Goodcole, Minister of the Word of God, and her Constant Visitor in the Jail of Newgate," published by authority in quarto format, 1621. This pamphlet is written in the form of a dialogue—question and answer—between Goodcole and the prisoner, who makes a full confession of her crimes.

In some ways, *The Witch of Edmonton* is the most interesting and valuable of the witch dramas because here we see the "hag" stripped of the slightest trace of glamour or romance, presented to us with the harshest realism. We see her living alone in a wretched hovel, "shunned and hated like a sickness," miserably poor, bent and stooped, dragging her trembling limbs wearily through the fields as she clutches her dirty rags around her withered body. And if she even dares to gather a few dried sticks in a corner, she is driven from the spot with harsh words and blows. Is it any wonder her mouth is full of curses and thoughts of revenge?

->It is all the same<-
->To be a witch as to be thought one.<-

Then the Black Dog appears and seals a contract with her blood. She blights the corn and sends a <term>murrain</term> <note>a plague or infectious disease affecting livestock</note> on the cattle of her persecutors; here a horse has the <term>glanders</term> <note>a contagious respiratory disease in horses</note>, there a sow loses her litter; a maid churns butter for nine hours and it will not form. Above all, a farmer’s wife, whom she hates, goes mad and dies in frantic agony; mischief and evil run riot through the town. But soon her familiar deserts her; she falls into the hands of human justice and, after a proper trial, is dragged to <term>Tyburn</term> <note>the primary location for public executions in London</note> shrieking and crying out in hideous despair. It is a sordid and terrible picture, but one cannot doubt it is a true one.

This subtle and minute study of weakness and degeneracy is wholly Ford’s work. Frank Thorney can be closely compared with Giovanni in *’Tis Pity She’s a Whore*. Winnifride, too, has all the sentimental charm of Ford’s heroines, Annabella and Penthea.

Carter is unmistakably the creation of Dekker. Simon Eyre and Orlando Friscobaldo are the same hearty, bluff, hospitable, and essentially honest old fellows. To Dekker, I would also assign the character of Mother Sawyer herself.

Rowley’s hand is especially noticeable in the scenes where Cuddy Banks and the clowns make their appearance.

It should be mentioned that Elizabeth Sawyer appears in Caulfield’s *Portraits, Memoirs, and Characters of Remarkable Persons (1794)*; she is also referred to in Robinson’s *History and Antiquities of the Parish of Edmonton* with a woodcut "from a rare print in the collection of W. Beckford, Esq."

A second drama that was also actually based on a contemporary trial is Heywood and Brome’s *The Late Lancashire Witches*, "A Well-Received Comedy" produced at the Globe Theatre in 1634. In the previous year, 1633, a number of witchcraft trials had drawn the attention of all England to Pendle Forest. A boy named Edmund Robinson, eleven years old, who lived there with his father, a poor woodcutter, told a long and detailed story which led to numerous arrests throughout the district. 

On All Saints’ Day, while gathering <term>bulloes</term> <note>original: "bulloes"—bullace, a variety of wild plum</note> in a field, he saw two greyhounds, one black and the other brown, each wearing a gold collar. They fawned upon him, and immediately a hare rose nearby. But the dogs refused to <term>course</term> <note>original: "course"—to hunt or chase game by sight rather than scent</note>, so he beat them with a small switch. At this, the black greyhound transformed into an old woman whom he recognized as Mother Dickenson, a notorious witch, and the other became a little boy he did not know. The <term>beldame</term> <note>original: "beldame"—an old woman, often used disparagingly for a witch</note> offered him money, either to buy his silence or as the price of his soul, but he refused. Taking a bridle "that jingled" from her pocket, she threw it over the little boy’s head, and he turned into a white horse. Seizing young Robinson in her arms, they mounted and were carried at great speed to a large house where some sixty other people had gathered. A bright fire was

Such was the story told to the justices and corroborated by Robinson's father. A reign of terror ensued. Mother Dickenson and Mother Lloynd were at once thrown into jail, and in the next few days, more than eighteen persons were arrested. The informer and his father earned a large sum by going round from church to church to point out, among the congregations, persons whom he recognized as having been in the house and barn to which he was led. A little quiet blackmail of the wealthier county families—threats to disclose the presence of various individuals at the witches' feast—brought in several hundreds of pounds.

The trial took place at the Lancaster <term>Assizes</term> <note>original: "Assizes"—periodic criminal courts held in England and Wales</note> and seventeen of the accused were <term>incontinently</term> <note>original: "incontinently"—immediately or without delay</note> found guilty. King Charles I himself also questioned one of these poor wretches and, discerning that the whole history was a fraud, immediately pardoned all who had been involved. Meantime...

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

Dr. John Bridgeman, the Bishop of Chester, had also been holding a special inquiry into the case. Young Robinson was lodged separately and was allowed to hold no communication with his relatives; when closely interrogated, he gave way and confessed that the scare, from beginning to end, had been maneuvered by his father, who carefully coached him in his lies. In spite of this fiasco, the gossip did not die down immediately, and there were many who continued to maintain that Mother Dickenson was indeed a witch, however false the evidence on this occasion might be. It must be remembered, moreover, that twenty-two years before, in the very same district, a coven of thirteen witches—the chief of whom was Elizabeth Demdike—had been brought to justice "at the <term>Assizes</term> <note>original: "Assizes"—periodic courts held in various counties of England and Wales for the trial of civil and criminal cases</note> and <term>General Gaol-Delivery</term> <note>original: "Generall Gaole-Delivery"—a court commission tasked with clearing out prisons by bringing inmates to trial</note>, held at Lancaster, before Sir Edward Bromley and Sir James Eltham." Old Demdike herself—she was blind and over eighty years of age—died in prison, but ten of the accused were executed, and the trial, which lasted two days, caused a tremendous stir.

It seems not at all improbable that Heywood had written a topical play in 1612 dealing with this first sensational prosecution, and that when practically the same events repeated themselves in the same place less than a quarter of a century later, he and the ever-ready Brome fashioned the old scenes anew. In the character of the honorable country gentleman Master Generous, whose wife is discovered to be guilty of witchcraft, there is something truly noble. His tender forgiveness of her crime when she repents is touched with the loving pathos that <term>informs</term> <note>original: "informs"—gives character or essence to; provides the underlying spirit of</note> *A Woman Killed with Kindness*, while his agony at her subsequent relapse is very real—although Heywood has wisely refrained from any attempt to show a broken heart except through a few quite simple but poignant words. The play as a whole is a faithful picture of country life, homely enough, yet not without a certain winsome beauty. The comic episodes are sufficiently broad in their humor; we see a household turned topsy-turvy by enchantment and a wedding breakfast bewitched. The kitchen is invaded by snakes, bats, frogs, beetles, and hornets, while to top it all off, the unfortunate bridegroom is rendered <term>impotent</term> <note>original: "impotent"—in this historical context, referring to a magical spell intended to prevent a man from consummating his marriage</note>. In Act II, we have the incident of a boy with a switch (young Edmund Robinson) and the two greyhounds.

All the witches are dragged in and, in spite of their charms and <term>bug-words</term> <note>original: "bug-words"—threatening, terrifying, or boastful language</note>, are identified by several witnesses, including the boy who "saw them all in the barn together, and many more, at their feast and witchery."

The play was evidently produced just after the Lancaster Assizes, while four of the accused were in the Fleet Prison in London for further examination, and the King’s pardon had not yet been pronounced. This is evident from the Epilogue, which commences:

> Now while the witches must expect their due,
> By lawful justice, we appeal to you
> For favorable judgment; what their crime
> May bring upon them is ripening yet, for time
> Has not revealed it. Perhaps great mercy may,
> After just condemnation, grant them a day
> Of longer life.

->THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT<-

It is helpful to consider in this connection a drama largely based upon the work of Heywood and Brome, produced nearly half a century later at the Duke’s House, Dorset Garden: Thomas Shadwell’s *The Lancashire Witches and Teague o’ Divelly, the Irish Priest*, which was first performed in the autumn of 1681 (probably in September). The idea of using magic in a play was obviously suggested to Shadwell by his idolized Ben Jonson’s *Masque of Queens*, performed at Whitehall on February 2, 1609. In close imitation of his model, Shadwell further added extensive notes to Acts one, two, three, and five, providing his references for the details of his enchantments. In the Preface (published in 1682), he naively confesses:

> “For the magical part, I had no hope of equaling Shakespeare in imagination <note>original: "fancy"</note>, who created his witchcraft mostly out of his own mind (a faculty in which no man ever excelled him). Therefore, I resolved to take mine from authority. To that end, there is not one action in the play—no, hardly even a word concerning it—that is not borrowed from some ancient or modern writer on witches <note>original: "witchmonger"</note>. You will find these in the notes, where I have presented you with a great part of the doctrine of witchcraft, whether you believe it or not.”

And indeed, he provides extensive citations from Vergil, Horace, Ovid, Propertius, Juvenal, Tibullus, Seneca, Tacitus, Lucan, Petronius, Pliny, Apuleius, Aristotle, Theocritus, Lucian, and Theophrastus; St. Augustine and St. Thomas Aquinas; Giambattista della Porta <note>original: "Baptista Porta"</note>; Ben Jonson (*The Sad Shepherd*); from the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Malleus Maleficarum"</note> by James Sprenger, a Dominican priest <note>original: "O.P."</note>, and Henry Institor (Heinrich Kramer), written around 1485–89; from Jean Bodin’s (1520–96) *The Demonomania of Sorcerers* <note>original: "La Demonomanie des Sorciers"</note>, 1580; the *Demonolatry* <note>original: "Dæmonolatria"</note>, 1595, by Nicolas Remy; *Six Books of Magical Investigations* <note>original: "Disquisitionum Magicarum libri sex"</note> by Martin Delrio, a Jesuit <note>original: "S.J."</note> (1551–1608); *History of Scottish Matters* <note>original: "Historia Rerum Scoticarum"</note>, Paris, 1527, by Hector Boece (1465–1536); *The Anthill* <note>original: "Formicarius"</note>, 5 volumes, Douai, 1602, by John Nider, a Dominican priest <note>original: "O.P."</note> (1380–1438); *On the Deceptions of Demons* <note>original: "De Præstigiis Dæmonum"</note>, 1563, by the celebrated John Weyer, physician to the Duke of Cleves; *On the Northern Nations* <note>original: "De Gentibus Septentrionalibus"</note>,13 Rome, 1555, by Olaus Magnus, the famous Archbishop of Uppsala; *The Discovery of Witchcraft*, 1584, by Reginald Scot; *Demon-Magic* <note>original: "Dæmonomagia"</note> by Philip Ludwig Elich, 1607; *On Witches and Magic* <note>original: "De Strigimagis"</note> by Sylvester Mazzolini, a Dominican priest <note>original: "O.P."</note> (1460–1523), Master of the Sacred Palace and champion of the Holy See against the heretic Luther; and the *Compendium of Witches* <note>original: "Compendium Maleficarum"</note> (Milan,

### WITCH IN DRAMATIC LITERATURE

*Compendium of Witches* <note>original: "Compendium Maleficarum"</note> (1608), by Francesco Maria Guazzo of the Congregation of Saint Ambrose; *A Debate on Magicians* <note>original: "Disputatio de Magis"</note> (Frankfort, 1584), by Johan Georg Godelmann; *Treatise on Sorceresses and Witches* <note>original: "Tractatus de Strigiis et Lamiis"</note> by Bartolommeo Spina, of the Dominican Order <note>original: "O.P."</note>; *The Decree* <note>original: "Decretum"</note> (about 1020) by Burchard, Bishop of Worms; *On Sorceries* <note>original: "De Sortilegiis"</note> (Lyons, 1533) by Paolo Grilland; *On Occult Philosophy* <note>original: "De Occulta Philosophia"</note> (Antwerp, 1531) by Cornelius Agrippa; the *Apology for All the Great Men Who Have Been Falsely Suspected of Magic* <note>original: "Apologie pour tous les Grands Hommes qui ont este faussement supconnez de Magie"</note> (1625) by Gabriel Naudé, librarian to Cardinal Mazarin; *On Subtlety* <note>original: "De Subtilitate"</note> (twenty-one books, Nuremberg, 1550) by Girolamo Cardano, the famous physician and astrologer; *On Great and Occult Philosophy* <note>original: "De magna et occulta Philosophia"</note> by Paracelsus; and *Four Books of Specters* <note>original: "IIII Livres des Spectres"</note> (Angers, 1586) by Pierre le Loyer, Lord of Brosse, of which Shadwell used the English version (1605), *A Treatise of Specters*, translated by Z. Jones.

It is clear that no fewer than forty-one authors—all authorities on magic—are quoted by Shadwell in these notes. Furthermore, he frequently cites the same author multiple times and provides lengthy extracts rather than merely general references.

Yet, despite all this parade of learning—and perhaps because of it—Shadwell’s witch scenes are intolerably clumsy. They are vulgar without being frightening. Shadwell was a talented dramatist who could draw a character, especially an eccentric one, with remarkable vigor, and his scenes are a triumph of realistic detail. It is true, however, that he could not distinguish between what to include and what to leave out; he threw his world onto the stage in a disorganized, haphazard fashion. And since even during the reign of the "Merry Monarch" <note>King Charles II</note> there were a few tedious people around, one occasionally—though not very often—comes across heavy, dull passages in Shadwell’s robust comedies.

On the other hand, *The Sullen Lovers*, *Epsom Wells*, *The Virtuoso*, *Bury Fair*, *The Squire of Alsatia*, and *The Volunteers*—in fact, all his original plays—are full of energy and fun, even if they are a bit rowdy and crude, as was the custom of the time. John Dryden, who knew exactly what he was doing, cleverly labeled Shadwell as "dull" for his own reasons. Because of Dryden, Shadwell has been called dull ever since by those who have not actually read his work. However, it is true that Shadwell did not have a single spark of poetry in his entire large frame. Consequently, his witches become farcical—yet farcical in a grimy, unpleasant way, for we are spared none of the loathsome details of their rituals.

Sabbat <note>A Sabbat is a supposed secret gathering of witches to worship the Devil.</note>, and should anyone object, why, there is the authority of Nicolas Rémy or Francesco Maria Guazzo—the precise passage from Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio <note>original: "Prierias"</note> or Burchard of Worms—to support the author. Indeed, we feel that these witches are very real despite the physical, literal way they are described. They present a clear picture of one side of the diabolic cult, however crude and insensitive it may be.

Even so, these incantation scenes are not, I venture to think, the worst thing in the play. The obscene caricature of the Catholic priest, Teague o’ Divelly, is frankly disgusting beyond words. He is represented as ignorant, idle, lustful, a liar, a coward, and a clown; he is too ape-like in his cunning to be a fool, yet too fundamentally mean to be a true villain. It is a filthy piece of writing, malicious and deliberately harmful <note>original: "harmful prepense"</note>.<sup>14</sup>

But Shadwell showed little respect for Protestants either, since Smerk—Sir Edward Hartfort’s chaplain—is described as "foolish, deceitful, pro-Catholic, arrogant, and insulting; yet for his own profit, he is a slave to others."

It is hardly surprising that after the play had been in the actors' hands for about two weeks, complaints from very high-ranking officials were lodged with Charles Killigrew, the Master of the Revels <note>The government official responsible for censoring plays.</note>. Killigrew promptly sent for the script—which at first he seems to have reviewed quite carelessly—and would only allow rehearsals to continue on the condition that a large amount of vulgar material was removed. Even with these cuts, the dialogue remains quite offensive and disrespectful. There was something like a riot in the theatre at the first performance, and the play was hissed as loudly as it deserved. Yet it managed to survive: those were the days of the Third Exclusion Bill <note>A political crisis (1679–1681) where Parliament tried to prevent the Catholic James II from inheriting the throne.</note> and widespread disloyalty to the King, but the political tide was turning. A rebellious Parliament had been dissolved on March 28th; on August 31st, Stephen College—a lying fanatic deeply involved in treason and every imaginable kind of criminal behavior—had met his just reward on the gallows. Meanwhile, the infamous Earl of Shaftesbury <note>A lead politician who opposed the King.</note> himself was to be arrested <note>original: "smartly laid by the heels"</note> the following November. Shadwell printed the parts of the dialogue that were not allowed to be spoken on stage in italics,<sup>15</sup> and from these, we can clearly see that the censor was fully justified in his demands. The political satire is of the lowest quality; the attacks against the Church are vulgar and spiteful.

Whatever success *The Lancashire Witches* had in the theatre—

—and it was frequently revived—was entirely due to the stage technician <note>original: "mechanist"</note> and the scenic effects, the "flyings" of the witches, and the music. This last element was such a prominent feature that Downes <note>John Downes (c. 1640–1712), a theater prompter and historian.</note> does not hesitate to call it "a kind of Opera."

In Shadwell’s Sabbat <note>A Sabbat is a supposed secret gathering of witches to worship the Devil.</note> scenes, the Devil himself appears, once in the form of a male goat <note>original: "Buck Goat"</note> and once in human shape, while his followers <note>original: "satellites"</note> adore him with revolting ceremonies. The witches are named Mother Demdike, Mother Dickenson, Mother Hargrave, Mal Spencer, Madge, and others who are not named.

Elizabeth Demdike and Jennet Hargreaves belonged to the first Lancashire witch trials, the prosecutions of 1612; Frances Dickenson and Mal Spencer were involved in the Robinson disclosures of 1633. Therefore, it is obvious that Shadwell has mixed the two incidents together. In his play, we have a hunting scene where the hare suddenly changes into Mother Demdike; the witches raise a storm and drink heavily in Sir Edward’s cellar, somewhat like the behavior of Madge Gray, Goody Price, and Goody Jones in *The Ingoldsby Legends* <note>A collection of myths and ghost stories written by Thomas Ingoldsby (Richard Harris Barham) in the 19th century.</note>. Mal Spencer puts a bridle on Clod, a country bumpkin <note>original: "yokel"</note>, and rides him to a witches’ festival, where Madge is admitted to the infernal sisterhood. The witches, disguised as cats, attack several people with horrible scratching and meowing; Tom Shacklehead strikes off an old cat's <note>original: "grimalkin's"</note> paw, and Mother Hargreave’s hand is later found to be missing. "The cutting off of the hand is an old story," says Shadwell in his notes. It can be seen that the later dramatist took many of his incidents from Thomas Heywood and Richard Brome <note>Authors of the 1634 play *The Late Lancashire Witches*.</note>, although it is only fair to add that he also drew heavily from original sources.

Shortly after the Restoration, a play was published dealing with one of the most famous of English prophetesses <note>original: "sibyls"</note>, *The Life of Mother Shipton*. It was described as: "A New Comedy. As it was Acted Nineteen days together with great Applause. . . . Written by T[homas] T[homson]." Among the characters <note>original: "Dramatis Personæ"</note> appear Pluto, the King of Hell, with Proserpina, his Queen; Radamon, a chief Spirit; and four other Devils. The scene is "The City of York, or Naseborough <note>Likely Knaresborough, the traditional home of Mother Shipton.</note> Grove in Yorkshire." It is a rough piece of work, largely compiled <note>original: "patched together"</note> from Thomas Middleton’s *A Chaste Maid in Cheapside* and Philip Massinger’s *The City Madam*. The episodes involving Mother Shipton seem to be based on one of the many old chap-books <note>Small, cheaply printed books containing popular stories or legends.</note> that relate her marvelous adventures and
