Agatha Shipton (whose name is usually given as Ursula) is complaining of her difficult life when she encounters Radamon, a demon who holds high rank in the court of Dis <note>Dis: A name for the Roman god of the underworld, Pluto, or the underworld itself.</note> <note>Radamon: Likely a variation of Rhadamanthus, a judge of the dead in Greek mythology.</note>. He arranges to meet her later and returns to his own place to boast of his success. He reappears to her dressed as a wealthy nobleman; he marries her, and for a while, she is seen living in great wealth and status. 

At the beginning of Act III, she finds herself in her poor cottage again. As she laments her situation, Radamon enters; he informs her who he really is and grants her magical powers. Her fame spreads far and wide, and as popular stories tell, the Abbot of Beverley visits her in disguise to test her art. She recognizes him immediately and, much to his great annoyance <note>original: "chagrin"</note>, foretells the dissolution of the monasteries <note>The closing of Catholic religious houses by Henry VIII between 1536 and 1541.</note> along with other future events. In the end, Mother Shipton outwits and frustrates the devils who attempt to seize her. She is granted a heavenly vision and turns to repentance and prayer. The whole play is a rather crude mixture <note>original: "commixture"</note>, possessing more historical interest than literary value.

There are some well-written episodes in Nevil Payne’s powerful tragedy *The Fatal Jealousy* <note>original: "The Fatal Jealousie"</note>, produced at the Dorset Garden Theatre <note>A major London theater known for its elaborate stage machinery and spectacles.</note> in early August 1672. Among the characters, we have a "Witch," who is the aunt of Jasper, the villain of the play. Jasper, who is Antonio’s servant, asks his aunt to help him with his evil schemes. At first, he believes she is a genuine sorceress, but she corrects his misunderstanding <note>original: "disabuses him"</note> and frankly acknowledges:

> ->I can raise no devils,<-
> ->Yet I associate with rogues and tailors,<-
> ->Things that can take the shape of elves,<-
> ->And goblins—<-

Her imps, named *Ranter*, *Swash*, *Dive*, *Fop*, *Snap*, *Gilt*, and *Pick-lock*, are actually slim boys in masquerade costumes <note>original: "masquing habits"</note> who have been trained in trickery. Nonetheless, they perform an incantation scene to deceive Antonio and persuade him that his wife, Celia, is unfaithful. An "Antic Dance of Devils" <note>Antic: Grotesque, bizarre, or clownish behavior.</note> which follows is interrupted by the forced entry of the Watch <note>The local night guard or police force.</note>. The Aunt shows Jasper a secret hiding place, whereupon he murders her and conceals the body in the hole. He pretends that she was truly a witch and has vanished by magic. The Captain of the Watch, however, had detected her fraud <note>original: "charlatanry"</note> long before, and soon a demon's mask <note>original: "vizor"</note> and a hooded cloak <note>original: "domino"</note> are found on the premises.

Later, a little boy who is caught in his devil’s costume confesses to the deceptions, and trembling, he adds that in one of their secret chambers they have discovered their mistress’s corpse stabbed to death. Finally, Jasper is unmasked and only escapes the severe punishment he deserves <note>original: "condign punishment"</note> by using his dagger. The character of the Witch is not unlike that of Thomas Heywood’s *The Wise Woman of Hogsdon*, although in *The Fatal Jealousy* <note>original: "The Fatal Jealousie"</note> the events take a tragic and bloody turn. The actor William Smith played Antonio; Mrs. Shadwell played Celia <note>original: "Caelia"</note>; Mrs. Norris played the Witch; and Samuel Sandford was famous in the role of Jasper.

There are scenes involving spells and incantations in John Dryden’s tragedies, but these hardly fall within our study <note>original: "survey"</note>, as the magicians are treated romantically—one might even say decoratively—and certainly no touch of realism is sought or intended here. We have the famous episode in *The Indian Queen* (produced at the Theatre Royal in January 1663–4), when Zempoalla seeks Ismeron the prophet, who summons the God of Dreams to prophesy her destiny. In the fourth act of *Tyrannic Love* <note>original: "Tyrannick Love"</note> (Theatre Royal, June 1669), the scene is an Indian cave where, at the prompting of Placidius, the magician Nigrinus summons a vision of the sleeping Saint Catherine. Various astral spirits appear, only to flee before the descent of Amariel, the Saint’s Guardian Angel. 

In *Oedipus* <note>original: "Œdipus"</note>, written by Dryden and Nathaniel Lee (Dorset Garden, December 1678), the prophet Tiresias <note>original: "Teresias"</note> plays a considerable part, and Act III is mainly concerned with a necromantic spell that summons the ghost of Laius in the depths of a sacred grove. In *The Duke of Guise*, moreover (Theatre Royal, December 1682), there is a sense of real horror in the figures of Malicorne and his familiar demon <note>A "familiar" was believed to be a demon or spirit that served a witch or wizard, often in the form of an animal.</note> Melanax. The scene where the miserable wizard, whose contract with the devil is now due, is carried shrieking to eternal torment <note>original: "endless bale"</note> cannot be read without a shudder, even after experiencing the final moments of Christopher Marlowe’s *Doctor Faustus*. 

Act IV of Lee’s *Sophonisba* (Theatre Royal, April 1675) begins in the temple of Bellona <note>Bellona was the ancient Roman goddess of war.</note>, where her priestesses are shown performing their terrifying rituals. The character Cumana is inspired by the divinity; she raves in the fury of her obsession, a dance of spirits occurs, and various visions are summoned.

In Thomas Otway’s curious adaptation <note>original: "rehandling"</note> of *Romeo and Juliet*, which he set in a Roman context <note>original: "Latinized"</note> as *The History and Fall of Caius Marius* (produced at Dorset Garden in the autumn of 1679), the Syrian witch Martha only appears for a moment to prophesy good fortune.

...fortune to Marius and to introduce a dance of spirits by the waving of her wand.

Charles Davenant’s operatic *Circe* (produced at Dorset Garden, March 1676–7) is an amazing distortion of mythological story. There are countless songs, a dance of magicians, storms, dreams, and an appearance of Pluto in a chariot drawn by black horses; however, all these are very much products of the theater—overly theatrical, born of candlelight and violins, and hardly bearable to read in cold print. Ragusa, the sorceress in Nahum Tate’s *Brutus of Alba: or the Enchanted Lovers* (Dorset Garden, May 1678), is a far more formidable figure. Tate managed his magic with some skill, and the conclusion of Act III, an incantation, was deservedly praised by the critic Charles Lamb. Curiously enough, the plot of *Brutus of Alba* is the story of Dido and Aeneas, with Virgil’s <note>original: "Vergil’s"</note> names being altered "rather than be guilty of a breach of modesty," as Tate says. But Tate also supplied Henry Purcell with the libretto for his opera *Dido and Aeneas*, in which witches also appear. It must not be forgotten that *Macbeth* was immensely popular throughout the whole of the Restoration period when, as noted above, the witch scenes were expanded and presented with every resource of scenery, mechanism, dance, song, and flashy decorations <note>original: "meretricious ornament"</note>. Revival followed revival, each more decorative than the last, and the theatre was constantly packed. Thomas Duffett undertook to parody <note>original: "burlesque"</note> this fashion, which he did in an extraordinary Epilogue to his skit *The Empress of Morocco* (produced at the Theatre Royal in the spring of 1674); but for all his jokes <note>original: "japeries"</note>, *Macbeth* never lost its favor with the public.

Spirits in abundance appear in the Earl of Orrery’s unpublished tragedy *Zoroastres*, where the principal character is described as the "King of Persia, the first Magician." He is attended by "several spirits in black with ghastly masks <note>original: "vizards"</note>," and at the end, furies and demons arise shaking dark torches at the monarch, whom they pull down to hell as the sky rains fire upon them. It was almost certainly never performed and is the wildest type of sensational melodrama <note>original: "transpontine melodrama"; a term for highly emotional and spectacular plays</note>.

Edward Ravenscroft’s "recantation play" *Dame Dobson, or, The Cunning Woman* <note>a "cunning woman" was a folk healer or practitioner of minor magic</note> (produced at Dorset Garden in the early autumn of 1683) is an English version of *The Fortune-Teller; or, The False Enchantments* <note>original: "La Devineresse ; ou les faux Enchantements"</note> (sometimes known as *Madame Jobin*), a brilliant comedy by Thomas Corneille and Jean

Donneau de Visé. This French original had been produced in 1679, and both the stagecraft and the clever way in which the various tricks and magic acts are handled must be admitted to be extremely skillful. An English comedy on a similar theme is *The Wise Woman of Hoxton* <note>original: "Hogsdon"</note>, where the complex plot is a triumph of technical skill. *The Female Fortune-Teller* <note>original: "La Devineresse"</note> was published in 1680 with a frontispiece showing an old cat <note>original: "grimalkin"</note>, a "hand of glory" <note>A macabre occult object made from the dried and pickled hand of a hanged criminal, believed to have magical properties.</note>, harmful weeds, two blazing torches, and other objects favored by necromancy. Furthermore, there are eight folding plates that decorate the small book; these are of significant interest as they depict scenes from the comedy. 

However, *Dame Dobson* cannot be considered a play about actual witchcraft; it is no more than an amusing study of skillful fraud <note>original: "charlatanry"</note>. The main character herself²⁰ belongs to that eternal sisterhood exemplified by the prophetess <note>original: "sibyl"</note> in Thomas Heywood’s play, of whom it is said: “She is a wise woman <note>original: "cunning woman," a term for a local practitioner of folk magic or herbalism</note>, and she didn't get her reputation for nothing; she can use her own ignorance to fool so many people who consider themselves wise.”

Mrs. Aphra Behn, in her amusing comedy *The Lucky Chance; or, An Alderman’s Bargain*—produced at Drury Lane in the late winter of 1686 and published in 1687—used pretended magic in the main scenes. In these, Gayman (played by Thomas Betterton) is secretly brought by the apprentice Bredwel (played by Bowman), who is disguised as a devil, to the house of Lady Fulbank (played by Elizabeth Barry). Here he is received by Pert, the maid, who is dressed as an old witch, and is led to the arms of his lover <note>original: "inamorata’s"</note>. But the entire episode is treated somewhat like a farce, and it is, of course, a complicated costume-play performed for the sake of a secret affair²¹.

In 1681, Thomas Shadwell took witchcraft seriously. Despite the hesitant denial in the address "To the Reader" that introduces his play *The Lancashire Witches*, I think he was sensible enough to recognize the truth at the heart of the matter, despite the ridiculous formulas and spells that senile <note>original: "doting"</note> hags and male witches <note>original: "warlocks"</note> usually employ. 

Witchcraft was still a crime punishable by death when, about fifteen years later, William Congreve lightly laughed it out of the courtroom. Foresight, a character in *Love for Love*, is described as "an uneducated old fellow, irritable and stubborn, superstitious, and claiming to understand astrology, palmistry, the study of facial features <note>original: "phisiognomy"</note>, omens, dreams, etc." He is seen in a private conversation <note>original: "confabulation"</note> with his young daughter’s nurse, when—

"You brat! You monster!" <note>original: "Hussy, Cockatrice"</note> storms the old man, beside himself with rage. To return for a short time to an earlier generation when it would have hardly been possible, or at least highly dangerous, to treat witchcraft with such a cheerful mood: we have only the names of two plays that would almost certainly have been of great interest in this regard: *The Witch of Islington*, performed in 1597, and *The Witch Traveller*, licensed in 1623.

In addition to *The Masque of Queens*, which, as has already been noted, served to some extent as a model for Shadwell when he was writing his encyclopedic notes on magic, Ben Jonson introduces a Scottish witch named Maudlin in that sweet pastoral play *The Sad Shepherd*. The character is drawn with vigorous strokes; realistic detail blends with folklore <note>original: "romance"</note>.

During the quarrel scene which opens *The Alchemist*, the character Face threatens Subtle:

> I'll bring you, you rogue, within
> the law against sorcery, from the *thirty-third* <note>original: "tricesimo tertio"</note> year
> of Henry the Eighth <note>The Witchcraft Act of 1541, the first to define witchcraft as a felony in England</note>.

Dapper, the foolish victim <note>original: "gull"</note>, asks Subtle for a familiar spirit, as Face explains (Act I, scene 2):

> Why, he only asks for one to help with gambling and horses,
> a minor spirit for games of chance <note>original: "rifling flye"</note>; none of your high-ranking spirits.

And later, in order to trick him thoroughly, Dol Common appears as the "Queen of Fairy." The Queen of Elphin or Elfhame, who is particularly mentioned in the Scottish <note>original: "Scotch"</note> witch trials, seems to be identical with the French Queen of the Sabbath <note>original: "Reine du Sabbat"</note>. In 1670, Jean Weir confessed: "That when she kept a school at Dalkeith, and taught children, a tall woman came to the declarant's house when the children were there; and that she had, as it appeared to her, a child upon her back, and one or two at her feet; and that the said woman desired that the declarant should employ her to speak for her to the Queen of Fairy, and strike and battle in her behalf with the said Queen (which were her own words)."22

Beaumont and Fletcher provide us with but few instances of witchcraft in the many dramas that conveniently go under their names. We have, it is true, a she-devil, Lucifera, in *The Prophetess*, but the incident is little better than clowning. Delphia herself is a severely classical pythoness <term>a female prophet or sorceress, traditionally associated with the Oracle of Delphi</term> far removed from the Sawyers, Demdikes, and Dickensons <note>Historical figures accused of witchcraft: Elizabeth Sawyer, the "Witch of Edmonton," and the Demdike and Dickenson families involved in the famous Lancashire witch trials of 1612</note>. Sulpitia, in *The Custom of the Country*, puts on a conjurer's robe and, at Hippolita's bidding, blasts Zenocia almost to death by her spells; yet she is more of a procuress <term>original: "bawd," a woman who manages a brothel or procures sexual partners</term> than a witch. Peter Vecchio in *The Chances*, "a reputed wizard," is as sharp and deceptive <note>original: "cozening"</note> a practitioner as Forobosco, the mountebank <term>a person who tricks others, often by selling fraudulent medicines or performing magic</term>—a petty thief who is exposed and sent to the galleys at the end of *The Fair Maid of the Inn*; or Shirley's Doctor Sharkino,23 whom silly serving-men consult about the loss of silver spoons and napkins; or Tomkis's *Albumazar*; or even Jonson's *Subtle* himself.24

In Marston's *Sophonisba* (published in quarto <term>a book format where the printing sheet is folded twice to create four leaves</term> in 1606) appears Erictho, a character borrowed from the Roman poet Lucan. The Friar in Chapman's *Bussy d'Ambois* (quarto, 1607) puts on a magician's robe and, after a sonorous Latin invocation, raises the spirits Behemoth and Cartophylax in the presence of Bussy and Tamyra.

A far more interesting drama than these is Shirley's *St. Patrick for Ireland*, acted in Dublin in 1639–40, which has as its theme the conversion of Ireland by St. Patrick and the opposition of the Druids under their leader Archimagus <note>A name meaning "chief magician," often used in literature to denote a powerful sorcerer</note>. The character of St. Patrick moves throughout the play with a quiet spiritual dignity that has true beauty, and the magicians, in their frustrated power to do evil, are only slightly less effective. Particularly impressive is the arrival of Saint Patrick: as the King and his two sons, his druids, and his nobles are gathered in anxious consultation at the gates of their temple, they see a fair company passing in solemn procession through the woods with gleaming crosses, silken banners, bright candles <note>original: "tapers"</note>, and incense. At the same time, the sweet music of a hymn strikes the ear:

Since Marlowe’s *Doctor Faustus* has already been discussed in this context, it may not be entirely irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent"</note> to briefly consider three or four other Elizabethan plays in which the Devil appears among the cast of characters <note>original: "Dramatis Personæ"</note>, even if he does not play a very prominent part. These for the most part fluctuate between serious drama and mere clowning <note>original: "buffoonery"</note>. Thus, the prologue of *The Merry Devil of Edmonton* (printed 1608), in which the magician <note>original: "enchanter"</note> Peter Fabell tricks the demon who has come to demand the fulfillment of his contract, begins with appropriate dignity, but it soon adopts a lighter and even trivial tone. William Rowley’s *The Birth of Merlin, or The Child has found his Father* (not printed until 1662) is a strange mixture <note>original: "medley"</note> of farce and romance, characterized by a certain clumsy strength and not entirely lacking in poetry. [If This Be Not a Good Play, the Devil is] in it (published in quarto format <note>original: "4to"</note>, 1612), which can be traced back to the old prose story *The History of Friar Rush*, depicts the adventures of three lesser demons who are dispatched to expand their master's kingdom in Naples. It is an inconsistent play, and its satire fails to land because it is clear that the poet was not truly committed to his outlandish theme.²⁵

Ben Jonson's *The Devil is an Ass*, performed in 1616, is entirely a comedy. Pug, "the lesser devil," who visits the earth and takes a job as a servant to a Norfolk landowner <note>original: "squire"</note> named Fabian Fitzdottrel, is hopelessly outsmarted at every turn by the cleverness of ordinary humans. Eventually, he finds himself imprisoned in Newgate <note>A famous London prison.</note>, and would be in danger of the gallows if he were not rescued by the "Vice" <term>a stock character in medieval and Renaissance plays who represented a particular sin or mischief</term> known as Iniquity, who carries him off happily back to the underworld. His fate can be compared to that of Roderigo in John Wilson's excellent comedy *Belphegor: or, The Marriage of the Devil* (produced at the Dorset Garden Theatre in the summer of 1690). In that play, Roderigo and his two demonic attendants fly back to their native hell to escape the miseries of life on earth.

In *The Devil's Charter*, however, by Barnaby Barnes (1607), we have what is undoubtedly a completely serious tragedy. While not an exact copy, it clearly takes many cues from Christopher Marlowe's *Doctor Faustus*. It is a showy melodrama and entirely historically inaccurate—a literal "Tophet" <term>a Hebrew term for a place of fire or hellish horror</term> of infernal horror. The main character is a disgusting caricature of Pope Alexander VI <note>Rodrigo Borgia, Pope from 1492–1503, often vilified in Protestant England.</note>, and, as might be expected, all the rumors and insults from Renaissance satirists and Protestant writers are piled together to portray an impossible monster of lust and crime. The most graphic scandals from the accounts of Burchard, Sanudo, Giustiniani, Filippo Nerli, Guicciardini, Paolo Giovio, Sannazzaro, and the Neapolitans <note>These were all contemporary chroniclers and historians who wrote about the scandals of the Borgia family.</note> have been used with what one might almost call a meticulous attention to detail. 

The "black arts" <term>dark magic or sorcery</term>, in particular, play a very prominent role in these gruesome scenes. Alexander has signed a contract with a demon named Astaroth, and all his success is attributed to this deal. In Act IV, there is a long ritual <note>original: "incantation"</note> where the Pope puts on his magical robes, takes his wand <note>original: "rod"</note> and pentacle <term>a five-pointed star or symbol used in magic to command spirits</term>, and, standing within the circle he has drawn, summons spirits using strange words. He begins with a formal Latin exorcism that dissolves into meaningless babble. Various demons appear, and he is shown a vision of the murder of the Duke of Gandia by his brother Caesar Borgia <note>original: "Cæsar"</note>, along with other horrific acts. At the high point of the play, we see the banquet with Cardinal...

Adrian of Corneto is present, and while the guests talk, "The Devil comes and swaps the Pope's bottles." The Borgias are poisoned, and in a far too long-winded "Final Scene" <note>original: "Scena Ultima"</note>, Alexander [Pope Alexander VI] discourses and disputes frantically with the demons who appear to mock and torment him. The play uses the old plot device of an unclear contract; soon, a "Devil like a Messenger" <note>original: "Poast"</note> enters, blowing a horn to summon the unhappy wretch, who raves and shrieks out meaningless cries as he is dragged away amid thunder and lightning. This sort of thing appealed to the most base appetites of the "groundlings" <term>the lower-class audience members who stood in the pit of the theater</term>, and *The Devil’s Charter* may be summed up as a disgusting parody <note>original: "burlesque"</note>, containing plenty of vile material that is so repulsive it is physically sickening.

Upon a careful consideration of those seventeenth-century plays which have witchcraft as their main theme—and leaving aside, for our purpose, the purely romantic treatment of the subject, however realistic some details of the picture may be—it is, I think, beyond dispute that *The Witch of Edmonton*, in the figure of Mother Sawyer, offers us the best contemporary illustration of the Elizabethan witch. The drama itself is of extraordinary merit and power; the understanding and restraint which set the play apart from its peers also raise it to the level of genuine tragedy. It should be noticed that we see a witch, so to speak, in the process of being made. Mother Sawyer is, in truth, the victim of the prejudices of the village laborers <term>hinds</term> and ignorant country folk. When she first appears, she is merely a poor old woman <note>original: "crone"</note> driven to desperation by her brutal neighbors; the farmers declare she is a witch, and at length, persecution makes her one. 

She is malicious and evil enough once the contract with the demon has been confirmed; she longs from the first to be revenged upon her enemies and mutters to herself, "By what magic may the thing called a Familiar <term>a supernatural spirit, often taking the form of an animal, believed to serve a witch</term> be purchased?" But, in one sense, she is urged and hounded to her destiny. The authors—although never doubting her contract with the powers of darkness or her vile and poisonous life—show a detached but very real sympathy for her. It is this touch of humanity, the pathos and pity for the poor old woman (repulsive, wicked, and menacing as she may be), which, in my opinion, places *The Witch of Edmonton* among the greatest and most moving of all Elizabethan plays.

<page-num>309</page-num>
<header>WITCH IN DRAMATIC LITERATURE</header>

It is not a pleasant task to turn our attention to the theater of the eighteenth century in this regard. The figure of the witch was degraded; she became a comic character, parodied and mocked—a mere prop for Christmas pantomimes. Examples include *Harlequin Mother Bunch*, *Mother Goose*, *Harlequin Dame Trot*, and Charles Dibdin’s *The Lancashire Witches, or The Distresses of Harlequin* <note>First performed in 1782.</note>. The flashy costumes, music, and theatrical nonsense <note>original: "mummery"</note> of Dibdin's play drew all the fashionable dandies <term>macaronis</term> and high-class prostitutes <term>cyprians</term> in London to the Circus during the winter of 1782–1783.

A certain foresight regarding the great success of Harrison Ainsworth’s powerful story *The Lancashire Witches* seems to have inspired the prolific Edward Fitzball. Ainsworth's novel, along with his macabre book *Rookwood*, are probably the best works of a talented writer who is now unfairly undervalued and criticized. Fitzball produced his "Legendary Drama in Three Acts," titled *The Lancashire Witches, A Romance of Pendle Forest*, at the Adelphi Theatre on January 3, 1848. This was remarkably quick work. Only a month earlier, on December 3, 1847, Ainsworth wrote to his friend Crossley of Manchester stating that he had accepted a generous offer from the *Sunday Times*—£1,000 plus the return of the copyright to the author upon completion—to publish his new romance *The Lancashire Witches* as a serial in the newspaper. 

Ainsworth had already sketched out the plan for the book, and he must have given Fitzball an idea of the plot, or at least allowed the dramatist to use some of his rough notes. Although the play and the novel have little—one might even say nothing essential—in common, the main character on stage, Bess of the Woods, is described as being "140 years old, formerly Abbess of S. Magdalen’s, doomed for her crimes to an unearthly age." This character is none other than the religious recluse <term>anchoress</term> Isolde de Heton.

The fourth scene of the second act presents the ruins of Whalley Abbey by moonlight. During a magical incantation, the scene gradually changes: the broken arches reconstruct themselves into perfect masonry; the ivy disappears from the windows to reveal the red and gold of stained glass; the decaying altar glitters with piles of silver plate and the light of thousands of candles <note>original: "tapers"</note>. A choir of nuns rises from the grave to dance with ghostly suitors <note>original: "spectral gallants"</note>. Among the participants <note>original: "votaries"</note> are Nutter, Demdike, and Chattox—"Three Weird Sisters, doomed for their weaknesses to become Witches." However, they do not speak and have no other role in the play's action.

# THE HISTORY OF WITCHCRAFT

This scene must have been extraordinarily effective on the stage. It owes much to the haunted convent in Giacomo Meyerbeer’s opera *Robert the Devil* <note>original: *Robert le Diable*</note>, which was first produced at the Royal Academy <note>original: *Académie Royale*</note> in November 1831, and appeared in unauthorized versions at both Drury Lane and Covent Garden within a few weeks. However, Fitzball's version does not compare to the original. In his melodrama, the actor O. Smith appeared as Gipsy Dallan—a new character—and Miss Faucit (Mrs. Bland) played Bess of the Woods. As a lurid, sensational production typical of the theaters south of the Thames <term>Surrey-side</term>, the play has some merit; however, it would be absurd to compare it to the works of Thomas Middleton or even Barnabe Barnes.

The genius of Percy Bysshe Shelley has, with wondrous beauty, translated scenes for us from Pedro Calderon’s *The Mighty Magician* <note>original: *El Mágico Prodigioso*</note>, one of the loveliest songs of the "Spanish nightingale." On a different level, certainly, but still possessing a simple grace of its own and a most poignant sorrow, is Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s New England tragedy, *Giles Corey of the Salem Farms*.³⁰ In this work, the characters are sketched with extraordinary power. A few quiet, effective touches make each person feel individual and alive: the honest sincerity of the minister Cotton Mather, the blunt and irritable heartiness of Giles Corey himself, the poorly timed skepticism of his wife—which many would consider sound common sense today—the hysteria of Mary Walcot, and the villainy of John Gloyd.

In the French theater, we find an early fourteenth-century play titled *The Miracle of Our Lady of Robert the Devil* <note>original: *Miracle de Nostre Dame de Robert le Dyable*</note>. Later, in 1505, *The Mystery of the Knight Who Gave His Wife to the Devil, for Ten Characters* <note>original: *Le mystère du Chevalier qui donna sa femme au Diable, à dix personnages*</note> was performed. As one might expect, witchcraft found no place in the works of French dramatists during the long "classical" period of the drama. To the writers of that era, it would have seemed far too wild and monstrous a fantasy. 

Consequently, it was not until June 11, 1805 <note>original: "24 floréal, An XIII," referring to the French Revolutionary calendar</note> that a play incorporating sorcery as its theme was seen at the French Theater <note>original: *Théâtre français*</note>. This was the production of François-Just-Marie Raynouard’s *The Templars* <note>original: *Les Templiers*</note>. A few years later, *The Vampire* <note>original: *Le Vampire*</note>, a thrilling melodrama by Charles Nodier and Carmouche produced on August 13, 1820, drew all of fashionable Paris to the Porte-Saint-Martin theater. In 1821, two prolific writers quick to satisfy the public's taste, Frédéric Dupetit-Méré and Victor Ducagne, found success with *The Witch, or the Scottish Orphan* <note>original: *La Sorcière, ou l’Orphelin écossais*</note>. # THE WITCH IN DRAMATIC LITERATURE

Auguste Maquet collaborated (if one can put it that way) on a grandiose five-act drama titled *Urbain Grandier* in 1850 <note>Urbain Grandier was a French priest executed for witchcraft following the Loudun possessions of 1634</note>. *The Witch Canidia* <note>original: *La Sorcière Canidie*</note>, a one-act play by Aurélien Vivie produced at Bordeaux in 1888, is of little importance. *The Queen of the Spirit* <note>original: *La Reine de l’Esprit*</note> (1891) by Maurice Pottecher is partially based on the *Count of Gabalis* <note>original: *Comte de Gabalis*, a 1670 satirical novel about elemental spirits</note>, while the same author’s three-act play *Everyone Seeks Their Treasure* <note>original: *Chacun cherche son Trésor*</note>, described as a "story of sorcerers" (1899), was significantly enhanced by the music of Lucien Michelet. One may easily justify merely mentioning *The Marriage of Satan* <note>original: *Les Noces de Sathan*</note> (1892), an "esoteric drama" by Jules Bois. Similarly, *The Basques, or the Witch of Espelette* <note>original: *Les Basques ou la Sorcière d’Espelette*</note>—a lyric drama in three acts by Loquin and Mégret de Belligny produced at Bordeaux in 1892—has an interest that is almost purely local. Alphonse Tavan’s *The Sorcerers* <note>original: *Les Mases*</note>, a legendary drama in five acts of alternating prose and verse performed in 1897, was supported by every theatrical resource: a ballet, a chorus, mechanical effects, and bold advertising. Serge Basset’s *Toward the Witches' Sabbath* <note>original: *Vers le Sabbat*</note>, a "conjuring of sorcery in one act" which appeared in the same year, does not require serious consideration. Nor does an elaborate episode titled "The Witches' Sabbath and the Infernal Portcullis" <note>original: "Le Sabbat et la Herse Infernale"</note>, in which Mr. Benglia appeared as Satan, call for more than the briefest mention; it was featured in the Folies Bergère revue *An Evening of Madness* <note>original: *Un Soir de Folie*</note> between 1925 and 1926.

In more recent days, Victorien Sardou’s *The Witch* <note>original: *La Sorcière*</note> is a violent but effective melodrama. Produced at the Sarah Bernhardt Theater on December 15, 1903, with De Max as Cardinal Ximenes and Sarah Bernhardt as the Moorish <note>original: "moresque"</note> Zoraya, it achieved a well-deserved success. The setting of the tragedy is Toledo in the year of our Lord <note>original: "anno domini"</note> 1506. The Inquisition scene in Act IV and the square before the Cathedral in Act V—featuring a grim funeral pyre ready for the torch—were truly harrowing, thanks to the genius of a great actress. Of course, the play is very flamboyant, very unbalanced, and very unhistorical; however, in its gaudy, theatrical way—employing all the old stage tricks—*The Witch* offered an exciting thrill for those who were willing to be simply entertained for a while.

John Masefield’s adaptation of the Norwegian play by Hans Wiers-Jenssen, *The Witch*<gloss>31</gloss>, a drama in four acts, is something quite different. Here we find psychological depth comparable to that of the Renaissance playwrights Thomas Dekker and John Ford. Nor will the performances of Miss Janet...

¹ The *Floralia*, the most lewd <note>original: wanton</note> of Roman festivals, began four days before the Kalends <note>The first day of the month</note> of May. During these celebrations, the spectators insisted that the female actors <note>original: *mimæ*</note> should perform naked. An old commentator on the poet Martial (Book I, 1) says, "[The Floralia] were performed by prostitutes stripped of all clothing, with every license of speech and obscenity of movement" <note>original: *agebantur [Floralia] a meretricibus ueste exutis omni cum uerborum licentia, motuumque obscænitate*</note>. The writer Ausonius calls them "The joyful Floralia of the lewd theater" <note>original: *Lasciui Floralia laeta theatri*</note> in his work *On Roman Festivals* <note>original: *De Feriis Romanis*</note>, 25. Lactantius, in *The Divine Institutes* <note>original: *De Institutionibus Diuinis*</note>, I, 20, writes: "Therefore those games are celebrated with all lewdness, fitting the memory of a prostitute. For besides the license of words, through which every obscenity is poured out, the prostitutes are even stripped of their clothes at the demand of the people; they then perform the role of actors; and in the sight of the people they are kept performing shameful movements until the lustful eyes are satisfied." <note>original: *Celebrantur ergo illi ludi...*</note> Both St. Augustine and Arnobius condemn <note>original: reprehend</note> the lewdness of these naked dances. **18** Dryden’s. He wrote the first scene of the first act, the whole of the fourth act, rather more than one-half of act five, and Lee is responsible for the rest of the tragedy.

**19** For a full analysis and critical examination of *Zoroastres*, see my article in the *Modern Language Review*, XII, Jan., 1917.

**20** The title role of Dame Dobson was played by Mrs. Corey, a mistress of broad comedy who was much admired for her humor by Samuel Pepys.

**21** Mrs. Behn owes a hint to Shirley’s *The Lady of Pleasure*, licensed by Sir Henry Herbert, October 15, 1635; Quarto, 1637. It must be confessed that she has managed her scenes with more wit and spirit than the older dramatist, whose charming verse is perhaps too seriously poetical for the actual situation.

Langbaine wrote: “The beginning of his Play seems to be written in imitation of Machiavelli’s <note>original: Matchiavel’s</note> *Novel of Belphegor*: where Pluto summons the Devils to Council <note>original: Councel</note>.”

**26** For a fitting account of Alexander VI, see *Pope Alexander VI and the Borgias* <note>original: *Le Pape Alexandre VI et les Borgia*</note>, Paris, 1870, by Father <note>original: Père</note> Ollivier, O.P.; also Leonetti's *Pope Alexander VI according to the documents and correspondence of the time* <note>original: *Papa Alessandro VI secondo documenti e carteggi del tempo*</note>, 3 volumes, Bologna, 1880. *Chronicles of the House of Borgia*, by Frederick, Baron Corvo, 1901, may be studied with profit. Monsignor de Roo’s *Material for a History of Pope Alexander VI*, 5 volumes, Bruges, 1924, is of the greatest value and completely authoritative.

**27** The murderer of the Duke of Gandia is unknown to history, if not to historians.

**28** The songs only are printed, Octavo <note>original: 8vo; a book size formed by folding a sheet of paper three times to create eight leaves</note>, 1783.

**29** Fosbrooke, in *British Monachism*, says that in the reign of Henry VI one Isolde de Heton petitioned the King to let her be admitted as an anchoress <note>term: a woman who lives in solitary religious seclusion</note> in the Abbey of Whalley. But afterward she left the enclosure and broke her vows, whereupon the King dissolved the hermitage.

**30** The incidents are historically correct. See Cotton Mather’s *Wonders of the Invisible World*. Corey, refusing to plead, was pressed to death <note>note: This refers to the legal torture of *peine forte et dure*, used to force a defendant to enter a plea</note>.

**31** Originally produced October 10, 1910, at the Royalty, Glasgow; in London, January 31, 1911, at the Court Theatre. Revived at the Court, October 29, 1913, when it ran for a month and was afterward included in the subsequent three weeks’ repertory season.

## BIBLIOGRAPHY

This bibliography does not aim to do anything more than provide a brief and convenient list of some of the more important books about witchcraft. It does not even claim to list all the specialized studies mentioned in the main body of this research. I considered it unnecessary to include a large number of books. For example, I have omitted general reference works like the *Encyclopædia Britannica*; Du Cange’s *Glossary for Writers of Medieval and Late Latin* <note>original: "Glossarium ad scriptores mediæ et infimæ latinitatis"</note>; and Dugdale’s *History of Monasteries* <note>original: "Monasticon"</note>. I also excluded daily religious companions such as the Missal, the Breviary, and the Bible; the works of Homer, Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Petronius, and Lucan; the writings of Shakespeare, Marlowe, Ford, and Dryden; Burton’s *Anatomy of Melancholy*; other English classics; and well-known histories found in every library by authors like Gibbon, Lingard, and Ranke, as well as the *Cambridge Modern History*.

On the other hand, I have intentionally included various books that might not seem at first glance to have much connection to witchcraft, though they are, in fact, relevant. To understand this vast subject in all its aspects, even a casual or amateur researcher should be well-grounded in theology, philosophy, and psychology. A serious student must also be a capable theologian.

I have paid particular attention to the works of the demonologists <term>scholars or writers who specialize in the study of demons and beliefs about evil spirits</term>. These works are now almost universally ignored, but studying them closely is essential for understanding occultism and recognizing the serious dangers that may be hidden there.

I am well aware of the many gaps <note>original: "lacunæ"</note> in this bibliography. However, attempting a complete catalog—if such a boundless task were even possible—would involve listing many thousands of books and would require a significant number of volumes <note>original: "no inconsiderable a tale of volumes"</note> itself.

<summary>The author introduces a selected bibliography on witchcraft, explaining that he has omitted general classics and reference works to focus on essential theological and demonological texts.</summary>
<keywords>bibliography, witchcraft, demonology, theology, research methods, occultism, academic sources</keywords>

# ENGLAND: THE PAMPHLET LITERATURE
->(Arranged in chronological order)<-

*The examination and confession of certain witches at Chelmsford in the County of Essex before the Queen's majesty's judges, the 26th day of July, Year of our Lord 1566.* <note>original: "Anno 1566"</note>

*A recital both strange and true of heinous and horrible acts committed by Elizabeth Style, alias Rockingham, Mother Dutten, Mother Devil, Mother Margaret. Four notorious witches apprehended at Windsor in the County of Berkshire, and at Abingdon arraigned, condemned, and executed on the 28th day of February last, year of our Lord 1579.* <note>original: "anno 1579"</note>

*A detection of damnable schemes* <note>original: "driftes"</note>*, practiced by three witches arraigned at Chelmsford in Essex... who were executed in April 1579.* 1579.

*The apprehension and confession of three notorious witches arraigned and by Justice condemned in the County of Essex the 5th day of July last past.* 1589.

*A true and just record of the information, examination, and confessions of all the witches taken at St. Osyth* <note>original: "St. Oses"</note> *in the county of Essex: whereby some were executed, and others treated according to the determination of the law... Written orderly, as the cases were tried by evidence, by W. W.* 1582.

*The most strange and admirable discovery of the three witches of Warboys, arraigned, convicted, and executed at the last court sessions* <note>original: "assizes"</note> *at Huntingdon.* London, 1593.

(This was one of the most famous cases of English witchcraft. A whole literature grew up in connection with it. In *Notes and Queries*, Twelfth Series, I, 1916, p. 283 and p. 304, will be found: "The Witches of Warboys: Bibliographical Note," where twenty-eight entries are made.)

*The most wonderful and true story of a certain witch named Alice Gooderidge of Stapenhill, who was arraigned and convicted at Derby... As also a true report of the strange torments of Thomas Darling, a boy of thirteen years of age, who was possessed by the Devil, with his horrible fits and terrible apparitions uttered by him at Burton-upon-Trent, in the county of Stafford, and of his marvelous deliverance.* London, 1597. [By John Denison.]

*The arraignment and execution of three detestable witches, John Newell, Joan his wife, and Helen Calles; two executed at Barnet, and one at Brentford, December 1, 1595.*

*The several acts of witchcraft proved against Margaret Hacket of Stanmore, 1585.* <term>Black letter</term> <note>Black letter refers to an early, ornate style of typeface that remained popular for cheap, sensational news pamphlets long after Roman type became standard for books.</note>.

*An account of Margaret Hacket, a notorious witch, who consumed a young man to death, rotted his bowels and backbone asunder, who was executed at Tyburn, February 19, 1585.* London, 1585.

*The examination and confession of a notorious witch named Mother Arnold, alias Whitecote, alias Glastonbury, at the court session* <note>original: "Assise"</note> *of Brentwood in July, 1574: who was hanged for witchcraft at Barking.* 1575.

(The four preceding pamphlets although referred to by Lowndes and other bibliographers apparently have not been traced.)

*A true report of three strange witches, lately found at Newnham Regis.*

(Not traced. Hazlitt, *Handbook*, p. 231.)

*A short treatise declaring the detestable wickedness of magical sciences, such as necromancy, conjuration of spirits, curious astrology, and the like... Made by Francis Coxe.* [London, 1561.] <term>Black letter</term>.

*The examination of John Walsh, before Master Thomas Williams, Commissary to the Reverend Father in God, William, Bishop of Exeter, upon certain interrogatories* <note>Legal questions or a formal examination.</note> *touching witchcraft and sorcery, in the presence of various gentlemen and others, the 20th of August, 1566.* 1566. <term>Black letter</term>.

*The disclosing of a recent counterfeit possession by the devil in two maidens within the City of London.* [1574.] <term>Black letter</term>.

*An Account of The Trials, Examination and Condemnation of Elinor Shaw and Mary Phillips (Two notorious Witches) on Wednesday the 7th of March, 1705, for Bewitching a Woman, and two children. . . With an Account of their strange Confessions.* This is signed at the end, “Ralph Davis, March 8, 1705.” It was followed very shortly by a more complete account, written after the execution, and titled:

*The Northamptonshire Witches, Being a true and faithful account of the Births, Educations, Lives, and Behavior <note>original: "Conversations." In the 18th century, this meant one's general conduct or way of life.</note> of Elinor Shaw and Mary Phillips (The two notorious Witches) That were Executed at Northampton on Saturday, March the 17th, 1705 . . . with their full Confession to the Minister, and last Dying Speeches at the place of Execution, the like never before heard of. . . Communicated in a Letter last Post, from Mr. Ralph Davis of Northampton, to Mr. William Simons, Merchant in London.* London, 1705.

*The Whole Trial and Examination of Mrs. Mary Hicks and her Daughter Elizabeth, only Nine Years of Age, who were Condemned the last Assizes <note>original: "Assizes," periodic courts held in England and Wales for civil and criminal cases.</note> held at Huntingdon for Witchcraft, and there Executed on Saturday, the 28th of July, 1716 . . . the like never heard before; their Behavior with several Divines who came to converse with them while under their sentence of Death; and last Dying Speeches and Confession at the place of execution.* London, 1716. There is a copy in the Bodleian Library.

(These last three pamphlets are almost certainly spurious <note>original: "spurious," meaning fake. Historians believe the 1716 execution of Mary Hicks never happened and was a sensationalist fabrication by publishers.</note>.)

*A Terrible and timely <note>original: "seasonable"</note> Warning to young Men. Being a very particular and True Relation of one Abraham Joiner, a young Man about 17 or 18 Years of Age, living in Shakesby’s Walks in Shadwell, being a Ballast Man <note>A laborer who loaded and unloaded ballast—heavy material like gravel or iron—into ships to keep them stable.</note> by Profession, who on Saturday Night last picked up a lewd Woman, and spent what Money he had on her, saying afterwards if she would have any more he must go to the Devil for it; and slipping out of her Company, he went to the Cock and Lion in King Street, where the Devil appeared to him, and gave him a gold coin <note>original: "Pistole," a gold coin of varying value used in Europe at the time.</note>, . . . appointing to meet him the next Night at the World’s End at Stepney; Also how his Brother persuaded him to throw the Money away, which he did; but was suddenly taken in a very strange manner; so that they were obliged <note>original: "fain"</note> to send for the Reverend Mr. Constable and other Ministers to pray with him, he appearing now to be very Penitent. . . .* Printed for J. Dulton, near Fleet Street. Circa 1718.

*A Timely Warning to Rash and Disobedient Children, Being a strange and wonderful Relation of a young Gentleman in the Parish of Stepney in the Suburbs of London, that sold himself to the Devil for 12 years to have the Power of being revenged on his Father and Mother, and how his Time being expired, he lay in a sad and deplorable Condition to the Amazement of all Spectators.* Edinburgh: Printed Anno 1721.

*The Kentish Miracle, Or, a Timely Warning to all Sinners Shown in The Wonderful Relation of one Mary Moore, whose Husband died some time ago, and left her with two Children, who was reduced to great Want. . . How the Devil appeared to her, and the many great Offers he made to her to deny Christ, and enter into his Service; and how she confounded Satan by powerful Arguments . . . with an Account how an Angel appeared to her and relieved her. . . .* Edinburgh: Printed in the Year 1741.

(This is probably a reprint. The style of the pamphlet seems some thirty or forty years earlier.)

->*In the sections devoted to* MODERN HISTORY, *the majority of titles*<-

The *New York Times* calls this series, "An adventure in literature and learning whose scope is so daring that it challenges the imagination to understand its full impact... It offers a new perspective on the entire field of historical science."

The *Chicago Evening Post* states: "The scope is intended to be comprehensive, and the work so far has been brilliant. Mr. Knopf <note>Alfred A. Knopf, a major American book publisher who helped bring international literature and scholarly works to the U.S. market.</note> will have performed an invaluable service for the public by providing an authoritative history of the world, written entirely in English, with each field covered by a man who has mastered it... *The History of Civilization* should prove to be a force not only in spreading knowledge but also in promoting international goodwill."

James T. Shotwell <note>A prominent historian and diplomat who played a key role in the creation of the International Labour Organization and the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.</note> writes: "The *History of Civilization*, edited by Mr. Ogden <note>C.K. Ogden of Magdalene College, Cambridge; a linguist and philosopher best known for creating 'Basic English.'</note> of Magdalene College, Cambridge, marks a new stage in the history of historical writing. Previously, we have had collaborative surveys of various sections of European history, but they have all suffered from limited space. Various contributors have been forced by editors to cram material into a single chapter that would normally require an entire volume. This great series gives the author true freedom to cover his subject adequately. Once this freedom is granted, the chief editorial challenge is simply to find the leading authority on that particular subject. The list of authors in this series could hardly be improved. Each writer can offer a unique contribution beyond just the data they present; every major phase of human evolution is presented here in a masterful survey that fits perfectly into the general overview.

"Looking at the work as a whole rather than just the individual volumes, one finds a concept of history that meets the needs of those interested in the social and intellectual development of Europe, while the traditional framework of the political story still runs alongside it. It is a living picture of a vast movement, brilliantly conceived and certain to be expertly executed."
